For `mauvais`, both `plus mauvais` and `pire` can mean worse; `pire` is especially useful for an unfavourable outcome or situation: `La situation est pire qu’hier`. With `mal`, normally use `plus mal`: `Elle dort plus mal depuis son déménagement`. Do not add `plus` to `meilleur`, `mieux`, or `pire` when they already mean better or worse.

Comparison of identity works differently from comparison of degree. `Le même` states that two things are identical, it agrees with the noun it introduces — `le même`, `la même`, `les mêmes` — and the second term is always introduced by `que`, never by `comme`: `J’ai les mêmes documents que toi`, `Elle suit le même cours que moi`, `Les consignes sont les mêmes que l’an dernier`. The agreement follows the noun and not the person compared, so the form is `le même formulaire` even when speaking to a woman.
points: Use `aussi` before an adjective or an adverb, `autant` after a verb, `autant de` before a noun.
For an adjective comparing different things or people, agree the superlative article with the noun; with a verb or adverb, use invariable `le`.
Use `de` to name the comparison group: `la plus calme de la classe`. `Dans` can still locate an event or situation; it is not forbidden from every sentence containing a superlative.
For the ordinary comparison better, use `meilleur` for `bon` and `mieux` for `bien`.
Check whether the word you are grading is an adjective or an adverb before choosing between `meilleur` and `mieux`.
Introduce the second term of `le même` with `que`, never with `comme`.
Agree `même` with the noun it introduces: `le même cours`, `les mêmes consignes`.

examples.french: Le transport en commun est aussi fiable que la voiture dans ce quartier.
examples.english: Public transit is as reliable as the car in this neighbourhood.
examples.note: « Aussi » before an adjective.

examples.french: Cette formation coûte autant que l’autre, mais elle propose plus de stages.
examples.english: This training course costs as much as the other one, but it offers more placements.
examples.note: « Autant » after a verb, « plus de » before a noun.

examples.french: Elle travaille moins rapidement que son collègue, mais elle relit davantage.
examples.english: She works less quickly than her colleague, but she proofreads more.
examples.note: « Moins » before an adverb.

examples.french: C’est la solution la plus efficace de toutes celles qui ont été proposées.
examples.english: It is the most effective solution of all those that were proposed.
examples.note: Superlative: definite article plus « de » for the group.

examples.french: Cette méthode est meilleure que l’autre, et elle fonctionne mieux en petit groupe.
examples.english: This method is better than the other one, and it works better in a small group.
examples.note: « Meilleure » grades a noun; « mieux » grades a verb.

examples.french: J’ai les mêmes documents que toi, et ce logement a le même loyer que l’autre.
examples.english: I have the same documents as you, and this unit has the same rent as the other one.
examples.note: Identity comparison agreeing with the noun and completed by « que ».

examples.french: Les consignes sont les mêmes que l’an dernier pour toutes les candidates.
examples.english: The instructions are the same as last year for all the applicants.
examples.note: « Les mêmes que » with a plural noun.

mistakes.avoid: Il travaille aussi que moi.
mistakes.prefer: Il travaille autant que moi.
mistakes.why: To compare how much someone works, use `autant que`. `Aussi` can mean also in other constructions, but it cannot fill this equality pattern by itself.

mistakes.avoid: Cette soupe est plus bonne que l’autre et elle est plus bien assaisonnée.
mistakes.prefer: Cette soupe est meilleure que l’autre et elle est mieux assaisonnée.
mistakes.why: For these ordinary comparisons, `bon` becomes `meilleur`, agreeing with `une soupe (f.)`, and `bien` becomes invariable `mieux`.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai le même formulaire comme toi.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai le même formulaire que toi.
mistakes.why: The second term of an identity comparison is introduced by `que`; `comme` expresses resemblance, not identity.

mistakes.avoid: Elle a rempli la même formulaire que moi.
mistakes.prefer: Elle a rempli le même formulaire que moi.
mistakes.why: `Un formulaire (m.)` is masculine, so use `le même formulaire`. The woman who completed it does not control the article’s gender.

sections.title: Si for degree: so… and not that…
paragraphs: Before an adjective or adverb, si can mean so: si calme, si rapidement. It is an invariable intensifier, not conditional si meaning if and not the answer Si! contradicting a negative question. It can stand without a result clause, or introduce one with que: si calme que je peux travailler.

Ne… pas si + adjective + que ça means not that…: Ce logement n’est pas si cher que ça. It rejects an assumed degree, not necessarily the quality altogether. The adjective still agrees with its noun; si and ça do not. This conversational frame differs from comparing two named things with aussi… que.
points: Identify si from its construction, not from one English translation.
Pas si… que ça lowers an assumed degree; it does not mean not at all.

examples.french: Cette bibliothèque est si calme!
examples.english: This library is so quiet!
examples.note: Si intensifies the adjective without stating a condition.

examples.french: Elle explique si clairement que tout le monde comprend.
examples.english: She explains so clearly that everyone understands.
examples.note: Si can intensify an adverb and lead to a result clause.

examples.french: Les démarches ne sont pas si compliquées que ça.
examples.english: The procedures are not that complicated.
examples.note: Compliquées agrees with des démarches (f. pl.); the expected degree is reduced.

mistakes.avoid: Les démarches ne sont pas si compliqué que ça.
mistakes.prefer: Les démarches ne sont pas si compliquées que ça.
mistakes.why: The adjective agrees even inside the degree construction.

mistakes.avoid: Cette salle est si calmes !
mistakes.prefer: Cette salle est si calme !
mistakes.why: `Une salle (f.)` is singular, so `calme` has no plural s.

vocabulary.example: Le transport en commun coûte moins cher que la voiture au quotidien.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; often used in the plural `les transports en commun`.

vocabulary.example: Une formation courte permet de compléter rapidement un profil professionnel.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `suivre une formation` means to take a course.

vocabulary.example: Une meilleure organisation réduit le nombre de rendez-vous manqués.
vocabulary.note: Comparative of `bon`; it agrees with the noun, unlike the adverb `mieux`.

vocabulary.french: le plus / la plus / les plus
vocabulary.example: C’est le quartier le plus vert de la ville.
vocabulary.note: Superlative marker; the group is introduced by `de`.

vocabulary.french: le même / la même / les mêmes
vocabulary.example: Les mêmes pièces justificatives sont exigées dans les deux bureaux.
vocabulary.note: Agrees with the noun; the second term is introduced by `que`.

practice.prompt: Complete: « Ce quartier a ___ services ___ le centre-ville, mais c’est le centre-ville qui reste ___ animé ___ la ville. »
practice.hint: Quantity first, then a superlative with its group.
practice.answer: Ce quartier a autant de services que le centre-ville, mais c’est le centre-ville qui reste le plus animé de la ville.

takeaways: Adjective or adverb: `aussi`. Verb: `autant`. Noun: `autant de`.
Superlative equals definite article plus `plus/moins`, with the group after `de`.
`Meilleur` grades nouns; `mieux` grades actions.
`Le même … que` for identity, agreeing with the noun, never with `comme`.
keywords: si intensif, pas si … que ça

lessons.title: Les nombres cardinaux et les nombres ordinaux
lessons.summary: Cardinal numbers count and are mostly unchanged; un/une varies in gender, while vingt and cent have particular plural rules. Million and milliard are nouns. Ordinals rank and agree: premier, première, premiers, premières. In the ordinary phrase meaning the first N items, put the cardinal before the ordinal: les trois premières étapes.
objectives: Recognise the limited written variation of cardinal numbers.
Treat `million` and `milliard` as nouns.
Agree an ordinal adjective with its noun.

sections.title: Counting, ranking, and number agreement
paragraphs: A cardinal counts (how many?) and an ordinal ranks (which position?). Most cardinals remain unchanged: `quatre étapes`, `quatre dossiers`. `Un` varies with gender, including at the end of a compound: `vingt et un dossiers`, `vingt et une étapes`. The number `mille` never adds a plural s: `trois mille personnes`.

In quantities, `vingt` and `cent` add s when multiplied and not immediately followed by another number word: `quatre-vingts`, `trois cents`, but `quatre-vingt-cinq`, `trois cent dix`, and `deux cent mille`. They keep s before the nouns `un million (m.)` and `un milliard (m.)`: `deux cents millions`, `quatre-vingts milliards`. When a cardinal labels a page, year, or item rather than counting a quantity, `vingt` and `cent` stay unchanged: `la page deux cent` means page 200.

`Un million (m.)` and `un milliard (m.)` take a plural s as ordinary nouns. When followed directly by the thing counted, use `de`: `deux millions de dollars`. When a smaller number completes the amount, no `de` appears before the counted noun: `deux millions trois cent mille dollars`. English billion is `un milliard`, not `un million`.

To form most ordinals, add `-ième`, dropping a final e: `trois/troisième`, `quatre/quatrième`. Note `cinq/cinquième` with qu and `neuf/neuvième` with v. First is `premier/première`, but compounds use `unième`: `la vingt et unième étape`. Second can be `deuxième` or `second/seconde`; `second` often suggests a pair, but it is not restricted to series of exactly two. Ordinals in `-ième` have the same masculine and feminine spelling and take s in the plural: `les troisièmes places`.

For the first N or last N items, use determiner + cardinal + ordinal + noun: `mes trois premiers jours`, `les cinq dernières pages`. The cardinal counts the group; `premier` or `dernier` agrees with the noun. English puts first before the number, so do not transfer its word order mechanically. The examples here use traditional number spelling; fully hyphenated forms such as `vingt-et-une` are also accepted under the 1990 recommendations.
points: Keep most cardinals unchanged; distinguish un/une and the special vingt/cent rules.
In quantities, `vingt` and `cent` take s when multiplied and not followed by another number word; `million` and `milliard` are nouns, not exceptions to that test.
Pluralise `million` and `milliard`; use `de` when they directly precede the counted noun.
Most ordinals use `-ième`; learn the special spellings `premier`, `cinquième`, `neuvième`, and the compound ending `unième`.
Agree `premier` and `dernier` in gender and number with the noun.

examples.french: Les deux premières étapes de la demande se font en ligne.
examples.english: The first two steps of the application are completed online.
examples.note: Cardinal invariable, ordinal agreeing in the feminine plural.

examples.french: Le programme a accueilli quatre-vingts participants et deux cents visiteurs.
examples.english: The program welcomed eighty participants and two hundred visitors.
examples.note: « Vingt » and « cent » take -s when multiplied and final.

examples.french: La ville a investi quatre-vingt-cinq millions de dollars dans le transport.
examples.english: The city invested eighty-five million dollars in transportation.
examples.note: No -s on « vingt » before another number; « millions » is a noun followed by « de ».

examples.french: La troisième entrevue aura lieu vendredi matin.
examples.english: The third interview will take place on Friday morning.
examples.note: Ordinals in -ième vary only in number.

examples.french: C’est la dernière semaine pour déposer un dossier complet.
examples.english: It is the last week to submit a complete application.
examples.note: « Dernier » agrees like an ordinary adjective.

examples.french: Mes trois premiers jours au bureau ont été très instructifs.
examples.english: My first three days at the office were very instructive.
examples.note: Trois counts; premiers agrees with des jours (m. pl.).

examples.french: Relisez les cinq dernières pages avant de signer.
examples.english: Reread the last five pages before signing.
examples.note: The same order applies to dernières, agreeing with des pages (f. pl.).

mistakes.avoid: Le projet coûte deux cents mille dollars.
mistakes.prefer: Le projet coûte deux cent mille dollars.
mistakes.why: `Cent` loses its `-s` when another number follows it.

mistakes.avoid: Les trois premiers étapes sont terminées.
mistakes.prefer: Les trois premières étapes sont terminées.
mistakes.why: `Premier` agrees with `des étapes (f. pl.)`, giving `premières`. The cardinal `trois` does not change.

vocabulary.example: Une étape essentielle consiste à relire la consigne avant de répondre.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `par étapes` means step by step.

vocabulary.example: Un participant sur trois a demandé une attestation de présence.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; feminine `une participante`.

vocabulary.example: La troisième inscrite a présenté un projet très structuré.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun from the participle of `inscrire`; masculine `un inscrit`.

vocabulary.example: Un million de dollars a été réservé au programme de rénovation.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun, not a determiner; it is followed by `de`.

practice.prompt: Write out: 80 participants, 82 participants, 300 dollars, 2 000 000 dollars.
practice.hint: `Vingt` keeps s in 80 but loses it in 82. `Cent` is multiplied and final in 300; `million` is an ordinary plural noun.
practice.answer: quatre-vingts participants, quatre-vingt-deux participants, trois cents dollars, deux millions de dollars

takeaways: Most cardinals are unchanged; check un/une and the vingt/cent plural rules.
`Million` and `milliard` are nouns and take `de`.
Put the cardinal before premier/dernier in les trois premières étapes; agree the ordinal with the noun.
keywords: cardinal avant ordinal, les trois premiers, les cinq dernières

modules.title: L’orthographe et la ponctuation
modules.description: Understand accents and other spelling marks, use capitals accurately, and punctuate sentences and documents.

lessons.title: Les accents et les signes diacritiques
lessons.summary: A diacritic is a mark added to a letter that guides pronunciation or distinguishes words. The five main French marks are the acute accent, only on `e` (`créé`); the grave accent (`une règle`, `à`, `où`); the circumflex, often marking a lost letter (`une forêt`); the diaeresis, which changes how a vowel sequence is read (`le maïs`, `aiguë/aigüe`); and the cedilla, which keeps `c` soft before `a`, `o`, `u` (`une leçon`, `un reçu`). Some words have accepted traditional and rectified spellings, including `maître/maitre`.
objectives: Name the five French diacritics and the job each one does.
Decide when a mark changes pronunciation and when it only separates two words.
Write the cedilla and the diaeresis where the spelling requires them.

sections.title: What each written mark changes
paragraphs: A diacritic is a mark attached to a letter, such as an accent or cedilla. The acute accent (`é`) appears only on e in ordinary French spelling. It indicates the vowel /e/, as in `été`, with the mouth less open than for /ɛ/. The grave accent on e (`è`) indicates the more open /ɛ/, as in `une règle`. Compare the two vowels in `un décès (m.)`: acute first, grave second. Other acute-accent examples are `créé`, `déjà`, `une épaule`, and `léger`.

A grave accent on a or u distinguishes words without necessarily changing their sound: `a` (has) versus `à` (to/at), `ou` (or) versus `où` (where), and `la` (the/her) versus `là` (there). An unaccented e is not always silent: compare `le` with `belle`. Learn the word’s spelling rather than adding an accent whenever you hear an e-like vowel.

The circumflex (`â/ê/î/ô/û`) often recalls a lost letter, especially s, as in `une forêt` and `une fête`; it can also distinguish words or pronunciations. The 1990 recommendations allow omission on i or u in many words, so `un maître` and `un maitre` are both accepted. This is not permission to remove every circumflex: a/e/o retain theirs, and distinctions such as masculine singular `dû/du`, `sûr/sur`, and `mûr/mur` remain, as do certain verb endings. Both traditional and rectified spellings are valid.

The diaeresis, `un tréma (m.)`, changes how a vowel sequence is read. In `le maïs (m.)`, `naïf`, `naïve`, `haïr`, `laïque`, `une faïence (f.)`, and `un canoë (m.)`, neighbouring vowels are pronounced separately. It does not always make the marked letter audible: in traditional `aiguë` and rectified `aigüe`, it signals that u is pronounced while the final e remains silent. Both spellings are accepted.

The cedilla, `une cédille (f.)`, makes c represent /s/, as at the start of `salut`, before a, o, or u: `une façade`, `une leçon`, `un reçu`, `un caleçon`, `nous commençons`. Without it, c before those vowels normally represents /k/. No cedilla is needed before e, i, or y, where c normally already represents /s/. Keep diacritics on capital letters too: `Ça commence`, `À demain`, `Émilie`.
points: Use the acute accent only on `e`, never on another vowel.
Use the grave accent to distinguish `a/à`, `ou/où`, and `la/là`; spelling and pronunciation distinctions do not always coincide.
Recognise the historical role of the circumflex and accepted variants such as `maître/maitre`.
Read the diaeresis by the word: separate vowels in `maïs`, but pronounced `u` and silent final `e` in `aiguë/aigüe`.
Add a cedilla to keep `c` soft before `a`, `o`, `u`, and never before `e` or `i`.

examples.french: J’ai déjà créé mon compte et ajouté ce fichier léger.
examples.english: I have already created my account and added this small file.
examples.note: Déjà, créé, and léger contain acute accents on e; déjà also has a grave accent on a. Léger describes a file with a small data size here.

examples.french: Où est la salle ? Elle est là, à côté du bureau.
examples.english: Where is the room? It is there, next to the office.
examples.note: The grave accent distinguishes « où » from « ou », « là » from « la », and « à » from « a ».

examples.french: Nous avons marché dans la forêt jusqu’à la fête du village.
examples.english: We walked in the forest as far as the village festival.
examples.note: The circumflex marks an « s » that has disappeared from the spelling.

examples.french: Le maïs est servi dans un bol en faïence.
examples.english: The corn is served in an earthenware bowl.
examples.note: The diaeresis separates the vowel sounds in le maïs (m.) and la faïence (f.); do not read aï like the usual ai sequence.

examples.french: Ce serait naïf de croire toutes les promesses de cette publicité.
examples.english: It would be naive to believe every promise in that advertisement.
examples.note: Naïf means too trusting or inexperienced here; naïve is the feminine form. Both keep the tréma and separate the a and i sounds.

examples.french: Nous commençons la leçon dès que le reçu est signé.
examples.english: We start the lesson as soon as the receipt is signed.
examples.note: The cedilla keeps « c » soft before « o »; « leçon » and « reçu » follow the same rule.

examples.french: Une douleur aiguë à l’épaule l’a empêché de travailler.
examples.english: A sharp pain in the shoulder prevented him from working.
examples.note: Traditional « aiguë » and rectified « aigüe » are both correct: the u is pronounced and the final e is silent.

mistakes.avoid: Nous commencons la leçon à neuf heures.
mistakes.prefer: Nous commençons la leçon à neuf heures.
mistakes.why: Before `o`, the letter `c` needs a cedilla to keep its soft sound.

mistakes.avoid: Je ne sais pas ou se trouve le bureau des permis.
mistakes.prefer: Je ne sais pas où se trouve le bureau des permis.
mistakes.why: `Ou` means or; the grave accent distinguishes `où`, which means where.

mistakes.avoid: Une douleur aigue l’a empêché de travailler.
mistakes.prefer: Une douleur aiguë l’a empêché de travailler.
mistakes.why: This feminine form needs a diaeresis: traditional `aiguë` and rectified `aigüe` are both accepted.

sections.title: Read the meaning as well as the accent
paragraphs: `Un mât (m.)` is a mast, the upright support for sails or sometimes a flag. `Un canoë (m.)` is a canoe, a small boat propelled with a paddle. The circumflex in `un mât` stays under both spelling conventions, whereas the tréma in `un canoë` tells you to pronounce the final vowel separately.

`Un maître (m.)` can mean a master with expertise or authority. In a primary-school context, `un maître d’école (m.)` means a schoolteacher. `Un décès (m.)` means a death or passing and is common in administrative or formal announcements.
points: Use context to select expert/master or schoolteacher for `maître`.
`Un décès` names the event of someone's death; `décédé/décédée` describes a person who has died.

examples.french: La voile est attachée au mât du bateau.
examples.english: The sail is attached to the boat’s mast.
examples.note: `Un mât` is a structural support.

examples.french: Nous avons loué un canoë pour traverser le lac.
examples.english: We rented a canoe to cross the lake.
examples.note: A boat propelled with a paddle.

examples.french: Le maître d’école lit une histoire à la classe.
examples.english: The schoolteacher reads a story to the class.
examples.note: The teaching sense of `maître`.

examples.french: Cet artisan est un maître dans son domaine.
examples.english: This craftsperson is a master in his field.
examples.note: Expertise, not a school job.

examples.french: La famille a annoncé son décès dans le journal.
examples.english: The family announced his death in the newspaper.
examples.note: `Un décès` is a death or passing, in a formal announcement.

mistakes.avoid: La voile est attachée au mat du bateau.
mistakes.prefer: La voile est attachée au mât du bateau.
mistakes.why: `Un mât (m.)`, a mast, keeps its circumflex on a. Do not confuse it with the adjective `mat`, meaning matt or non-glossy.

sections.title: Secular, to hate, and a hero or heroine
paragraphs: `Laïque` means secular, particularly when an institution or education is independent of religious authority. It does not mean that every person in that institution is an atheist. `Haïr` means hate, a strong feeling rather than simple dislike; `détester` is more common in many everyday situations. Notice the spelling change in the present: `je hais`, `tu hais`, `il/elle hait` have no tréma, but `nous haïssons`, `vous haïssez`, and `ils/elles haïssent` keep it.

`Un héros (m.)` and `une héroïne (f.)` mean a hero and heroine. They can identify someone admired for courage or the central character of a story; that character is not necessarily morally perfect. The h behaves differently: write `le héros` without elision, but `l’héroïne` with elision. The tréma in `héroïne` separates the o and i sounds.
points: Secular describes the institution's relationship to religion, not each person's private belief.
Distinguish a heroic person from the central character of a story through context.

examples.french: Cette école est laïque et accueille des élèves de différentes convictions.
examples.english: This school is secular and welcomes pupils with different beliefs.
examples.note: `Laïque` does not mean that all pupils have no religion.

examples.french: Elle dit haïr la violence sous toutes ses formes.
examples.english: She says she hates violence in all its forms.
examples.note: `Haïr` expresses strong hatred, not a mild preference.

examples.french: Les habitants considèrent le sauveteur comme un héros.
examples.english: The residents regard the rescuer as a hero.
examples.note: Admiration for a courageous person.

examples.french: L’héroïne du roman cherche à comprendre la disparition de son amie.
examples.english: The novel’s heroine is trying to understand her friend’s disappearance.
examples.note: The main female character in a story.

mistakes.avoid: L’héroine du roman raconte son enfance.
mistakes.prefer: L’héroïne du roman raconte son enfance.
mistakes.why: `Une héroïne (f.)` needs a tréma to separate o and i. Its h permits elision, unlike the h in `le héros (m.)`.

sections.title: A sound, a voice, and a high pitch
paragraphs: `Un son (m.)` means a sound, something heard; it is a noun, unlike possessive `son` before a noun. `Une voix (f.)` is a voice, the sound produced by a person speaking or singing. It is different from `une voie (f.)`, a way, route, or track.

`Aigu/aiguë` describes a high pitch in a sound or voice. It does not necessarily mean loud. With pain, `aiguë` means sharp or acute instead: `une douleur aiguë` is not a high-pitched pain. These are distinct senses of the same adjective. The feminine spelling `aigüe` is also accepted.
points: For pitch, compare `un son aigu` with `un son grave`, a low-pitched sound.
Separate pitch from volume and from the sharp-pain meaning.

examples.french: Quel est ce son ? On dirait une alarme.
examples.english: What is that sound? It sounds like an alarm.
examples.note: `Un son` is something heard.

examples.french: Je reconnais sa voix, même au téléphone.
examples.english: I recognise her voice, even on the phone.
examples.note: `Une voix` identifies a person's vocal sound.

examples.french: L’appareil émet un son aigu, mais peu fort.
examples.english: The device emits a high-pitched but quiet sound.
examples.note: A sound can be high in pitch without being loud.

examples.french: Sa voix est plus aiguë quand elle est surprise.
examples.english: Her voice is higher-pitched when she is surprised.
examples.note: The high-pitch meaning with a feminine noun.

examples.french: Le médecin parle d’une douleur aiguë, pas d’un son aigu.
examples.english: The doctor is talking about a sharp pain, not a high-pitched sound.
examples.note: The noun changes which meaning of the adjective applies.

mistakes.avoid: Sa voix est aigu.
mistakes.prefer: Sa voix est aiguë.
mistakes.why: `Une voix (f.)` requires feminine `aiguë` (or `aigüe`), meaning high-pitched. `Forte` would describe a loud voice instead; pitch and volume are different properties.

vocabulary.example: Un accent aigu ne se place jamais sur une autre voyelle que le « e ».
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase; the mark appears in `créé` and `déjà`.

vocabulary.example: Un accent circonflexe rappelle souvent un « s » disparu, comme dans « forêt ».
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase; found in `fête`, `pâte`, `mât`, and traditional `maître` (also accepted as `maitre`).

vocabulary.example: Un tréma sépare les deux voyelles de « maïs » et de « naïf ».
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun despite its final -a.

vocabulary.example: Une cédille garde le son doux du « c » dans « leçon » et « façade ».
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; used only before `a`, `o`, `u`.

vocabulary.example: Une forêt protégée borde le nord de la municipalité.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the circumflex replaces an older `s`.

vocabulary.example: Un décès doit être déclaré à l’état civil dans les jours qui suivent.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; identical in the plural, with an acute accent on the first `e` and a grave accent on the second.

practice.prompt: Add the missing marks: « Nous commencons la lecon des que le recu est signe. »
practice.hint: Three cedillas, one acute accent on a past participle, and one grave accent.
practice.answer: Nous commençons la leçon dès que le reçu est signé.

takeaways: Acute accent: only on `e`.
Grave accent: opens `e`, or separates `a`/`à`, `ou`/`où`, `la`/`là`.
The circumflex can mark history or a distinction; traditional `maître` and rectified `maitre` are both accepted.
The diaeresis guides vowel reading; the cedilla softens `c` before `a`, `o`, `u`.
keywords: un mât, un maître, un canoë, un décès, haïr, laïque
un héros, une héroïne, une voix, un son, aigu, aiguë

lessons.title: Les majuscules en français
lessons.summary: French uses capitals more sparingly than English. Days, months, seasons, languages, religions, professions, and nationality adjectives are lowercase. Proper place names and official names take capitals, as do nouns naming inhabitants. Generic words such as `rue`, `fleuve`, `ministère`, or `université` take a capital only when the official name requires it.
objectives: Distinguish common labels from proper names before choosing a capital.
Apply the nationality, language, title, profession, institution, and geographic-name rules.
Write dates, holidays, historical names, religious terms, and titles of works consistently.
Distinguish ordinary compass directions from proper geographical names.
Use initialisms, professional abbreviations, academic abbreviations, and unit symbols in their established forms.

sections.title: Common words versus proper names
paragraphs: Inside an ordinary sentence, a capital usually marks a proper name, not importance. Write weekdays, months, and seasons in lowercase: `le lundi`, `le mois de janvier`, `le printemps`. Languages and religions are common nouns: `le français`, `l’anglais`, `le christianisme`, `l’islam`. A nationality adjective stays lowercase (`une candidate canadienne`), while the noun naming an inhabitant takes a capital (`une Canadienne`). The normal first-letter capital at the start of a sentence still applies: `Lundi, je reprends le travail`.

Titles and professions normally remain lowercase when an article introduces them: `le premier ministre`, `la docteure Tremblay`, `le professeur Dubois`. In direct address and formal correspondence, titles of civility may take a capital: `Madame, Monsieur`. For geographic names, capitalise the identifying element and keep the generic category lowercase: `le fleuve Saint-Laurent`, `la rue Sainte-Catherine`, `le mont Royal`. Follow the official spelling of an institution: `l’Université de Montréal`, but `une université montréalaise`.

Historical names and titles of works follow established forms rather than one mechanical rule. Write `le Moyen Âge`, `la Renaissance`, `la Révolution française`, and `la Première Guerre mondiale`; centuries stay lowercase. Sacred texts take capitals (`la Bible`, `le Coran`), but names of religions and their followers, when referring to religious affiliation, are lowercase. For books and films, follow the required editorial convention or the published title rather than English title case; familiar forms include `Le Petit Prince`, `Les Misérables`, `La Belle et la Bête`, and `L’Étranger`.

Capital letters retain their accents and other marks: `Émilie`, `À bientôt`, `Ça va`. Write `ÉTÉ` in capitals, not `ETE`, when the format supports French characters. A capital does not erase an accent that distinguishes words or guides pronunciation.
points: Lowercase weekdays, months, seasons, languages, religions, professions, and nationality adjectives.
Capitalise the noun naming an inhabitant: `une Canadienne`, but `une candidate canadienne`.
Keep a geographic generic word lowercase and capitalise the identifying proper name.
Use the institution’s official spelling; a generic description remains lowercase.
Preserve the established capitalisation of historical names and published titles.

examples.french: La réunion aura lieu lundi 15 janvier, au début de l’hiver.
examples.english: The meeting will take place on Monday, January 15, at the start of winter.
examples.note: Weekday, month, and season are lowercase.

examples.french: Une candidate canadienne a parlé français avec une Canadienne de Montréal.
examples.english: A Canadian candidate spoke French with a Canadian woman from Montreal.
examples.note: The adjective and language are lowercase; the inhabitant noun is capitalised.

examples.french: La docteure Tremblay rencontrera le ministre de la Santé.
examples.english: Dr. Tremblay will meet the minister of health.
examples.note: Professional and political titles remain lowercase after an article.

examples.french: Elle étudie à l’Université de Montréal, près du mont Royal.
examples.english: She studies at the Université de Montréal, near Mount Royal.
examples.note: The official institution name is capitalised; the geographic generic remains lowercase.

examples.french: La Première Guerre mondiale a profondément marqué le vingtième siècle.
examples.english: The First World War profoundly shaped the twentieth century.
examples.note: The event name is capitalised; the century is lowercase.

examples.french: Des musulmans et des chrétiens participent à une discussion sur le Coran et la Bible.
examples.english: Some Muslims and Christians are taking part in a discussion about the Quran and the Bible.
examples.note: Followers and religions are lowercase; sacred texts are proper titles.

mistakes.avoid: Je pars Lundi 15 Janvier.
mistakes.prefer: Je pars lundi 15 janvier.
mistakes.why: French writes weekdays and months in lowercase.

mistakes.avoid: Cette candidate Canadienne parle le Français.
mistakes.prefer: Cette candidate canadienne parle le français.
mistakes.why: `Canadienne` describes `une candidate (f.)`, so it is an adjective here and takes lowercase. The language name `le français (m.)` is also lowercase.

mistakes.avoid: Le Christianisme s’est développé pendant le moyen âge.
mistakes.prefer: Le christianisme s’est développé pendant le Moyen Âge.
mistakes.why: Religion names are lowercase, while the established historical name `Moyen Âge` takes capitals.

sections.title: Holidays, directions, and names of deities
paragraphs: Holiday names have established capitals: Noël, Pâques, le Nouvel An. This does not capitalise the ordinary weekday or season around them: le lundi après Pâques, les vacances d’hiver. Follow the actual holiday name rather than capitalising every nearby word.

An ordinary direction is lowercase: au nord de Montréal, le sud de la France, un vent d’ouest. A direction forming part of a proper geographical name keeps the name’s capital, as in l’Afrique du Sud. A named region may also use a capital; the question is whether the word is a name or merely a direction.

Dieu takes a capital when it functions as the proper name of the monotheistic deity. A generic deity is un dieu (m.), plural des dieux; une déesse (f.) is a goddess. Mythological names such as Zeus, Aphrodite, and Thor are proper names. This does not change the lowercase spelling of religions or their followers.
points: Preserve the established capitals in holiday names.
Distinguish a direction from an element of a proper geographical name.
Write Dieu as a proper name, but un dieu and des dieux as common nouns.

examples.french: Le centre ferme pour Noël et rouvre après le Nouvel An.
examples.english: The centre closes for Christmas and reopens after New Year.
examples.note: The holiday names retain their established capitals.

examples.french: La réunion est prévue le lundi après Pâques.
examples.english: The meeting is scheduled for the Monday after Easter.
examples.note: The weekday is lowercase, while the holiday name has a capital.

examples.french: Elle habite au nord de Montréal et prépare un voyage en Afrique du Sud.
examples.english: She lives north of Montreal and is planning a trip to South Africa.
examples.note: Nord is a direction; Sud is part of a proper country name.

examples.french: Dans ce récit, le personnage prie Dieu avant son départ.
examples.english: In this story, the character prays to God before leaving.
examples.note: Dieu functions as a proper name in this monotheistic context.

examples.french: Le texte présente Zeus parmi les dieux grecs et Aphrodite parmi les déesses.
examples.english: The text presents Zeus among the Greek gods and Aphrodite among the goddesses.
examples.note: Proper names are capitalised; generic dieux and déesses remain lowercase.

mistakes.avoid: Le centre ferme pour noël.
mistakes.prefer: Le centre ferme pour Noël.
mistakes.why: Noël is the established proper name of the holiday.

mistakes.avoid: Elle prépare un voyage en Afrique du sud.
mistakes.prefer: Elle prépare un voyage en Afrique du Sud.
mistakes.why: Sud belongs to the proper country name Afrique du Sud.

sections.title: Initialisms, symbols, abbreviations, and letter openings
paragraphs: `Un sigle (m.)` is formed from initials. Common established forms include `l’ONU (f.)` (the United Nations), `l’OTAN (f.)` (NATO), `l’UE (f.)` (the European Union), and `un PDG (m.)` (a company’s chair and chief executive), normally without periods. Some are pronounced as words, others letter by letter. Follow the organisation’s chosen spelling; not every acronym must be all capitals, especially once it has become a common word, as with `un radar (m.)`.

Abbreviations do not all end in a period: M. shortens monsieur, whereas Mme, Dr, and Dre retain their final letters. Academic forms such as M.A., B.A., and Ph.D. follow institutional and regional conventions; reproduce the degree’s established form instead of applying the professional-title rule mechanically.

Unit symbols have their own exact case and do not take a plural s or an abbreviation point: 5 kg, 12 km, 30 cm, 2 m. The full nouns do agree: cinq kilogrammes, douze kilomètres. Not every symbol is lowercase: W for watt, Pa for pascal, and °C for degree Celsius. Both l and L are accepted litre symbols. Put a space between the number and symbol. A sentence-ending period after a symbol is ordinary punctuation, not part of that symbol.

A salutation or standalone closing begins with a capital: Madame, Monsieur; Chère Marie; Cordialement; Bien à vous. Within a sentence, ordinary words remain lowercase: Je vous remercie cordialement. A rule about lowercase profession names does not override sentence-initial capitals.
points: Use each organisation’s established initialism rather than inventing capitals or periods.
Distinguish abbreviation points from punctuation ending a sentence.
Keep unit symbols unchanged in the plural and preserve their exact case.
Capitalise standalone salutations and closings.

examples.french: L’ONU publie un rapport, et la bibliothèque en conserve une copie.
examples.english: The UN publishes a report, and the library keeps a copy of it.
examples.note: ONU is an established uppercase initialism without periods.

examples.french: Le document compare le rôle de l’UE à celui de l’OTAN.
examples.english: The document compares the role of the EU with that of NATO.
examples.note: Use the established initialisms, not a rule about capitalising every word in ordinary prose.

examples.french: Mme Roy remet le dossier au Dr Martin, puis téléphone à M. Dubois.
examples.english: Ms. Roy gives the file to Dr. Martin, then calls Mr. Dubois.
examples.note: Mme and Dr do not need an abbreviation point; M. does.

examples.french: Le colis pèse 5 kg et doit parcourir douze kilomètres, soit 12 km.
examples.english: The parcel weighs 5 kg and must travel twelve kilometres, that is, 12 km.
examples.note: Symbols stay unchanged; the full noun un kilomètre (m.) takes plural s.

examples.french: La lampe consomme 10 W et la température de la pièce est de 20 °C.
examples.english: The lamp uses 10 W and the room temperature is 20°C.
examples.note: W and °C show why unit symbols cannot all be made lowercase.

examples.french: Elle indique « M.A. » après son nom, conformément à l’usage de son université.
examples.english: She puts “M.A.” after her name, following her university’s convention.
examples.note: Academic abbreviations follow the awarding institution’s established style.

examples.french:
Madame, Monsieur,
Voici les documents demandés.
Cordialement,
Léa Martin
examples.english:
Dear Sir or Madam,
Here are the requested documents.
Kind regards,
Léa Martin
examples.note: A standalone closing begins with a capital; Cordialement is not obligatorily lowercase.

mistakes.avoid: Le colis pèse 5 kgs.
mistakes.prefer: Le colis pèse 5 kg.
mistakes.why: The symbol kg does not take a plural s. The final period ends the sentence.

mistakes.avoid: Le colis parcourt douze kilomètre.
mistakes.prefer: Le colis parcourt douze kilomètres.
mistakes.why: Unlike the symbol `km`, the full countable noun `un kilomètre (m.)` takes plural s after `douze`.

vocabulary.example: Une majuscule distingue le nom propre du nom commun.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun.

vocabulary.example: Une minuscule convient au nom d’une langue ou d’une profession.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun.

vocabulary.example: Un nom propre désigne une personne, un lieu ou une institution précise.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase.

vocabulary.example: Un nom d’habitant comme « Canadienne » prend une majuscule.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase; the adjective of nationality stays lowercase.

vocabulary.example: Un titre d’œuvre conserve la graphie choisie par l’éditeur.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase.

practice.prompt: Correct the capitals: « Une Canadienne étudie le Français à l’université de Montréal depuis Septembre. »
practice.hint: Inhabitant noun, language, official institution, and month each follow a different rule.
practice.answer: Une Canadienne étudie le français à l’Université de Montréal depuis septembre.

takeaways: Capitalise proper names, not categories or titles merely because they seem important.
Person noun uppercase; nationality adjective and language lowercase.
For institutions, historical names, holidays, and works, follow the established form.
Ordinary directions are lowercase; proper geographical names keep their capitals.
Distinguish Dieu as a proper name from generic un dieu and des dieux.
Initialisms, abbreviations, and unit symbols follow different conventions; symbols do not take plural s.
keywords: proper names, nationalities, institutions, and titles
fêtes, points cardinaux, noms de dieux, sigles, abréviations, symboles d’unités
un kilomètre, ONU, OTAN, UE, PDG, formules de politesse

lessons.title: La ponctuation et les espaces typographiques
lessons.summary: Typography varies by region and publication. Quebec commonly omits spaces before `;`, `?`, and `!`, but also accepts narrow spaces; France commonly uses non-breaking spaces, often narrow, before these marks. This lesson illustrates the no-space Quebec convention. Both conventions use a non-breaking space before a colon and spaces inside French guillemets. Apostrophes stay attached to the words they join. Hyphens link inversion and affirmative imperative pronouns; traditional and rectified number spellings are both accepted.
objectives: Apply the Quebec spacing convention illustrated here and recognise accepted regional alternatives.
Use French guillemets, typographic apostrophes, dialogue dashes, and hyphens correctly.
Format percentages, currency amounts, times, abbreviations, and lists consistently.
Handle ellipses, nested quotations, parentheses, and the restricted elision of si.
Use a consistent citation, footnote, and bibliography style without treating house-style variants as grammar errors.

sections.title: Spaces, quotation marks, and hyphens
paragraphs: Distinguish grammar from typographic convention. The Office québécois de la langue française favours no space before `;`, `?`, and `!`, while also accepting a narrow space when available. France commonly uses a non-breaking space, often narrow, before these marks. Neither regional convention makes a sentence ungrammatical. The examples here use the no-space Quebec convention. Keep periods and commas attached to the preceding word, and put a non-breaking space before a colon so it cannot begin a new line.

In polished French typography, prefer guillemets with non-breaking spaces inside: `« texte »`, and curly apostrophes in `l’école`, `d’accord`, and `qu’il`. Straight quotation marks and apostrophes are common in plain text and are not grammar errors. Whichever apostrophe you use, do not insert spaces around an elision. Do not elide before an aspirated `h` or certain number words: `le héros`, `le onze`. Dialogue commonly starts each speaker’s turn on a new line with an em dash; some publications use an en dash instead.

A hyphen joins the verb and subject pronoun in inversion: `vient-il?`, `pouvez-vous?`. In forms such as `va-t-il?` and `parle-t-elle?`, an extra `t` links a third-person singular verb to `il`, `elle`, or `on`, with a hyphen on each side. Do not add this extra letter when the verb already ends in t or d: `vient-il?`, `prend-elle?`. A hyphen also joins an affirmative imperative to its pronouns (`donnez-le-moi`, `vas-y`, `prends-en`). Under the 1990 spelling recommendations, compound number elements are hyphenated (`vingt-et-un`, `cent-vingt-trois`); traditional spellings such as `vingt et un` and `cent vingt-trois` remain accepted.

Symbols and abbreviations follow their own patterns: write a non-breaking space before `%`, `$`, and `€`; write time as `14 h 30`; write `M.` because the abbreviation cuts off the end of `monsieur`, but `Dr` and `Dre` without a period because their final letters remain. The abbreviation `etc.` already includes its period.
points: Keep periods and commas attached to the preceding word; before `;`, `?`, and `!`, follow the chosen regional convention.
Insert a non-breaking space before `:` and inside `«  »`.
Keep apostrophes attached to both sides; choose a consistent dialogue-dash convention.
Use hyphens in inversion, affirmative imperative pronoun groups, and rectified compound numbers.
Keep a non-breaking space between a number and `%`, `$`, or `€`, and around the `h` in a written time.

examples.french: Le dossier est complet : nous pouvons l’envoyer aujourd’hui.
examples.english: The file is complete: we can send it today.
examples.note: A non-breaking space precedes the colon.

examples.french: Avez-vous reçu mon courriel? Merci de me répondre rapidement!
examples.english: Did you receive my email? Please reply quickly!
examples.note: Canadian French normally places no space before the question or exclamation mark.

examples.french: La conseillère a répondu : « Votre demande est complète. »
examples.english: The adviser replied, “Your application is complete.”
examples.note: French guillemets contain non-breaking spaces.

examples.french:
— Avez-vous une pièce d’identité?
— Oui, je l’ai apportée.
examples.english: “Do you have a piece of identification?” “Yes, I brought it.”
examples.note: Each change of speaker is marked by an em dash; every reply starts a new line.

examples.french: Préparez votre réponse et joignez-y les documents demandés.
examples.english: Prepare your reply and attach the requested documents to it.
examples.note: The affirmative imperative pronoun y refers clearly to votre réponse and is joined to joignez with a hyphen.

examples.french: Le taux est de 15 %, les frais sont de 20 $ et le rendez-vous est fixé à 14 h 30.
examples.english: The rate is 15%, the fee is $20, and the appointment is set for 2:30 p.m.
examples.note: A non-breaking space separates a number from a symbol; written time uses `h`.

mistakes.avoid: « Votre dossier est prêt, dit-elle.
mistakes.prefer: « Votre dossier est prêt », dit-elle.
mistakes.why: Close the quotation before the narrator’s reporting clause. Opening and closing quotation marks must be paired.

mistakes.avoid: Je vais à l’ école demain.
mistakes.prefer: Je vais à l’école demain.
mistakes.why: An apostrophe is attached to the elided word and to the following word; no space is inserted.

mistakes.avoid: Va il venir à la réunion?
mistakes.prefer: Va-t-il venir à la réunion?
mistakes.why: Inversion takes hyphens, and a euphonic `t` separates the two vowel sounds.

sections.title: Ellipses, nested quotations, parentheses, and si
paragraphs: An ellipsis normally attaches to the preceding word, with a space before the next word: Je pensais venir… mais je travaille. Three periods (...) are a plain-text alternative to the single character (…). Do not add another full stop merely because the ellipsis ends the sentence. A following capital depends on whether a new sentence begins.

For a quotation inside French guillemets, a common convention uses English-style double quotation marks: « Elle a dit “bonjour”. » The inner marks have no internal spaces. Publishers may adopt other nested-quotation styles; the essential point is to keep the two levels identifiable and correctly paired.

Parentheses contain no space immediately after the opening mark or before the closing one: (voir page 3). A parenthetical phrase inside a sentence leaves the sentence’s final period outside. A complete independent sentence enclosed in parentheses keeps its own final period inside.

Conjunction si elides specifically before il and ils: s’il, s’ils. It does not elide before elle, elles, on, or a general vowel-initial word: si elle vient, si on attend. This restriction differs from the broader elision of que. Also learn lexical hyphens as part of a word’s spelling: un arc-en-ciel (m., rainbow), un chef-d’œuvre (m., masterpiece), un sous-sol (m., basement); not every compound noun has hyphens.
points: Attach an ellipsis to the preceding word and distinguish continuation from a new sentence.
Keep nested quotation levels identifiable and pair every opening mark with a closing mark.
Use no internal spaces in parentheses.
Elide si only before il and ils in these conjunction uses.

examples.french: Je pensais venir… mais mon horaire a changé.
examples.english: I was planning to come… but my schedule has changed.
examples.note: The ellipsis touches venir; the same sentence continues with lowercase mais.

examples.french: « La conseillère a dit “revenez demain” avant de fermer le guichet. »
examples.english: “The adviser said ‘come back tomorrow’ before closing the counter.”
examples.note: English-style inner marks distinguish the quoted words from the outer quotation.

examples.french: La liste des pièces (voir page 3) accompagne le formulaire.
examples.english: The list of documents (see page 3) accompanies the form.
examples.note: No internal spaces in the parentheses; the sentence’s period remains outside.

examples.french: (Le bureau sera fermé lundi.)
examples.english: (The office will be closed on Monday.)
examples.note: A complete independent parenthetical sentence keeps its period inside.

examples.french: S’il arrive tôt, prévenez-moi; si elle arrive plus tard, gardez une place.
examples.english: If he arrives early, let me know; if she arrives later, keep a place.
examples.note: Si elides before il but not before elle.

examples.french: S’ils confirment leur présence, nous ouvrirons le sous-sol au public.
examples.english: If they confirm that they are coming, we will open the basement to the public.
examples.note: S’ils uses the same restricted elision; sous-sol keeps its lexical hyphen.

mistakes.avoid: S’elle téléphone, donnez-lui mon numéro.
mistakes.prefer: Si elle téléphone, donnez-lui mon numéro.
mistakes.why: Si does not elide before elle.

mistakes.avoid: Si ils arrivent, ouvrez la salle.
mistakes.prefer: S’ils arrivent, ouvrez la salle.
mistakes.why: Si elides before ils.

mistakes.avoid: La liste (voir page 3 accompagne le formulaire.
mistakes.prefer: La liste (voir page 3) accompagne le formulaire.
mistakes.why: The opening parenthesis needs a closing parenthesis.

sections.title: References, note markers, and lists
paragraphs: A bibliography identifies sources in a consistent order. One French book-reference style separates author, title, and publication details with periods, and place from publisher with a colon. Other required styles use different punctuation or place the year earlier. Follow the assignment or publisher’s style rather than claiming that every bibliography must use one universal pattern. Italicise a standalone book title where the format permits.

A footnote marker is normally a small raised number attached to the relevant word or passage, not separated by a space. In the convention illustrated here it precedes the following punctuation: Selon le guide¹, la règle s’applique. Placement around quotation marks can differ between editorial styles. The marker must point to an actual note; quotation marks alone do not identify a source.

A list continuing an introductory sentence can start with a colon, use lowercase phrases, end intermediate items with semicolons, and end the final item with a period. Complete-sentence items normally start with capitals and end with periods. Short labels may omit final punctuation under another consistent house style. These choices do not turn valid regional spacing into a grammar error.
points: Follow the required bibliography style consistently instead of assuming one universal format.
Attach each footnote marker to the relevant passage and supply its note.
Distinguish list fragments continuing a sentence from independent sentence items.

examples.french: Martin, Léa. Guide du quartier. Montréal : Éditions du Canal, 2025.
examples.english: Martin, Léa. Neighbourhood Guide. Montreal: Éditions du Canal, 2025.
examples.note: Invented reference demonstrating one bibliography style, not a real source citation or a mandatory universal format.

examples.french:
Selon le guide¹, la demande doit être signée.
¹ Exemple de note : préciser ici l’auteur, le titre et la page consultée.
examples.english:
According to the guide¹, the application must be signed.
¹ Example note: give the author, title, and page consulted here.
examples.note: The attached superscript points to an explanatory note; a real citation must supply real source details.
A list continuing the introductory sentence: lowercase items, semicolons, then a period. The spacing follows this lesson’s Quebec convention.

examples.french:
Deux règles s’appliquent :
– Chaque candidat signe son formulaire.
– Le service conserve une copie.
examples.english:
Two rules apply:
– Each applicant signs their form.
– The department keeps a copy.
examples.note: These list items are complete sentences, with capitals and periods.

mistakes.avoid: Pour préparer le dossier, il faut : vérifier les pièces; signez le formulaire; conserver une copie.
mistakes.prefer: Pour préparer le dossier, il faut : vérifier les pièces; signer le formulaire; conserver une copie.
mistakes.why: Each item completes il faut and therefore needs an infinitive. This is a syntactic error, not a preference between punctuation styles.

mistakes.avoid: Chaque candidat signent son formulaire.
mistakes.prefer: Chaque candidat signe son formulaire.
mistakes.why: A complete-sentence list item still needs subject–verb agreement: chaque candidat is singular.

vocabulary.example: La ponctuation claire rend une lettre officielle plus facile à lire.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the ending `-tion` is a strong feminine clue.

vocabulary.example: Une espace insécable empêche le deux-points de commencer une nouvelle ligne.
vocabulary.note: In typography, `espace` is feminine.

vocabulary.example: Un guillemet français a la forme d’un petit chevron.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; normally used in the plural when naming the pair.

vocabulary.example: Une apostrophe remplace la voyelle supprimée dans « l’école ».
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; use the typographic apostrophe `’` in polished writing.

vocabulary.example: Un trait d’union relie le verbe et le pronom dans « vient-il ».
vocabulary.note: Masculine compound noun.

practice.prompt: Apply this lesson’s Quebec typography convention and correct the missing inversion hyphen: « Votre dossier est prêt : pouvez vous venir à 14h30 ? »
practice.hint: Use non-breaking spaces inside guillemets and before the colon, a hyphen in `pouvez-vous`, spaces around `h`, and this lesson’s no-space convention before `?`.
practice.answer: « Votre dossier est prêt : pouvez-vous venir à 14 h 30? »

takeaways: Quebec often omits spaces before `;`, `?`, and `!`, but accepts narrow spaces; France commonly uses non-breaking spaces.
Prefer guillemets and curly apostrophes in polished typography without treating plain-text alternatives as grammar errors.
Inversion and affirmative imperative pronouns require hyphens.
Si elides before il/ils, not elle/elles/on.
Pair nested quotation marks and parentheses; keep ellipses attached to the preceding word.
Follow a consistent reference and list style, and make every footnote marker point to a real note.
keywords: points de suspension, parenthèses, citations imbriquées, élision de si
bibliographie, appel de note, note de bas de page, énumération, espaces insécables, France, Québec

modules.title: La conjugaison, les temps et les modes
modules.description: Move from present and past forms to future, conditions, instructions and the subjunctive, then study participles, passive voice and causative constructions.

lessons.title: Les modèles du présent
lessons.summary: The present can describe current actions, habits, general truths, scheduled future events, and vivid historical narration. Learn the parler, finir, and attendre patterns, but do not infer a verb's whole conjugation from its infinitive ending. Frequent irregular verbs provide further useful families.
objectives: Produce the present-tense patterns of parler, finir, and attendre.
Group frequent irregular verbs into families instead of memorising them singly.
Predict which written forms are pronounced alike.
Recognise the present used for current, habitual, future, general, and historical meaning.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A simple verb form combines a stem carrying the meaning with an ending marking person and tense. The infinitive is the unconjugated dictionary form, such as `parler` (to speak). Three useful present patterns are `parler`: `je parle, tu parles, il parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils parlent`; `finir`: `je finis, tu finis, il finit, nous finissons, vous finissez, ils finissent`; and `attendre`: `j’attends, tu attends, il attend, nous attendons, vous attendez, ils attendent`. Remove `-er`, `-ir`, or `-re` to find the starting stem in these models; `finir` adds `-iss-` in the plural. An infinitive ending alone is not a guarantee: `aller` is irregular, and many `-ir` and `-re` verbs follow other patterns.

Irregular verbs are often learned in families, because one pattern then covers several verbs. `Tenir` and `venir` share `je tiens / nous tenons` and `je viens / nous venons`, and so do their derivatives `obtenir`, `maintenir`, `devenir`, `revenir`. `Ouvrir`, `offrir`, and `souffrir` end in `-ir` but take `-er` present endings: `j’ouvre`, `il offre`. In `je parle`, `tu parles`, `il parle`, and `ils parlent`, the verb forms sound alike. The subject often helps, but `il parle` and `ils parlent` also sound alike: context supplies the number.

Context decides the time meaning. `Je travaille maintenant` is current; `Je travaille chaque samedi` is habitual; `L’eau bout à 100 °C` is a general truth; `Le train part demain` uses the present for a scheduled near future. In historical narration, the present can make a past event vivid, but ordinary personal narration normally uses past tenses.
points: Identify the infinitive type before choosing an ending set.
Use `-issons`, `-issez`, `-issent` for `-ir` verbs of the `finir` type only.
Learn `tenir` and `venir` together with their derivatives.
Remember that `ouvrir`, `offrir`, and `souffrir` take `-er` endings.
The verb forms parle, parles, and parlent sound the same; subject pronouns or context help distinguish them.
Use a time marker such as `maintenant`, `chaque semaine`, or `demain` to make the intended present meaning clear.
Use the historical present as a narrative effect, not as the default past tense.
Study the spelling families — `-ayer`, `-oyer`, `-uyer`, `-indre`, `-aître`, `cueillir`, `vivre`, `suivre`, `servir`, `courir` — in the dedicated lesson that follows.

examples.french: Nous parlons français au travail, vous finissez le formulaire et ils attendent la réponse.
examples.english: We speak French at work, you finish the form, and they wait for the answer.
examples.note: One sentence showing the -er, -ir, and -re endings.

examples.french: Nous suivons un cours de français offert par le centre communautaire.
examples.english: We are taking a French course offered by the community centre.
examples.note: « Suivre » keeps its stem in the plural: nous suivons.

examples.french: Les familles reçoivent une réponse dans un délai de dix jours ouvrables.
examples.english: Families receive an answer within ten business days.
examples.note: « Recevoir » changes its stem in the third-person plural.

examples.french: J’obtiens mon attestation aujourd’hui et nous obtenons les nôtres demain.
examples.english: I am getting my certificate today and we are getting ours tomorrow.
examples.note: The `tenir` family alternates between « obtiens » and « obtenons ».

examples.french: Elle ouvre le dossier et elle offre son aide aux nouveaux arrivants.
examples.english: She opens the file and offers her help to newcomers.
examples.note: « Ouvrir » and « offrir » take -er endings despite their infinitive.

examples.french: Je travaille actuellement au service des permis.
examples.english: I currently work in the permits department.
examples.note: Current situation.

examples.french: Chaque samedi, nous faisons du bénévolat au centre communautaire.
examples.english: Every Saturday, we volunteer at the community centre.
examples.note: Habitual present.

examples.french: Le train part demain à huit heures.
examples.english: The train leaves tomorrow at eight o’clock.
examples.note: Present used for a scheduled near-future event.

examples.french: L’eau bout à 100 °C au niveau de la mer.
examples.english: Water boils at 100°C at sea level.
examples.note: Present used for a general scientific truth.

examples.french: En 1969, les premiers humains marchent sur la Lune.
examples.english: In 1969, the first humans walk on the Moon.
examples.note: Historical present used to make a past event vivid.

mistakes.avoid: Nous finons le formulaire avant midi.
mistakes.prefer: Nous finissons le formulaire avant midi.
mistakes.why: `Finir` belongs to the group that inserts `-iss-` in the plural forms.

mistakes.avoid: Nous ouvrez la porte du bureau chaque matin.
mistakes.prefer: Nous ouvrons la porte du bureau chaque matin.
mistakes.why: With nous, the present ending is -ons. Ouvrir uses the same present endings as an -er verb.

sections.title: Seven complete irregular present patterns
paragraphs: Use these six-person patterns as reference points rather than guessing from an infinitive ending. Il, elle, and on share the third-person singular form; ils and elles share the third-person plural. Read each line aloud, then use the form with a meaningful complement.

Être describes identity or a state; avoir expresses possession and many fixed states. Aller names movement or forms the near future with an infinitive. Faire names an action or activity. Pouvoir, vouloir, and devoir can modify the meaning of another verb; this use is called modal. They take an infinitive directly, commonly expressing ability or permission, desire, and obligation respectively. Devoir can also express probability: il doit être chez lui means he is probably at home. With a noun object, devoir means owe: je dois vingt dollars.
points: Être — to be: je suis; tu es; il/elle/on est; nous sommes; vous êtes; ils/elles sont.
Avoir — to have: j’ai; tu as; il/elle/on a; nous avons; vous avez; ils/elles ont.
Aller — to go: je vais; tu vas; il/elle/on va; nous allons; vous allez; ils/elles vont.
Faire — to do/make: je fais; tu fais; il/elle/on fait; nous faisons; vous faites; ils/elles font.
Pouvoir — to be able to: je peux; tu peux; il/elle/on peut; nous pouvons; vous pouvez; ils/elles peuvent.
Vouloir — to want: je veux; tu veux; il/elle/on veut; nous voulons; vous voulez; ils/elles veulent.
Devoir — to have to/owe: je dois; tu dois; il/elle/on doit; nous devons; vous devez; ils/elles doivent.

examples.french: Nous sommes disponibles lundi, mais vous êtes déjà en réunion.
examples.english: We are available on Monday, but you are already in a meeting.
examples.note: Sommes and êtes are whole irregular forms, not a regular stem plus predictable endings.

examples.french: Tu as une copie du contrat, et les autres candidats ont les leurs.
examples.english: You have a copy of the contract, and the other applicants have theirs.
examples.note: As is singular; ont is plural. A copy is une copie (f.); a contract is un contrat (m.).

examples.french: Je vais à la bibliothèque pendant que mes voisins vont au marché.
examples.english: I am going to the library while my neighbours are going to the market.
examples.note: Vais and vont belong to aller despite looking unlike its infinitive.

examples.french: Vous faites la réservation et nous faisons les préparatifs.
examples.english: You make the reservation and we make the preparations.
examples.note: Use vous faites, not a form invented from faisons.

examples.french: Nous pouvons attendre ici, mais les enfants peuvent entrer.
examples.english: We can wait here, but the children can enter.
examples.note: The stem changes between pouvons and peuvent; both take an infinitive without de.

examples.french: Vous voulez une réponse écrite; elles veulent aussi connaître le délai.
examples.english: You want a written answer; they also want to know the processing time.
examples.note: Vouloir can take a noun or an infinitive: une réponse (f.) or connaître.

examples.french: Je dois vérifier la facture, et nous devons encore trente dollars.
examples.english: I have to check the invoice, and we still owe thirty dollars.
examples.note: Modal devoir takes an infinitive; lexical devoir takes what is owed. A named creditor is optional.

mistakes.avoid: Vous faisez la réservation.
mistakes.prefer: Vous faites la réservation.
mistakes.why: The irregular vous form of faire is faites.

mistakes.avoid: Les candidats veullent une réponse.
mistakes.prefer: Les candidats veulent une réponse.
mistakes.why: The third-person plural of vouloir is veulent, with one l.

vocabulary.example: Je suis un cours de conversation deux soirs par semaine.
vocabulary.note: Irregular: `je suis`, `nous suivons`; identical to `être` in the first person singular.

vocabulary.example: Les candidats reçoivent une confirmation par courriel.
vocabulary.note: Stem change in the plural: `nous recevons`, `ils reçoivent`.

vocabulary.example: J’obtiens enfin une réponse du service d’immigration.
vocabulary.note: Belongs to the `tenir` family: `j’obtiens`, `nous obtenons`.

vocabulary.example: Un centre communautaire offre des cours de français gratuits.
vocabulary.note: Masculine compound noun; learn it as one unit.

vocabulary.example: Un délai de traitement de six semaines est indiqué sur le site.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; false friend, it does not mean delay in the sense of lateness.

practice.prompt: Conjugate for `nous` and `ils`: `parler`, `finir`, `attendre`, `venir`.
practice.hint: Only one of the four inserts `-iss-`.
practice.answer: nous parlons / ils parlent, nous finissons / ils finissent, nous attendons / ils attendent, nous venons / ils viennent

takeaways: Use parler, finir, and attendre as models, but check which family a verb belongs to.
`Ouvrir`, `offrir`, `souffrir` take `-er` endings in the present.
Parle, parles, and parlent sound alike; il parle and ils parlent need context to distinguish number.
The present can locate an action now, regularly, tomorrow, generally, or in vivid historical narration.
Keep complete six-person reference patterns for être, avoir, aller, faire, pouvoir, vouloir, and devoir.
keywords: être, avoir, aller, faire, pouvoir, vouloir, devoir, conjugaison complète du présent

lessons.title: Les familles orthographiques du présent
lessons.summary: Learn present-tense stem and ending patterns together: nettoie/nettoyons, crains/craignons, connais/connaissons, and cueillir with -er endings. Rire and courir keep their present stems; dire has exceptional vous dites, unlike vous interdisez. Conduire models a common -uire family. Future forms need separate checking: je verrai but je prévoirai.
objectives: Apply the `y` to `i` change to `-oyer` and `-uyer` verbs and recognise the double spelling allowed for `-ayer`.
Conjugate the `-indre`, `-aître`, `-ivre`, and `servir` families in the singular and the plural.
Distinguish `je verrai` from the futures `je prévoirai`, `je pourvoirai`, and `je fuirai`.
Conjugate the present -uire family and the exceptional vous forms in the dire family.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A silent ending is one that is not pronounced: the `-e`, `-es`, and `-ent` of `je nettoie`, `tu nettoies`, `ils nettoient` are all silent, while the `-ons` and `-ez` of `nous nettoyons` and `vous nettoyez` are heard. Several families change their stem exactly at that boundary. Verbs in `-oyer` and `-uyer` write `i` instead of `y` before a silent ending: `je nettoie`, `nous nettoyons`; `j’essuie`, `vous essuyez`; `j’envoie`, `nous envoyons`. Verbs in `-ayer` accept both spellings, so `je paie` and `je paye` are equally correct, as are `j’essaie` and `j’essaye`. One irregularity is worth memorising separately: `envoyer` builds its future on `enverr-`, giving `j’enverrai`, not `j’envoierai`.

Three more families change the stem between singular and plural. Verbs in `-indre` — `craindre`, `joindre`, `peindre`, `atteindre`, `éteindre` — drop the `d` and write `-gn-` in the plural: `je crains`, `nous craignons`; `je joins`, `nous joignons`. Verbs in `-aître` — `connaître`, `paraître`, `disparaître`, `apparaître`, `naître` — double the `s` in the plural: `je connais`, `nous connaissons`; `vous paraissez`. `Cueillir`, `accueillir`, and `recueillir` end in `-ir` but take the `-er` endings, so `j’accueille`, `nous cueillons`, never `nous cueillissons`.

The last group is short but very frequent. `Vivre` and `suivre` give `je vis / nous vivons` and `je suis / nous suivons`; note that `je suis` is also the present of `être`, and context tells the two apart: `Je suis un cours de français` means *I am taking a French course*. `Servir` and its derivatives alternate stems too: `je sers / nous servons`. `Desservir` can mean to serve a place, as a transit line does, or to clear a table. In contrast, `rire`, `sourire`, and `courir` keep their written stems in the present: `je ris / nous rions`, `je souris / nous sourions`, `je cours / nous courons`; only the endings change. Do not extend the future of `voir` to every similar verb: `je verrai`, `je reverrai`, and `j’entreverrai`, but `je prévoirai`, `je pourvoirai`, and `je fuirai`.
points: Write `i` instead of `y` before a silent ending in `-oyer` and `-uyer` verbs.
Accept both `je paie` and `je paye`, and both `j’essaie` and `j’essaye`, for `-ayer` verbs.
Build the future of `envoyer` on `enverr-`: `j’enverrai`.
Replace `-nd-` with `-gn-` in the plural of `-indre` verbs: `nous craignons`, `nous joignons`.
Double the `s` in the plural of `-aître` verbs: `nous connaissons`, `vous paraissez`.
Give `cueillir`, `accueillir`, and `recueillir` the `-er` endings: `j’accueille`, `nous cueillons`.
Learn `je vis / nous vivons`, `je suis / nous suivons`, `je ris / nous rions`, `je sers / nous servons`, `je cours / nous courons` as fixed pairs.
Distinguish stem changes from ending changes: `rire` and `courir` keep `ri-` and `cour-` in the present.
Learn the futures `je verrai`, `je prévoirai`, `je pourvoirai`, and `je fuirai` separately.

examples.french: Je paie mon loyer par virement le premier du mois, et nous nettoyons les bureaux avant l’inspection.
examples.english: I pay my rent by transfer on the first of the month, and we clean the offices before the inspection.
examples.note: « Paie » with a silent ending, « nettoyons » with a pronounced one.

examples.french: J’envoie les documents numérisés ce soir et je vous enverrai l’original par la poste.
examples.english: I am sending the scanned documents tonight and I will send you the original by mail.
examples.note: Present « envoie », irregular future « enverrai ».

examples.french: Je crains un retard, mais nous joignons déjà toutes les pièces au dossier.
examples.english: I am afraid of a delay, but we are already attaching all the supporting documents to the file.
examples.note: « Crains » in the singular, « joignons » with -gn- in the plural.

examples.french: Elle connaît bien les services offerts aux nouveaux arrivants, et vous paraissez inquiets avant l’entretien.
examples.english: She knows the services offered to newcomers well, and you look worried before the interview.
examples.note: Traditional spelling has « connaît »; rectified « connait » is also accepted. « Paraissez » has a doubled s in either spelling system.

examples.french: J’accueille les participants à la réception pendant que mes collègues cueillent les fruits du jardin communautaire.
examples.english: I welcome the participants at reception while my colleagues pick the fruit from the community garden.
examples.note: The « cueillir » family takes -er endings in the present.

examples.french: Je suis un cours de français le mardi soir et je vis dans ce quartier depuis deux ans.
examples.english: I take a French course on Tuesday evenings and I have lived in this neighbourhood for two years.
examples.note: « Je suis » is here the present of « suivre », not of « être ».

examples.french: Cette ligne d’autobus dessert le centre-ville toutes les dix minutes.
examples.english: This bus line serves the downtown area every ten minutes.
examples.note: « Desservir » in its transit meaning: to serve or link a place.

examples.french: Nous verrons la conseillère à quatorze heures, et les enfants courent déjà dans le parc.
examples.english: We will see the adviser at two o’clock, and the children are already running in the park.
examples.note: Future stem « verr- » for « voir »; « courent » for « courir ».

examples.french: Je prévoirai une journée de congé pour le déménagement.
examples.english: I will plan a day off for the move.
examples.note: « Prévoir » keeps prévoir- in the future; it does not follow « je verrai ».

mistakes.avoid: Je nettoye la cuisine avant l’inspection du logement.
mistakes.prefer: Je nettoie la cuisine avant l’inspection du logement.
mistakes.why: `-oyer` and `-uyer` verbs must write `i` before a silent ending; only `-ayer` verbs allow both spellings.

mistakes.avoid: Je vous envoierai les documents demain matin.
mistakes.prefer: Je vous enverrai les documents demain matin.
mistakes.why: `Envoyer` builds its future on the irregular stem `enverr-`.

mistakes.avoid: Je préverrai une journée de congé pour le déménagement.
mistakes.prefer: Je prévoirai une journée de congé pour le déménagement.
mistakes.why: `Prévoir` uses the future stem `prévoir-`, unlike `voir`, which uses `verr-`.

mistakes.avoid: Nous craindons un retard dans le traitement du dossier.
mistakes.prefer: Nous craignons un retard dans le traitement du dossier.
mistakes.why: `-indre` verbs replace `-nd-` with `-gn-` in the plural of the present.

mistakes.avoid: Nous connaisons bien cette procédure et nous recueillissons les documents à l’accueil.
mistakes.prefer: Nous connaissons bien cette procédure et nous recueillons les documents à l’accueil.
mistakes.why: `Connaître` has the plural stem `connaiss-`. `Recueillir` (to collect) takes the present ending `-ons`, without the `-iss-` of `finir`: `nous recueillons`.

sections.title: Dire and its derivatives: check vous
paragraphs: Dire has je dis, tu dis, il/elle/on dit, nous disons, vous dites, ils/elles disent. Redire follows this pattern: vous redites. Do not extend dites to every derivative: vous prédisez (predict), interdisez (forbid), médisez (speak ill), and contredisez (contradict). Médire takes de before the person criticised.

In the present, maudire follows a finir-like pattern: je maudis, tu maudis, il maudit, nous maudissons, vous maudissez, ils maudissent. This comparison concerns the present only; its past participle is maudit, not a form invented from finir.
points: Dire/redire: vous dites/redites.
Prédire/interdire/médire/contredire: vous forms in -disez.
Maudire inserts -iss- in the present plural.

examples.french: Vous dites la date, puis vous redites l’adresse plus lentement.
examples.english: You say the date, then repeat the address more slowly.
examples.note: Dire and redire share the exceptional vous form.

examples.french: Vous prédisez une hausse des prix, mais vous contredisez le dernier rapport.
examples.english: You predict a price rise, but you contradict the latest report.
examples.note: Prédire and contredire use -disez, not -dites.

examples.french: Vous interdisez les interruptions, mais vous médisez de vos collègues.
examples.english: You forbid interruptions, but you speak ill of your colleagues.
examples.note: Interdire takes a direct object; médire takes de.

examples.french: Dans le récit, les voyageurs maudissent la pluie qui les retarde.
examples.english: In the story, the travellers curse the rain delaying them.
examples.note: Maudissent shows the -iss- present plural.

mistakes.avoid: Vous redisez la consigne.
mistakes.prefer: Vous redites la consigne.
mistakes.why: Redire follows dire: vous redites.

mistakes.avoid: Vous interdites le stationnement.
mistakes.prefer: Vous interdisez le stationnement.
mistakes.why: Interdire has the vous form interdisez.

sections.title: The present pattern of conduire
paragraphs: Learn the full pattern: je conduis, tu conduis, il/elle/on conduit, nous conduisons, vous conduisez, ils/elles conduisent. The singular endings are -s, -s, -t; the plural uses conduis- before -ons, -ez, -ent. The final t in il conduit belongs to a present form that also happens to look like the past participle conduit.

Common verbs following this pattern include produire (produce), cuire (cook), traduire (translate), construire (build), détruire (destroy), séduire (appeal to or attract), and déduire (deduct or infer). Learn the full word, not only a shared suffix: nous cuisons, vous traduisez, ils construisent.
points: Singular: conduis, conduis, conduit; plural: conduisons, conduisez, conduisent.
Do not transfer the plural's s into the third-person singular.

examples.french: Je conduis jusqu’au centre, puis vous conduisez jusqu’à la gare.
examples.english: I drive to the centre, then you drive to the station.
examples.note: Conduis versus conduisez.

examples.french: Nous produisons la brochure et nos collègues traduisent les consignes.
examples.english: We produce the brochure and our colleagues translate the instructions.
examples.note: Produisons and traduisent use the plural pattern.

examples.french: Le pain cuit pendant que nous construisons les étagères.
examples.english: The bread is baking while we build the shelves.
examples.note: Cuire has il cuit; construire has nous construisons.

examples.french: Les travaux détruisent l’ancien mur, et vous déduisez leur coût du budget.
examples.english: The work demolishes the old wall, and you deduct its cost from the budget.
examples.note: Détruisent and déduisez follow the same present family.

mistakes.avoid: Nous conduions les visiteurs à la gare aujourd’hui.
mistakes.prefer: Nous conduisons les visiteurs à la gare aujourd’hui.
mistakes.why: The present nous form of conduire is conduisons.

mistakes.avoid: Elle traduis le formulaire.
mistakes.prefer: Elle traduit le formulaire.
mistakes.why: The third-person singular ends in t.

vocabulary.example: Nous nettoyons la salle communautaire après chaque activité.
vocabulary.note: `Y` becomes `i` before a silent ending: `je nettoie`.
