examples.note: Soyons and ayez are irregular; une pièce d’identité (f.) is an identification document.

examples.french: Je souhaite que vous sachiez où aller et que vous puissiez obtenir de l’aide.
examples.english: I want you to know where to go and to be able to get help.
examples.note: Savoir and pouvoir have the subjunctive stems sach- and puiss-.

mistakes.avoid: Il faut que nous prennions une décision.
mistakes.prefer: Il faut que nous prenions une décision.
mistakes.why: The nous/vous stem comes from prenons: prenions has one n.

mistakes.avoid: Je comprends que vous veuilliez vérifier.
mistakes.prefer: Je comprends que vous vouliez vérifier.
mistakes.why: The standard vous subjunctive of vouloir is vouliez, not veuilliez.

sections.title: Past subjunctive: a completed action
paragraphs: Form the past subjunctive with the present subjunctive of avoir or être plus the past participle: que j’aie envoyé, que nous ayons fini, qu’elle soit partie. The trigger selects the mood; the timeline selects present or past. Je suis heureux qu’elle vienne welcomes her coming, whereas Je suis heureux qu’elle soit venue welcomes a visit already made.

The compound form presents an action as completed relative to the relevant moment. That moment may still be in the future: Il faut que vous ayez terminé avant vendredi means the task must be complete by Friday. With avant que, the main event can prevent the subordinate action from ever being completed: Il est parti avant que j’aie pu lui parler does not assert that a conversation occurred.

Keep the ordinary auxiliary and agreement rules. Arriver uses être and agrees with its subject: qu’elles soient arrivées. With avoir, agreement depends on a preceding direct object, not simply on the subject’s gender. Pronominal verbs retain their own patterns: qu’elles se soient lavées, but qu’elles se soient parlé. Negation surrounds the auxiliary: qu’il n’ait pas répondu.
points: Form the past subjunctive with a present-subjunctive auxiliary and a past participle.
Interpret completion relative to the reference point, which may be a future deadline.
Keep ordinary auxiliary, negation, and participle-agreement rules.

examples.french: Je suis contente que vous ayez reçu les documents hier.
examples.english: I am glad that you received the documents yesterday.
examples.note: Present emotion concerns an earlier completed receipt: ayez + reçu.

examples.french: Je doute que les conseillères soient déjà arrivées.
examples.english: I doubt that the advisers have already arrived.
examples.note: Être is the auxiliary of arriver; arrivées agrees with the feminine plural subject.

examples.french: Il faut que nous ayons terminé le dossier avant vendredi.
examples.english: We must have completed the application by Friday.
examples.note: Past subjunctive marks completion by a future deadline, not necessarily before now.

examples.french: Le responsable est parti avant que j’aie pu lui poser ma question.
examples.english: The manager left before I could ask him my question.
examples.note: Aie pu presents the opportunity as not yet achieved when he left.

examples.french: Je regrette qu’elle n’ait pas répondu à mon courriel.
examples.english: I regret that she did not reply to my email.
examples.note: Ne… pas surrounds ait; répondu remains after the negative.

mistakes.avoid: Je suis ravi que tu aies recevoir la lettre.
mistakes.prefer: Je suis ravi que tu aies reçu la lettre.
mistakes.why: A compound tense requires a past participle after its auxiliary, not an infinitive.

mistakes.avoid: Je suis heureux qu’elles aient arrivées.
mistakes.prefer: Je suis heureux qu’elles soient arrivées.
mistakes.why: Arriver uses être: the subjunctive auxiliary is soient.

vocabulary.example: Il faut que vous fournissiez une preuve de résidence.
vocabulary.note: Impersonal verb, used only with `il`; followed by an infinitive or by `que` plus subjunctive.

vocabulary.example: Il faut que j’aille au bureau des permis avant midi.
vocabulary.note: Irregular subjunctive: `que j’aille`, `que nous allions`.

vocabulary.example: Nous devons décider avant que le délai expire.
vocabulary.note: Takes the subjunctive, unlike `après que`, which takes the indicative.

vocabulary.example: Une décision favorable a été communiquée par courriel.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the ending -sion is a feminine hint.

vocabulary.english: to wish that, to hope that
vocabulary.example: Nous souhaitons que chaque famille reçoive une réponse avant l’été.
vocabulary.note: Trigger of will, so it takes the subjunctive; `souhaiter` plus infinitive when the subject is the same.

vocabulary.example: Veillez à ce que rien ne soit oublié dans le dossier.
vocabulary.note: The sequence `à ce que` is obligatory and is followed by the subjunctive.

vocabulary.example: Je m’attends à ce que la réponse arrive avant la fin du mois.
vocabulary.note: S’attendre à ce que takes the subjunctive; formal s’attendre que is also correct. S’attendre à takes a noun or an infinitive: s’attendre à une réponse, à réussir.

vocabulary.example: Nous craignons que le délai soit trop court pour rassembler les pièces.
vocabulary.note: Takes the subjunctive and may have an optional expletive `ne`; distinguish genuine negatives such as `ne… jamais`.

practice.prompt: Choose the mood: « Je reste jusqu’à ce que le guichet (fermer). » and « Après que le guichet (fermer), je suis rentré. »
practice.hint: One conjunction takes the subjunctive, the other the indicative.
practice.answer: Je reste jusqu’à ce que le guichet ferme. Après que le guichet a fermé, je suis rentré.

takeaways: The trigger, not the meaning of the verb, calls the subjunctive.
Check separate stems for nous/vous: que je prenne, but que nous prenions.
The past subjunctive uses a subjunctive auxiliary plus a participle and marks completion relative to a reference point.
An infinitive often keeps the same actor with desire or purpose; après que keeps the indicative.
Learn the common à ce que constructions; s’attendre que is also correct in formal usage.
An expletive `ne` is optional and non-negative; the absence of `pas` alone does not identify it.
keywords: subjonctif présent, subjonctif passé, deux radicaux, nous et vous, antériorité

lessons.title: Les infinitifs : temps, but, sujets et adjectifs
lessons.summary: Infinitives express timing and purpose, can act as sentence subjects, and follow adjective constructions. Compare Il est difficile de lire ce texte with Ce texte est difficile à lire; heureux de venir with heureux que vous veniez. Learn each preposition with its construction rather than translating every English to alike.
objectives: Build a past infinitive with the correct auxiliary.
Choose between an infinitive and a subjunctive clause for purpose.
Avoid the bare après plus simple infinitive pattern.
Choose purpose alternatives by register and distinguish purpose from actual result.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: An infinitive has no person ending; its actor is supplied by the construction and context. Avant de signer le bail, elle a vérifié les conditions puts checking before signing. Avant de commonly takes a simple infinitive, but a past infinitive can emphasise completion: avant d’avoir terminé. Après takes a past infinitive for an earlier completed action: Après avoir rempli le formulaire, je l’ai envoyé. Choose the auxiliary as in the compound past: après être arrivée, après avoir couru, après s’être installée. Movement alone does not determine the auxiliary.

With an action and its purpose, an infinitive normally keeps the same actor: `Je suis cette formation pour améliorer mon français`. To name a different actor explicitly, use `pour que` or `afin que` plus the subjunctive: `Je vous écris afin que vous compreniez ma situation`. This is a useful construction pattern, not a rule for every infinitive: in `Ce manuel est utile pour apprendre le français` (This textbook is useful for learning French), the understood learner is its user, not the textbook.

With a time phrase placed at the start, make the actor clear: `Après avoir signé, la locataire a envoyé le bail` means the tenant signed and sent the lease. If someone else signed, name that person: `Après que la propriétaire a signé, la locataire a envoyé le bail` (After the landlady signed, the tenant sent the lease). For this temporal meaning, `après` takes a past infinitive, not a bare simple infinitive.
points: Use avant de to introduce the later action; the main action happens before it.
Use `après` plus `avoir` or `être` plus participle for a completed action.
Choose the past-infinitive auxiliary with the compound-past rules.
Use `après s’être` plus participle with a reflexive verb, agreeing where required.
Use pour que or afin que plus subjunctive to give the purpose clause its own explicit subject.
The usual order with ne… pas is before the infinitive auxiliary: après ne pas avoir dormi.

examples.french: Après avoir rempli le formulaire, je l’ai envoyé au ministère.
examples.english: After completing the form, I sent it to the ministry.
examples.note: Past infinitive with avoir.

examples.french: Après s’être installée à Montréal, elle a cherché un emploi bilingue.
examples.english: After settling in Montreal, she looked for a bilingual job.
examples.note: Reflexive past infinitive; the participle agrees with the subject.

examples.french: Avant de signer le bail, elle a vérifié toutes les conditions.
examples.english: Before signing the lease, she checked all the conditions.
examples.note: Avant de takes a simple infinitive here; avant d’avoir signé is also possible when completion matters.

examples.french: Je suis cette formation pour améliorer mon français professionnel.
examples.english: I am taking this course to improve my professional French.
examples.note: One subject, so an infinitive is enough.

examples.french: La ville a modifié l’horaire afin que les familles puissent participer.
examples.english: The city changed the schedule so that families could take part.
examples.note: Two subjects, so a conjunction plus the subjunctive.

examples.french: Après ne pas avoir dormi de la nuit, elle a reporté son entrevue.
examples.english: After not having slept all night, she postponed her interview.
examples.note: The negation stands in front of the entire past infinitive, auxiliary included.

mistakes.avoid: Après courir, je me repose quelques minutes.
mistakes.prefer: Après avoir couru, je me repose quelques minutes.
mistakes.why: `Après` requires the past infinitive when the action is already completed.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai écrit une lettre pour que vous comprenez ma situation.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai écrit une lettre pour que vous compreniez ma situation.
mistakes.why: Pour que introduces a purpose clause in the subjunctive: compreniez.

mistakes.avoid: Après avoir ne pas dormi, elle a reporté son entrevue.
mistakes.prefer: Après ne pas avoir dormi, elle a reporté son entrevue.
mistakes.why: The usual order is ne pas avoir dormi: ne precedes the infinitive auxiliary rather than following it. The more literary n’avoir pas dormi is also possible; avoir ne pas dormi is not.

sections.title: Purpose alternatives: construction, register, and result
paragraphs: Pour plus infinitive is the neutral purpose frame; afin de is more formal. De manière à and de façon à plus infinitive describe acting in a way intended to achieve an outcome. Dans le but de explicitly announces a goal and suits formal explanations. Before a vowel, de elides: dans le but d’améliorer. These infinitives normally share the actor of the main action.

En vue de means in preparation for or with a view to. It accepts a noun (en vue de l’inspection) or an infinitive (en vue d’améliorer l’accueil), and is common in administrative writing. Histoire de plus infinitive gives a casual, often modest reason: histoire de discuter means just to chat. It is useful in conversation, but less suited to a formal application.

A purpose clause can name its own subject: pour que, afin que, de manière que, de façon que, and de sorte que take the subjunctive when they express an intended outcome. The last three can instead describe an actual consequence with the indicative. Compare Nous réorganisons l’accueil de manière que chacun puisse entrer (our goal) with Nous avons réorganisé l’accueil, de manière que chacun peut maintenant entrer (the observed result). Neither mood is a universal rule for these connectors.
points: Use an infinitive after de manière à, de façon à, dans le but de, and histoire de.
En vue de accepts either a noun phrase or an infinitive.
Distinguish formal goal statements from conversational histoire de.
After de manière que or de sorte que, separate subjunctive purpose from indicative result.

examples.french: Placez les affiches de manière à les rendre visibles depuis l’entrée.
examples.english: Position the posters so as to make them visible from the entrance.
examples.note: De manière à takes an infinitive. A poster is une affiche (f.); an entrance is une entrée (f.).

examples.french: Nous adaptons les horaires de façon à accueillir les familles après le travail.
examples.english: We are adapting the hours so as to welcome families after work.
examples.note: De façon à presents an intended outcome of the action.

examples.french: Le centre organise un atelier dans le but d’améliorer l’accès aux services.
examples.english: The centre is organising a workshop with the aim of improving access to services.
examples.note: A formal explicit goal; de elides before améliorer.

examples.french: Nous classons les dossiers en vue de l’inspection et recueillons des avis en vue d’améliorer l’accueil.
examples.english: We are sorting the files in preparation for the inspection and gathering feedback with a view to improving reception services.
examples.note: En vue de accepts both a noun phrase and an infinitive.

examples.french: Restons quelques minutes, histoire de discuter avec nos voisins.
examples.english: Let’s stay a few minutes, just to chat with our neighbours.
examples.note: Histoire de gives a conversational reason and takes an infinitive.

examples.french: Nous réorganisons l’accueil de manière que chacun puisse entrer sans attendre.
examples.english: We are reorganising reception so that everyone can enter without waiting.
examples.note: Intended purpose: subjunctive puisse.

examples.french: Nous avons réorganisé l’accueil, de manière que chacun peut maintenant entrer sans attendre.
examples.english: We have reorganised reception, with the result that everyone can now enter without waiting.
examples.note: An observed result: indicative peut.

examples.french: Le service ajoute une permanence de sorte que les salariés puissent venir le soir.
examples.english: The department is adding a staffed session so that employees can come in the evening.
examples.note: De sorte que also takes the subjunctive for an intended purpose, rather than the indicative used for an actual result.

mistakes.avoid: Nous agissons dans le but de améliorer l’accueil.
mistakes.prefer: Nous agissons dans le but d’améliorer l’accueil.
mistakes.why: De elides before the vowel in améliorer.

mistakes.avoid: Placez les affiches de manière à elles sont visibles.
mistakes.prefer: Placez les affiches de manière qu’elles soient visibles.
mistakes.why: A clause with its own subject needs de manière que; the intended purpose selects soient. With à, use an infinitive such as les rendre visibles.

sections.title: An activity as subject; difficult to do
paragraphs: An infinitive phrase can name an activity as the subject of a sentence. English often uses -ing where French uses an infinitive: Lire régulièrement aide la mémoire. One activity takes singular agreement. A pronominal infinitive keeps se when its actor is general: Se lever tôt demande un effort.

With an impersonal evaluation, use adjective + de + infinitive: Il est difficile de comprendre ce texte. Il is a placeholder. If the sentence instead makes the object of comprendre its subject, use Ce texte est difficile à comprendre. The text is what someone understands, not the person doing the understanding. This de/à contrast applies to constructions such as facile/difficile, not mechanically to every adjective with a named subject.
points: An infinitive can name a subject activity, with singular agreement for one activity.
Impersonal il est difficile de contrasts with an object-subject that is difficile à.

examples.french: Lire régulièrement aide à reconnaître les mots.
examples.english: Reading regularly helps you recognise words.
examples.note: The whole infinitive phrase is the singular subject of aide.

examples.french: Se lever tôt demande un effort au début.
examples.english: Getting up early takes an effort at first.
examples.note: Se remains attached to the pronominal infinitive.

examples.french: Il est difficile de comprendre ce texte sans contexte.
examples.english: It is difficult to understand this text without context.
examples.note: Impersonal evaluation: difficile de.

examples.french: Ces textes sont difficiles à comprendre sans contexte.
examples.english: These texts are difficult to understand without context.
examples.note: The texts become the subject and govern plural sont difficiles.

mistakes.avoid: Lire régulièrement aident la mémoire.
mistakes.prefer: Lire régulièrement aide la mémoire.
mistakes.why: One infinitive activity requires singular aide.

mistakes.avoid: Ces textes sont difficiles de comprendre.
mistakes.prefer: Ces textes sont difficiles à comprendre.
mistakes.why: Here the texts are the understood objects of comprendre: use à.

sections.title: Heureux/content de: glad to do something
paragraphs: Heureux de and content de take an infinitive when the person feeling the emotion is also the infinitive’s actor: Je suis content de participer. A past infinitive marks an earlier completed action: Elle est heureuse d’être venue. Choose avoir or être as in other compound forms.

A que clause can name its own actor and takes the subjunctive after these emotional adjectives: Je suis heureuse que vous veniez. The infinitive is the normal concise choice when the actors coincide; this is a construction preference, not a claim that every same-subject que clause is impossible.
points: Heureux/content de + infinitive normally keeps the same actor.
Heureux/content que introduces a subjunctive clause with an explicit subject.

examples.french: Je suis contente de participer à cet atelier.
examples.english: I am glad to take part in this workshop.
examples.note: A female speaker is both pleased and participating.

examples.french: Elle est heureuse d’être venue à la réunion.
examples.english: She is glad she came to the meeting.
examples.note: The past infinitive marks her completed arrival.

examples.french: Nous sommes contents que vous puissiez rester.
examples.english: We are glad you can stay.
examples.note: The named second subject takes subjunctive puissiez.

mistakes.avoid: Elle est heureuse de être venue.
mistakes.prefer: Elle est heureuse d’être venue.
mistakes.why: De elides before être.

mistakes.avoid: Nous sommes contents que vous pouvez rester.
mistakes.prefer: Nous sommes contents que vous puissiez rester.
mistakes.why: The emotional adjective selects the subjunctive in this clause.

sections.title: Good at, bad at, or good for?
paragraphs: Conversational nul pour plus infinitive expresses poor ability at an activity: Je suis nul pour retenir les prénoms. It is a fairly strong, informal self-assessment, not a neutral test score. With a subject or field, bon en and nul en are common: bonne en maths, nul en dessin.

Bon pour may express suitability or benefit rather than a person’s skill: un livre bon pour débuter, la marche bonne pour la santé. Choose the construction from the intended meaning; do not replace every English good at with bon pour or declare other idiomatic prepositions incorrect.
points: Nul pour + infinitive can describe poor activity skills in conversation.
Bon en names a field; bon pour can mean suitable or beneficial.

examples.french: Je suis nul pour retenir les prénoms, alors je les note.
examples.english: I am terrible at remembering first names, so I write them down.
examples.note: A conversational self-assessment with pour + infinitive.

examples.french: Elle est bonne en maths, mais elle préfère le dessin.
examples.english: She is good at maths, but she prefers drawing.
examples.note: En introduces the field of skill.

examples.french: Ce livre est bon pour débuter; la marche est bonne pour la santé.
examples.english: This book is good for getting started; walking is good for your health.
examples.note: Suitability and benefit are not the same as ability.

mistakes.avoid: Elle est bon en maths.
mistakes.prefer: Elle est bonne en maths.
mistakes.why: The adjective agrees with elle; en maths does not change that agreement.

vocabulary.example: Après s’être installés, ils ont inscrit les enfants à l’école du quartier.
vocabulary.note: Reflexive verb; the past infinitive is `après s’être installé(e)(s)`.

vocabulary.example: Avant de signer, vérifiez la durée du bail et le montant du loyer.
vocabulary.note: Regular `-er` verb; frequent in administrative instructions.

vocabulary.example: Un bail de douze mois a été signé par les deux parties.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; irregular plural `des baux`.

vocabulary.example: Un ministère provincial gère les demandes de reconnaissance de diplôme.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; not to be confused with `une ministre`, the person.

vocabulary.example: Il regrette de ne pas avoir joint toutes les pièces.
vocabulary.note: Negative past infinitive; both negative words precede the auxiliary.

practice.prompt: Rewrite with a past infinitive: « Elle est arrivée, puis elle a téléphoné au bureau. »
practice.hint: `Arriver` takes `être`, so the participle agrees.
practice.answer: Après être arrivée, elle a téléphoné au bureau.

takeaways: `Avant de` plus infinitive, `après` plus past infinitive.
The past infinitive follows the compound-past auxiliary rules.
Use an infinitive when its actor is understood; a purpose clause can name another actor.
Purpose takes the subjunctive after de manière que/de sorte que; an actual result takes the indicative.
En vue de accepts a noun or infinitive; histoire de is conversational.
keywords: infinitive constructions for sequence and purpose
avant de, après avoir, après être, afin de, afin que, pour que
de manière à, de façon à, de manière que, de façon que, de sorte que, dans le but de, en vue de, histoire de
infinitif sujet, difficile de, difficile à, heureux de, content de, nul pour, bon en, bon pour

lessons.title: Le participe présent et le gérondif
lessons.summary: Form the present participle from the present nous form minus -ons plus -ant, with irregular ayant, étant, and sachant. Adding en gives the gerund, which can express simultaneity, manner, means, or a condition. In ordinary use it shares the main verb’s subject. Without en, a participle can express cause or a relative-like description.
objectives: Form the present participle, including the three irregular verbs.
Distinguish simultaneity, manner, means, and a conditional reading of en plus participle.
Keep the subject of the gerund identical to the subject of the main verb.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The present participle is the `-ant` form. It is built on the present `nous` stem, so it inherits any spelling change from that form: `nous commençons` gives `commençant`, `nous mangeons` gives `mangeant`. Only `avoir`, `être`, and `savoir` are irregular, giving `ayant`, `étant`, and `sachant`.

Adding en produces the gerund. It can express simultaneity or means: En travaillant, elle a appris beaucoup de vocabulaire; Elle a trouvé un logement en consultant les annonces. In ordinary careful writing, make its understood subject the same as the main verb’s subject: En arrivant, j’ai trouvé le dossier prêt. If different actors are intended, name them in a clause: Pendant que la conseillère parlait, je prenais des notes. Without en, a participle can give a cause: Ayant acquis une solide expérience, elle a dirigé le projet. Here ayant acquis is a compound participle: having gained experience before leading the project.

A present participle can also describe a noun: `Les personnes travaillant ici ont un badge` (The people working here have a badge). Used as a verb, `travaillant` does not agree, even with plural `personnes`. Distinguish an adjective derived from a verb, which does agree: `des tâches fatigantes` (tiring tasks), but `des tâches fatiguant les yeux` (tasks tiring the eyes). The spelling can differ too: adjective `fatigant`, verbal participle `fatiguant`.
points: Take the present `nous` form and replace `-ons` with `-ant`.
Keep the spelling change of the `nous` form: `commençant`, `mangeant`.
Memorise `ayant`, `étant`, `sachant`.
Add en for simultaneity, manner, means, or a condition inferred from context.
Check that the gerund and the main verb share the same subject.

examples.french: En travaillant avec une équipe bilingue, elle a enrichi son vocabulaire.
examples.english: By working with a bilingual team, she expanded her vocabulary.
examples.note: Gerund of means, same subject as the main verb.

examples.french: Elle a trouvé un logement en consultant les annonces du quartier.
examples.english: She found housing by looking through the local listings.
examples.note: Gerund of manner.

examples.french: En arrivant au bureau, j’ai remarqué que la file était déjà longue.
examples.english: On arriving at the office, I noticed that the queue was already long.
examples.note: Simultaneity; the subject of both verbs is « je ».

examples.french: Ayant acquis une solide expérience, elle a dirigé le projet avec assurance.
examples.english: Having gained solid experience, she led the project confidently.
examples.note: Participle without « en »: cause rather than simultaneity.

examples.french: Ne sachant pas où déposer le dossier, il a téléphoné à la mairie.
examples.english: Not knowing where to submit the file, he phoned the town hall.
examples.note: Irregular participle « sachant » in a causal construction.

mistakes.avoid: En arrive au guichet, j’avais déjà un dossier complet.
mistakes.prefer: En arrivant au guichet, j’avais déjà un dossier complet.
mistakes.why: The gerund uses en plus the participle arrivant, not the finite form arrive.

mistakes.avoid: En savant où chercher, vous gagneriez du temps.
mistakes.prefer: En sachant où chercher, vous gagneriez du temps.
mistakes.why: The participle of savoir is sachant. Here en sachant has a conditional reading: if you knew where to look.

sections.title: A gerund can mean if
paragraphs: The gerund does not always describe an action already taking place. With a predicted or hypothetical result, it can state the condition for that result: En réservant tôt, vous paierez moins means If you book early, you will pay less. The same form can also suggest the means of achieving the result; those readings may overlap.

The main verb supplies the time or hypothetical perspective. A future can present a realistic consequence; a conditional can present a more tentative possibility. The gerund itself does not conjugate for either perspective. Do not mechanically translate every en + -ant as while.
points: Test whether the gerund can be paraphrased by an if-clause.
Read the main verb for the time and hypothetical perspective.
Keep the gerund invariable even when the main verb is conditional.

examples.french: En réservant avant lundi, vous obtiendrez le tarif réduit.
examples.english: If you book before Monday, you will get the reduced rate.
examples.note: The booking is a condition, not an action asserted to be happening now. A rate is un tarif (m.).

examples.french: En partant un peu plus tôt, tu éviterais les embouteillages.
examples.english: If you left a little earlier, you would avoid the traffic jams.
examples.note: A conditional result makes the suggestion hypothetical; partant stays unchanged.

examples.french: En connaissant mieux les besoins du quartier, nous pourrions proposer un service adapté.
examples.english: If we knew the neighbourhood’s needs better, we could offer a suitable service.
examples.note: A state of knowledge can supply the condition; a gerund is not restricted to physical actions.

mistakes.avoid: En vous inscrivez cette semaine, vous aurez une place.
mistakes.prefer: En vous inscrivant cette semaine, vous aurez une place.
mistakes.why: Use the participle inscrivant after en, with the reflexive pronoun vous.

mistakes.avoid: En consultant le plan, vous trouverions l’entrée.
mistakes.prefer: En consultant le plan, vous trouveriez l’entrée.
mistakes.why: The main verb agrees with vous: trouveriez. The gerund consultant does not carry a person ending.

vocabulary.example: Ayant acquis de l’expérience à l’étranger, elle a été retenue immédiatement.
vocabulary.note: Irregular verb; participle `acquis`, present participle `acquérant`.

vocabulary.example: En consultant le site du ministère, j’ai trouvé la liste des documents.
vocabulary.note: Regular `-er` verb; very useful with the gerund of means.

vocabulary.example: Un stage en milieu bilingue complète utilement une formation.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `un stagiaire` is the intern.

vocabulary.example: Une équipe bilingue répond aux appels du lundi au vendredi.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; takes a singular verb in French.

practice.prompt: Join with a gerund: « Elle prépare son entrevue. Elle relit les annonces. »
practice.hint: Both actions belong to the same subject.
practice.answer: Elle prépare son entrevue en relisant les annonces.

takeaways: `Nous` form minus `-ons` plus `-ant`, with three irregular verbs.
En plus participle can express simultaneity, manner, means, or a condition.
Keep the same understood subject in ordinary gerund constructions; name different actors in full clauses.
keywords: the present participle and en + participle
gérondif de condition, participe présent, simultanéité

lessons.title: L’accord du participe passé avec un complément placé avant
lessons.summary: With `avoir`, the past participle normally agrees with a preceding direct object: `les lettres que j’ai écrites`. With a non-pronominal verb using `être`, it agrees with the subject: `elles sont arrivées`. For ordinary reflexive or reciprocal uses, identify the direct object and its position: `elles se sont lavées`, but `elles se sont lavé les mains` and `elles se sont parlé`. Other pronominal meanings have their own pattern: `elles se sont plaintes`, but `elles se sont rendu compte`.
objectives: Locate the direct object and check whether it precedes the participle.
Apply subject agreement only where the auxiliary licenses it.
Analyse a reflexive pronoun before agreeing with it.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A direct object completes a verb without a linking preposition: `envoyer une demande` (send an application). With `avoir`, the participle normally agrees with a direct object placed before it. Common cases include object pronouns (`le`, `la`, `les`, `me`, `te`, `nous`, `vous`), the relative pronoun `que`, and an object moved to the front of a question: `Quelles lettres avez-vous envoyées ?` (Which letters did you send?). In `Nous les avons envoyées`, `les` stands for `les demandes`, so the participle takes `-es`. Do not agree with an indirect object: `les personnes à qui j’ai parlé` (the people I spoke to).

With `être` and a non-pronominal verb, agreement is with the subject. Ordinary reflexive and reciprocal uses need another step: find the direct object and check its position. In `elles se sont lavées`, `se` is the preceding direct object, so the participle agrees. In `elles se sont lavé les mains`, the direct object `les mains` follows and `se` is indirect, so there is no agreement. Moving that object before the verb restores agreement: `les mains qu’elles se sont lavées`. In `elles se sont parlé`, `parler à` makes `se` indirect, so there is no agreement.

Some verbs are normally used only with a subject-linked pronoun, such as `s’enfuir` and `se méprendre`; these are called essentially pronominal. Others acquire a distinct meaning with the pronoun, such as `se plaindre` (to complain) and `s’apercevoir` (to realise). These examples agree with the subject: `Elles se sont enfuies`, `Elles se sont méprises sur la date`, `Elle s’est plainte du bruit`. `Plaindre` also exists without `se`: `Je plains cette famille` means I feel sorry for this family. Check fixed expressions separately: in `se rendre compte`, the direct object is `compte`, placed after the participle, so `rendu` stays unchanged: `Elle s’est rendu compte de l’erreur`.

Two pronouns need special care. When en represents an indefinite quantity, the participle normally stays unchanged: `Des lettres ? J’en ai reçu trois` (Letters? I received three). But another preceding direct object still governs agreement: `les conclusions que j’en ai tirées` (the conclusions I drew from it). Le/l’ can also refer to a whole idea rather than a gendered noun: `La procédure est plus longue que je l’avais prévu` (The procedure is longer than I had expected) keeps prévu unchanged. Contrast `La réunion ? Je l’avais prévue pour lundi` (The meeting? I had scheduled it for Monday), where l’ replaces feminine réunion.

Before an infinitive, check which verb owns the preceding object. `Les musiciennes que j’ai entendues jouer` (the musicians I heard playing) agrees because the musicians are heard and are the understood subject of jouer. `Les chansons que j’ai entendu jouer` (the songs I heard being played) does not: the songs are the object of jouer, not its performers. Fait before an infinitive is always unchanged: `les documents que j’ai fait traduire` (the documents I had translated). For laisser, both spelling systems are accepted: traditional `Je les ai laissées partir` for a group of women, and rectified `Je les ai laissé partir` (I let them leave). Do not mark either accepted spelling as an error.
points: Identify the auxiliary before looking for anything else.
With `avoir`, search to the left of the participle for a direct object.
Agree with a preceding `le`, `la`, `les`, or with the relative `que`.
With non-reflexive `être`, agree with the subject.
For ordinary reflexive or reciprocal uses, agree with a preceding direct object, not with an indirect `se`.
Learn subject agreement in forms such as `elle s’est enfuie` and `elle s’est plainte`; `plaindre quelqu’un` has a different meaning.
Leave `se rendre compte` invariable, because `compte` is the direct object and follows the participle.
Remember that `monter`, `descendre`, `sortir`, `rentrer`, `passer`, and `retourner` switch to `avoir` with a direct object, and then follow the `avoir` rule.

examples.french: Les demandes ? Nous les avons envoyées hier après-midi.
examples.english: The applications? We sent them yesterday afternoon.
examples.note: The preceding direct object « les » is feminine plural.

examples.french: La lettre que j’ai écrite est restée sans réponse.
examples.english: The letter that I wrote went unanswered.
examples.note: The relative « que » is the preceding direct object.

examples.french: Les formulaires que nous avons remplis sont maintenant complets.
examples.english: The forms that we filled in are now complete.
examples.note: Masculine plural agreement after « que ».

examples.french: Elle s’est lavé les mains avant le rendez-vous.
examples.english: She washed her hands before the appointment.
examples.note: The direct object « les mains » follows, so no agreement.

examples.french: Les deux conseillères se sont parlé avant la réunion.
examples.english: The two advisers spoke to each other before the meeting.
examples.note: « Parler à » makes « se » indirect, so the participle does not agree.

examples.french: Elle s’est plainte du bruit, et elles se sont méprises sur la date de l’audience.
examples.english: She complained about the noise, and they were mistaken about the hearing date.
examples.note: These pronominal meanings take subject agreement; « plaindre quelqu’un » without se means to feel sorry for someone.

examples.french: Elle s’est rendu compte de l’erreur avant l’envoi du dossier.
examples.english: She realised the mistake before sending the file.
examples.note: « Compte » is the direct object and follows, so the participle stays invariable.

examples.french: Nous avons retourné le formulaire signé, puis nous sommes retournés au bureau des permis.
examples.english: We returned the signed form, then we went back to the permits office.
examples.note: « Retourner » takes « avoir » with a direct object and « être » without one.

mistakes.avoid: Les documents ? Elle les a envoyé hier.
mistakes.prefer: Les documents ? Elle les a envoyés hier.
mistakes.why: `Les` stands for the masculine plural `les documents` and precedes the participle.

mistakes.avoid: Elles se sont lavées les mains avant de partir.
mistakes.prefer: Elles se sont lavé les mains avant de partir.
mistakes.why: The direct object is `les mains`, which follows the verb; `se` is indirect.

mistakes.avoid: Elle s’est plaint du bruit auprès du propriétaire.
mistakes.prefer: Elle s’est plainte du bruit auprès du propriétaire.
mistakes.why: In the pronominal meaning to complain, `se plaindre` takes subject agreement: feminine singular `plainte`.

mistakes.avoid: Elle s’est rendue compte de l’erreur trop tard.
mistakes.prefer: Elle s’est rendu compte de l’erreur trop tard.
mistakes.why: In `se rendre compte`, the direct object `compte` comes after the participle, so there is no agreement.

vocabulary.example: Les formulaires que nous avons remplis étaient en double exemplaire.
vocabulary.note: Regular `-ir` verb of the `finir` type; participle `rempli`.

vocabulary.example: La lettre que j’ai écrite est partie ce matin.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; triggers a feminine singular participle when placed before.

vocabulary.example: Les pièces justificatives que j’ai jointes figurent en annexe.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun, usually plural in administrative language.

vocabulary.example: Une annexe détaillée accompagne le rapport final.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `en annexe` means attached.

vocabulary.example: Plusieurs locataires se sont plaints du chauffage insuffisant.
vocabulary.note: This pronominal meaning takes subject agreement; non-pronominal `plaindre quelqu’un` means to feel sorry for someone.

practice.prompt: Agree if required: « Les attestations que j’ai (recevoir) », « Elle s’est (couper) le doigt », « Elles sont (partir) ».
practice.hint: One preceding direct object, one following direct object, one subject agreement.
practice.answer: Les attestations que j’ai reçues, Elle s’est coupé le doigt, Elles sont parties

takeaways: `Avoir` agrees only with a direct object placed before the participle.
Non-reflexive `être` agrees with the subject, automatically.
For ordinary reflexive and reciprocal uses, locate the direct object before deciding agreement.
Learn the pattern of each pronominal meaning: `elles se sont plaintes`, but `elles se sont rendu compte`.
keywords: past-participle agreement with a preceding object

lessons.title: La voix passive et les tournures pronominales
lessons.summary: The passive uses être plus a past participle agreeing with the subject. Alternatives include a pronominal construction for a general process and on for an unnamed human agent. Distinguish real subjects in Les maisons se vendent from the singular placeholder il in established expressions such as Il se dit que and Il se passe.
objectives: Build a passive sentence with the correct agreement.
Replace a heavy passive with a pronominal construction where it is idiomatic.
Use `on` for an unnamed human agent.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: In a passive sentence the grammatical subject receives the action instead of performing it. French forms it with `être` in the required tense plus the past participle, which agrees with that subject: `Le formulaire a été envoyé`, `Les demandes ont été traitées`. The performer, called the agent, is usually introduced by `par`: `Le rapport a été rédigé par le comité`. Some verbs also allow `de`, especially for states or feelings: `Elle est appréciée de ses collègues` (She is appreciated by her colleagues).

The ordinary French passive turns the active verb's direct object into its subject: `Le comité examine les demandes → Les demandes sont examinées par le comité`. An indirect recipient cannot normally make this switch as it can in English. For I was given a form, use `On m’a donné un formulaire`, not a word-for-word passive of donner with je as its subject.

The passive is useful in academic and administrative writing when the result or affected item matters most; it is not inherently bad style. Two alternatives suit other contexts. A pronominal construction with `se` often describes a general process or property without naming an agent: `Cette démarche se fait entièrement en ligne`, `Ce produit se vend bien`. In speech, `on` plus an active verb often expresses an unnamed human agent: `On m’a indiqué que le service fermerait plus tôt`. These choices change the focus and are not mechanically interchangeable.
points: Conjugate `être` in the tense you need, then add the participle.
Agree the participle with the subject, not with the agent.
Usually introduce a named agent with par; some state or feeling verbs also allow de.
Use `se` plus verb for a general process with no agent.
Use `on` plus an active verb when the agent is human but unnamed.
Use the pronominal passive for what is normally done, sold, or said: `se vendre`, `se dire`, `s’écrire`, `se manger`.

examples.french: Le formulaire a été envoyé par voie électronique.
examples.english: The form was sent electronically.
examples.note: Passive with a masculine singular subject.

examples.french: Les demandes ont été traitées en priorité cette semaine.
examples.english: The applications were processed as a priority this week.
examples.note: Traitées agrees with the feminine plural subject. Été, the participle of être after ont, stays unchanged.

examples.french: Le rapport a été rédigé par le comité de quartier.
examples.english: The report was written by the neighbourhood committee.
examples.note: The agent is introduced by « par ».

examples.french: Cette démarche se fait entièrement en ligne.
examples.english: This procedure is completed entirely online.
examples.note: Pronominal construction for a general process.

examples.french: On m’a indiqué que le service fermerait plus tôt aujourd’hui.
examples.english: I was told that the service would close earlier today.
examples.note: « On » replaces an English passive with an unnamed agent.

examples.french: Ce produit local se vend très bien, et cela ne se dit pas dans une lettre officielle.
examples.english: This local product sells very well, and that is not said in an official letter.
examples.note: The pronominal passive states a general norm with no agent in view.

mistakes.avoid: Les demandes ont été traité la semaine dernière.
mistakes.prefer: Les demandes ont été traitées la semaine dernière.
mistakes.why: In the passive the participle agrees with the subject, here feminine plural.

mistakes.avoid: Le formulaire a été envoyer par voie électronique.
mistakes.prefer: Le formulaire a été envoyé par voie électronique.
mistakes.why: The passive is built with a past participle, `envoyé`, not with the infinitive `envoyer`, which sounds identical.

sections.title: Il se dit and il se passe: a singular placeholder
paragraphs: Il se dit que means it is being said that, often introducing an unconfirmed report. Il does not refer to a man or to the people doing the talking. Il se passe quelque chose means something is happening; this established impersonal use of se passer is not itself a passive.

The placeholder il keeps the verb singular, even in Il se passe des choses étranges. Compare Des choses étranges se passent, where the plural noun phrase is the grammatical subject. Likewise, Les maisons se vendent has a real plural subject. Learn these established constructions individually: adding il se does not make every French verb impersonal.
points: Impersonal il is singular and has no person as its referent.
A real plural subject instead governs a plural verb.

examples.french: Il se dit que la bibliothèque va prolonger ses horaires.
examples.english: It is being said that the library will extend its opening hours.
examples.note: A reported claim, not a guarantee that it has been confirmed.

examples.french: Il se passe des choses intéressantes dans ce quartier.
examples.english: Interesting things are happening in this neighbourhood.
examples.note: The impersonal subject keeps passe singular.

examples.french: Des choses intéressantes se passent dans ce quartier.
examples.english: Interesting things are happening in this neighbourhood.
examples.note: Here des choses intéressantes is the plural subject.

examples.french: Les maisons se vendent rapidement dans cette rue.
examples.english: Houses sell quickly on this street.
examples.note: A personal-subject pronominal passive, not impersonal il.

mistakes.avoid: Il se passent des choses intéressantes.
mistakes.prefer: Il se passe des choses intéressantes.
mistakes.why: Impersonal il requires a singular verb.

mistakes.avoid: Les maisons se vend rapidement.
mistakes.prefer: Les maisons se vendent rapidement.
mistakes.why: The real plural subject maisons requires vendent.

vocabulary.example: Les dossiers sont traités dans l’ordre d’arrivée.
vocabulary.note: Regular `-er` verb; `le traitement` is the related noun.

vocabulary.english: to be done, to take place
vocabulary.example: L’inscription se fait en ligne jusqu’au 30 juin.
vocabulary.note: Pronominal construction used instead of a passive with no agent.

vocabulary.example: Un avis officiel a été publié sur le site de la municipalité.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; identical in the plural.

vocabulary.example: Un comité consultatif examine les projets de rénovation.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; the ending -té is usually feminine, so this one must be learned.

vocabulary.example: Les billets se vendent en ligne à partir du 1er mars.
vocabulary.note: Pronominal passive; the subject is the thing sold, not the seller.

vocabulary.english: to be said, to be the usual way of saying
vocabulary.example: « Bonne journée » se dit couramment à la fin d’un échange.
vocabulary.note: Frequently used to comment on usage and register.

practice.prompt: Rewrite without a passive: « Les décisions sont prises par une commission. » and « The forms are filled in online. »
practice.hint: One keeps a named agent, the other has none.
practice.answer: Une commission prend les décisions. Les formulaires se remplissent en ligne.

takeaways: `Être` plus participle, agreeing with the subject; agent after `par`.
`Se` plus verb for a process with no agent.
`On` plus active verb is the everyday equivalent of an English passive.
keywords: construction impersonnelle, il se dit que, il se passe

lessons.title: La construction causative « faire + infinitif »
lessons.summary: `Faire` plus an infinitive expresses causing an action: `Je fais réparer mon ordinateur` means I am having my computer repaired. Object pronouns normally precede `faire` (`Je le fais réparer`), but follow it in an affirmative imperative (`Faites-le réparer`). Adverbs can come between the verbs. The performer can be a direct object (`Je fais venir Paul`) or follow `à/par` when the infinitive already has a direct object (`Je fais réparer la porte par Paul`). `Fait` stays unchanged before an infinitive, including in `Elle s’est fait rembourser`.
objectives: Express an action carried out by someone else.
Place object pronouns with `faire`, accounting for the affirmative imperative.
Use `se faire + infinitif` and leave its participle unchanged.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A causative construction says that the subject causes an action rather than necessarily performing it. French builds it with `faire` plus an infinitive: `Je fais réparer mon ordinateur` means I am having my computer repaired. Keep the noun object after the infinitive, not between the two verbs. This does not prohibit adverbs: `Cela fait souvent rire les enfants` is correct. `Laisser` plus an infinitive expresses permission instead: `Le gardien laisse entrer les visiteurs`; it also allows the order `Le gardien laisse les visiteurs entrer`.

Object pronouns normally precede `faire`: `Je le fais réparer`, `Elle nous a fait remplir un formulaire`. In an affirmative imperative, they follow it: `Faites-le réparer`. The performer’s construction depends on the infinitive: `Je fais venir Paul` has no separate direct object for `venir`, so `Paul` is direct. When the infinitive already has a direct object, introduce the performer with `à` or `par`: `J’ai fait signer le contrat à la directrice`, `J’ai fait traduire le document par un traducteur agréé`. The pronominal `se faire` plus an infinitive presents the subject as someone who benefits or suffers: `Elle s’est fait rembourser ses frais`, `Il s’est fait voler son vélo`. The participle `fait` stays unchanged before an infinitive.

The difference appears in pronouns: `Je le fais venir` (I am having him come), but `Je lui fais signer le contrat` (I am having him or her sign the contract). Replacing both the contract and its signer gives `Je le lui fais signer`; le represents the contract, lui the signer. Negative commands restore the pronoun before faire: `Ne le faites pas réparer` (Do not have it repaired).
points: Do not insert the noun object between `faire` and the infinitive; adverbs can intervene.
Place object pronouns before `faire`, except in affirmative commands: `Je le fais réparer`, `Faites-le réparer`.
Use a direct performer with an intransitive infinitive (`faire venir Paul`); use `à/par` when the infinitive already has a direct object.
Use `laisser + infinitif` when the meaning is to let rather than to make.
Use se faire + infinitive for an action done for or to the subject; it need not be intentional, as in Il s’est fait voler son vélo (His bicycle was stolen).
Leave the participle `fait` unchanged in `elle s’est fait rembourser`.

examples.french: Je fais réparer mon ordinateur avant la reprise des cours.
examples.english: I am having my computer repaired before classes start again.
examples.note: The subject causes the action; someone else performs it.

examples.french: Ce formulaire est illisible, alors je le fais refaire.
examples.english: This form is illegible, so I am having it redone.
examples.note: In this statement, le precedes faire. In an affirmative command it follows faire: Faites-le refaire.

examples.french: La municipalité a fait construire une passerelle par une entreprise locale.
examples.english: The city had a footbridge built by a local company.
examples.note: « Par » names the performer and avoids any ambiguity.

examples.french: J’ai fait signer le contrat à la directrice avant l’échéance.
examples.english: I had the director sign the contract before the deadline.
examples.note: The thing is the direct object; the person takes « à ».

examples.french: Elle s’est fait rembourser ses frais de déplacement.
examples.english: She got her travel expenses reimbursed.
examples.note: « Se faire » plus infinitive; the participle « fait » stays invariable.

examples.french: Le gardien laisse entrer les visiteurs à partir de huit heures.
examples.english: The security guard lets visitors in from eight o’clock.
examples.note: « Laisser + infinitif » means to let, not to make.

examples.french: Ce jeu fait souvent rire les enfants.
examples.english: This game often makes the children laugh.
examples.note: An adverb can intervene; with intransitive rire, the children are the direct performer.

examples.french: Votre ordinateur est en panne ? Faites-le réparer avant lundi.
examples.english: Is your computer broken? Have it repaired before Monday.
examples.note: In an affirmative imperative, le follows faire and precedes the infinitive.

mistakes.avoid: Je fais mon ordinateur réparer cette semaine.
mistakes.prefer: Je fais réparer mon ordinateur cette semaine.
mistakes.why: This noun object belongs after réparer in the causative: faire réparer mon ordinateur. That restriction does not ban intervening adverbs or the pronoun in an affirmative command such as Faites-le réparer.

mistakes.avoid: Elle s’est faite rembourser ses frais.
mistakes.prefer: Elle s’est fait rembourser ses frais.
mistakes.why: In `se faire + infinitif` the participle `fait` is invariable, so it never agrees with the subject.

vocabulary.example: Nous avons fait réparer la porte d’entrée la semaine dernière.
vocabulary.note: Model of the causative; object pronouns attach to `faire`, not to `réparer`.

vocabulary.example: Elle s’est fait rembourser le titre de transport.
vocabulary.note: The participle `fait` never agrees in this construction.

vocabulary.example: L’agent laisse entrer les candidats dès l’ouverture.
vocabulary.note: `Laisser + infinitif` expresses permission, unlike causative `faire`.

vocabulary.example: Une passerelle relie le parc au quartier voisin.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; also used figuratively for a link between two services.

vocabulary.example: Un traducteur agréé a certifié la traduction de mon diplôme.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase; feminine `une traductrice agréée`.

practice.prompt: Say that you are having your diplomas translated, then replace the object with a pronoun.
practice.hint: The pronoun goes in front of `faire`.
practice.answer: Je fais traduire mes diplômes. Je les fais traduire.

takeaways: `Faire + infinitif` equals having something done by someone else.
Pronouns normally precede `faire`, but follow it in affirmative imperatives; adverbs can intervene before the infinitive.
The performer is direct with `faire venir Paul`, but follows `à/par` when the infinitive already has a direct object.
`Se faire + infinitif` keeps `fait` invariable.

modules.title: Les pronoms, les questions et la négation
modules.description: Identify what pronouns replace, place them correctly, build relative clauses and questions, and distinguish negation from affirmative or contrasting replies.

lessons.title: Les pronoms toniques, réfléchis et emphatiques
lessons.summary: Stressed pronouns (`moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles`) are used after a preposition, in a coordinated subject, after `c’est`, and for emphasis. Naming yourself last is a courtesy convention, not a grammar requirement. `Lui et toi avez répondu` and `Toi et lui, vous avez répondu` are both correct. Reflexive pronouns (`me, te, se, nous, vous, se`) belong to the verb and refer back to its subject. `Soi` is useful with an indefinite or general subject.
objectives: Use a stressed pronoun in each of its four contexts.
Distinguish courtesy conventions from grammatical agreement in a coordinated subject.
Choose `soi` and `soi-même` with an indefinite subject.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A stressed pronoun can stand independently rather than forming a short pronoun group attached to a verb. The forms are `moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles`. Common uses include as the complement of a preposition (`avec lui`, `chez elle`, `pour eux`), in a coordinated subject (`Elle et moi participerons`), after `c’est` (`C’est moi`), and for contrast (`Moi, je préfère attendre`). Adding `-même` emphasises identity or personal involvement: `moi-même`, `eux-mêmes`. With polite vous referring to one person, write `vous-même`, not plural `vous-mêmes`.

A coordinated subject does not have a compulsory order by person. Naming yourself last is courteous (`Ma collègue et moi`), but reversing the order is not ungrammatical. Repeating the group with a subject pronoun is also optional: `Lui et toi avez répondu` and `Toi et lui, vous avez répondu` are both correct. Agreement depends on the people included, not their order: a group including `moi` takes the `nous` form; without a first person, a group including `toi` takes the `vous` form. Reflexive pronouns instead belong to the verb: `elle se prépare`, `nous nous inscrivons`. With an indefinite or general subject, `soi` is useful: `Il vaut mieux vérifier le formulaire soi-même`.
points: Use a stressed form when the personal pronoun itself is a preposition's complement: avec moi, pour elle.
Naming yourself last (`Elle et moi`) is a courtesy convention, not a required word order.
Agree by the people included: `Lui et moi avons répondu`, `Lui et toi avez répondu`.
Repeat the group with a matching subject pronoun if desired: `Toi et lui, vous avez répondu`.
Use `c’est moi`, `c’est lui`, `ce sont eux` to identify.

A reflexive pronoun refers back to the verb's subject: je me prépare, tu te prépares, elle se prépare, nous nous préparons, vous vous préparez, ils se préparent. Contrast Elle me prépare un café (She makes me a coffee): me refers to someone other than elle and is not reflexive there.
Add `-même` for emphasis, agreeing in number: `nous-mêmes`, `eux-mêmes`.
Use soi/soi-même for a general or indefinite referent. When on means a specific we, nous-mêmes is possible: On l’a fait nous-mêmes.

examples.french: Elle et moi participerons à la consultation publique de jeudi.
examples.english: She and I will take part in Thursday’s public consultation.
examples.note: Naming yourself last is courteous; the verb takes the nous form because moi is included.

examples.french: Le rendez-vous a lieu chez elle, pas au bureau.
examples.english: The appointment is at her place, not at the office.
examples.note: Stressed pronoun after a preposition.

examples.french: Ils ont préparé le dossier eux-mêmes, sans aide extérieure.
examples.english: They prepared the file themselves, without outside help.
examples.note: Emphatic form agreeing in number.

examples.french: Il vaut mieux vérifier le formulaire soi-même avant de l’envoyer.
examples.english: It is better to check the form oneself before sending it.
examples.note: « Soi » with an impersonal subject.

examples.french: Moi, je préfère déposer le dossier en personne.
examples.english: Personally, I prefer to submit the file in person.
examples.note: Stressed pronoun in front for contrast.

examples.french: Toi et lui, vous présenterez le projet devant le conseil de quartier.
examples.english: You and he will present the project to the neighbourhood council.
examples.note: Second person before third, resumed by « vous ».

examples.french: Ma femme et toi, vous êtes les meilleures amies du monde.
examples.english: You and my wife are the best of friends.
examples.note: The coordinated subject is resumed by « vous »; the attribute agrees in the feminine plural.

mistakes.avoid: Ma collègue et je avons rédigé le rapport.
mistakes.prefer: Ma collègue et moi avons rédigé le rapport.
mistakes.why: Use the stressed form `moi`, not `je`, in this coordinated subject.

mistakes.avoid: Ils ont préparé le dossier eux-même.
mistakes.prefer: Ils ont préparé le dossier eux-mêmes.
mistakes.why: The emphatic form agrees in number: plural `eux-mêmes`.

mistakes.avoid: Lui et toi a rempli les mêmes formulaires.
mistakes.prefer: Lui et toi avez rempli les mêmes formulaires.
mistakes.why: This coordinated subject includes `toi` and no first person, so it takes the second-person plural verb `avez`. Its order is grammatical without a repeated `vous`.

vocabulary.example: Une consultation publique permet à chacun de s’exprimer sur le projet.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun phrase; the gender comes from `consultation`.

vocabulary.example: Elle se prépare seule pour l’entrevue de mardi.
vocabulary.note: Reflexive verb; the pronoun changes with the subject.

vocabulary.example: Il vaut mieux relire son dossier soi-même avant de l’envoyer.
vocabulary.note: Used with `on`, `chacun`, or an impersonal construction.

vocabulary.example: Ma collègue et moi partageons le même bureau.
vocabulary.note: Feminine form; the masculine is `un collègue`, with the same spelling.

practice.prompt: Rewrite politely: « Moi et lui avons déposé la demande. »
practice.hint: Only the order changes; the original is grammatical, but naming yourself last is courteous.
practice.answer: Lui et moi avons déposé la demande.

takeaways: Preposition, coordination, `c’est`, emphasis: four homes for stressed pronouns.
Subject order is flexible; agreement follows the people included, and a repeated subject pronoun is optional.
Indefinite subject equals `soi` and `soi-même`.

lessons.title: Les pronoms compléments directs et indirects
lessons.summary: Learn object pronouns with the French verb's construction: voir quelqu’un gives le/la/les; parler à quelqu’un gives lui/leur. Not every à + person phrase becomes lui/leur: penser à elle keeps a stressed pronoun. Pronouns normally precede their verb or auxiliary; affirmative imperatives use a different order after the verb.
objectives: Test a verb’s construction before choosing a pronoun.
Position a single pronoun correctly in simple, compound, and infinitive structures.
Apply the fixed order when two pronouns appear together.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: An object completes a verb's meaning. A direct object connects without a preposition: `voir quelqu’un` (see someone), `regarder quelque chose` (look at something). An indirect object uses a preposition: `parler à quelqu’un`, `téléphoner à quelqu’un`, `répondre à quelqu’un`, `envoyer quelque chose à quelqu’un`. Choose the pronoun from the French construction, not its English translation.

Direct forms are `me, te, le, la, nous, vous, les`; indirect forms for the people in the à constructions just listed are `me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur`. `Le` is masculine singular, `la` feminine singular, and `les` plural for either gender. Indirect `lui` means to him or to her; `leur` means to them, without a plural s. Before a vowel or mute h, `me, te, le, la` become `m’, t’, l’, l’`: `je l’écoute`. Not every à + person phrase becomes lui: `penser à Léa → penser à elle`, `s’intéresser à Paul → s’intéresser à lui`. Learn the verb's complete pattern.

Placement follows the verb group. Before a single conjugated verb: `Elle nous reçoit`. Before the auxiliary in a compound tense: `Elle nous a reçus`. Before the infinitive when the pronoun belongs to it: `Je dois le remplir`. For pronouns placed before a verb, use these ordered slots: `me/te/se/nous/vous`, then `le/la/les`, then `lui/leur`, then `y`, then `en`. Not every slot must or can be filled in every construction. Thus `Je les lui remettrai` combines a direct and an indirect object; `Oui, elle les y a posées` combines a direct object and a place. A preceding direct object still controls agreement with `avoir`: `posées` agrees with `les` when it replaces `les clés`.

Affirmative commands put these pronouns after the verb, joined by hyphens: le/la/les, then moi/toi/lui/nous/vous/leur, then y, then en. Compare `Donnez-le-moi` (Give it to me) with the negative `Ne me le donnez pas` (Do not give it to me), which restores the ordinary preverbal order. Before en or y, moi/toi become m’/t’: `Donne-m’en deux` (Give me two), `Va-t’en` (Go away). Only pronouns belonging to the command verb move after it: `Allez le chercher` (Go and get him/it) keeps le before chercher, without a hyphen after allez.
points: Check whether the French verb takes a direct object or `à` plus a person.
Use le/la/les for a third-person direct object; use lui/leur with verbs such as parler à and répondre à, but à + stressed pronoun with penser à.
Place the pronoun before the conjugated verb, or before the auxiliary in a compound tense.
Attach the pronoun to the infinitive it completes: `Je vais le remplir`.
Follow the fixed sequence `me/te/nous/vous`, then `le/la/les`, then `lui/leur`.
Remember that `attendre` and `écouter` are direct in French, with no preposition at all.
Follow the full five-slot order when several pronouns meet: `me/te/nous/vous`, `le/la/les`, `lui/leur`, `y`, `en`.
Agree the participle with the direct-object pronoun standing in front of it.

examples.french: La conseillère nous reçoit à neuf heures.
examples.english: The adviser is meeting us at nine o’clock.
examples.note: « Recevoir quelqu’un » is direct.

examples.french: Je leur envoie les documents demandés dès ce soir.
examples.english: I am sending them the requested documents this evening.
examples.note: « Envoyer à quelqu’un » is indirect, so « leur ».

examples.french: Ce formulaire est long, mais je dois le remplir avant vendredi.
examples.english: This form is long, but I have to complete it before Friday.
examples.note: The pronoun goes before the infinitive it belongs to.

examples.french: Les documents ? Je les lui remettrai demain matin.
examples.english: The documents? I will hand them to him tomorrow morning.
examples.note: Direct pronoun before indirect pronoun.

examples.french: Elle m’a téléphoné hier pour confirmer le rendez-vous.
examples.english: She phoned me yesterday to confirm the appointment.
examples.note: « Téléphoner à quelqu’un » is indirect in French, unlike its English equivalent.

examples.french: J’attends la conseillère depuis vingt minutes ; je l’attends devant le guichet.
examples.english: I have been waiting for the adviser for twenty minutes; I am waiting for her in front of the counter.
examples.note: « Attendre quelqu’un » is direct in French, so the pronoun is « la », not « lui ».

examples.french: Les clés du local ? Oui, elle les y a posées ce matin.
examples.english: The keys to the room? Yes, she put them there this morning.
examples.note: When replacing the keys with a pronoun, les precedes y and triggers agreement. Keeping the noun is also correct: « Elle y a posé les clés ».

examples.french: Les documents ? Elle me les a envoyés par courriel, mais ne les leur transmettez pas avant la vérification.
examples.english: The documents? She sent them to me by email, but do not forward them to the others before the check.
examples.note: « Me » before « les »; in a negative command the pronouns keep their normal order before the verb.

mistakes.avoid: Je l’ai téléphoné pour confirmer.
mistakes.prefer: Je lui ai téléphoné pour confirmer.
mistakes.why: `Téléphoner à quelqu’un` takes an indirect object, so the pronoun is `lui`.

mistakes.avoid: Je vais remplir le demain.
mistakes.prefer: Je vais le remplir demain.
mistakes.why: The pronoun stands before the infinitive it completes, not after it.

mistakes.avoid: J’attends pour la conseillère depuis vingt minutes.
mistakes.prefer: J’attends la conseillère depuis vingt minutes.
mistakes.why: `Attendre` takes a direct object in French; the English preposition for has no equivalent here.

mistakes.avoid: Je lui le remettrai demain matin au guichet.
mistakes.prefer: Je le lui remettrai demain matin au guichet.
mistakes.why: `Le/la/les` always comes before `lui/leur` in the fixed sequence.

mistakes.avoid: Oui, elle y les a posées ce matin.
mistakes.prefer: Oui, elle les y a posées ce matin.
mistakes.why: When both pronouns are used, the direct object `les` precedes `y`. Repeating the noun instead is also grammatical.

sections.title: Me voilà, les voilà: here I am, there they are
paragraphs: Voilà can present or point out someone or something. With a pronoun, use me, te, le, la, nous, vous, or les before voilà: Me voilà, La voilà, Les voilà. This is a presentative expression, not an imperative telling someone to look, and voilà does not change for plural people or objects.
Context decides between English here and there. An added adjective or phrase can describe the person or thing presented: Les voilà ensemble means There they are together.
points: Place the direct-form pronoun before voilà.
Voilà stays invariable; the following description may need agreement.

examples.french: Me voilà enfin à la gare !
examples.english: Here I am at the station at last!
examples.note: Me presents the speaker.

examples.french: Tu cherchais la responsable ? La voilà près de l’entrée.
examples.english: Were you looking for the person in charge? There she is near the entrance.
examples.note: La, not lui, presents the woman.

examples.french: Les enfants ? Les voilà ensemble devant l’école.
examples.english: The children? There they are together in front of the school.
examples.note: Les presents a plural group without changing voilà.

mistakes.avoid: Tu cherchais Paul ? Lui voilà.
mistakes.prefer: Tu cherchais Paul ? Le voilà.
mistakes.why: This presentative construction uses le, not indirect lui.

mistakes.avoid: Les voilàs ensemble.
mistakes.prefer: Les voilà ensemble.
mistakes.why: Voilà does not take a plural s.

vocabulary.example: J’ai téléphoné à la conseillère, puis je lui ai envoyé un courriel.
vocabulary.note: Indirect in French even though the English verb is direct.

vocabulary.example: Je les lui remettrai avant la fin de la semaine.
vocabulary.note: Follows `mettre`; participle `remis`.

vocabulary.example: Un document numérisé est accepté pour la première étape.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `un justificatif` is the narrower administrative term.

vocabulary.example: Un rendez-vous en personne reste nécessaire pour la signature.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; invariable in the plural.

vocabulary.example: Nous attendons la décision du comité depuis trois semaines.
vocabulary.note: Direct object with no preposition, so the pronoun is `le`, `la`, or `les`.

practice.prompt: Replace le dossier and à la conseillère with pronouns: « J’envoie le dossier à la conseillère. »
practice.hint: Direct pronoun first, then indirect.
practice.answer: Je le lui envoie.

takeaways: The French verb decides: direct object or `à` plus person.
Learn lui/leur with verbs such as parler à; penser à a person instead keeps à plus a stressed pronoun.
Fixed order: `me/te/nous/vous`, `le/la/les`, `lui/leur`, `y`, `en`.
Five slots in order: `me/te/nous/vous`, `le/la/les`, `lui/leur`, `y`, `en`.
keywords: voilà, me voilà, te voilà, le voilà, la voilà, les voilà

lessons.title: Les pronoms « y » et « en »
lessons.summary: `Y` replaces a place or a non-person complement introduced by `à`: `Je vais au bureau` gives `J’y vais`; `Je pense au projet` gives `J’y pense`. `En` replaces a complement introduced by `de`, a partitive phrase, or a counted noun: `Je parle du projet` gives `J’en parle`; `J’ai deux dossiers` gives `J’en ai deux`. Stressed forms make personal references clear (`Je pense à elle`, `Je parle d’elle`), while `en` can also count people (`Des collègues ? J’en connais plusieurs`).
objectives: Find the preposition of the phrase you want to replace.
Keep the quantity expression when using `en`.
Use stressed pronouns for clear personal reference and recognise that `en` can also count people.
Place `y` correctly inside a pronominal verb in a compound tense.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: `Y` and `en` replace references to places, things, or quantities; they are often called adverbial pronouns. `Y` commonly replaces a place introduced by `à`, `dans`, `chez`, or `sur`: `Elle travaille dans ce bureau → Elle y travaille` (She works there). A place of origin with `de` instead gives `en`: `Elle revient du bureau → Elle en revient` (She is coming back from there). `Y` also replaces an à complement referring to a thing: `Je pense au projet → J’y pense`. `En` commonly replaces a de complement: `Je parle du projet → J’en parle`. Check the construction rather than treating every prepositional phrase alike.

En also replaces an indefinite or partitive object: `Je bois du café → J’en bois` (I drink some). Keep an expressed quantity: `J’en veux deux`, `Il y en a beaucoup`, `J’ai un dossier → J’en ai un`. With ordinary negation, `Je n’ai pas de dossier → Je n’en ai pas` drops un because it no longer specifies one. To refer clearly to a person, stressed forms are useful: `Je pense à elle`, `Je parle de lui`. En can nevertheless refer to people, not only when counting them: `Des collègues ? J’en connais plusieurs` (I know several), and `Mes enfants ? J’en suis fière` (I am proud of them) are both correct.

Normally place y and en before their conjugated verb or auxiliary, or before the infinitive they complete: `Je vais en acheter deux` (I am going to buy two). In affirmative commands they follow the verb: `Allez-y`, `Prenez-en deux`; negative commands keep them before it: `N’y allez pas`, `N’en prenez pas`. With quantitative en as the direct object, the past participle normally stays unchanged: `Des formations ? J’en ai suivi deux`, not agreement as in `Ces formations, je les ai suivies`.

`S’habituer à` illustrates placement with a pronominal verb. `Je m’habitue à la nouvelle procédure` can become `Je m’y habitue`; in a compound tense, `y` sits between the reflexive pronoun and the auxiliary: `Je m’y suis habitué`. Keeping `à ça` is also grammatical: `Je me suis habitué à ça`. With `s’habituer`, the reflexive pronoun is direct, so the participle agrees: a woman writes `Je m’y suis habituée`. Do not generalise this agreement to every pronominal verb: `elles se sont parlé` stays unchanged because `se` is indirect.
points: Identify the preposition before choosing between `y` and `en`.
Y can replace a destination or location; en can replace an origin. Also learn y with penser à and en with parler de.
Use `en` for a partitive article and for any counted noun.
Repeat the number or quantity after `en`.
Stressed forms such as à elle and de lui make personal reference clear; en can also refer to people.
Place `y` between the reflexive pronoun and the auxiliary: `je m’y suis habitué`.
With `s’habituer`, agree with the direct reflexive pronoun: `je m’y suis habituée` for a woman; other pronominal verbs need their own agreement analysis.

examples.french: Vous allez au centre de services ? Oui, j’y vais cet après-midi.
examples.english: Are you going to the service centre? Yes, I am going there this afternoon.
examples.note: « Y » replaces « au centre de services ».

examples.french: Avez-vous besoin de renseignements ? Oui, j’en ai besoin.
examples.english: Do you need information? Yes, I need some.
examples.note: « Avoir besoin de » becomes « en ».

examples.french: Elle a suivi deux formations cette année ; elle en a suivi deux.
examples.english: She took two training courses this year; she took two of them.
examples.note: The number stays after « en ».

examples.french: Ce projet est important : nous y pensons depuis des mois.
examples.english: This project is important: we have been thinking about it for months.
examples.note: « Penser à » plus a thing gives « y ».

examples.french: Ma conseillère est excellente ; je pense souvent à elle.
examples.english: My adviser is excellent; I often think about her.
examples.note: With a person, a stressed pronoun replaces « y ».

examples.french: Le froid me surprenait au début, mais je m’y suis habituée en quelques mois.
examples.english: The cold surprised me at first, but I got used to it within a few months.
examples.note: « Y » sits before the auxiliary; the participle agrees with a female subject.

examples.french: La nouvelle procédure est plus longue, mais nous nous y sommes habitués rapidement.
examples.english: The new procedure takes longer, but we got used to it quickly.
examples.note: Same structure in the plural, with agreement on « habitués ».

mistakes.avoid: J’en vais à l’école chaque matin.
mistakes.prefer: J’y vais chaque matin.
mistakes.why: A place introduced by `à` is replaced by `y`, not by `en`.

mistakes.avoid: Ma sœur habite ici ; je pense souvent à la.
mistakes.prefer: Ma sœur habite ici ; je pense souvent à elle.
mistakes.why: After the preposition `à`, use the stressed pronoun `elle`, not the object pronoun `la`.

mistakes.avoid: C’était difficile au début, mais je me suis y habitué.
mistakes.prefer: C’était difficile au début, mais je m’y suis habitué.
mistakes.why: When using `y`, place it before the auxiliary and elide `me` to `m’`. The alternative `je me suis habitué à ça` is also correct.

vocabulary.example: Nous parlons du projet en réunion, et nous en parlons aussi entre nous.
vocabulary.note: Built with `de`, so the complement is replaced by `en`.

vocabulary.example: Je pense à ma prochaine entrevue, et j’y pense chaque soir.
vocabulary.note: `Y` for a thing, but `à lui` or `à elle` for a person.

vocabulary.example: Un renseignement précis évite un déplacement inutile.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun, frequently used in the plural: `des renseignements`.

vocabulary.example: Un centre de services regroupe plusieurs démarches administratives.
vocabulary.note: Masculine compound noun; learn it as one unit.

practice.prompt: Answer with `y` or `en`: « Combien de dossiers avez-vous déposés ? » (three) and « Allez-vous à la mairie ? » (yes).
practice.hint: One answer keeps a number.
practice.answer: J’en ai déposé trois. Oui, j’y vais.

takeaways: `À` plus thing gives `y`; `de` plus thing gives `en`.
`En` also covers partitives and counted nouns, and the number stays.
Stressed pronouns clarify personal references (`à elle`, `de lui`); `en` can also count people.
`Y` precedes the auxiliary in `je m’y suis habitué`; it does not determine the participle’s agreement rule.

lessons.title: Les différents emplois de « on »
lessons.summary: `On` is an indefinite subject pronoun and always takes a third-person singular verb. It has three everyday readings: we in conversation, people in general, and someone unspecified. It is also the natural French replacement for an English passive with an unnamed human agent. In formal writing, prefer `nous` when the reference must be explicit.
objectives: Keep the verb in the third-person singular after `on`.
Interpret `on` from the context of the sentence.
Choose between `on` and `nous` according to register.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: `On` is grammatically singular, whatever it means: `On y va`, `On a annoncé une consultation`. Its meaning is supplied by the context. In conversation it usually replaces `nous`: `On part à huit heures`. In a general statement it means people as a whole: `Au Canada, on peut recevoir certains services en français`. In a report about an unidentified person it means someone: `On a frappé à la porte`.

On is a useful active alternative to an English passive with an unnamed human actor: On m’a dit que le bureau fermait (I was told the office was closing), On a annoncé la décision (The decision was announced). French passives remain grammatical and may better keep the focus on the affected thing: La décision a été annoncée. In formal writing, nous often identifies the writer’s group more clearly; on is not itself forbidden there.

The conjugated verb stays singular, but an adjective or a participle that agrees with a known group can reflect that group: On est prêts (We are ready, male or mixed group), On est arrivées (We arrived, all-female group). For a general, unspecified person, use the usual singular: Quand on est fatigué, on se repose (When one is tired, one rests). When on means we, object and reflexive forms are not on: On se prépare, and Cela nous aide.
points: Conjugate the verb in the third-person singular after `on`.
Read `on` as we in conversation and as people in a general statement.
Consider on + active verb for an unnamed human actor; keep a passive when its focus better suits the context.
Prefer `nous` in formal writing when the reference is specific.
Write a following adjective in the plural when `on` means we.

examples.french: Au Canada, on peut recevoir certains services en français.
