examples.english: In Canada, people can receive certain services in French.
examples.note: General statement; the verb stays singular.

examples.french: On a annoncé une consultation publique pour lundi prochain.
examples.english: A public consultation was announced for next Monday.
examples.note: « On » replaces an English passive with an unnamed agent.

examples.french: Dans ce quartier, on organise souvent des activités gratuites.
examples.english: In this neighbourhood, people often organise free activities.
examples.note: People in general.

examples.french: On est prêts à déposer le dossier dès demain matin.
examples.english: We are ready to submit the file as early as tomorrow morning.
examples.note: « On » meaning we, with a plural adjective.

examples.french: Nous avons examiné la demande et nous vous répondrons sous huit jours.
examples.english: We have reviewed the application and we will reply within eight days.
examples.note: Formal writing prefers « nous » when the reference is explicit.

mistakes.avoid: On sont arrivés en retard à la réunion.
mistakes.prefer: On est arrivés en retard à la réunion.
mistakes.why: `On` always takes a third-person singular verb, even when the participle is plural in meaning.

mistakes.avoid: Dans notre lettre, on demandons un rendez-vous.
mistakes.prefer: Dans notre lettre, on demande un rendez-vous.
mistakes.why: On takes demande, even when it means we. Nous demandons un rendez-vous is also correct and often preferable in a formal letter; that is a register choice, not a ban on on.

vocabulary.example: Un usager peut déposer une plainte directement en ligne.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; feminine `une usagère`.

vocabulary.example: Un service bilingue accueille les usagers du lundi au vendredi.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `un service public` is a public service.

vocabulary.example: Une activité gratuite est proposée chaque samedi à la bibliothèque.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the ending -té is a feminine hint.

vocabulary.example: On organise une séance d’information chaque premier lundi du mois.
vocabulary.note: Regular `-er` verb; frequently used with `on` in general statements.

practice.prompt: Rewrite without a passive: « The forms were sent yesterday. » Then say that your own group sent them, using nous.
practice.hint: On can leave the human actor unidentified; nous explicitly includes the speaker’s group, so this step adds information.
practice.answer: On a envoyé les formulaires hier. Nous avons envoyé les formulaires hier.

takeaways: `On` is always singular, whatever it means.
Context decides between we, people, and someone.
On is one alternative to a passive with a human actor; nous explicitly identifies the speaker’s group and often suits formal writing.

lessons.title: Les indéfinis « tout », « quelqu’un », « chacun », « n’importe » et « autre »
lessons.summary: Tout agrees as a determiner and is usually invariable as an intensifying adverb, with feminine-adjective exceptions. Quelqu’un and quelque chose take de before an adjective; chacun/chacune are singular. N’importe expresses unrestricted choice in statements, questions, and negatives; N’importe quoi ! can also dismiss something as nonsense. Distinguish unspecified d’autres from de + les autres, which contracts to des autres.
objectives: Agree `tout` correctly and recognise its invariable adverbial use.
Insert `de` before an adjective after `quelqu’un` and `quelque chose`.
Select the right form of `autre` and of the `n’importe` series.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: An indefinite word refers without identifying a precise person or thing. Before a noun, `tout` has four determiner forms — `tout`, `toute`, `tous`, `toutes`: `tout le dossier`, `toutes les candidates`. As a pronoun it can mean everything (`Tout est prêt`). When it intensifies an adjective or adverb, it is usually unchanged: `tout simplement`, `tout près`, `tout émue`. Before a feminine adjective beginning with a consonant or an aspirated h, however, it agrees: `toute contente`, `toutes honteuses`. An aspirated h is silent but blocks ordinary linking, as in `honteuse`; it is not a pronounced English h.

`Quelqu’un` and `quelque chose` are singular and take `de` before an adjective: `quelqu’un de disponible`, `quelque chose d’utile`, `quelqu’un d’autre`. `Chacun` and `chacune` are singular and take `de` or `d’entre` before a group: `chacune des candidates`, `chacun d’entre vous`. The `n’importe` series expresses unrestricted choice: `n’importe qui`, `n’importe quoi`, `n’importe quel formulaire`. It can occur in questions and negatives too; it is not interchangeable with `personne` or `rien`. Finally, `autre` varies by specificity: `un autre` (another one), `l’autre` (the other specific one), `les autres` (the others), `d’autres` (some others).

Three quantifiers distinguish number and amount. `Quelques` introduces a small number and is plural: `J’habite à quelques rues de la station de métro`. `Plusieurs` means several and never changes form: `Plusieurs organismes offrent des cours de français gratuits`. `De nombreux` and `de nombreuses` mean many and agree with the noun: `De nombreuses familles attendent encore un logement abordable`. In careful writing, indefinite plural des normally becomes de before a preposed plural adjective. This does not remove a definite article: `Profitez des nombreux services` retains the contraction de + les.
points: Distinguish determiner agreement from adverbial tout, including toute/toutes before feminine adjectives beginning with a consonant or aspirated h.
Add `de` between `quelqu’un` or `quelque chose` and any adjective.
Keep `chacun` and `chacune` singular, followed by `de` or `d’entre`.
Use n’importe for unrestricted choice, including in questions and negatives when that meaning fits.
Choose among `un autre`, `l’autre`, `les autres`, and `d’autres` by specificity.
Use `plusieurs` for an unspecified number greater than one, and `quelque part` for an unidentified place.
Pronounce the final `s` of `tous` when it is a pronoun (`ils sont tous venus`) and keep it silent in the determiner (`tous les dossiers`).

Choose the relative form by its role: Tout ce qui manque est indiqué (Everything that is missing is listed): qui is the subject of manque. Tout ce que vous envoyez sera vérifié (Everything you send will be checked): que is the object of envoyez. Voilà tout ce dont vous avez besoin (Here is everything you need): dont supplies de in avoir besoin de.

Quelque chose takes a masculine adjective despite the feminine noun une chose: quelque chose d’important (something important). N’importe quel agrees with its noun: quel document, quelle date, quels documents, quelles dates.
Use `quelques` for a small plural number and `plusieurs` for several; the pronoun can introduce a subset with `de`: `plusieurs de mes collègues`.
Agree nombreux/nombreuses with the noun; distinguish indefinite de from the contraction de + les.

examples.french: Toutes les candidates ont reçu les mêmes consignes écrites.
examples.english: All the candidates received the same written instructions.
examples.note: « Tout » agrees with the noun group it introduces.

examples.french: Quelqu’un d’autre pourra-t-il m’expliquer cette démarche ?
examples.english: Will someone else be able to explain this procedure to me?
examples.note: « De » is required before the adjective.

examples.french: Chacun d’entre vous peut proposer une solution concrète.
examples.english: Each of you can suggest a concrete solution.
examples.note: « Chacun » stays singular and takes « d’entre ».

examples.french: Prenez n’importe quel formulaire vert ; les autres sont périmés.
examples.english: Take any green form at all; the others are out of date.
examples.note: Free choice in a positive sentence, then « les autres » for a known group.

examples.french: Personne n’a répondu et rien n’a été décidé pendant la réunion.
examples.english: Nobody answered and nothing was decided during the meeting.
examples.note: Personne and rien mean nobody and nothing; they are not automatic replacements for n’importe under negation.

examples.french: Plusieurs candidats attendent encore une réponse, et le dossier manquant est quelque part dans les archives.
examples.english: Several applicants are still waiting for an answer, and the missing file is somewhere in the archives.
examples.note: « Plusieurs » is invariable in form and always plural; « quelque part » names an unidentified place.

examples.french: Tout ce que vous avez fourni est conforme, et les candidats sont tous convoqués lundi.
examples.english: Everything you provided is compliant, and the candidates are all summoned on Monday.
examples.note: « Tout ce que » for everything that; in « tous convoqués » the pronoun « tous » is pronounced with its final s.

examples.french: J’habite à quelques rues de la station de métro, et plusieurs organismes offrent des cours de français gratuits dans le secteur.
examples.english: I live a few streets from the subway station, and several organisations offer free French courses in the area.
examples.note: « Quelques » for a small number, invariable « plusieurs » for several.

examples.french: De nombreuses familles attendent encore un logement abordable dans ce quartier.
examples.english: Many families are still waiting for affordable housing in this neighbourhood.
examples.note: « De » instead of « des » before the preposed plural adjective « nombreuses ».

examples.french: Plusieurs de mes collègues suivent ce cours du soir.
examples.english: Several of my colleagues take this evening course.
examples.note: As a pronoun, plusieurs can take de before the group from which a subset is selected.

examples.french: Elle est toute contente et tout émue de nous revoir.
examples.english: She is very happy and very moved to see us again.
examples.note: Intensifying tout agrees before feminine contente, but not before vowel-initial émue.

mistakes.avoid: Je cherche quelqu’un de disponibles cet après-midi.
mistakes.prefer: Je cherche quelqu’un de disponible cet après-midi.
mistakes.why: Quelqu’un is singular, so disponible must be singular.

mistakes.avoid: Chacune des candidates ont reçu une réponse.
mistakes.prefer: Chacune des candidates a reçu une réponse.
mistakes.why: `Chacune` is singular, so the verb stays in the singular.

mistakes.avoid: Tout que vous avez envoyé est arrivé ce matin.
mistakes.prefer: Tout ce que vous avez envoyé est arrivé ce matin.
mistakes.why: `Tout` needs the relative group `ce que`, `ce qui`, or `ce dont` before a clause.

mistakes.avoid: De nombreuse services sont offerts gratuitement aux nouveaux arrivants.
mistakes.prefer: De nombreux services sont offerts gratuitement aux nouveaux arrivants.
mistakes.why: Services is masculine plural and requires nombreux.

mistakes.avoid: Plusieurs personne attend encore une réponse du service.
mistakes.prefer: Plusieurs personnes attendent encore une réponse du service.
mistakes.why: `Plusieurs` is invariable but the noun and the verb that follow it are plural.

sections.title: Not just anyone is not nobody
paragraphs: N’importe qui/quoi means anyone/anything without restriction; n’importe quel agrees with a following noun. A question can ask whether that freedom exists. A negative can reject unrestricted choice: Je ne confie pas mes clés à n’importe qui means I do not trust just anyone with my keys, not I trust nobody.

Standalone N’importe quoi ! dismisses a claim or action as nonsense, and can sound blunt. In dire n’importe quoi or faire n’importe quoi, context often gives a careless or nonsensical reading rather than permission to say or do anything.
points: Questions and negatives are compatible with n’importe.
Distinguish unrestricted choice from the dismissive nonsense reading.

examples.french: Peut-on choisir n’importe quelle date pour la visite ?
examples.english: Can we choose any date at all for the visit?
examples.note: A valid question asking whether the choice is unrestricted.

examples.french: Je ne donne pas mon code à n’importe qui.
examples.english: I do not give my code to just anyone.
examples.note: A valid negative: the speaker is selective, not necessarily refusing everyone.

examples.french: Je ne donne mon code à personne.
examples.english: I do not give my code to anyone.
examples.note: Personne excludes every recipient, unlike not just anyone.

examples.french: « Ce trajet prend cinq minutes à pied ? N’importe quoi ! Il faut une heure. »
examples.english: “This journey takes five minutes on foot? Nonsense! It takes an hour.”
examples.note: A dismissive conversational reaction, not a neutral request for clarification.

mistakes.avoid: Peut-on choisir n’importe quel date ?
mistakes.prefer: Peut-on choisir n’importe quelle date ?
mistakes.why: Quelle agrees with the feminine noun date; the question itself is valid.

sections.title: Other items, or the other known items?
paragraphs: D’autres introduces unspecified additional or different people or things: J’ai d’autres questions. Les autres identifies the remaining members of a known set. If a preceding construction requires de, de + les autres contracts to des autres: J’ai besoin des autres documents.

Compare avoir besoin d’autres documents (need some other documents, not yet identified) with avoir besoin des autres documents (need the other known documents). Des autres is therefore not universally wrong; identify the preposition and the definite article before choosing.
points: D’autres leaves the other items unspecified.
Des autres can be de + les autres, with a specific known set.

examples.french: Avez-vous d’autres questions avant de partir ?
examples.english: Do you have any other questions before leaving?
examples.note: The additional questions are not identified in advance.

examples.french: J’ai besoin d’autres documents pour prouver mon adresse.
examples.english: I need some other documents to prove my address.
examples.note: Unspecified alternatives after avoir besoin de.

examples.french: J’ai reçu votre passeport, mais j’ai encore besoin des autres documents de la liste.
examples.english: I received your passport, but I still need the other documents on the list.
examples.note: The list identifies the remaining documents; de + les becomes des.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai besoin de les autres documents.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai besoin des autres documents.
mistakes.why: De contracts with the definite plural article les.

vocabulary.example: Une consigne claire évite beaucoup d’erreurs pendant l’épreuve.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `suivre les consignes` means to follow instructions.

vocabulary.example: Une candidate motivée pose des questions précises en entrevue.
vocabulary.note: Feminine form; the masculine is `un candidat`.

vocabulary.example: N’importe quelle pièce d’identité officielle est acceptée.
vocabulary.note: Determiner form; it agrees with the noun that follows.

vocabulary.example: Chacun d’entre nous doit relire son dossier avant l’envoi.
vocabulary.note: Always singular, even when the group is plural.

vocabulary.example: Plusieurs mesures ont été annoncées lors de la consultation.
vocabulary.note: Invariable and plural; determiner in `plusieurs personnes`, pronoun in `plusieurs de mes collègues`.

vocabulary.example: J’ai rangé l’attestation quelque part dans ce classeur.
vocabulary.note: Invariable; the negative counterpart is `nulle part`.

vocabulary.example: Tout ce que vous déposez avant midi est traité le jour même.
vocabulary.note: Use `tout ce qui` when the element is the subject of the clause.

vocabulary.example: La consigne est claire, et nos valises sont à la consigne de la gare.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun with two meanings decided by context; `les consignes` are usually instructions.

vocabulary.example: De nombreuses demandes ont été déposées avant la date limite.
vocabulary.note: Agrees with the noun; `de` replaces `des` because the adjective comes first.

practice.prompt: Complete: « ___ les documents sont prêts, mais il manque ___ d’important : ___ des candidats doit signer. »
practice.hint: Agreement, then `de` before an adjective, then a singular indefinite.
practice.answer: Tous les documents sont prêts, mais il manque quelque chose d’important : chacun des candidats doit signer.

takeaways: Tout agrees as a determiner; as an intensifier, note the feminine consonant/aspirated-h exception.
`Quelqu’un` and `quelque chose` need `de` before an adjective.
N’importe expresses unrestricted choice even in questions and negatives; personne/rien mean nobody/nothing.
D’autres is unspecified; des autres can be de + the other known items.
`Quelques` a few, `plusieurs` several and invariable, `de nombreux` many and agreeing.
keywords: tout, quelqu’un, chacun, n’importe, and autre
n’importe qui, n’importe quoi, n’importe quel, d’autres, des autres, tout adverbe
n'importe qui, n'importe quoi, n'importe quel, d'autres, des autres

lessons.title: Les pronoms relatifs « qui », « que », « dont » et « où »
lessons.summary: A relative pronoun links a noun, its antecedent, to a clause that describes it. Choose by the role of the missing element in that clause: `qui` is its subject, `que` its direct object, `dont` replaces a complement built with `de`, and `où` replaces a complement of place or time. `Que` elides to `qu’` before a vowel; `qui` never elides.
objectives: Identify the antecedent and the missing role inside the relative clause.
Select among `qui`, `que`, `dont`, and `où` on that basis.
Avoid eliding `qui` and avoid repeating `de` after `dont`.

sections.title: Choose the relative pronoun from its role
paragraphs: A relative clause is a group with a verb that gives information about a noun: in `la conseillère qui vous reçoit`, it tells you which adviser is meant. That noun is called the antecedent. Rebuild the clause as an independent sentence. If the repeated noun is the subject, use `qui`: `La conseillère vous reçoit` → `la conseillère qui vous reçoit`. If it is the direct object, linked to the verb without a preposition, use `que`: `Vous devez remplir le formulaire` → `le formulaire que vous devez remplir`.

Choose from the noun’s role, not whether it names a person or thing: `la personne que j’appelle`, but `le téléphone qui sonne`. A place name is not automatically followed by `où`: compare `la ville que je visite` (I visit the city, a direct object) and `la ville où j’habite` (I live in the city, a location). French keeps the relative pronoun where English can omit it: `le livre que je lis`, the book I am reading.

`Dont` replaces a complement linked by plain `de`, whether it depends on a verb (`parler de`), a noun (`le titre de`), or an adjective (`fier de`). Do not repeat the same link with `de`, `en`, or a possessive: `le quartier dont les services sont excellents`, not `dont ses services`. With a longer preposition such as `près de`, keep that whole preposition and use another relative form: `le parc près duquel j’habite`. The ending `de` does not by itself justify `dont`.

`Où` can express place or time: `la ville où j’habite`, `l’année où je suis arrivé`. It has an accent, unlike `ou` meaning or. `Que` elides before a vowel or mute h (`qu’il`, `qu’elle`), while relative `qui` keeps its form (`qui a`).
points: Rebuild the clause as a full sentence to see which element is missing.
Use `qui` for the missing subject and `que` for the missing direct object.
Use `dont` for a link with plain `de`; do not duplicate that link inside the clause. Longer prepositions such as `près de` need a different construction.
Use `où` for a place and also for a moment in time.
Elide `que` to `qu’` before a vowel, but never write `qu’` for `qui`.

examples.french: La conseillère qui vous reçoit connaît bien le programme.
examples.english: The adviser who is meeting with you knows the program well.
examples.note: The missing element is the subject of « reçoit ».

examples.french: Le formulaire que vous devez remplir se trouve en ligne.
examples.english: The form that you must complete is online.
examples.note: The missing element is the direct object of « remplir ».

examples.french: Le programme dont je vous ai parlé accepte encore des candidatures.
examples.english: The program I told you about is still accepting applications.
examples.note: « Parler de » becomes « dont »; the preposition is not repeated.

examples.french: C’est un quartier dont les services de proximité sont excellents.
examples.english: It is a neighbourhood whose local services are excellent.
examples.note: « Dont » also renders whose with a noun complement.

examples.french: La ville où je me suis installé offre des cours de français gratuits.
examples.english: The city where I settled offers free French classes.
examples.note: « Où » replaces a complement of place.

examples.french: L’année où j’ai obtenu mon permis, tout est devenu plus simple.
examples.english: The year when I got my permit, everything became easier.
examples.note: « Où » also covers time, where English uses when.

mistakes.avoid: Le dossier dont j’ai besoin de est incomplet.
mistakes.prefer: Le dossier dont j’ai besoin est incomplet.
mistakes.why: `Dont` already contains `de`, so the preposition must not be repeated.

mistakes.avoid: La candidate qu’a déposé son dossier attend une réponse.
mistakes.prefer: La candidate qui a déposé son dossier attend une réponse.
mistakes.why: The missing element is the subject, and `qui` never elides.

vocabulary.example: Une conseillère en emploi aide à préparer les entrevues.
vocabulary.note: Feminine form; the masculine is `un conseiller`.

vocabulary.example: Un programme d’intégration accompagne les familles pendant un an.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; can also mean an event programme or schedule. Use `un horaire (m.)` when referring specifically to times.

vocabulary.example: Le service dont je parle a déménagé au rez-de-chaussée.
vocabulary.note: Relative pronoun replacing a complement linked by plain `de`; longer prepositions such as `près de` require another construction.

vocabulary.example: Le jour où j’ai reçu la réponse, j’ai appelé toute ma famille.
vocabulary.note: Relative pronoun of place and of time.

practice.prompt: Join with the right pronoun: « C’est un quartier. Je rêve de ce quartier. » and « Voici le bureau. J’ai déposé le dossier à ce bureau. »
practice.hint: One complement begins with `de`, the other is a place.
practice.answer: C’est un quartier dont je rêve. Voici le bureau où j’ai déposé le dossier.

takeaways: Missing subject: `qui`. Missing direct object: `que`.
Complement with `de`: `dont`, and never repeat `de`.
Place or moment: `où`.
keywords: relative pronouns qui, que, dont, and où

lessons.title: Le pronom « lequel » et ses formes contractées
lessons.summary: `Lequel`, `laquelle`, `lesquels`, and `lesquelles` replace a noun and ask or specify which one of a known set. `Quel` instead relates to a noun, either directly (`quel formulaire`) or across `être` (`Quel est votre nom ?`). After `à` and `de`, the forms are `auquel`, `à laquelle`, `auxquels`, `auxquelles`; `duquel`, `de laquelle`, `desquels`, `desquelles`. They also serve as relative pronouns after prepositions; for a person, `qui` is often a simpler alternative.
objectives: Select the form of `lequel` that matches the noun it replaces.
Apply the obligatory contractions after `à` and `de`.
Use `lequel` as a relative pronoun after a preposition.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: `Quel` often stands directly before a noun (`quel formulaire`, `quelles conditions`), but it can also be separated from that noun by `être`: `Quel est votre nom ?`, `Quelles sont vos disponibilités ?`. `Lequel` replaces the noun entirely and asks which one out of a known set. It agrees with that noun in gender and number: `lequel`, `laquelle`, `lesquels`, `lesquelles`. The set is often named with `de`: `Lequel de ces formulaires faut-il signer ?`, `Parmi ces trois formations, laquelle correspond le mieux à votre projet ?`

Lequel contains forms corresponding to the definite article, so `à` and `de` contract with it: `à + lequel → auquel`, `à + lesquels → auxquels`, `à + lesquelles → auxquelles`. Feminine singular stays in two words: `à laquelle`. With `de`, use `duquel`, `de laquelle`, `desquels`, `desquelles`. These forms also link a describing clause to an earlier noun, called its antecedent: `le service auquel je me suis adressé`, `les documents sans lesquels la demande est incomplète`.

For people, qui after a simple preposition is often lighter, but lequel is also grammatical: `la conseillère à qui j’ai parlé` and `la conseillère à laquelle j’ai parlé` both mean the adviser I spoke to. Use lequel forms with people as well in constructions such as `les collègues parmi lesquels je travaille` (the colleagues among whom I work). For a relative clause with a simple de relationship, dont is usually the natural choice: `le dossier dont je parle` (the file I am talking about). After a multiword preposition such as près de, keep the full construction: `le bâtiment près duquel nous attendons` (the building near which we are waiting).
points: Use `quel` with a noun, directly or across être; use `lequel` to replace a noun and select from a set.
Agree `lequel`, `laquelle`, `lesquels`, `lesquelles` with the noun replaced.
Introduce the known set with `de`: `lequel de ces documents`.
Contract obligatorily: `auquel`, `auxquels`, `auxquelles`, `duquel`, `desquels`, `desquelles`.
Keep `à laquelle` and `de laquelle` in two words.
Lequel forms can refer to things or people. Qui is often simpler after a preposition with people; près de and similar phrases need their full construction.

examples.french: Parmi ces trois formations, laquelle correspond le mieux à votre projet ?
examples.english: Of these three training courses, which one best matches your plan?
examples.note: Feminine singular, agreeing with « formation ».

examples.french: Voici les formulaires ; lesquels faut-il signer aujourd’hui ?
examples.english: Here are the forms; which ones have to be signed today?
examples.note: Masculine plural, standing alone where « quel » would be impossible.

examples.french: Vous avez reçu deux convocations ; à laquelle devez-vous répondre en premier ?
examples.english: You received two summonses; which one do you have to answer first?
examples.note: Feminine singular stays in two words after « à ».

examples.french: Le service auquel je me suis adressé m’a répondu en deux jours.
examples.english: The department I contacted replied within two days.
examples.note: Relative use after a preposition, with the obligatory contraction.

examples.french: Ce sont les pièces sans lesquelles votre dossier restera incomplet.
examples.english: These are the documents without which your file will remain incomplete.
examples.note: « Lesquelles » after another preposition, agreeing with « pièces ».

examples.french: La conseillère à qui j’ai parlé connaît bien le programme.
examples.english: The adviser I spoke to knows the program well.
examples.note: With a person, French prefers « à qui » to « à laquelle ».

examples.french: Quelle est votre adresse actuelle ?
examples.english: What is your current address?
examples.note: Quelle agrees with adresse even though est separates them.

mistakes.avoid: Quel de ces documents dois-je fournir ?
mistakes.prefer: Lequel de ces documents dois-je fournir ?
mistakes.why: Selecting one item from `ces documents` requires the pronoun `lequel`, not `quel`.

mistakes.avoid: Le service à lequel j’ai écrit n’a pas répondu.
mistakes.prefer: Le service auquel j’ai écrit n’a pas répondu.
mistakes.why: `À` and `lequel` must contract to `auquel`; the two-word form does not exist.

mistakes.avoid: Voici deux formations ; lequel préférez-vous ?
mistakes.prefer: Voici deux formations ; laquelle préférez-vous ?
mistakes.why: The pronoun agrees with the noun it replaces, and `une formation` is feminine.

vocabulary.example: Lequel de ces deux bureaux traite les demandes de permis ?
vocabulary.note: Contracts to `auquel` and `duquel` after `à` and `de`.

vocabulary.example: Laquelle de ces attestations faut-il joindre ?
vocabulary.note: Stays in two words after a preposition: `à laquelle`, `de laquelle`.

vocabulary.example: Lesquelles de ces pièces sont obligatoires ?
vocabulary.note: Contract to `auxquels`, `auxquelles`, `desquels`, `desquelles`.

vocabulary.example: Le programme auquel elle s’est inscrite commence en septembre.
vocabulary.note: Obligatory contraction of `à + lequel`.

vocabulary.example: Une convocation écrite précise la date et le lieu de l’entrevue.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `convoquer` is the related verb.

practice.prompt: Complete: « Voici deux services ; ___ faut-il écrire ? Et ___ de ces formulaires est le bon ? »
practice.hint: One needs a contraction after `à`, the other stands alone.
practice.answer: Voici deux services ; auquel faut-il écrire ? Et lequel de ces formulaires est le bon ?

takeaways: `Quel` relates to a noun, sometimes across être; `lequel` replaces a noun to select from a set.
Four agreeing forms, and the contractions `auquel`, `auxquels`, `duquel`, `desquels` are obligatory.
After prepositions, lequel forms can refer to people too; distinguish simple de + relative dont from phrases such as près duquel.

lessons.title: Les questions et les exclamations
lessons.summary: Questions use statement order, est-ce que, or inversion according to context and register; writing does not require inversion. Distinguish subject qu’est-ce qui from object qu’est-ce que, and noun-linked quel from selecting lequel. Quel also introduces agreeing exclamations, while Vive…! celebrates or expresses support.
objectives: Match a question structure to the register of the situation.
Choose the right question word for a person, a thing, a quantity, or a choice.
Recognise common inversions with `je` without treating a short example list as exhaustive.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Register is the level of formality suited to the audience. Statement-order questions (`Vous avez un rendez-vous ?`) are common in conversation and written dialogue; final question words (`Tu habites où ?`) often sound informal. `Est-ce que` is a useful neutral choice. Putting the subject after the verb is called inversion: `Où habitez-vous ?`. It often sounds more formal, but some inverted questions are ordinary everyday language (`Combien coûte ce service ?`). Writing does not require inversion in every question. Compare `Tu pars quand ?`, `Quand est-ce que tu pars ?`, and `Quand pars-tu ?`.

For a person, `qui` can appear alone or after a preposition: `Qui vous a reçu ?`, `Avec qui travaillez-vous ?`, `À qui dois-je m’adresser ?`. Compare subject `Qui est-ce qui vous attend ?` (Who is waiting for you?) and object `Qui est-ce que vous attendez ?` (Who are you waiting for?). For a thing, `qu’est-ce qui` marks the subject and `qu’est-ce que` the object; inverted `que` is another object form. After a preposition use `quoi`: `À quoi pensez-vous ?` (What are you thinking about?). `Quel` agrees with its noun (`quel formulaire`, `quelles conditions`, `Quelles sont vos disponibilités ?`), while `lequel` selects from a known set (`Lequel de ces documents faut-il joindre ?`). It contracts with `à` and `de` to give forms such as `auquel` and `duquel`. `N’est-ce pas` asks for confirmation.

With a subject pronoun, join the inverted verb and pronoun by a hyphen: `Avez-vous reçu la lettre ?`. If the third-person singular verb does not already end in t or d, add `-t-` before il, elle, or on: `A-t-elle répondu ?`, but `Prend-elle le train ?`. A noun subject often stays in front and is repeated by a pronoun: `La responsable a-t-elle répondu ?`. Inversion with je depends on the verb and tense: common forms include ai-je, suis-je, dois-je, puis-je, sais-je, vais-je, and future Pourrai-je venir ? These are not an exhaustive list; the present of pouvoir uses puis-je, not peux-je.

An indirect question reports what someone asks or wants to know. It normally uses statement order, without est-ce que: `Je voudrais savoir où vous habitez` (I would like to know where you live), not an embedded où habitez-vous. For a yes/no question, use si meaning whether: `Je voudrais savoir si vous avez reçu la lettre`. This si is not the si of an if-condition.
points: Use statement-order questions in conversation and written dialogue; a final question word often sounds informal.
Use `est-ce que` as a neutral way to form a direct question.
Choose inversion when it suits the wording and register, not merely because the question is written.
Use `qui` for a person in any role, including after a preposition: `avec qui`, `à qui`.
Choose `qu’est-ce qui` for an unknown subject and `qu’est-ce que` for an unknown object.
Agree `quel` with its noun, and use `lequel` to ask which one of a known set.
Recognise forms such as `Que sais-je ?`, `Où vais-je ?`, and `Pourrai-je venir ?`; use `puis-je` for present-tense `pouvoir`.
For the full `lequel` system and its contracted forms, see the dedicated lesson on `lequel`.

examples.french: Tu pars quand ? — Quand est-ce que tu pars ? — Quand pars-tu ?
examples.english: When are you leaving? (statement order, est-ce que, inversion)
examples.note: The same tu addressee across three structures. Changing tu to vous is a separate choice about number or politeness.

examples.french: Avec qui travaillez-vous sur ce dossier, et à qui dois-je m’adresser ?
examples.english: Who are you working with on this file, and who should I speak to?
examples.note: « Qui » after a preposition, and the fixed inversion « dois-je ».

examples.french: Qu’est-ce qui bloque la demande, et qu’est-ce que le service recommande ?
examples.english: What is holding up the application, and what does the department recommend?
examples.note: Subject form, then object form.

examples.french: Quelles conditions faut-il remplir, et lequel de ces formulaires dois-je joindre ?
examples.english: Which conditions have to be met, and which of these forms should I attach?
examples.note: « Quelles » determines a noun; « lequel » selects from a known set.

examples.french: Combien coûte le permis, et combien de pièces justificatives faut-il fournir ?
examples.english: How much does the permit cost, and how many supporting documents must be provided?
examples.note: « Combien » alone before a verb, « combien de » before a noun.

examples.french: Puis-je déposer mon dossier en ligne ? Vous acceptez les copies numérisées, n’est-ce pas ?
examples.english: May I submit my file online? You accept scanned copies, don’t you?
examples.note: « Puis-je » is the accepted inversion; « n’est-ce pas » asks for confirmation.

examples.french: Pourrai-je retirer mon attestation demain ?
examples.english: Will I be able to collect my certificate tomorrow?
examples.note: Future-tense inversion with je is not limited to the short list of common present forms.

mistakes.avoid: Qu’est-ce que se passe au guichet ?
mistakes.prefer: Qu’est-ce qui se passe au guichet ?
mistakes.why: The missing element is the subject of `se passe`, which requires `qui`.

mistakes.avoid: Quel mesures avez-vous prises ?
mistakes.prefer: Quelles mesures avez-vous prises ?
mistakes.why: `Quel` is a determiner and agrees with the feminine plural noun `mesures`.

mistakes.avoid: Peux-je déposer ma demande aujourd’hui ?
mistakes.prefer: Puis-je déposer ma demande aujourd’hui ?
mistakes.why: For the present-tense inversion of `pouvoir` with `je`, the standard form is `puis-je`, not `peux-je`.

sections.title: What a…! and Long live…!
paragraphs: Quel can express surprise or admiration rather than ask a question. It agrees with the noun: quel soulagement, quelle nouvelle, quels tableaux, quelles journées. Unlike English what a, French normally puts no un/une between exclamative quel and its noun: Quelle surprise !

Vive introduces an enthusiastic wish or celebration: Vive la lecture ! Before a plural noun, invariable Vive les vacances ! is widely used; Vivent les vacances ! is also accepted when vive is treated as the subjunctive verb agreeing with its subject. Neither variant should be treated as a grammar mistake.
points: Exclamative quel agrees in gender and number.
Vive…! expresses enthusiasm; accepted plural variants include vive and vivent.

examples.french: Quel soulagement de retrouver nos documents !
examples.english: What a relief to find our documents again!
examples.note: Un soulagement (m.) is a relief; exclamative quel has no added un.

examples.french: Quelle bonne nouvelle pour le quartier !
examples.english: What good news for the neighbourhood!
examples.note: Une nouvelle (f.) is a piece of news.

examples.french: Quels beaux tableaux ! Quelles couleurs lumineuses !
examples.english: What beautiful paintings! What luminous colours!
examples.note: Un tableau (m.) contrasts with une couleur (f.); both phrases are plural.

examples.french: Vive la bibliothèque et ses bénévoles !
examples.english: Long live the library and its volunteers!
examples.note: Vive expresses enthusiastic support.

examples.french: Vive les vacances ! / Vivent les vacances !
examples.english: Hooray for the holidays! / Long live the holidays!
examples.note: Both the fixed exclamation and the agreeing verb are accepted.

mistakes.avoid: Quelle une bonne nouvelle !
mistakes.prefer: Quelle bonne nouvelle !
mistakes.why: Do not copy the English article in what a after exclamative quelle.

mistakes.avoid: Quelles beaux tableaux !
mistakes.prefer: Quels beaux tableaux !
mistakes.why: Tableaux is masculine plural, so use quels.

vocabulary.example: Est-ce que vous acceptez les documents numérisés ?
vocabulary.note: Neutral question opener; elides to `est-ce qu’` before a vowel.

vocabulary.example: Combien de pièces justificatives faut-il joindre ?
vocabulary.note: `Combien` alone stands before a verb; `combien de` stands before a noun.

vocabulary.example: Puis-je obtenir une attestation aujourd’hui ?
vocabulary.note: Fixed formal inversion; `peux-je` does not exist.

vocabulary.example: Le dossier est complet, n’est-ce pas ?
vocabulary.note: Invariable tag placed at the end of a statement.

vocabulary.example: Le prix affiché sur ce devis comprend toutes les taxes.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; identical in the plural.

practice.prompt: Ask formally: how much the service costs, who you should contact, and which of two forms to sign.
practice.hint: Use inversion, `qui` after a preposition, and `lequel`.
practice.answer: Combien coûte ce service ? À qui dois-je m’adresser ? Lequel de ces deux formulaires faut-il signer ?

takeaways: Choose question structure by context and register; inversion is not compulsory in writing.
`Qui` for people in any role; `qu’est-ce qui` and `qu’est-ce que` for things.
`Quel` relates to a noun, `lequel` picks from a set; valid je inversions extend beyond ai-je, suis-je, dois-je, and puis-je.
Quel also introduces exclamations; Vive…! expresses celebration or support.

lessons.title: La négation et la place des pronoms
lessons.summary: In careful written French, `ne` precedes the verb group and words such as `pas`, `jamais`, and `plus` follow the conjugated verb or auxiliary. Object and reflexive pronouns sit between `ne` and the verb; an object `personne` follows the past participle. Before an infinitive, place `ne pas` together: `ne pas déranger`. Signs may use either an infinitive or an imperative (`Ne dérangez pas`). Keep `ne` in formal prose; its omission belongs to informal usage. `Si` contradicts a negative statement or question.
objectives: Position both negative elements in simple and compound tenses.
Place `ne pas` before an infinitive and recognise the imperative as another valid sign format.
Judge when the spoken omission of `ne` is acceptable.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The basic formal negative has two parts, `ne… pas`: `Nous ne pouvons pas venir ce soir`, `Je ne t’attends pas`. Put ne before the pronouns belonging to the conjugated verb, and pas after that verb. In a compound tense, pas follows the auxiliary: `Je n’ai pas mangé`, `Je n’ai pas marché dans la forêt`, `Je ne suis pas allé en France le mois dernier`. Ne becomes n’ before a vowel or mute h. This pattern describes pas and similar adverbs, not every negative expression.

Change the second word to change the meaning: `Je n’ai jamais reçu de réponse` (I have never received an answer), `Le guichet n’accepte plus les espèces` (The counter no longer accepts cash), `Je n’ai rien reçu` (I received nothing). Jamais, plus, and object rien normally go before the participle; object personne goes after it: `Je n’ai vu personne` (I saw nobody). Do not add pas to these ordinary negatives. Two negatives can reinforce each other rather than cancel out: `Je n’ai jamais rien reçu` (I have never received anything).

As subjects, personne and rien come before ne and a singular verb: `Personne n’a répondu` (Nobody answered), `Rien n’a changé` (Nothing has changed). `Ne… que` instead restricts, meaning only: `Je n’ai que deux copies` (I have only two copies). The position of que identifies what is restricted. `Ni… ni` joins excluded alternatives: `Je ne bois ni café ni thé` (I drink neither coffee nor tea).

Before an infinitive, `ne pas` stays together: `Ne pas déranger`, `Ne pas fumer`. An imperative is equally grammatical on a sign: `Ne dérangez pas`, `Ne fumez pas`. The choice is a matter of presentation, not a rule banning commands from signs. An object `personne` follows the past participle: `Je n’ai vu personne`. The more formal `ne… guère` means hardly, and `ne… nullement` means not at all. Dropping `ne` is common in relaxed speech and informal messages, but keep it in formal letters and exam prose. Finally, use `si` to contradict a negative question or statement.
points: Write `ne` before the pronouns and the conjugated verb.
Place pas, jamais, plus, guère, or nullement after the conjugated verb or auxiliary; do not extend that placement to object personne.
Keep `ne pas` together in front of an infinitive: `Ne pas déranger`, `Ne pas fumer`.
Place `personne` after the past participle when it is the object.
Keep `ne` in formal writing; distinguish that register choice from informal speech or messages.
Use `si` when contradicting a negative question or statement.

examples.french: Nous ne pouvons pas venir ce soir, et je ne t’attends pas après dix-huit heures.
examples.english: We cannot come this evening, and I am not waiting for you after six o’clock.
examples.note: Simple tenses, with the object pronoun inside the negation.

examples.french: Je n’ai pas mangé et je ne suis pas allé en France le mois dernier.
examples.english: I have not eaten and I did not go to France last month.
examples.note: In compound tenses the second element follows the auxiliary, whatever the auxiliary.

examples.french: Sur la porte, on lit « Ne pas déranger » et, dans le hall, « Ne pas fumer ».
examples.english: On the door it reads “Do not disturb” and, in the lobby, “No smoking”.
examples.note: Before an infinitive the two negative words stand together.

examples.french: Le service n’a guère de personnel cette semaine et n’accepte nullement les retards.
examples.english: The department has hardly any staff this week and does not tolerate lateness at all.
examples.note: « Ne… guère » and « ne… nullement » belong to a formal register.

examples.french: Dans une lettre officielle, j’écris « Je ne parle pas français » ; dans un message familier, on peut lire « Je parle pas français ».
examples.english: In an official letter I write “I do not speak French”; in an informal message you may see the same statement without ne.
examples.note: Both quoted French forms mean I do not speak French. The distinction is formal versus informal usage, not simply writing versus speech.

examples.french: Vous n’avez pas encore soumis le formulaire ? Si, je l’ai soumis ce matin.
examples.english: Have you not submitted the form yet? Yes, I submitted it this morning.
examples.note: « Si » contradicts a negative question.

mistakes.avoid: Je le ne connais pas et je ne l’ai jamais vu.
mistakes.prefer: Je ne le connais pas et je ne l’ai jamais vu.
mistakes.why: The object pronoun belongs between `ne` and the verb, not before `ne`.

mistakes.avoid: Il a ne pas répondu à ma demande.
mistakes.prefer: Il n’a pas répondu à ma demande.
mistakes.why: In a compound tense, `ne` precedes the auxiliary and `pas` follows it.

mistakes.avoid: Sur la porte, on lit « Ne pas dérangez » comme consigne générale.
mistakes.prefer: Sur la porte, on lit « Ne pas déranger » comme consigne générale.
mistakes.why: Use the infinitive after `ne pas`: `Ne pas déranger`. The imperative `Ne dérangez pas` is another correct option.

vocabulary.example: Je ne connais pas encore la décision du comité.
vocabulary.note: Basic frame; `ne` precedes the verb group, `pas` follows the conjugated verb.

vocabulary.example: Elle n’a jamais manqué une séance de formation.
vocabulary.note: Rules out every occurrence; same placement as `ne… pas`.

vocabulary.example: Le guichet n’accepte plus les paiements en espèces.
vocabulary.note: Marks a situation that has stopped.

vocabulary.example: Ce rapport n’apporte guère d’éléments nouveaux.
vocabulary.note: Formal register; close in meaning to `presque pas`.

vocabulary.english: not at all, in no way
vocabulary.example: La municipalité n’est nullement responsable de ce retard.
vocabulary.note: Formal register; stronger than `pas du tout` in writing.

vocabulary.example: Un portail sécurisé permet de suivre l’état de sa demande.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; also means a gate.

practice.prompt: Write the sign meaning “no smoking”, then say formally that you did not walk in the forest.
practice.hint: An infinitive sign, then a compound tense.
practice.answer: Ne pas fumer. Je n’ai pas marché dans la forêt.

takeaways: `Ne` hugs the verb group; the second word follows the conjugated verb.
`Ne pas` stands together in front of an infinitive, as on signs.
Keep `ne` in formal prose; both infinitive and imperative instructions are valid on signs.
`Si` is the yes that contradicts a negative.

lessons.title: Répondre avec « moi aussi », « moi non plus » et « moi, si »
lessons.summary: Echo an affirmative statement with moi aussi and a negative statement with moi non plus. Distinguish sharing the same situation from contrasting your own situation with Moi, non or Moi, si. Grammatical affirmation is not the same thing as a positive feeling.
objectives: Identify whether the first statement is positive or negative.
Respond with the matching stressed pronoun and particle.
Add a second excluded element with `non plus`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Whether a statement affirms or denies is called its polarity. In a standard short reply expressing the same situation, echo a positive statement with `aussi` and a negative one with `non plus`. Put the stressed pronoun first in these models: `moi aussi`, `toi non plus`, `eux aussi`.

The same pattern works inside a sentence when you add another person. After a positive clause: `Elle participe à l’atelier, et son conjoint aussi`. After a negative clause: `Elle n’utilise pas la voiture, et son conjoint non plus`. English uses too and either; for a clear standard short reply meaning me neither, use `moi non plus`.

Judge the grammatical statement, not whether the feeling is positive: `Je déteste attendre. — Moi aussi` (I hate waiting. — So do I). Nor does every ne signal denial: `Je n’ai que deux jours de congé. — Moi aussi` (I have only two days off. — So do I) uses restrictive ne… que. To contrast your situation instead of agreeing, use `Moi, non` after an affirmative statement, or `Moi, si` after a negative one: `Je ne travaille pas demain. — Moi, si` (I am not working tomorrow. — I am).
points: Read the first statement and label it positive or negative.
Echo a positive statement with `aussi`.
Echo a negative statement with `non plus`.
Start with the stressed pronoun: `moi`, `toi`, `lui`, `elle`, `nous`, `vous`, `eux`, `elles`.
Use `non plus` to add a second excluded element after a negative clause.

examples.french: Je participe à l’atelier du samedi. — Moi aussi !
examples.english: I go to the Saturday workshop. — So do I!
examples.note: Positive statement echoed with « aussi ».

examples.french: Je ne peux pas travailler dimanche. — Moi non plus !
examples.english: I cannot work on Sunday. — Neither can I!
examples.note: Negative statement echoed with « non plus ».

examples.french: Elle n’utilise pas la voiture, et son conjoint non plus.
examples.english: She does not use the car, and neither does her partner.
examples.note: A second excluded element inside the same sentence.

examples.french: Il a déposé sa demande en ligne, et sa sœur aussi.
examples.english: He submitted his application online, and so did his sister.
examples.note: A second included element after a positive clause.

examples.french: Nous n’avons pas reçu la confirmation. — Nous non plus.
examples.english: We have not received the confirmation. — Neither have we.
examples.note: The stressed pronoun comes first.

mistakes.avoid: Je n’ai pas compris la consigne. — Moi aussi.
mistakes.prefer: Je n’ai pas compris la consigne. — Moi non plus.
mistakes.why: For the standard short reply meaning I did not understand either, echo the negative statement with non plus.

mistakes.avoid: Elle n’aime pas les longues réunions, et son collègue aussi.
mistakes.prefer: Elle n’aime pas les longues réunions, et son collègue non plus.
mistakes.why: The added element is also excluded, so it takes `non plus`.

vocabulary.example: Je ne travaille pas le dimanche. — Moi non plus.
vocabulary.note: Reply used only after a negative statement.

vocabulary.example: Je suis un cours du soir. — Moi aussi.
vocabulary.note: Reply used only after a positive statement.

vocabulary.example: Un conjoint peut accompagner le demandeur à l’entrevue.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; feminine `une conjointe`.

vocabulary.example: Un horaire de fin de semaine ne convient pas à tout le monde.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun despite its final -e.

practice.prompt: Reply agreeing: « Je n’ai pas encore reçu ma carte. » then « J’ai déjà pris rendez-vous. »
practice.hint: Opposite polarities require opposite particles.
practice.answer: Moi non plus. / Moi aussi.

takeaways: Positive equals `aussi`; negative equals `non plus`.
In the short reply models here, place the stressed pronoun first.
`Non plus` also adds a second excluded element.
keywords: agreeing with positive and negative statements

modules.title: Le temps, le lieu et les prépositions
modules.description: Express origins, destinations, location, transport and duration; choose prepositions and the verb mood after time conjunctions.

lessons.title: Les pays, les régions, les villes et l’origine
lessons.summary: Most cities use à/de, but articles within names produce forms such as à La Rochelle and au/du Havre. Country prepositions usually follow gender, number, and initial sound: en France, au Canada, aux États-Unis. Learn regional usage as well: dans le Yorkshire, au Texas, en Californie. An -e ending is only a gender hint, not a guarantee.
objectives: Store each country name together with its article.
Derive the location and origin forms from gender, number, and initial sound.
Recall the four frequent masculine countries ending in `-e`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Cities normally take no article, so both location and destination use à Montréal, while origin uses de Montréal. Most country names have a usual article, and gender and number guide their prepositions: feminine singular generally gives en/de; masculine singular gives au/du; plural gives aux/des. Masculine vowel-initial names take en, as in en Iran and en Israël; their origin forms are d’Iran and d’Israël. De becomes d’ before a vowel or silent h. Some country names normally lack an article: à Cuba / de Cuba, but en Israël / d’Israël. Learn these established constructions rather than inventing an article.

The -e ending is a strong hint of a feminine country (la France, la Suisse, la Belgique, la Roumanie) but not a guarantee: le Mexique, le Cambodge, le Mozambique, and le Zimbabwe are masculine and take au. Many Canadian provincial constructions are analogous: au Québec, en Ontario, en Colombie-Britannique. For ordinary origin, de before a feminine country usually has no article: Je viens de France.
points: Learn the country with its article: `la France`, `le Canada`, `les États-Unis`.
Use `en` and `de/d’` for a feminine country or a masculine one starting with a vowel: en France / de France; en Italie / d’Italie; en Iran / d’Iran.
Use `au` and `du` for other masculine countries.
Use `aux` and `des` for plural country names.
Memorise `le Mexique`, `le Cambodge`, `le Mozambique`, `le Zimbabwe` as masculine exceptions.
Distinguish au Québec / du Québec (the province) from à Québec / de Québec (Quebec City).

examples.french: J’habite au Canada et je travaille à Montréal.
examples.english: I live in Canada and work in Montreal.
examples.note: Masculine country with « au », city with « à ».

examples.french: Elle va en France pour poursuivre ses études de droit.
examples.english: She is going to France to continue her law studies.
examples.note: Feminine country with « en ».

examples.french: Je viens du Sénégal et ma collègue vient du Mexique.
examples.english: I come from Senegal and my colleague comes from Mexico.
examples.note: « Le Mexique » is masculine despite its -e ending.

examples.french: Ils sont revenus des États-Unis après une conférence de trois jours.
examples.english: They came back from the United States after a three-day conference.
examples.note: Plural country name with « des ».

examples.french: Nous nous sommes installés en Ontario avant de déménager au Québec.
examples.english: We settled in Ontario before moving to Quebec.
examples.note: Learn the established provincial forms en Ontario and au Québec.

mistakes.avoid: Je vais au France pour trois semaines.
mistakes.prefer: Je vais en France pour trois semaines.
mistakes.why: `La France` is feminine, so location and destination take `en`.

mistakes.avoid: Elle arrive de le Mexique demain matin.
mistakes.prefer: Elle arrive du Mexique demain matin.
mistakes.why: `Le Mexique` is masculine, and `de + le` must contract to `du`.

sections.title: Articles inside city names and regional usage
paragraphs: The city rule à/de has exceptions when an article belongs to the name. Keep La in à La Rochelle and de La Rochelle. With Le Havre, contract à + Le to au and de + Le to du: au Havre, du Havre. The uncontracted city name still has its capital: Le Havre.

Region and state names have established constructions, not one rule covering every masculine region. Learn dans le Yorkshire, au Texas, en Californie, and en Ontario in context. Dans le Yorkshire describes location within the region; it is not restricted to entering a building. Gender helps, but does not by itself predict every regional preposition.
points: Keep an article that belongs to a city name and apply the appropriate contraction.
Learn a region together with its established prepositional phrase.

examples.french: Elle vient de La Rochelle et travaille maintenant au Havre.
examples.english: She comes from La Rochelle and now works in Le Havre.
examples.note: La stays separate; à + Le contracts to au.

examples.french: Le train revient du Havre avant de repartir vers La Rochelle.
examples.english: The train returns from Le Havre before leaving again towards La Rochelle.
examples.note: De + Le contracts to du; vers does not make that contraction.

examples.french: Sa famille vit dans le Yorkshire; lui a travaillé au Texas puis en Californie.
examples.english: His family lives in Yorkshire; he worked in Texas and then in California.
examples.note: Three established regional constructions; a masculine name does not always take au.

mistakes.avoid: Elle travaille à Le Havre.
mistakes.prefer: Elle travaille au Havre.
mistakes.why: À and the article Le contract in this city name.

mistakes.avoid: Il revient de le Havre.
mistakes.prefer: Il revient du Havre.
mistakes.why: De and Le contract to du.

vocabulary.example: La France accueille chaque année de nombreux étudiants étrangers.
vocabulary.note: Feminine country; `en France`, `de France`.

vocabulary.example: Le Mexique attire les voyageurs pour son patrimoine archéologique.
vocabulary.note: Masculine even though it ends in -e; `au Mexique`, `du Mexique`.

vocabulary.example: Les États-Unis partagent une longue frontière avec le Canada.
vocabulary.note: Masculine plural; `aux États-Unis`, `des États-Unis`.

vocabulary.example: Le Québec offre des cours de français gratuits aux nouveaux arrivants.
vocabulary.note: Masculine; `au Québec` for the province, `à Québec` for the city.

practice.prompt: Complete: « Il vient ___ Portugal, il travaille ___ Belgique et il retourne ___ Philippines l’an prochain. »
practice.hint: Masculine, feminine, plural.
practice.answer: Il vient du Portugal, il travaille en Belgique et il retourne aux Philippines l’an prochain.

takeaways: Most cities: à/de; preserve or contract an article within a name, as in à La Rochelle and au Havre.
Typical country patterns: feminine en/de; masculine au/du, but vowel-initial en/de; plural aux/des.
Regional prepositions also depend on established usage, not gender alone.
`Le Mexique`, `le Cambodge`, `le Mozambique`, `le Zimbabwe` break the `-e` pattern.
keywords: Le Havre, du Havre, de La Rochelle, en Ontario

lessons.title: Les lieux, les destinations et « chez »
lessons.summary: `Chez` commonly names someone’s home or workplace: `chez ma tante`, `chez le coiffeur`, `chez elle`. It can also introduce a company name or mean among a group. To name an establishment directly, use `à` with its article: `à la piscine`, `à la banque`, `à la boulangerie`, `au théâtre`, `aux toilettes`. `Dans` often marks an interior; `en` appears in fixed expressions such as `en ville`. Position words include `sous`, `sur`, `devant`, `derrière`, `à côté de`, `en face de`, `au fond de`, `à l’intérieur de`, and `en dehors de`.
objectives: Distinguish chez with people, trades, or company names from à plus an establishment.
Contract the article correctly in a destination.
Use the frequent position words, including their `de`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: `Chez` commonly refers to someone’s home or workplace: `chez ma tante`, `chez le coiffeur`, `chez le médecin`, `chez nous`. When you name an establishment such as a pool or bank directly, use `à` with its article: `à la piscine`, `à la banque`, `à la boulangerie`, `au théâtre`, `au concert`, `au magasin`, `au spectacle`, `au musée`, `aux toilettes`. Thus `chez le boulanger` and `à la boulangerie` can describe the same errand. The use of `chez` is broader than individual people: `travailler chez Renault` names a company, and `une habitude fréquente chez les jeunes` means a habit common among young people. `Dans` can name a physical interior (`dans le bureau`, `dans le tiroir`); learn `en` through common fixed expressions (`en ville`, `en classe`, `en réunion`, `en ligne`) rather than assuming it always excludes an article.

Position words are learned as blocks, and several keep a `de` that contracts: `sous la table`, `sur le comptoir`, `devant la mairie`, `derrière l’immeuble`, `à côté de la fenêtre`, `en face de l’ascenseur`, `au fond du couloir`, `à l’intérieur du tiroir`, `au bout de la rue`, `en arrière`. Two of them have a second, figurative life. `Au fond de` is physical (`au fond de la boîte`), but standalone `au fond` means deep down or in reality (`Au fond, la démarche est simple`), and it can also mean at the back of a room. `En dehors de` is literally outside (`en dehors du bâtiment`) and figuratively apart from (`en dehors de cette réserve, le dossier est complet`).

One pair of prepositions has to be separated by meaning rather than by translation, because English *before* covers both. `Avant` and `après` situate something in time: `Mon rendez-vous est avant le vôtre`, `Après la réunion, nous irons au bureau des inscriptions`. `Devant` and `derrière` situate something in space: `Je suis assis devant vous dans la salle d’attente`, `Le stationnement se trouve derrière l’immeuble`. Using `avant` for a physical position, as in a word-for-word rendering of *he is sitting before me*, is one of the most recognisable English-speaker errors in French.
points: Use `chez` plus a person, a stressed pronoun, or a trade: `chez ma tante`, `chez le coiffeur`.
Use `à la`, `au`, `à l’`, or `aux` plus the place: `à la piscine`, `au théâtre`, `aux toilettes`.
Compare a physical interior (`dans le bureau`) with a fixed contextual expression (`en réunion`).
Keep the `de` inside `à côté de`, `en face de`, `au fond de`, `à l’intérieur de`, `en dehors de`.
Standalone `au fond` can mean fundamentally/deep down, at the back, or at the bottom when the place is understood: Le sac est ouvert ; les clés sont au fond.
Read `en dehors de` as literally outside or figuratively apart from.
Use `avant` and `après` for time, `devant` and `derrière` for space.

examples.french: Je vais chez ma tante, puis chez le coiffeur avant d’aller à la banque.
examples.english: I am going to my aunt’s, then to the hairdresser’s, before going to the bank.
examples.note: « Chez » for a person and a trade, « à la » for the establishment.

examples.french: Les enfants sont à la piscine et les parents sont au théâtre.
examples.english: The children are at the pool and the parents are at the theatre.
examples.note: « À + la » and « à + le » contracted to « au ».

examples.french: Les toilettes sont au fond du couloir, à côté de l’ascenseur.
examples.english: The toilets are at the end of the corridor, next to the lift.
examples.note: Two position phrases, each keeping its « de ».

examples.french: L’araignée est sous le banc, derrière la boîte posée devant la porte.
examples.english: The spider is under the bench, behind the box placed in front of the door.
examples.note: Three position words in one sentence: sous, derrière, devant.

examples.french: Le dossier est à l’intérieur du tiroir, en dehors du classeur principal.
examples.english: The file is inside the drawer, outside the main binder.
examples.note: « En dehors de » in its literal sense.

examples.french: Au fond, la démarche est simple : en dehors de cette pièce manquante, tout est prêt.
examples.english: Basically, the procedure is simple: apart from this missing document, everything is ready.
examples.note: Figurative uses of « au fond » and « en dehors de ».

examples.french: Mon rendez-vous est avant le vôtre, et je suis assis devant vous dans la salle d’attente.
examples.english: My appointment is before yours, and I am sitting in front of you in the waiting room.
examples.note: « Avant » in time, « devant » in space, in the same sentence.

examples.french: Après la réunion, nous irons au bureau des inscriptions situé derrière l’immeuble.
examples.english: After the meeting, we will go to the registration office located behind the building.
examples.note: « Après » in time, « derrière » in space.

mistakes.avoid: Je vais chez la piscine avec les enfants.
mistakes.prefer: Je vais à la piscine avec les enfants.
mistakes.why: Here la piscine names an establishment, so use à la piscine. Chez commonly introduces a person or professional, and also has broader uses such as chez Renault and chez les jeunes.

mistakes.avoid: Elle attend dans la salle d’attente en face du ascenseur.
mistakes.prefer: Elle attend dans la salle d’attente en face de l’ascenseur.
mistakes.why: `De` does not contract before an elided `l’`.

mistakes.avoid: Le formulaire est au fond de, dans le tiroir.
mistakes.prefer: Le formulaire est au fond du tiroir.
mistakes.why: `Au fond de` needs a complement. If the drawer is already identified, Le formulaire est au fond is also possible: au fond then means at its back or bottom.

mistakes.avoid: Il est assis devant de moi dans la salle d’attente.
mistakes.prefer: Il est assis devant moi dans la salle d’attente.
mistakes.why: Devant takes the stressed pronoun directly, without de. It describes spatial position.

mistakes.avoid: Derrière le rendez-vous, j’ai rempli le formulaire à l’accueil.
mistakes.prefer: Après le rendez-vous, j’ai rempli le formulaire à l’accueil.
mistakes.why: `Derrière` is spatial; what follows an event in time is introduced by `après`.

sections.title: Against, beside, and on the other side
paragraphs: Contre can describe contact with a surface, opposition to an idea, or the opposing player or team in a game. Its complement follows directly: contre le mur, contre cette proposition, contre une autre équipe. It does not by itself mean beside.

À côté de means beside or next to. De l’autre côté de means on the other side of a boundary or space: de l’autre côté de la rue, de l’autre côté du fleuve. Keep both instances of de in the phrase; the final de contracts with le to du. En face de focuses on being opposite or facing something, while de l’autre côté de identifies the intervening street, river, or other boundary.
points: Read contre as contact, opposition, or an opponent according to context.
À côté de is beside; de l’autre côté de places a boundary between the locations.

examples.french: Le vélo est appuyé contre le mur.
examples.english: The bicycle is leaning against the wall.
examples.note: Contre describes physical contact.

examples.french: Je suis contre cette proposition, mais je veux en discuter.
examples.english: I oppose this proposal, but I want to discuss it.
examples.note: Contre introduces an idea opposed.

examples.french: Notre équipe joue contre celle du quartier voisin.
examples.english: Our team is playing against the team from the neighbouring district.
examples.note: Contre introduces the sporting opponent.

examples.french: La pharmacie est à côté de la banque, mais l’école est de l’autre côté de la rue.
examples.english: The pharmacy is next to the bank, but the school is across the street.
examples.note: Beside contrasts with across a boundary.

examples.french: Ils habitent de l’autre côté du fleuve.
examples.english: They live on the other side of the river.
examples.note: Un fleuve (m.) is a river flowing to the sea; de + le becomes du.

mistakes.avoid: Notre équipe joue contre de l’autre équipe.
mistakes.prefer: Notre équipe joue contre l’autre équipe.
mistakes.why: Contre introduces the opponent directly; no de is needed.

mistakes.avoid: Ils habitent de l’autre côté de le fleuve.
mistakes.prefer: Ils habitent de l’autre côté du fleuve.
mistakes.why: The final de contracts with le to du.

sections.title: Inside it, and at the post office
paragraphs: `Dedans` means inside or in it when the container or place is already understood. Unlike ordinary `dans`, it normally stands without a following noun complement: `dans le sac`, but `Le sac est ouvert ; mets le document dedans`. It can describe a position or a destination.

`La poste (f.)` can name the post office as a place for postal services; `un bureau de poste (m.)` is an explicit name for a particular branch. `Aller à la poste` is a physical errand, whereas `envoyer quelque chose par la poste` describes sending something by post.
points: Name the container after `dans`; use standalone `dedans` when it has already been identified.
Distinguish a destination (`à la poste`) from a delivery method (`par la poste`).

examples.french: Tu vois le sac bleu ? Mes documents sont dedans.
examples.english: Do you see the blue bag? My documents are inside it.
examples.note: The bag supplies the understood container.

examples.french: Voici l’enveloppe ; mets la lettre dedans.
examples.english: Here is the envelope; put the letter inside it.
examples.note: A destination, with no repeated noun after `dedans`.

examples.french: La boîte est vide ; il n’y a rien dedans.
examples.english: The box is empty; there is nothing inside.
examples.note: A location rather than an action.

examples.french: Je vais à la poste pour envoyer cette lettre.
examples.english: I am going to the post office to send this letter.
examples.note: The post office is a physical destination.

examples.french: Le bureau de poste est encore ouvert ; mon frère est dedans.
examples.english: The post office is still open; my brother is inside.
examples.note: The understood interior is now a building.

mistakes.avoid: La lettre est dans de l’enveloppe.
mistakes.prefer: La lettre est dans l’enveloppe. / L’enveloppe est là ; la lettre est dedans.
mistakes.why: Dans introduces the noun complement directly, without de. Dedans normally stands alone in neutral modern French; dedans followed by a noun also occurs in familiar or older usage.

vocabulary.example: Une piscine municipale ouvre gratuitement le dimanche matin.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `à la piscine` for the destination.

vocabulary.example: Un coiffeur du quartier accepte les rendez-vous en ligne.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `chez le coiffeur` because it names a person.

vocabulary.example: Une boîte d’archives est rangée sous le comptoir.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; also means a nightclub in familiar speech.

vocabulary.example: Une araignée s’est installée derrière le banc du jardin.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; useful in describing a position.

vocabulary.example: Un banc en bois se trouve devant l’entrée du parc.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; the final `c` is silent.

vocabulary.example: Un plafond bas rend la salle plus sombre.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; the opposite of `le plancher`, the floor surface.

vocabulary.example: Un musée régional propose une entrée gratuite le premier dimanche du mois.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun despite its final -e; `au musée` for the destination.

vocabulary.example: En dehors du bâtiment, le stationnement est payant.
vocabulary.note: Literal and figurative; the article contracts after `de`.

practice.prompt: Complete: « Je passe ___ le dentiste, puis ___ la banque, et j’attends ___ la salle, ___ de la fenêtre. »
practice.hint: Person, establishment, bounded interior, position word.
practice.answer: Je passe chez le dentiste, puis à la banque, et j’attends dans la salle, à côté de la fenêtre.

takeaways: `Chez` commonly introduces a person’s home or workplace; `à la`, `au`, `aux` introduce establishments directly.
Learn location phrases as complete chunks: `dans le bureau`, `en réunion`, `chez le médecin`, `à la banque`.
Position words keep their `de`; `au fond` and `en dehors de` also have figurative uses.
`Avant`/`après` order time; `devant`/`derrière` order space.
keywords: contre, de l’autre côté de, de l'autre côté de
dedans, dans, la poste, un bureau de poste

lessons.title: Les transports et les adresses
lessons.summary: Learn transport phrases such as à pied, à vélo, à cheval, en voiture, en autobus, en métro, en train, and en avion. The astride/inside distinction is a useful guide, not a universal rule; en vélo and en moto also occur. Dans le bus identifies the vehicle containing you. Getting off uses descendre de, with normal articles and contractions.
objectives: Produce the transport chunks without translating word by word.
Separate the means of transport from being inside a vehicle.
Use `monter dans` and `descendre de` with the right article.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A means of transport answers how you travel. Learn the usual phrases without an article: `à pied`, `à vélo`, `à cheval`, `à moto`; `en voiture`, `en autobus`, `en métro`, `en train`, `en avion`, `en taxi`. The idea of sitting astride something versus being inside helps you remember many of them, but it is not an absolute rule: en tandem is established usage. En vélo and en moto also occur widely, including in dictionaries; à vélo and à moto remain safe choices in careful writing because some authorities still criticise the en forms.

When the point is not how you travel but where you physically are, the chunk disappears and an ordinary preposition returns with its article: `Nous sommes dans le bus qui dessert le centre-ville`. Boarding and alighting use their own verbs: `monter dans` plus article, `descendre de` plus article, with contraction where required: `monter dans le train`, `descendre du train`, `descendre de l’autobus`. For an address, both `J’habite rue Pasteur` and `J’habite dans la rue Pasteur` occur, the first being the neutral administrative form.
points: Learn `à pied`, `à vélo`, and `à cheval`; use `en` in the listed vehicle phrases rather than applying a universal enclosure rule.
Leave out the article inside a transport chunk.
Switch to `dans le` or `dans la` when you mean physically inside.
Use `monter dans` and `descendre de`, contracting `de + le` to `du`.

Without a house number: J’habite rue Pasteur / dans la rue Pasteur. With a number: J’habite au 12, rue Pasteur. The no-preposition pattern also works with une avenue (f.) and un boulevard (m.): J’habite avenue Victor-Hugo / boulevard Saint-Michel.

examples.french: Je vais au travail en autobus et je reviens à pied.
examples.english: I go to work by bus and walk back.
examples.note: Two frozen transport chunks with no article.

examples.french: Nous sommes dans le bus qui dessert le centre-ville.
examples.english: We are on the bus that serves downtown.
examples.note: Dans le bus identifies the particular vehicle containing us; en bus would identify how we are travelling.

examples.french: Les passagers sont descendus du train à la gare centrale.
examples.english: The passengers got off the train at the central station.
examples.note: « Descendre de » with the contracted article.

examples.french: Elle prend le métro tous les matins, sauf quand elle circule à vélo.
examples.english: She takes the subway every morning, except when she cycles.
examples.note: « Prendre » plus the article, contrasted with the chunk « à vélo ».

examples.french: J’habite rue Pasteur, à deux pas de l’arrêt d’autobus.
examples.english: I live on rue Pasteur, a stone’s throw from the bus stop.
examples.note: Standard address form without a preposition before « rue ».

mistakes.avoid: Je vais au travail en pied quand il fait beau.
mistakes.prefer: Je vais au travail à pied quand il fait beau.
mistakes.why: `À pied` is the fixed expression for on foot; the choice cannot be derived from English by.

mistakes.avoid: Les passagers sont descendus de le train à Laval.
mistakes.prefer: Les passagers sont descendus du train à Laval.
mistakes.why: `De + le` must contract to `du`.

vocabulary.example: Un autobus express relie la banlieue au centre-ville en vingt minutes.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun used in Canada; `un bus` is the common form in France.

vocabulary.example: Une gare rénovée facilite les correspondances entre le train et le métro.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; a bus terminal is `une gare routière`.

vocabulary.english: to get off, to get out of
vocabulary.example: Je descends de l’autobus à l’arrêt suivant.
vocabulary.note: Takes `être` when intransitive; the article contracts after `de`.

vocabulary.example: La rue principale devient piétonne pendant le marché du samedi.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; an address is normally written without a preposition.

practice.prompt: Complete: « Elle voyage ___ train, mais aujourd’hui elle est ___ le train de 8 h et elle descendra ___ train à Laval. »
practice.hint: Chunk, physical location, then a contraction.
practice.answer: Elle voyage en train, mais aujourd’hui elle est dans le train de 8 h et elle descendra du train à Laval.

takeaways: `À pied`, `à vélo`; `en autobus`, `en voiture`, `en métro`.
No article in the chunk; `dans le` when you are inside.
`Descendre de` plus a contracted article.

lessons.title: Les moments, les durées et les échéances
lessons.summary: Use `à` for clock time. `Depuis` links an ongoing situation to its starting point; `depuis que` introduces a clause. `Pendant` states a bounded span; `pour` an intended span; `en` the time needed to complete something; `dans` a delay before an event; `il y a` means ago. `À partir de` opens a range and `jusqu’à` closes it. A measured value uses `de` in `Le loyer est de 900 $`. Distinguish `en avance` (ahead of schedule), `à l’heure` (on schedule), `en retard` (late), and `à temps` (before it is too late).
objectives: Separate a starting point, a bounded span, and an intended span.
Distinguish the completion time `en` from the future delay `dans`.
Use `depuis` with the imperfect and `depuis que` with a clause.
Insert `de` between `être` and a measured amount.
Frame a range with `à partir de` and `jusqu’à`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: English uses for and in across several distinct relationships, so choose the French preposition by meaning. `Depuis` connects a continuing situation to its starting point or elapsed duration, normally with the present: `J’habite au Québec depuis cinq ans`. `Pendant` measures a bounded span, whether past, habitual, or future: `Nous avons discuté pendant deux heures` (we talked for two hours); `Demain, je travaillerai pendant deux heures` (tomorrow, I will work for two hours). `Pour` announces an intended span: `Je suis ici pour deux semaines` (I am here for two weeks).

Three further contrasts complete the set. `En` states how long an action takes to complete: `J’ai rempli le formulaire en dix minutes`. `Dans` places a future event after a delay: `Votre permis sera envoyé dans cinq jours ouvrables`. `Il y a` counts backwards from now: `J’ai déposé ma demande il y a trois jours`. For a range, `à partir de` opens it and `jusqu’à` closes it: `Le service est ouvert à partir de neuf heures jusqu’à dix-sept heures`.

With the imperfect, `depuis` describes a situation that was still ongoing at a past moment: `J’attendais une réponse depuis six semaines quand le courriel est arrivé` (I had been waiting for an answer for six weeks when the email arrived). Do not mechanically copy the English perfect into French. A compound tense is nevertheless possible with depuis when it reports completed events within the period (`J’ai envoyé trois messages depuis lundi` — I have sent three messages since Monday), or no event within it (`Je n’ai pas reçu de réponse depuis lundi` — I have not received an answer since Monday). `Depuis que` introduces a clause with a subject and verb in the indicative: `Depuis que le règlement a changé, les délais sont plus courts`.

Two fixed patterns complete the topic. In careful writing, a measured value after `être` uses `de`: `Le loyer est de 900 $ par mois`, `Le délai de traitement est de trente jours ouvrables`, `Les frais de dossier sont de 85 $`. Punctuality then requires a distinction of meaning: `être en avance` means ahead of schedule, `être à l’heure` means on schedule, and `être en retard` means late. `À temps` means in time, before it is too late to do something; it is not universally interchangeable with `à l’heure`, but it is not an error. `Je serai à temps pour le rendez-vous` stresses not being too late, while `Je serai à l’heure` stresses punctuality. The fixed phrase `à l’heure` includes the definite article `l’`. A measured delay can be expressed as `L’autobus avait dix minutes de retard`, `Je suis arrivé avec dix minutes de retard`, or `Je suis en retard de dix minutes`.
points: Use `à` plus the hour for clock time: `à neuf heures`.
Use `depuis` with the present when the situation still holds.
Use `depuis` with the imperfect when the situation still held at a past moment.
Use `depuis que` plus a clause when the starting point is an event rather than a duration.
