Use `il se peut que` plus the subjunctive for an open possibility.
Separate `douter de` (to be unsure) from `se douter de` (to suspect it is true).

examples.french: La demande sera peut-être traitée avant vendredi.
examples.english: The application will perhaps be processed before Friday.
examples.note: Neutral position, after the conjugated verb.

examples.french: Peut-être que le service rouvrira la semaine prochaine.
examples.english: Perhaps the service will reopen next week.
examples.note: Peut-être que keeps the ordinary subject–verb order; do not add inversion after que.

examples.french: Peut-être viendra-t-il en personne déposer le dossier.
examples.english: Perhaps he will come in person to submit the file.
examples.note: Formal alternative: inversion instead of « que ».

examples.french: — Le bureau est-il ouvert samedi ? — Peut-être pas ; je vous conseille d’appeler.
examples.english: “Is the office open on Saturday?” “Perhaps not; I would advise you to call.”
examples.note: « Peut-être pas » is the fixed short negative answer.

examples.french: Il se peut que le délai soit prolongé, mais ce retard est sans doute temporaire.
examples.english: The deadline may be extended, but this delay is probably temporary.
examples.note: « Il se peut que » takes the subjunctive; « sans doute » means probably.

examples.french: Je doute de l’exactitude de ce chiffre, mais je me doutais déjà du résultat.
examples.english: I doubt this figure is accurate, but I already suspected the result.
examples.note: « Douter de » to be unsure, « se douter de » to suspect it is true.

mistakes.avoid: Peut-être qu’il viendra-t-il demain matin.
mistakes.prefer: Peut-être qu’il viendra demain matin.
mistakes.why: Choose que with ordinary word order, or inversion without que: Peut-être viendra-t-il demain matin. Do not combine the two constructions.

mistakes.avoid: Le bureau est-il ouvert samedi ? — Peut-être ne.
mistakes.prefer: Le bureau est-il ouvert samedi ? — Peut-être pas.
mistakes.why: Ne cannot stand alone as the negative answer. Peut-être pas is the usual expression for perhaps not.

mistakes.avoid: Je doute que de ce chiffre : il me semble trop élevé.
mistakes.prefer: Je doute de ce chiffre : il me semble trop élevé.
mistakes.why: Douter de takes a noun phrase; douter que takes a clause. Do not combine que and de before ce chiffre.

vocabulary.example: Peut-être que la décision sera annoncée cette semaine.
vocabulary.note: A standard sentence-initial form without inversion; initial peut-être with ordinary word order also occurs in conversation.

vocabulary.example: Ce retard est sans doute lié au nombre de demandes.
vocabulary.note: Often probably, but can also concede a point or express certainty in context; sans aucun doute is explicitly certain.

vocabulary.example: Il se peut que le guichet ferme plus tôt aujourd’hui.
vocabulary.note: Always followed by the subjunctive.

vocabulary.english: to doubt, to be unsure of
vocabulary.example: Je doute de la fiabilité de cette source.
vocabulary.note: `Douter que` also takes the subjunctive.

vocabulary.example: Je me doutais de sa réponse avant même de lire le courriel.
vocabulary.note: Opposite meaning to `douter de`, despite the shared root.

practice.prompt: Hedge the claim three ways: the office will perhaps close earlier today.
practice.hint: Neutral position, `peut-être que`, and formal inversion.
practice.answer: Le bureau fermera peut-être plus tôt aujourd’hui. Peut-être que le bureau fermera plus tôt aujourd’hui. Peut-être le bureau fermera-t-il plus tôt aujourd’hui.

takeaways: `Peut-être` after the verb, or first with `que` or inversion.
`Peut-être pas` is the usual short negative; sans doute often means probably, but context can give it other nuances.
`Douter de` equals unsure; `se douter de` equals suspecting it is true.

modules.title: Le sens des mots et les expressions
modules.description: Distinguish easily confused verbs and nouns, learn common constructions, understand idioms, and choose natural everyday replies and register.

lessons.title: Les tournures fréquentes avec « avoir », « faire », « il faut » et « valoir »
lessons.summary: French expresses many states with `avoir`: `avoir faim`, `avoir froid`, `avoir peur de`, `avoir besoin de`, `avoir l’air`. Both `avoir de la chance` and `avoir la chance de` can express being fortunate. Necessity uses impersonal `il faut` plus an infinitive, with the person understood from context, or `il faut que` plus a subjunctive clause. `Il me faut` and `il vous faut` name a personal need. `Il vaut mieux` gives advice, `avoir lieu` means to take place, and `faire` supplies expressions such as `faire mal` and `faire la queue`.
objectives: Use `avoir` for physical and emotional states.
Choose the right structure after `il faut` and read `il vous faut` correctly.
Use `avoir lieu` and `il vaut mieux` in their fixed forms.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Learn these word combinations as units rather than translating the English verb be. French uses `avoir faim` (be hungry), `avoir soif` (be thirsty), `avoir froid` (feel cold), `avoir sommeil` (be sleepy), `avoir raison` (be right), `avoir tort` (be wrong), `avoir peur de` (be afraid of), `avoir honte de` (be ashamed of), `avoir besoin de` (need), and `avoir envie de` (feel like/want). Their listed nouns take no article: J’ai faim, not j’ai la faim for I am hungry. `Avoir l’air` plus an adjective means look or seem, and `avoir lieu` means take place: La réunion a lieu mardi.

`Il faut` is impersonal: `il` refers to nothing. Three structures follow it. With an infinitive it states a general obligation: `Il faut remplir ce formulaire`. With an indirect pronoun and a noun it names who needs something: `il me faut deux pièces d’identité`, and `il vous faut un sac` means you need a bag, not would you like a bag. With `que` and a subjunctive it names the person concerned: `Il faut que vous fournissiez une preuve de résidence`. The related impersonal `valoir` gives advice rather than obligation: `Il vaut mieux arriver en avance`, and with `que` it also takes the subjunctive: `Il vaut mieux que vous appeliez d’abord`.

Before a verb, expressions such as `avoir peur de` take an infinitive: `J’ai peur de me perdre dans le métro`, `Vous avez peur d’échouer à l’entretien`. They can also take nouns or stressed pronouns: `avoir peur du bruit`, `avoir peur d’eux`. Learn articles with the expression. `Avoir de la chance` means to be lucky; `avoir la chance de` means to be fortunate enough to, and can also describe a favourable opportunity. Thus `Nous avons la chance d’avoir trouvé ce logement rapidement` is fully correct. The simple expressions `avoir raison` and `avoir tort` use bare nouns.

Impersonal `il faut` does not force every possessive to be generic. `Il faut ranger sa chambre avant l’inspection` can state a general rule, while `Il faut ranger ta chambre` refers to the listener’s room and leaves the person doing the tidying to context. `Il faut que tu ranges ta chambre` explicitly says that the listener must do it. Choose the possessive for the intended possessor, not mechanically from the impersonal `il`.
points: Use `avoir` plus a bare noun for states: `avoir faim`, `avoir raison`.
Add `de` before an infinitive with `avoir besoin`, `avoir envie`, `avoir peur`, `avoir honte`.
Il faut + infinitive leaves the actor to context: it can state a general rule or tell a particular person what they need to do. Il me faut partir means I need to leave.
Read `il me faut` and `il vous faut` plus a noun as a statement of need, not an offer.
Use `il faut que` and `il vaut mieux que` plus the subjunctive.
Use `avoir lieu` for an event that takes place.
Before a verb, follow `avoir peur de` with an infinitive; noun and stressed-pronoun complements are also possible.
Learn both `avoir de la chance` and `avoir la chance de`; both can express good fortune.
Choose a possessive according to its referent: `Il faut ranger sa chambre` and `Il faut ranger ta chambre` are both grammatical.
Use `il faut que` plus subjunctive to explicitly name the subject of the required action.
Distinguish Il ne faut pas entrer (You must not enter) from Il n’est pas nécessaire d’entrer (You do not need to enter): prohibiting an action is different from saying it is optional.

examples.french: Il faut remplir ce formulaire avant vendredi, et il me faut deux pièces d’identité.
examples.english: This form must be completed before Friday, and I need two pieces of identification.
examples.note: General obligation, then a personal need.

examples.french: Pour transporter ces documents, il vous faut un sac solide.
examples.english: To carry these documents, you need a sturdy bag.
examples.note: « Il vous faut » states a need; it is not an offer.

examples.french: Il faut que vous fournissiez une preuve de résidence récente.
examples.english: You must provide recent proof of residence.
examples.note: The que clause explicitly names the person who must provide the proof.

examples.french: La séance d’information a lieu mardi à la bibliothèque municipale.
examples.english: The information session takes place on Tuesday at the municipal library.
examples.note: « Avoir lieu » is the fixed expression for an event.

examples.french: Il vaut mieux arriver en avance, et il vaut mieux que vous appeliez d’abord.
examples.english: It is better to arrive early, and it is better for you to call first.
examples.note: « Il vaut mieux » plus infinitive, then plus « que » and the subjunctive.

examples.french: Elle a l’air fatiguée et le dos lui fait mal depuis ce matin.
examples.english: She looks tired and her back has been hurting since this morning.
examples.note: « Avoir l’air » plus adjective, and « faire mal » with an indirect pronoun.

examples.french: J’ai peur de me perdre dans le métro, et mon voisin a peur d’échouer à l’entretien.
examples.english: I am afraid of getting lost in the subway, and my neighbour is afraid of failing the interview.
examples.note: « Avoir peur de » is followed by an infinitive, never by an -ant form.

examples.french: Nous avons de la chance : le bureau est encore ouvert et vous avez raison de vérifier les délais.
examples.english: We are lucky: the office is still open, and you are right to check the deadlines.
examples.note: « Avoir de la chance » keeps the partitive; « avoir raison » stays bare.

examples.french: Il faut ranger ta chambre avant l’inspection ; il faut que tu ranges aussi le couloir.
examples.english: Your room needs tidying before the inspection; you also need to tidy the hallway.
examples.note: Ta is valid with an impersonal infinitive; the second clause explicitly assigns the action to tu.

examples.french: Nous avons la chance d’avoir trouvé ce logement rapidement.
examples.english: We are fortunate to have found this home quickly.
examples.note: Avoir la chance de can express good fortune, not only an opportunity.

examples.french: J’ai sommeil et j’ai envie de rentrer, mais nous devons encore faire la queue.
examples.english: I am sleepy and feel like going home, but we still have to queue.
examples.note: Avoir envie de takes an infinitive; faire la queue means stand in line. The line itself is une file d’attente (f.).

mistakes.avoid: J’ai besoin une attestation de travail.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai besoin d’une attestation de travail.
mistakes.why: `Avoir besoin` is always followed by `de` before its complement.

mistakes.avoid: Il faut que je dois partir plus tôt.
mistakes.prefer: Il faut que je parte plus tôt.
mistakes.why: `Il faut que` already carries the obligation and is followed directly by the subjunctive.

mistakes.avoid: La réunion prend lieu mardi matin.
mistakes.prefer: La réunion a lieu mardi matin.
mistakes.why: The fixed expression is `avoir lieu`; `prendre lieu` does not exist in French.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai peur de perdant mon chemin dans le quartier.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai peur de me perdre dans le quartier.
mistakes.why: To name the feared action after `avoir peur de`, use the infinitive `se perdre`, not the present participle `perdant`.

mistakes.avoid: Nous avons la chance de avoir trouvé ce logement rapidement.
mistakes.prefer: Nous avons la chance d’avoir trouvé ce logement rapidement.
mistakes.why: `De` elides before the vowel of `avoir`. The expression `avoir la chance de` is correct and means to be fortunate enough to.

mistakes.avoid: Il faut que tu range ta chambre avant chaque inspection.
mistakes.prefer: Il faut que tu ranges ta chambre avant chaque inspection.
mistakes.why: After `il faut que`, the subjunctive with `tu` is `ranges`. The possessive `ta` correctly refers to the listener’s room.

sections.title: Faire exprès: on purpose, not quickly
paragraphs: Faire exprès means do something deliberately. It can stand alone when the action is understood, or take de plus an infinitive to name it. It has nothing to do with express delivery or speed.

Compare Il a fait exprès (he did it on purpose), Il a fait exprès de partir tôt (he deliberately left early), and Il n’a pas fait exprès (he did not mean to). The last expression denies intention, not necessarily the action itself.
points: Faire exprès can stand alone or take de + infinitive.
Negating it denies deliberate intention.

examples.french: J’ai fait exprès de laisser une page blanche pour vos notes.
examples.english: I deliberately left a blank page for your notes.
examples.note: De introduces the intentional action.

examples.french: Le titre est en gros caractères; je l’ai fait exprès.
examples.english: The heading is in large print; I did that on purpose.
examples.note: The action is already known, so no infinitive is needed.

examples.french: Il a renversé son verre, mais il n’a pas fait exprès.
examples.english: He knocked over his glass, but he did not do it on purpose.
examples.note: The action occurred accidentally.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai fait exprès laisser une page blanche.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai fait exprès de laisser une page blanche.
mistakes.why: When the action is named by an infinitive, faire exprès takes de.

sections.title: Causing fear is not feeling fear
paragraphs: Faire peur à quelqu’un means frighten someone. The cause is the subject; the frightened person is introduced by à or an indirect pronoun: Ce bruit fait peur à Léa → Ce bruit lui fait peur. Avoir peur de instead makes the frightened person the subject: Léa a peur de ce bruit.
Use me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur for the person frightened. The indirect pronoun does not cause past-participle agreement: Les enfants ? Ce bruit leur a fait peur.
points: Faire peur à: the cause frightens someone.
Avoir peur de: someone feels fear of the cause.

examples.french: L’orage fait peur aux enfants.
examples.english: The storm frightens the children.
examples.note: À + les gives aux before the frightened people.

examples.french: Les enfants ont peur de l’orage.
examples.english: The children are afraid of the storm.
examples.note: The frightened people are now the subject.

examples.french: La porte a claqué et ce bruit lui a fait peur.
examples.english: The door slammed, and the noise frightened her.
examples.note: Lui is indirect; fait remains unchanged.

mistakes.avoid: Ce bruit la fait peur.
mistakes.prefer: Ce bruit lui fait peur.
mistakes.why: Faire peur à takes an indirect person pronoun, lui, not direct la.

vocabulary.example: Nous avons besoin d’une confirmation écrite avant la réunion.
vocabulary.note: Always takes `de` before a noun or an infinitive.

vocabulary.english: to be afraid of, to be afraid to
vocabulary.example: Elle a peur de manquer une étape de la procédure.
vocabulary.note: Followed by an infinitive, a noun, or a stressed pronoun: `peur d’eux`.

vocabulary.example: Vous avez de la chance : il reste une place à la séance de ce soir.
vocabulary.note: Keeps the partitive; `avoir la chance de` is also correct and means to be fortunate enough to or to have a favourable opportunity.

vocabulary.example: Le dossier a l’air complet, mais il manque une signature.
vocabulary.note: Followed by an adjective; agreement with the subject is the common usage.

vocabulary.example: L’atelier a lieu chaque premier mardi du mois.
vocabulary.note: Fixed expression; never `prendre lieu`.

vocabulary.example: Il vaut mieux déposer la demande en ligne que par la poste.
vocabulary.note: Impersonal form of `valoir`; takes an infinitive or `que` plus subjunctive.

vocabulary.english: to queue, to stand in line
vocabulary.example: Nous avons fait la queue pendant vingt minutes au guichet.
vocabulary.note: Fixed expression; `une file d’attente` is the queue itself.

vocabulary.example: Un accompagnement personnalisé facilite les premières démarches.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; the ending -ment is a masculine hint.

practice.prompt: Say that the session takes place on Thursday, that you need two documents, and that it is better to arrive early.
practice.hint: `Avoir lieu`, `il me faut`, `il vaut mieux`.
practice.answer: La séance a lieu jeudi. Il me faut deux documents. Il vaut mieux arriver en avance.

takeaways: Learn each avoir expression with its article pattern: `avoir faim`, `avoir l’air`, `avoir de la chance`.
`Il faut` plus infinitive, `il me/vous faut` plus noun, `il faut que` plus subjunctive.
`Avoir lieu` equals to take place; `il vaut mieux` gives advice.
`Avoir peur de` takes an infinitive for an action; `avoir de la chance` and `avoir la chance de` can both express good fortune.
Impersonal `il faut` allows possessives such as `ta`; use a que clause when you want to name the actor explicitly.
keywords: faire exprès, faire exprès de, faire peur à

lessons.title: Les verbes « savoir », « connaître », « croire » et « penser »
lessons.summary: Use savoir for information and learned abilities, including clauses, indirect questions, and infinitives. Connaître commonly introduces a person, place, or field of familiarity. Some information nouns allow both: savoir or connaître la réponse. Croire à often stresses reality or effectiveness; croire en stresses faith or trust. Penser à means think about or remember to.
objectives: Split `savoir` and `connaître` by the type of complement.
Use `savoir` with a question word for information.
Distinguish `croire à`, `croire en`, and `penser à`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Choose by meaning as well as by what follows the verb. Connaître describes familiarity with a person, place, or field: Je connais cette conseillère; Je connais Montréal; Je connais les services offerts. Savoir introduces information in a que clause (Je sais que le bureau ferme à midi), an indirect question (Je ne sais pas où déposer ma demande), or a learned ability with an infinitive (Je sais remplir ce formulaire). Use savoir, not connaître, for these clause and skill patterns. Information nouns can follow either verb: Je sais la réponse / Je connais la réponse (I know the answer).

`Croire à` often stresses belief in existence, reality, or effectiveness: Je crois à l’efficacité de cette mesure. `Croire en` often stresses trust or faith: Je crois en toi (I believe in you). These uses overlap with some abstract nouns; changing à to en can change emphasis rather than create an error. `Croire quelqu’un` means believe what someone says, and `croire que` introduces a belief about a situation. Penser à means have someone or something in mind: Je pense à ma prochaine entrevue. Use y for a thing; à lui / à elle makes a person reference explicit. With an infinitive, penser à can mean remember to: Pense à signer (Remember to sign).
points: Connaître commonly takes a noun or its pronoun: Je connais cette personne → Je la connais. Some information nouns also take savoir.
Use `savoir` before a clause, a question word, or an infinitive.
Read `savoir` plus infinitive as an acquired ability, not as permission.
Use `croire à` for effectiveness and `croire en` for trust.
Replace `à` plus thing with `y`, but keep `à elle` and `à lui` for people.
Use `se demander` for an internal question and `croire à` for accepting that something is real or effective.
Use `croire quelqu’un` with no preposition when you believe what a person says.

examples.french: Savez-vous remplir ce formulaire en ligne ?
examples.english: Do you know how to complete this form online?
examples.note: « Savoir » plus infinitive: an acquired ability.

examples.french: Je ne sais pas où déposer ma demande de logement.
examples.english: I do not know where to submit my housing application.
examples.note: « Savoir » plus a question word.

examples.french: Je connais bien les services offerts aux nouveaux arrivants.
examples.english: I am familiar with the services offered to newcomers.
examples.note: « Connaître » plus a noun phrase.

examples.french: Je crois en l’importance de l’éducation publique, et je crois à l’efficacité de ce programme.
examples.english: I believe in the importance of public education, and I believe this programme is effective.
examples.note: En foregrounds a conviction here; à foregrounds effectiveness. This distinction is a tendency, not a ban on overlap.

examples.french: Mon entrevue ? J’y pense souvent. La conseillère ? Je pense à elle depuis notre rencontre.
examples.english: My interview? I often think about it. The adviser? I have been thinking about her since we met.
examples.note: Y refers to the interview; à elle unambiguously refers to the adviser.

examples.french: Je me demande si le service est ouvert le samedi, mais je crois à l’efficacité du portail en ligne.
examples.english: I wonder whether the service is open on Saturdays, but I believe the online portal is effective.
examples.note: « Se demander si » introduces an indirect question; « croire à » accepts something as real or effective.

examples.french: Je le crois : son explication est cohérente et vérifiable.
examples.english: I believe him: his explanation is coherent and verifiable.
examples.note: Believing what a person says is direct, so the pronoun is « le », not « lui ».

mistakes.avoid: Je connais parler français depuis trois ans.
mistakes.prefer: Je sais parler français depuis trois ans.
mistakes.why: An acquired ability expressed by an infinitive requires `savoir`.

mistakes.avoid: Je sais cette conseillère depuis longtemps.
mistakes.prefer: Je connais cette conseillère depuis longtemps.
mistakes.why: Acquaintance with a person is expressed by `connaître` plus a noun phrase.

mistakes.avoid: Son explication est claire : je lui crois.
mistakes.prefer: Son explication est claire : je le crois.
mistakes.why: `Croire quelqu’un` is transitive, so the pronoun is `le` or `la`; `lui` would require a preposition the verb does not take.

sections.title: Apprendre can mean learning or teaching
paragraphs: When the subject acquires knowledge, `apprendre` means learn: `J’apprends le français`, `J’apprends à cuisiner`. When the subject gives someone knowledge, `apprendre quelque chose à quelqu’un` means teach someone something. For a skill, use `apprendre à quelqu’un à faire quelque chose`.

The recipient may be a noun or an indirect pronoun: `Elle apprend cette chanson aux enfants`, `Elle leur apprend cette chanson`. Context can also give the knowledge-transfer construction the meaning tell or inform, as in `Elle m’apprend la nouvelle`. `Enseigner` is a more explicitly instructional verb, especially for a school subject.
points: Without a learner receiving the teaching, `J’apprends à nager` means I am learning to swim.
With the recipient, `Je lui apprends à nager` means I am teaching that person to swim.

examples.french: J’apprends cette chanson pour la fête de samedi.
examples.english: I am learning this song for Saturday’s party.
examples.note: The subject is the learner.

examples.french: J’apprends cette chanson aux enfants.
examples.english: I am teaching this song to the children.
examples.note: The children receive the teaching.

examples.french: Tu peux m’apprendre à préparer ce plat ?
examples.english: Can you teach me how to prepare this dish?
examples.note: `M’` identifies the learner; the speaker asks someone else to teach.

examples.french: Mon frère apprend à conduire, et notre mère lui apprend à se garer.
examples.english: My brother is learning to drive, and our mother is teaching him to park.
examples.note: Learning and teaching contrasted in one situation.

examples.french: Cette formatrice enseigne le français et nous apprend à rédiger des courriels professionnels.
examples.english: This trainer teaches French and teaches us how to write professional emails.
examples.note: `Enseigner` names the subject taught; `apprendre à quelqu’un à` introduces a particular skill.

mistakes.avoid: Je lui apprends de conduire.
mistakes.prefer: Je lui apprends à conduire.
mistakes.why: The skill follows apprendre with à + infinitive. Lui identifies the learner: I am teaching that person to drive. Without a recipient, J’apprends à conduire normally means I am learning to drive.

vocabulary.english: to know (a fact), to know how to
vocabulary.example: Je sais où se trouve le bureau et je sais remplir la demande.
vocabulary.note: Followed by a clause, a question word, or an infinitive.

vocabulary.english: to know, to be familiar with
vocabulary.example: Elle connaît bien le quartier et ses services de proximité.
vocabulary.note: Commonly takes a noun or pronoun naming what is familiar. Use savoir + infinitive for a learned ability.

vocabulary.example: Nous croyons en la valeur de ce programme d’intégration.
vocabulary.note: `Croire à` instead expresses belief in the reality or effectiveness of something.

vocabulary.example: Une procédure clairement expliquée réduit le nombre de questions.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `une démarche` is the step you take within it.

vocabulary.example: Elle se demande combien de temps prendra le traitement du dossier.
vocabulary.note: Pronominal; followed by `si` or by a question word, never by `que`.

vocabulary.english: to believe in (the reality or effectiveness of)
vocabulary.example: Nous croyons à l’utilité de cette mesure pour le quartier.
vocabulary.note: `Croire en` expresses trust in a person or a value instead.

vocabulary.example: Les membres du comité l’ont crue sans hésiter.
vocabulary.note: Direct object; distinct from `croire à` (effectiveness) and `croire en` (trust).

practice.prompt: Choose the verb: « Je ___ cette procédure, mais je ne ___ pas comment la commencer. »
practice.hint: A noun phrase, then a question word.
practice.answer: Je connais cette procédure, mais je ne sais pas comment la commencer.

takeaways: Connaître expresses familiarity; savoir introduces information or a learned ability. Some information nouns, such as la réponse, allow both.
`Croire à` for effectiveness, `croire en` for trust.
`Penser à` plus thing becomes `y`, plus person stays stressed.
keywords: apprendre quelque chose à quelqu’un, apprendre à quelqu’un à faire, enseigner

lessons.title: Arriver, parvenir et les verbes d’événement
lessons.summary: Arriver can mean arrive or happen; arriver à/parvenir à plus infinitive mean manage to. Parvenir also means reach a place or recipient. Se passer and se dérouler describe events; se tenir describes an event being held. An artist se produit on stage, whereas a task is performed with effectuer or réaliser.
objectives: Read `arriver` correctly as arrival or as occurrence.
Use `arriver à` and `parvenir à` for successful effort.
Ask and answer about what happened with `se passer`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: `Arriver` can mean arrive: Elle est arrivée au Canada l’an dernier. It can also mean happen: Il est arrivé quelque chose d’important dans mon quartier (Something important happened in my neighbourhood), Ça m’est arrivé une fois (That happened to me once). Both senses use être in compound tenses. For a change taking place, Un changement s’est produit is more idiomatic than un changement est arrivé.

Followed by à plus an infinitive, arriver expresses success after effort: Je suis arrivé à joindre le service. Parvenir à is a more formal equivalent: Je suis parvenu à trouver un logement. When the goal is already known, y can replace it: C’était difficile, mais j’y suis arrivé. Se passer asks what happened: Qu’est-ce qui s’est passé ? uses an interrogative subject; the more formal Que s’est-il passé ? uses impersonal il. Not every se passer question is impersonal.
points: Use `être` as the auxiliary for `arriver` in every meaning.
Read `arriver` plus a place as arrival, and `arriver` plus an event or pronoun as occurrence.
Use `arriver à` or `parvenir à` plus infinitive for success after effort.
Use `y arriver` when the goal is already known.
Ask about an event with `Qu’est-ce qui s’est passé ?` or `Que s’est-il passé ?`.

examples.french: Je suis parvenu à trouver un logement près de mon travail.
examples.english: I managed to find housing near my workplace.
examples.note: Formal register for a goal reached after effort.

examples.french: C’était difficile au début, mais j’y suis arrivé.
examples.english: It was difficult at first, but I managed it.
examples.note: « Y arriver » resumes a goal already mentioned.

examples.french: Il est arrivé quelque chose d’important dans mon quartier cette année : la bibliothèque a rouvert.
examples.english: Something important happened in my neighbourhood this year: the library reopened.
examples.note: Arriver means happen, with être. Here il is an impersonal subject, not a man being described.

examples.french: Qu’est-ce qui s’est passé pendant la réunion de quartier ?
examples.english: What happened during the neighbourhood meeting?
examples.note: Standard question with « se passer ».

examples.french: Ça m’est arrivé une fois, et depuis je vérifie toujours mes documents.
examples.english: It happened to me once, and since then I always check my documents.
examples.note: Occurrence with an indirect pronoun.

mistakes.avoid: Que s’est passé pendant la réunion de quartier ?
mistakes.prefer: Que s’est-il passé pendant la réunion de quartier ?
mistakes.why: In the inverted question, `se passer` keeps its impersonal subject `il`, which is inverted after the verb.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai arrivé à joindre le service ce matin.
mistakes.prefer: Je suis arrivé à joindre le service ce matin.
mistakes.why: `Arriver` always takes the auxiliary `être` in the compound past.

sections.title: Parvenir: reaching a place or a recipient
paragraphs: Parvenir à does not always mean manage to. With a place, it means reach; with a recipient, a letter or information reaches that person. The recipient can become an indirect pronoun: La lettre est parvenue à Léa → La lettre lui est parvenue. The letter remains the subject, so parvenue agrees with lettre, not with the recipient.

This delivery sense is common in formal correspondence. Contrast parvenir à terminer (manage to finish), parvenir au sommet (reach the summit), and parvenir au service (reach the department). All use être in compound tenses.
points: Read the complement: infinitive, destination, or recipient.
With an indirect recipient pronoun, agreement still follows the subject.

examples.french: Après deux heures de marche, nous sommes parvenus au sommet.
examples.english: After two hours of walking, we reached the summit.
examples.note: Un sommet (m.) is a summit; au introduces the destination.

examples.french: Votre lettre nous est parvenue ce matin.
examples.english: Your letter reached us this morning.
examples.note: Nous is the recipient; lettre is the feminine singular subject.

examples.french: Les informations leur parviendront avant lundi.
examples.english: The information will reach them before Monday.
examples.note: Leur replaces à plus the recipients.

mistakes.avoid: Votre lettre nous a parvenu.
mistakes.prefer: Votre lettre nous est parvenue.
mistakes.why: Parvenir takes être, and parvenue agrees with lettre.

sections.title: Events being held and artists performing
paragraphs: Avoir lieu states that an event takes place. Se tenir is common for an organised meeting or conference being held at a place or time. Se dérouler can describe both when an event takes place and how it unfolds: La réunion s’est déroulée dans le calme. The event is the subject, so plural events take plural verbs.

For a stage performance, use an artist or group with se produire: Le groupe se produit ce soir. To carry out a task, use effectuer une tâche or réaliser un travail. Se produire also means occur in other contexts, as in Un incident s’est produit; it is not restricted to artists.
points: Se tenir: an organised event is held; se dérouler: it takes place or unfolds.
Distinguish an artist performing from someone carrying out a task.

examples.french: Les entretiens se tiendront mardi dans la grande salle.
examples.english: The interviews will be held on Tuesday in the large room.
examples.note: Plural entretiens governs se tiendront.

examples.french: La consultation s’est déroulée dans une ambiance calme.
examples.english: The consultation took place in a calm atmosphere.
examples.note: Se dérouler describes how the event unfolded.

examples.french: Le groupe se produit sur scène pendant que les techniciens effectuent les derniers réglages.
examples.english: The group performs on stage while the technicians make the final adjustments.
examples.note: Stage performance differs from carrying out technical work.

examples.french: Nous réalisons le travail demandé avant le début du spectacle.
examples.english: We carry out the requested work before the show begins.
examples.note: Réaliser takes the task as a direct object.

mistakes.avoid: Les entretiens se tiendra mardi.
mistakes.prefer: Les entretiens se tiendront mardi.
mistakes.why: The plural event subject requires tiendront.

mistakes.avoid: La réunion s’est déroulé dans le calme.
mistakes.prefer: La réunion s’est déroulée dans le calme.
mistakes.why: Déroulée agrees with the feminine subject réunion in this construction.

vocabulary.english: to manage to, to succeed in
vocabulary.example: Elle est parvenue à obtenir un rendez-vous en moins d’une semaine.
vocabulary.note: Formal register; conjugated like `venir` and taking `être`.

vocabulary.example: La démarche était longue, mais nous y sommes arrivés.
vocabulary.note: `Y` stands for a goal already mentioned.

vocabulary.example: La consultation s’est bien passée malgré le nombre de participants.
vocabulary.note: Pronominal verb; the auxiliary is `être`.

vocabulary.example: Un événement imprévu a interrompu la cérémonie d’accueil.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; also written `un évènement`.

practice.prompt: Ask what happened, then answer that you managed to finish the file anyway.
practice.hint: The question needs a subject form; the answer can use `y arriver`.
practice.answer: Qu’est-ce qui s’est passé ? Malgré tout, j’y suis arrivé et le dossier est terminé.

takeaways: `Arriver` equals to arrive and to happen, always with `être`.
Arriver à/parvenir à plus infinitive mean manage to; parvenir can also describe reaching a place or recipient.
Se dérouler describes an event’s course; se tenir describes it being held; se produire can describe an artist performing.
`Qu’est-ce qui s’est passé ?` is the standard question.
keywords: arriver, parvenir, y arriver, and se passer
parvenir à un lieu, se produire sur scène, se dérouler, se tenir, effectuer, réaliser

lessons.title: Verbes transitifs et formes pronominales : « terminer », « asseoir » et leurs paires
lessons.summary: Compare a verb’s constructions rather than assuming that every pronominal form removes its object. `Terminer le rapport` names what is completed, while `J’ai terminé` can leave it understood and `La séance se termine` describes an event ending. `Asseoir quelqu’un` means to seat another person; `s’asseoir` means to sit down. Other pairs include `ouvrir/s’ouvrir` and `arrêter/s’arrêter`, but their possible uses must be learned individually.
objectives: Decide whether an agent or the affected subject drives the sentence.
Use `asseoir` for seating someone else and `s’asseoir` for sitting down.
Transfer the pattern to comparable verb pairs.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A direct-transitive construction links a verb to an object without a preposition: Je termine le rapport. That object can be understood from context, so J’ai terminé is complete and correct. A pronominal verb includes a pronoun matching its subject, such as me in je me lave or se in la séance se termine. In La séance se termine à dix-sept heures, the event itself is the subject. This does not mean all pronominal verbs lack objects: Elle se lave les mains still has the direct object les mains.

`Asseoir quelqu’un` means to seat another person: `L’infirmière assoit le patient dans le fauteuil`. `S’asseoir` means to sit down: `Asseyez-vous, je vous en prie`. The pronominal form takes `être` (`elle s’est assise`, with agreement), while the transitive form takes `avoir` (`elle a assis l’enfant`). Learn other pairs in context: `Le conducteur arrête le bus` versus `Le bus s’arrête`. Some verbs also have non-pronominal intransitive uses: `Le guichet ouvre à neuf heures` is correct without an object or a reflexive pronoun.
points: Name the object when needed, but allow it to be understood in expressions such as `J’ai terminé`.
Learn each pronominal construction separately; some still take a direct object.
Use `asseoir quelqu’un` for seating someone else and `s’asseoir` for sitting down.
Compare `ouvrir/s’ouvrir` and `arrêter/s’arrêter` in full sentences rather than applying one universal object rule.

In these ending and sitting constructions, the past participle agrees with the subject: La séance s’est terminée; Elles se sont assises. Do not extend this blindly to every pronominal verb: Elle s’est lavé les mains keeps lavé unchanged because les mains is a following direct object.
Both present forms are standard: elle s’assoit / elle s’assied; both imperative families exist: assois-toi / assieds-toi, assoyez-vous / asseyez-vous.
Separate the action `s’asseoir` from the resulting state `être assis(e)`, which uses the participle as an adjective.

examples.french: Je termine le rapport avant la réunion de quinze heures.
examples.english: I am finishing the report before the three o’clock meeting.
examples.note: Transitive use with a direct object.

examples.french: La séance se termine à dix-sept heures précises.
examples.english: The session ends at five o’clock sharp.
examples.note: The event itself is the subject.

examples.french: L’infirmière assoit le patient dans le fauteuil avant l’examen.
examples.english: The nurse seats the patient in the chair before the examination.
examples.note: « Asseoir » with a direct object: someone seats someone else.

examples.french: « Asseyez-vous, je vous en prie. » La patiente s’est assise près de la fenêtre.
examples.english: “Please sit down.” The patient sat down near the window.
examples.note: « S’asseoir » for sitting down, with agreement in the compound past.

examples.french: Le bus s’arrête devant la mairie, puis le conducteur arrête le moteur.
examples.english: The bus stops in front of the town hall, then the driver switches off the engine.
examples.note: The same contrast with « arrêter ».

examples.french: Le guichet ouvre à neuf heures et la porte s’ouvre automatiquement.
examples.english: The counter opens at nine o’clock and the door opens automatically.
examples.note: Ouvre is intransitive here; s’ouvre is pronominal. Neither sentence needs a direct object.

examples.french: Elle s’assoit à côté de la fenêtre ; dix minutes plus tard, elle est toujours assise au même endroit.
examples.english: She sits down next to the window; ten minutes later, she is still sitting in the same place.
examples.note: « S’asseoir » is the action of sitting down; « être assis(e) » is the state that follows.

examples.french: Avez-vous terminé le rapport ? — Oui, j’ai terminé.
examples.english: Have you finished the report? — Yes, I have finished.
examples.note: The answer leaves the object understood instead of repeating it.

mistakes.avoid: La réunion se termines à midi.
mistakes.prefer: La réunion se termine à midi.
mistakes.why: The third-person singular present is `termine`, not the second-person form `termines`.

mistakes.avoid: Asseyez-se dans le fauteuil, s’il vous plaît.
mistakes.prefer: Asseyez-vous dans le fauteuil, s’il vous plaît.
mistakes.why: The vous imperative takes the matching reflexive pronoun `vous`, not third-person `se`.

vocabulary.example: Je termine la lettre de motivation avant la date limite.
vocabulary.note: Takes a direct object here; the object can be understood in `J’ai terminé`.

vocabulary.english: to end, to come to an end
vocabulary.example: La formation se termine par une évaluation écrite.
vocabulary.note: Pronominal; takes `être` in compound tenses.

vocabulary.example: L’agent assoit les visiteurs dans la salle d’attente.
vocabulary.note: Transitive; two accepted present forms, `il assoit` and `il assied`.

vocabulary.example: Les candidats s’assoient dès que leur nom est appelé.
vocabulary.note: Pronominal; imperative `assieds-toi`, `asseyez-vous`.

vocabulary.example: Un fauteuil confortable est réservé aux personnes à mobilité réduite.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `un siège` is the general word for a seat.

vocabulary.english: to be seated, to be sitting
vocabulary.example: Les candidats sont assis dans la salle depuis huit heures.
vocabulary.note: State resulting from `s’asseoir`; the participle agrees like an adjective.

practice.prompt: Say that the receptionist seats the visitors, then invite one visitor to sit down.
practice.hint: Transitive first, pronominal imperative second.
practice.answer: La réceptionniste assoit les visiteurs. Asseyez-vous, s’il vous plaît.

takeaways: A transitive object can be understood; a pronominal verb can also have an object.
`Asseoir quelqu’un` seats another person; `s’asseoir` is sitting down.
Learn the possible constructions of `ouvrir`, `fermer`, and `arrêter` individually.
keywords: transitive verbs and their pronominal pairs

lessons.title: La famille du verbe « rendre »
lessons.summary: `Rendre quelque chose` means to give something back. `Rendre visite à quelqu’un` means to visit a person. `Se rendre quelque part` means to go somewhere, in a formal register. `Se rendre compte de` plus a noun and `se rendre compte que` plus a clause both mean to realise. `Rendre compte de`, without the reflexive pronoun, means to report on or account for something.
objectives: Separate the five frequent constructions built on `rendre`.
Choose between `se rendre compte de` and `se rendre compte que`.
Keep `rendre compte de` apart from its reflexive counterpart.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: `Rendre` means to give back in `Je rends le formulaire à la conseillère`, with a direct object and an indirect recipient. Adding a fixed noun changes the meaning. `Rendre visite à quelqu’un` is the usual expression for an ordinary social visit. `Visiter` often takes a place, but it can also take people, notably in `visiter les malades` or `visiter les prisonniers`. This is a distinction of usage, not an absolute ban on visiting a person with `visiter`. `Rendre service à quelqu’un` means to do someone a favour.

The reflexive forms are a second family. `Se rendre` plus a place means to go there and belongs to a formal or administrative register: `Veuillez vous rendre au guichet 4`. `Se rendre compte` means to realise, and its complement decides the structure: `de` plus a noun (`Je me rends compte de la difficulté`) or `que` plus a clause (`Je me rends compte que le délai est court`). Dropping the reflexive pronoun gives a different verb again: `rendre compte de` means to report on or to account for, as in `Le comité doit rendre compte de ses dépenses`. Note that in `se rendre compte`, `compte` is invariable and the past participle never agrees: `elle s’est rendu compte`.
points: Use `rendre` plus a direct object for giving something back.
Prefer `rendre visite à` for a social visit; recognise accepted uses of `visiter` with people.
Se rendre uses an ordinary destination phrase, not a direct place object: se rendre au bureau, en France, chez le médecin. Aller is the simpler everyday alternative.
Use se rendre compte de before a noun and se rendre compte que before an indicative clause stating what is realised: Elle se rend compte que le bureau est fermé.
Use `rendre compte de` when the meaning is to report on something.
Leave the participle unchanged in `elle s’est rendu compte`.

examples.french: Je rends le formulaire à la conseillère avant midi.
examples.english: I am giving the form back to the adviser before noon.
examples.note: Basic meaning: to give something back.

examples.french: J’ai rendu visite à une famille nouvellement arrivée dans le quartier.
examples.english: I visited a family that has recently arrived in the neighbourhood.
examples.note: Rendre visite à is the ordinary expression for a social visit.

examples.french: Veuillez vous rendre au guichet 4 avec votre pièce d’identité.
examples.english: Please go to counter 4 with your identification.
examples.note: « Se rendre » plus a place, in a formal instruction.

examples.french: Je me rends compte de la difficulté et je me rends compte que le délai est très court.
examples.english: I realise how difficult it is, and I realise that very little time is available.
examples.note: « De » before a noun, « que » before a clause.

examples.french: Le comité doit rendre compte de ses dépenses devant le conseil.
examples.english: The committee has to account for its spending before the council.
examples.note: Without the reflexive pronoun, the meaning is to report on.

examples.french: Elle s’est rendu compte de l’erreur en relisant son dossier.
examples.english: She realised the mistake while rereading her file.
examples.note: The participle stays unchanged in this fixed expression.

examples.french: Les bénévoles visitent les malades à l’hôpital.
examples.english: The volunteers visit patients at the hospital.
examples.note: Visiter can take people; this accepted usage does not describe touring a place.

examples.french: Tu peux me rendre service en déposant cette lettre à la poste ?
examples.english: Can you do me a favour by dropping this letter off at the post office?
examples.note: Me is the person receiving the favour: rendre service à quelqu’un. The action after en explains what the favour consists of.

mistakes.avoid: Je me rends compte que la difficulté de cette démarche.
mistakes.prefer: Je me rends compte de la difficulté de cette démarche.
mistakes.why: `Que` introduces a clause; before a noun phrase the expression takes `de`.

mistakes.avoid: Elle s’est rendue compte de son erreur trop tard.
mistakes.prefer: Elle s’est rendu compte de son erreur trop tard.
mistakes.why: In `se rendre compte`, the direct object is `compte`, which follows the verb, so the participle does not agree.

vocabulary.example: Nous nous rendons compte de l’ampleur du problème.
vocabulary.note: `De` before a noun, `que` before a clause; the participle never agrees.

vocabulary.english: to go (formal), to make one’s way
vocabulary.example: Les candidats doivent se rendre à la salle B avant huit heures.
vocabulary.note: Formal register; `aller` is the neutral equivalent.

vocabulary.english: to report on, to account for
vocabulary.example: La directrice rend compte de ses décisions chaque trimestre.
vocabulary.note: Without the reflexive pronoun the meaning changes completely.

vocabulary.example: Ce nouveau service rend service à toutes les familles du quartier.
vocabulary.note: Fixed expression; the person is introduced by `à`.

vocabulary.example: Une dépense imprévue doit être justifiée dans le rapport annuel.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `dépenser` is the related verb.

practice.prompt: Translate: « She realised that the office was closed, so she went to the other counter and gave the form back. »
practice.hint: Three different members of the `rendre` family.
practice.answer: Elle s’est rendu compte que le bureau était fermé ; elle s’est donc rendue à l’autre guichet et elle a rendu le formulaire.

takeaways: `Rendre` alone equals to give back.
`Rendre visite à` a person, `se rendre` to a place.
`Se rendre compte de` a noun, `que` a clause; `rendre compte de` equals to report on.

lessons.title: Les constructions de « cacher » et de « rapporter »
lessons.summary: `Cacher quelque chose à quelqu’un` means to hide something from someone, so French uses `à` where English uses from. `Se cacher de quelqu’un` means to hide oneself from that person. `Rapporter` has three readings: to bring back, to report information, and to yield a return. `Se rapporter à` means to relate or refer to.
objectives: Use `à` after `cacher` where English would use from.
Distinguish the pronominal and non-pronominal forms.
Read `rapporter` correctly from its complement.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The preposition belongs to the French verb, not to the English translation. `Cacher` is built as `cacher quelque chose à quelqu’un`, so `The company must not hide this information from employees` becomes `L’entreprise ne doit pas cacher cette information aux employés`. Adding the reflexive pronoun changes both the meaning and the preposition: `se cacher de quelqu’un` means to hide oneself from that person.

Read the whole construction of rapporter. Bringing back: Rapportez le formulaire signé. Reporting information: Le témoin a rapporté les faits. Yielding a return: Ce placement rapporte peu, where the investment is the subject, not an object being brought back. An amount and recipient can follow: Ce placement lui rapporte cent euros par an (This investment earns that person a hundred euros a year). Se rapporter à means relate to or concern: Cette statistique se rapporte au marché du travail canadien.

Cacher quelque chose à quelqu’un makes the person an indirect object: Il cache la vérité à ses collègues → Il leur cache la vérité (He hides the truth from them). When both complements are pronouns, Il la leur cache means He hides it from them. The à belongs to the French verb pattern; do not translate English from mechanically.
points: Build `cacher` as `cacher quelque chose à quelqu’un`.
Use `se cacher de quelqu’un` when the subject hides itself.
Read `rapporter` plus object as bring back.
Read `rapporter` plus information as report.
Use `se rapporter à` for a reference or a relationship between ideas.

examples.french: L’entreprise ne doit pas cacher cette information aux employés.
examples.english: The company must not hide this information from employees.
examples.note: French uses « à » where English uses from.

examples.french: Il se cachait de ses créanciers depuis plusieurs mois.
examples.english: He had been hiding from his creditors for several months.
examples.note: Pronominal form with « de ».

examples.french: Rapportez le formulaire signé au guichet avant seize heures.
examples.english: Bring the signed form back to the counter before four o’clock.
examples.note: « Rapporter » plus a concrete object.

examples.french: Le journal a rapporté les propos de la porte-parole sans les commenter.
examples.english: The newspaper reported the spokesperson’s words without commenting on them.
examples.note: « Rapporter » plus information.

examples.french: Cette statistique se rapporte au marché du travail canadien.
examples.english: This statistic relates to the Canadian labour market.
examples.note: « Se rapporter à » for a relationship between ideas.

mistakes.avoid: Il les cache la vérité.
mistakes.prefer: Il leur cache la vérité.
mistakes.why: The people kept uninformed take à or an indirect pronoun: à ses collègues → leur. Les would be a direct object, but la vérité is already the thing hidden.

mistakes.avoid: Ce chapitre rapporte à la question du logement.
mistakes.prefer: Ce chapitre se rapporte à la question du logement.
mistakes.why: In the sense of relating to, the verb is pronominal: `se rapporter à`.

vocabulary.example: Elle n’a rien caché à son employeur au sujet de son horaire.
vocabulary.note: The person is introduced by `à`, never by `de`.

vocabulary.english: to relate to, to refer to
vocabulary.example: Ce paragraphe se rapporte aux conditions d’admission.
vocabulary.note: Pronominal; the complement is introduced by `à`.

vocabulary.example: Un employé à temps partiel a demandé une copie de son contrat.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; feminine `une employée`.

vocabulary.example: Une statistique récente montre une hausse du nombre de demandes.
vocabulary.note: Une statistique is an individual numerical result; les statistiques are numerical data. La statistique names the discipline, although faire des statistiques also occurs.

practice.prompt: Translate: « She did not hide the delay from the committee, and this note refers to the same file. »
practice.hint: One `à` after `cacher`, one pronominal verb.
practice.answer: Elle n’a pas caché le retard au comité, et cette note se rapporte au même dossier.

takeaways: `Cacher quelque chose à quelqu’un`, not `de`.
`Se cacher de` for hiding oneself.
`Se rapporter à` equals to relate to.
keywords: cacher, se cacher, rapporter, and se rapporter

lessons.title: Les distinctions entre des verbes proches
lessons.summary: Learn each verb with its meaning and construction: leaving, bringing, visiting, owing, retaining or removing, walking, serving or using, and making a commitment. Distinguish direct objects from à/de complements and impersonal patterns such as Il me manque deux euros. A similar English translation does not guarantee the same French syntax.
objectives: Store each verb together with the complement it accepts.
Separate leaving a place, leaving a person, and leaving something behind.
Read `disposer de` and `disposer` as two different verbs.

sections.title: Bringing, leaving, remembering, and owing
paragraphs: Use this long lesson as a reference in several sittings. Each section groups verbs around a particular meaning or activity. A complement is what completes a verb’s meaning: a direct object follows without a preposition (quitter le bureau); other complements require one (partir du bureau). Learn that construction along with the meaning.

Apporter commonly means carry something to a destination, while amener means lead or bring someone there: apporter un document, amener un enfant. The distinction is not strictly thing versus person: amener une voiture is possible, and apporter un bébé describes carrying a baby. For ordinary social visits, use rendre visite à un ami; visiter un musée means visit a museum. Convaincre quelqu’un de and persuader quelqu’un de can both mean persuade someone to do something: Je l’ai convaincu de venir / Je l’ai persuadé de venir. Convaincre often suggests reasons or evidence and persuader winning someone over, but they overlap rather than forming a strict reason-versus-emotion opposition.

Departure splits three ways. `Partir` is intransitive: `Je pars à huit heures`. `Quitter` takes a direct object in `Je quitte le bureau à dix-sept heures` and `Elle a quitté son emploi`; this construction does not mean that every use requires an explicitly named object. `Laisser` means to leave something or someone behind, and it also means to let: `J’ai laissé mon dossier à l’accueil`, `Laissez-moi vérifier`. `Croiser quelqu’un` is to run into someone by chance: `J’ai croisé ma voisine au marché`. `Disposer de` means to have something available (`Le centre dispose de deux salles`), while `disposer` with a direct object means to arrange (`Elle a disposé les chaises en cercle`). `S’équiper de` means to equip oneself with something: `Il faut s’équiper de bonnes bottes pour l’hiver`. For remembering a thing expressed by a noun, compare `Je me souviens de cette réunion` / `Je m’en souviens` with the careful French construction `Je me rappelle cette réunion` / `Je me la rappelle`.

`Devoir` followed directly by an infinitive can express obligation or probability: `Je dois déposer ma demande avant vendredi`. With a thing or amount owed, it means to owe: `Il doit 200 $`, `Tu dois de l’argent depuis le mois dernier`. Naming the creditor is optional: add `à la banque`, or use an indirect pronoun in `Tu me dois de l’argent`, when that information is relevant. `Patrick me doit une faveur` shows that the object need not be money. Another useful overlap concerns inclusion: both `Le prix inclut les taxes` and `Le prix comprend les taxes` are correct. `Inclure` can describe incorporating an item or what a whole includes; `comprendre` also means to understand.
points: Apporter foregrounds carrying; amener foregrounds bringing or leading to a destination. The thing/person rule is a useful first guide, not absolute.
Use `rendre visite à` for ordinary social visits; `visiter` also takes people in contexts such as visiting patients or prisoners.
Use `partir` with no object, `quitter` with an object, and `laisser` for what stays behind.
Use `croiser quelqu’un` for an unplanned meeting.
Read `disposer de` as to have available and `disposer` as to arrange.
Use `s’équiper de` for acquiring the equipment you need.
Use either `inclure` or `comprendre` for what a whole includes; use `comprendre` for understanding.
Before a noun naming what is remembered, use `se souvenir de`; in careful French, `se rappeler` takes that noun directly.

With an infinitive, devoir can express necessity (Je dois partir — I must leave) or an inference (Elle doit être chez elle — She is probably at home / She must be at home). It can also state what is expected or scheduled. Context decides.
With something owed, devoir means owe: Patrick me doit une faveur (Patrick owes me a favour). Naming the creditor is optional.

examples.french: J’amène ma fille à la garderie et j’apporte son dossier médical.
examples.english: I take my daughter to daycare and bring her medical file.
examples.note: A person is « amenée », a thing is « apportée ».

examples.french: J’ai rendu visite à une famille nouvellement installée dans le quartier.
examples.english: I visited a family that has recently settled in the neighbourhood.
examples.note: Rendre visite à is the usual expression for a social visit.

examples.french: Je quitte le bureau à dix-sept heures, mais je laisse mon dossier à l’accueil.
examples.english: I leave the office at five, but I leave my file at reception.
examples.note: « Quitter » takes an object; « laisser » names what stays behind.

examples.french: J’ai croisé ma voisine au marché et elle m’a parlé du nouveau service.
examples.english: I ran into my neighbour at the market and she told me about the new service.
examples.note: « Croiser » marks an unplanned meeting.

examples.french: Le centre dispose de deux salles, et la bénévole a disposé les chaises en cercle.
examples.english: The centre has two rooms available, and the volunteer arranged the chairs in a circle.
examples.note: « Disposer de » to have available, « disposer » to arrange.

examples.french: Il faut s’équiper de bonnes bottes avant le premier verglas.
examples.english: You need to get yourself a good pair of boots before the first ice.
examples.note: De introduces the equipment. Without naming it, Il faut s’équiper (You need to get equipped) is also complete.

examples.french: Le tarif comprend l’assurance, et nous avons inclus une copie du bail dans le dossier.
examples.english: The price includes insurance, and we included a copy of the lease in the file.
examples.note: These examples illustrate containing and incorporating; both inclure and comprendre can describe what a price includes.

examples.french: Je me souviens de l’entrevue, mais je ne me rappelle plus le nom du recruteur.
examples.english: I remember the interview, but I no longer remember the recruiter’s name.
examples.note: « Se souvenir » keeps « de »; « se rappeler » takes a direct object.

examples.french: Je dois déposer ma demande avant vendredi, et je dois encore 200 $ à la coopérative.
examples.english: I have to submit my application before Friday, and I still owe $200 to the co-op.
examples.note: Modal « devoir » plus infinitive, then lexical « devoir » plus amount plus « à ».

examples.french: Je dois encore deux mois de loyer.
examples.english: I still owe two months’ rent.
examples.note: The creditor can remain unexpressed; the amount owed is the direct object.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai rendu visite ma sœur pendant les vacances.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai rendu visite à ma sœur pendant les vacances.
mistakes.why: In `rendre visite à quelqu’un`, the person is introduced by `à`.

mistakes.avoid: Je pars le bureau à dix-sept heures.
mistakes.prefer: Je quitte le bureau à dix-sept heures.
mistakes.why: Use the direct construction `quitter le bureau`, or the prepositional alternative `partir du bureau`.

mistakes.avoid: Le centre dispose de les deux salles de réunion.
mistakes.prefer: Le centre dispose des deux salles de réunion.
mistakes.why: Disposer de means have available. With the definite article les, de contracts to des; de deux salles, without les, instead means two unspecified rooms.

mistakes.avoid: Le prix inclut les taxes, mais je ne inclus pas votre question.
mistakes.prefer: Le prix inclut les taxes, mais je ne comprends pas votre question.
mistakes.why: `Le prix inclut les taxes` is correct. To mean understand in the second clause, use `comprendre`, not `inclure`.

mistakes.avoid: Je me rappelle que notre conversation de mardi.
mistakes.prefer: Je me rappelle notre conversation de mardi.
mistakes.why: Before a noun phrase, careful French uses se rappeler directly; que needs a clause, as in Je me rappelle que nous avons parlé mardi. Se rappeler de is common in conversation but is traditionally discouraged before a noun.

mistakes.avoid: Je dois de partir avant la fin de la réunion.
mistakes.prefer: Je dois partir avant la fin de la réunion.
mistakes.why: Modal `devoir` is followed directly by the infinitive, with no preposition.

mistakes.avoid: Tu doit de l’argent depuis le mois dernier.
mistakes.prefer: Tu dois de l’argent depuis le mois dernier.
mistakes.why: The present form with `tu` is `dois`, not `doit`. No explicit creditor is required.

sections.title: Retenir is not retirer
paragraphs: Retenir can mean hold back or delay someone, retain something in memory, or reserve a place in a somewhat formal register. Retirer means remove or withdraw; context can also make it mean collect something that was waiting for you. Both take direct objects, but they describe different actions.

Compare retenir une date (remember a date), retenir une table (reserve a table), retirer une pièce du dossier (remove a document), and retirer de l’argent (withdraw money). Do not choose a verb just because its spelling resembles an English word.
points: Read retenir from its object and context: holding back, remembering, or reserving.
Retirer concerns removal, withdrawal, or collection.

examples.french: Une dernière question m’a retenu au bureau.
examples.english: One final question kept me at the office.
examples.note: Retenir can delay someone without physically restraining them.

examples.french: Je retiens facilement les dates et j’ai retenu une table pour vendredi.
examples.english: I remember dates easily, and I have reserved a table for Friday.
examples.note: Memory and reservation are distinct readings of retenir.

examples.french: Elle retire une ancienne attestation du dossier, puis retire de l’argent au guichet.
examples.english: She removes an old certificate from the file, then withdraws money at the counter.
examples.note: Une attestation (f.) is a certificate; retirer describes removal or withdrawal.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai reteni une table.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai retenu une table.
mistakes.why: The participle of retenir is retenu.

mistakes.avoid: Elle a retiru l’ancienne attestation.
mistakes.prefer: Elle a retiré l’ancienne attestation.
mistakes.why: Retirer is an -er verb with the participle retiré.

sections.title: Walking: action, transport, an outing, and taking someone out
paragraphs: Marcher describes walking itself or the way someone walks. Aller à pied presents walking as the means of transport; its destination may be stated or understood. Se promener describes a stroll or outing, often on foot, without necessarily going to accomplish an errand.

Promener takes the person or animal being taken out as a direct object: promener le chien. Compare Je me promène (I am taking a stroll) and Je promène le chien (I am walking the dog). In a compound tense, the pronominal construction uses être; transitive promener uses avoir.
points: Marcher names the action; aller à pied names the transport.
Se promener has a reflexive pronoun; promener names who or what you take out.

examples.french: Elle marche lentement depuis son opération.
examples.english: She has been walking slowly since her operation.
examples.note: Marcher describes the manner of walking.

examples.french: Le bureau est proche; nous y allons à pied.
examples.english: The office is nearby; we walk there.
examples.note: The destination is represented by y, not necessarily repeated as a noun.

examples.french: Après le repas, nous nous promenons au bord du canal.
examples.english: After the meal, we take a stroll beside the canal.
examples.note: The focus is an outing rather than transport to an errand.

examples.french: Elle a promené le chien, puis elle s’est promenée seule.
examples.english: She walked the dog, then went for a walk on her own.
examples.note: Transitive avoir contrasts with pronominal être and agreement.

mistakes.avoid: Nous se promenons près du canal.
mistakes.prefer: Nous nous promenons près du canal.
mistakes.why: The reflexive pronoun must match nous.

mistakes.avoid: Elle est promené le chien.
mistakes.prefer: Elle a promené le chien.
mistakes.why: Transitive promener uses avoir, with le chien as its object.

sections.title: What is missing and what escapes someone
paragraphs: Manquer changes meaning with its construction: manquer le train means miss the train; manquer de temps means lack time. In impersonal Il manque une signature au formulaire, il is a grammatical placeholder and manquer stays singular. An indirect pronoun can express the person affected: Il me manque deux euros. Compare Deux euros me manquent, where the missing euros are the plural subject. For missing someone emotionally, that person is also the subject: Ma sœur me manque (I miss my sister), Tu me manques (I miss you), not the other way round.

Échapper à means escape from or evade someone or something: échapper au chien, échapper à un danger. It can also mean escape someone’s notice or understanding: Ce détail m’échappe. The complement takes à or an indirect pronoun, unlike a direct object. Reflexive s’échapper is another construction, not an obligatory replacement.
points: Impersonal il manque stays singular even before plural missing items.
Use indirect pronouns for the affected person with manquer and échapper à.

examples.french: Il me manque deux euros pour acheter le billet.
examples.english: I am two euros short of buying the ticket.
examples.note: Me identifies the person short of money; deux euros is what is missing.

examples.french: Il manque une signature au formulaire.
examples.english: The form is missing a signature.
examples.note: Une signature (f.) is the missing item; au formulaire names the affected document.

examples.french: Le chat échappe au chien en passant sous la clôture.
examples.english: The cat escapes the dog by going under the fence.
examples.note: À + le contracts to au.

examples.french: Les raisons de ce refus m’échappent.
examples.english: I cannot understand the reasons for this refusal.
examples.note: The reasons are the plural subject; me is the indirect person concerned.

mistakes.avoid: Il me manquent deux euros.
mistakes.prefer: Il me manque deux euros.
mistakes.why: The impersonal subject il requires singular manque.

mistakes.avoid: Le chat échappe le chien.
mistakes.prefer: Le chat échappe au chien.
mistakes.why: Échapper introduces the pursuer with à, not as a direct object.

sections.title: Serving, helping yourself, and using a tool
paragraphs: Servir can take what is served as a direct object and the recipient with à: servir du thé aux invités. Se servir can mean help yourself, often in a food or self-service context. Se servir de, with an instrument or resource, means use: se servir de cet outil.

A known de complement can be replaced by en: Je me sers de ce logiciel → Je m’en sers. Keep the reflexive pronoun; it belongs to the verb. Contrast using a tool with its purpose: Je me sers de cette clé (I use this key), Cette clé sert à ouvrir la réserve (This key is used to open the storeroom). Servir à + infinitive states what something is for. Food context can instead make se servir mean help oneself.
points: Servir: serve something to someone.
Se servir: help yourself; se servir de an instrument: use it.

examples.french: La bénévole sert du thé aux visiteurs.
examples.english: The volunteer serves tea to the visitors.
examples.note: The drink is served; aux visiteurs identifies the recipients.

examples.french: Les visiteurs se servent eux-mêmes au buffet.
examples.english: The visitors help themselves at the buffet.
examples.note: The pronominal form describes self-service.

examples.french: Je me sers de ce logiciel chaque jour; mes collègues s’en servent aussi.
examples.english: I use this software every day; my colleagues use it too.
examples.note: Un logiciel (m.) is software; de ce logiciel becomes en.

mistakes.avoid: Je me sers ce logiciel.
mistakes.prefer: Je me sers de ce logiciel.
mistakes.why: In the sense use, the construction is se servir de.

sections.title: Engager: hire, initiate, get involved, or commit
paragraphs: Engager quelqu’un means hire someone; engager une conversation means initiate a conversation. S’engager dans un projet describes involvement. S’engager à plus infinitive expresses a commitment to do something. Keep the construction with its meaning rather than treating every use as an English engagement.
In compound tenses, compare Elle a engagé une avocate with Elle s’est engagée à répondre. The latter is pronominal and agrees with the subject in this commitment construction.
points: Engager takes a person hired or an activity initiated as a direct object.
S’engager dans introduces involvement; s’engager à introduces a promised action.

examples.french: L’association a engagé une avocate pour examiner le contrat.
examples.english: The association hired a lawyer to examine the contract.
examples.note: Une avocate (f.) is a female lawyer; the hired person is a direct object.

examples.french: Nous engageons une conversation avec les nouveaux voisins.
examples.english: We start a conversation with the new neighbours.
examples.note: Engager can mean initiate, without employment.

examples.french: Elle s’engage dans le projet et s’est engagée à répondre avant vendredi.
examples.english: She is getting involved in the project and has committed to replying before Friday.
examples.note: Dans introduces the project; à introduces the action promised.

mistakes.avoid: Elle s’est engagée répondre avant vendredi.
mistakes.prefer: Elle s’est engagée à répondre avant vendredi.
mistakes.why: Commitment to an action requires à before the infinitive.

sections.title: Drawing, attending, and avoiding misleading English lookalikes
paragraphs: `Dessiner` means draw, making an image or sketch; designing a system is more often `concevoir`. `Mentir` means lie in the sense of saying something untrue, not lying down. `Assister à` means attend an event. Helping a person is normally aider quelqu’un; assister quelqu’un also means assist someone, especially in formal or professional contexts. Its direct object distinguishes it from attending an event with assister à.

`Un patron (m.)` or `une patronne (f.)` is a boss or employer in everyday speech, not an ordinary customer. `Une allure (f.)` can mean pace or speed; in other contexts it describes someone's appearance or bearing. `Éventuellement` means possibly or if needed. English eventually, meaning in the end, is usually `finalement` or `finir par`.
points: Store `assister à` with its event-attendance meaning.
Separate possibility (`éventuellement`) from the eventual outcome (`finalement`).

examples.french: Elle dessine le bâtiment avant de le peindre.
examples.english: She draws the building before painting it.
examples.note: Making a drawing, not designing the building.

examples.french: Il a menti sur son âge, puis il a dit la vérité.
examples.english: He lied about his age, then told the truth.
examples.note: `Mentir` concerns a false statement.

examples.french: J’assiste à la réunion, mais je n’aide pas à l’organiser.
examples.english: I am attending the meeting, but I am not helping to organise it.
examples.note: Attendance and assistance are different actions.

examples.french: Ma patronne m’a proposé un nouvel horaire.
examples.english: My boss offered me a new work schedule.
examples.note: An everyday word for the person in charge.

examples.french: Nous marchons à une allure modérée pour rester ensemble.
examples.english: We are walking at a moderate pace so that we stay together.
examples.note: `Allure` means pace here.

examples.french: Je pourrai éventuellement venir vendredi ; je te confirmerai demain.
examples.english: I may possibly be able to come on Friday; I will confirm tomorrow.
examples.note: An uncertain possibility, not an action certain to happen eventually.

mistakes.avoid: J’assiste de la réunion demain.
mistakes.prefer: J’assiste à la réunion demain.
mistakes.why: Attendance takes assister à. For helping a colleague, use J’aide mon collègue or the more formal Je l’assiste, without à.

sections.title: Who lends, who borrows, and what happens to an object
paragraphs: `Prêter quelque chose à quelqu’un` means lend something to someone: the subject supplies it temporarily. `Emprunter quelque chose à quelqu’un` means borrow it: the subject receives it temporarily. The same exchange can therefore be described from opposite viewpoints.

`Lancer` means throw; `attraper` means catch or grab. `Ramasser` means pick up from a surface or gather items together. `Serrer` means grip, squeeze, or tighten according to context. For hugging a person, the full expression `serrer quelqu’un dans ses bras` makes the intended action clear.
points: Lender: `Je te prête mon livre`. Borrower: `Je t’emprunte ton livre`.
A thrown object is caught with `attraper`; a fallen object is picked up with `ramasser`.

examples.french: Nora me prête son dictionnaire jusqu’à lundi.
examples.english: Nora is lending me her dictionary until Monday.
examples.note: Nora supplies the dictionary.

examples.french: Tu peux me prêter ton livre ? Je te le rendrai lundi.
examples.english: Can you lend me your book? I will return it to you on Monday.
examples.note: The owner lends: tu me prêtes. The recipient borrows: je t’emprunte. Choose the verb for whose action the sentence describes.

examples.french: J’emprunte le dictionnaire de Nora ; je le lui rendrai lundi.
examples.english: I am borrowing Nora’s dictionary; I will return it to her on Monday.
examples.note: The same exchange from the borrower's viewpoint.

examples.french: Lance-moi la balle ; je vais essayer de l’attraper.
examples.english: Throw me the ball; I will try to catch it.
examples.note: Throwing and catching are complementary actions.

examples.french: La balle est tombée derrière toi ; peux-tu la ramasser ?
examples.english: The ball fell behind you; can you pick it up?
examples.note: Picking up something that has fallen.

examples.french: Elle a ramassé tous les papiers tombés du dossier.
examples.english: She picked up all the papers that had fallen out of the folder.
examples.note: `Ramasser` can describe gathering several scattered objects.

examples.french: Elle serre la corde entre ses doigts pour ne pas la lâcher.
examples.english: She grips the rope between her fingers so she does not let go of it.
examples.note: `Serrer` describes a firm grip.

examples.french: Ne serre pas trop le tube, sinon tout va sortir.
examples.english: Do not squeeze the tube too hard, or everything will come out.
examples.note: Squeezing an object.

examples.french: Il a serré sa sœur dans ses bras pour la réconforter.
examples.english: He hugged his sister to comfort her.
examples.note: The arms phrase gives `serrer` its hugging interpretation.

sections.title: Checking a box, losing time, and spying
paragraphs: `Cocher` means tick or check a box by marking it. It does not mean every kind of checking: verifying an answer is `vérifier une réponse`. `Perdre le match` means lose the game, while `perdre du temps` means lose or waste time.
`Espionner quelqu’un` means spy on someone, secretly observing them or gathering information about them. It is stronger and more intrusive than simply looking at someone or checking a public fact.
points: A mark in a box is `cocher`; a verification is `vérifier`.
Translate `perdre` with its object: a defeat is not the same as wasted time.

examples.french: Cochez la case qui correspond à votre situation.
examples.english: Tick the box that matches your situation.
examples.note: An instruction to make a mark.

examples.french: Nous avons perdu le match malgré un bon début.
examples.english: We lost the game despite a good start.
examples.note: The result of a contest.

examples.french: J’ai perdu du temps en cherchant la mauvaise adresse.
examples.english: I wasted time looking for the wrong address.
examples.note: Time used unproductively.

examples.french: Il lisait leurs messages en secret pour les espionner.
examples.english: He was secretly reading their messages to spy on them.
examples.note: Covert observation, not ordinary communication.

mistakes.avoid: Je vais cocher si l’adresse est correcte.
mistakes.prefer: Je vais vérifier si l’adresse est correcte.
mistakes.why: `Cocher` marks a choice; `vérifier` checks whether something is correct.

sections.title: Discovering something, seeing it appear, and reacting
paragraphs: `Découvrir` means discover or find out: something becomes known to the person discovering it. `Apparaître` means appear: the subject comes into view or becomes visible. `S’écrier` means cry out or exclaim, often in a narrative; it is not `s’écrire`, to write to one another or to be spelled.

`S’éteindre` describes a light, screen, or flame going out. It differs from `éteindre`, where someone switches something off or extinguishes it. `Grimper` means climb in a physical context, such as climbing a ladder or climbing up into a tree; that sense is distinct from prices rising.
points: A person discovers a detail; the detail appears on a screen.
`S’écrier` belongs to speech or a vocal reaction, not writing.

examples.french: J’ai découvert un passage que je ne connaissais pas.
examples.english: I discovered a passageway I did not know about.
examples.note: A place becomes known to the speaker.

examples.french: Son nom apparaît sur la liste après quelques secondes.
examples.english: Her name appears on the list after a few seconds.
examples.note: The name becomes visible.

examples.french: « Voilà la sortie ! » s’est-elle écriée.
examples.english: “There is the exit!” she exclaimed.
examples.note: A spoken exclamation, not written correspondence.

examples.french: La lumière s’est éteinte au milieu de la réunion.
examples.english: The light went out in the middle of the meeting.
examples.note: No person switching it off is named.

examples.french: Le technicien éteint la lampe avant de la remplacer.
