examples.english: The technician switches off the lamp before replacing it.
examples.note: Transitive `éteindre` names the person doing the action.

examples.french: Elle grimpe à l’échelle pour atteindre l’étagère.
examples.english: She climbs the ladder to reach the shelf.
examples.note: Literal upward movement, not a figurative increase.

mistakes.avoid: Elle s’est écrite : « Attention ! »
mistakes.prefer: Elle s’est écriée : « Attention ! »
mistakes.why: `S’écrire` concerns writing; `s’écrier` introduces a cry or exclamation.

sections.title: Apologising, cooperating, and reaching agreement
paragraphs: `Excuser quelqu’un` means excuse or forgive someone; `s’excuser` means apologise. `Excusez-moi` asks the other person to excuse you, whereas `Je m’excuse` performs an apology. `Se comporter mal`, often ordered `mal se comporter`, means behave badly or misbehave.

`Changer d’opinion` means change one's view. `Collaborer avec quelqu’un` means work together with someone. `Convenir de quelque chose` means agree on something, and `convenir de faire quelque chose` means agree to do it. Do not transfer that meaning to `convenir à`, which means suit or be suitable for.
points: Read who receives the excuse: `Je l’excuse` forgives someone else; `Je m’excuse` is an apology.
Keep the distinction `convenir de` = agree on/to, `convenir à` = suit.

examples.french: Je m’excuse pour mon retard ; le bus n’est pas passé.
examples.english: I apologise for being late; the bus did not come.
examples.note: The speaker offers an apology.

examples.french: Je l’excuse, car elle ne connaissait pas la règle.
examples.english: I excuse her because she did not know the rule.
examples.note: The speaker excuses another person.

examples.french: Il s’est mal comporté pendant la visite et a ensuite présenté ses excuses.
examples.english: He misbehaved during the visit and later apologised.
examples.note: A judgement about behaviour.

examples.french: Après avoir lu les résultats, j’ai changé d’opinion.
examples.english: After reading the results, I changed my opinion.
examples.note: A revised view.

examples.french: Nous collaborons avec une autre équipe sur ce projet.
examples.english: We are collaborating with another team on this project.
examples.note: Working together, with the partner introduced by `avec`.

examples.french: Nous convenons d’une date, puis nous confirmons la réservation.
examples.english: We agree on a date, then confirm the booking.
examples.note: `Convenir de` introduces the point agreed on.

examples.french: Nous convenons de nous revoir lundi ; cet horaire convient à tout le monde.
examples.english: We agree to meet again on Monday; that time suits everyone.
examples.note: Agreement with `de`, suitability with `à`, in the same situation.

mistakes.avoid: Cet horaire convient de tout le monde.
mistakes.prefer: Cet horaire convient à tout le monde.
mistakes.why: The time suits people; it does not agree on them. `Convenir de` introduces an agreement's content.

mistakes.avoid: Je me excuse pour mon retard.
mistakes.prefer: Je m’excuse pour mon retard.
mistakes.why: Me elides before excuse. Je l’excuse is also grammatical, but it means I excuse that person, not I apologise.

sections.title: What grows and what someone grows
paragraphs: For plants and hair, `pousser` means grow. The growing thing is the subject: `Les plantes poussent`. When a person cultivates plants, use `faire pousser`: `Elle fait pousser des tomates`. This differs from the ordinary transitive meaning of `pousser`, to push.
The contrast is lexical: `pousser une porte` moves a door by pressure; `faire pousser une plante` brings about its growth. A plant can grow without anyone cultivating it.
points: Plant as subject: `pousser`. Person cultivating plants: `faire pousser`.
Do not turn English grow vegetables into transitive `pousser des légumes`.

examples.french: Ces plantes poussent bien près de la fenêtre.
examples.english: These plants grow well near the window.
examples.note: The plants themselves are growing.

examples.french: Elle fait pousser des tomates sur son balcon.
examples.english: She grows tomatoes on her balcony.
examples.note: A person cultivates the plants.

examples.french: Ses cheveux poussent vite depuis quelques mois.
examples.english: Her hair has been growing quickly for a few months.
examples.note: `Pousser` also describes hair growth.

examples.french: L’herbe pousse toute seule ici ; personne ne la cultive.
examples.english: The grass grows by itself here; nobody cultivates it.
examples.note: Growth does not require a human grower.

mistakes.avoid: Je pousse des tomates dans le jardin.
mistakes.prefer: Je fais pousser des tomates dans le jardin.
mistakes.why: For cultivating a crop, French uses `faire pousser`, not the direct-object construction meaning push.

vocabulary.example: J’amène mon fils au centre communautaire chaque mercredi.
vocabulary.note: Usually bringing or leading a person to a destination; also possible with movable things such as a vehicle. Apporter emphasises carrying.

vocabulary.english: to leave (a place or a person)
vocabulary.example: Elle a quitté son emploi pour suivre une formation à temps plein.
vocabulary.note: Takes a direct object in quitter son emploi or quitter le bureau; partir du bureau uses de.

vocabulary.example: J’ai laissé une copie du formulaire à l’accueil.
vocabulary.note: Also used for permission: `laissez-moi vérifier`.

vocabulary.example: Nous avons croisé la conseillère devant la bibliothèque.
vocabulary.note: Marks an unplanned meeting; `rencontrer` is neutral.

vocabulary.example: Nous disposons de trois semaines pour compléter le dossier.
vocabulary.note: Without `de`, `disposer` means to arrange or lay out.

vocabulary.example: Les bénévoles se sont équipés de vestes réfléchissantes.
vocabulary.note: Equipment is introduced by de; the verb can stand alone when equipment is understood. Équiper quelqu’un de is the non-reflexive form.

vocabulary.example: Ce quartier manque de places en garderie.
vocabulary.note: Manquer + direct object can mean miss a train or event; manquer à someone can mean be missed by that person.

vocabulary.example: Veuillez inclure une preuve de résidence dans votre envoi.
vocabulary.note: Participle `inclus`, feminine `incluse`; also describes inclusion in `Le prix inclut les taxes`.

vocabulary.english: to comprise, to include (of a whole)
vocabulary.example: Le forfait comprend le transport et les repas.
vocabulary.note: Overlaps with `inclure` for what a whole includes; `comprendre` also means to understand.

vocabulary.example: Je me souviens de la date limite indiquée sur la lettre.
vocabulary.note: Before a noun, use de; before a clause, se souvenir que is also possible. In careful French, se rappeler takes a noun directly.

vocabulary.example: Le locataire doit encore deux mois de loyer à la propriétaire.
vocabulary.note: Lexical use; the creditor after à can be left understood. Modal devoir is followed directly by an infinitive.

vocabulary.example: Une offre d’emploi bilingue a été publiée hier sur le site du centre.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun. Une proposition (f.) is a proposal and can also be commercial; une offre is the usual term in offre d’emploi and offre promotionnelle.

practice.prompt: Complete: « Je ___ le bureau à midi, je ___ le dossier à l’accueil et j’ai ___ un collègue dans l’ascenseur. »
practice.hint: Object of departure, what stays behind, an unplanned meeting.
practice.answer: Je quitte le bureau à midi, je laisse le dossier à l’accueil et j’ai croisé un collègue dans l’ascenseur.

takeaways: Apporter commonly describes carrying a thing; amener commonly describes bringing a person. Rendre visite à is the usual social-visit phrase.
`Partir` without an object, `quitter` with one, `laisser` for what stays.
`Disposer de` equals to have available; `s’équiper de` equals to get equipped.
`Se souvenir de` keeps the preposition; `se rappeler` does not.
`Devoir` plus infinitive is modal; with something owed it means owe, whether or not the creditor is named.
keywords: retenir, retirer, marcher, aller à pied, se promener, promener
manquer, il me manque, échapper à, servir, se servir, se servir de
engager, s’engager dans, s’engager à, s'engager dans, s'engager à
dessiner, mentir, assister à, un patron, une allure, éventuellement
prêter, emprunter, attraper, cocher, perdre le match, perdre du temps, espionner
lancer, s’écrier, ramasser, s’éteindre, excuser, s’excuser
changer d’opinion, collaborer, serrer, pousser, faire pousser, se comporter mal

lessons.title: La différence entre « la part » et « une partie »
lessons.summary: `La part` is someone’s share, allocation, or contribution, and appears in the fixed expressions `faire sa part`, `prendre part à`, and `de la part de`. `Une partie` is a section of a whole, a game or match, or one side in a dispute. English part covers both, so the choice must be made on meaning rather than on translation.
objectives: Choose `la part` when a share is distributed or contributed.
Choose `une partie` for a section of a whole.
Use the frequent fixed expressions built on `part`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Une part often means a share, contribution or portion: faire sa part du travail, payer sa part des dépenses, une part de gâteau. Une partie often identifies a section or an unspecified portion of a whole: la deuxième partie du rapport, une partie du quartier, une partie des candidats. The meanings overlap: giving someone une partie du gâteau is grammatical too. The choice is not a rule that distribution among people always requires part.

Learn the expression and the emphasis: faire sa part means contribute one’s share; rédiger sa partie du rapport means write one’s assigned section. Une partie also names a game or a side in a dispute. Three fixed expressions use part: faire sa part, prendre part à (participate in), and de la part de (on behalf of/from). Distinguish prendre parti, without an e, which means take sides.
points: Use une part for a share or portion, and learn fixed expressions such as faire sa part.
Use `une partie` for a section, a chapter, or a proportion.
Learn `faire sa part`, `prendre part à`, and `de la part de` as blocks.
Use `une partie` for a game and for a side in a negotiation.
Use share versus section as a helpful cue, not an absolute test; check the whole expression.

examples.french: Chacun doit faire sa part du travail dans le projet collectif.
examples.english: Everyone must do their share of the work in the group project.
examples.note: A distribution among people.

examples.french: Dans la deuxième partie du rapport, l’autrice propose trois solutions.
examples.english: In the second part of the report, the author proposes three solutions.
examples.note: A section of a whole.

examples.french: Une partie des candidats a déjà reçu une réponse écrite.
examples.english: Some of the candidates have already received a written answer.
examples.note: A proportion of a group.

examples.french: Je vous appelle de la part de la conseillère en emploi.
examples.english: I am calling on behalf of the employment adviser.
examples.note: Fixed expression « de la part de ».

examples.french: Plus de deux cents personnes ont pris part à la consultation.
examples.english: More than two hundred people took part in the consultation.
examples.note: Fixed expression prendre part à: participate in.

examples.french: J’ai pris une part de gâteau ; une partie du gâteau est restée au réfrigérateur.
examples.english: I took a slice of cake; part of the cake stayed in the refrigerator.
examples.note: Une part presents an individual portion; une partie presents some of the whole without defining a serving.

examples.french: Léa rédige sa partie du rapport, puis nous vérifierons ensemble le document complet.
examples.english: Léa is writing her section of the report, then we will check the complete document together.
examples.note: Partie is valid for a section assigned to a particular person.

examples.french: Je souhaite prendre part à la discussion sans prendre parti dans votre désaccord.
examples.english: I would like to take part in the discussion without taking sides in your disagreement.
examples.note: Prendre part à means participate; prendre parti means take sides.

mistakes.avoid: Nous prenons partie à la consultation.
mistakes.prefer: Nous prenons part à la consultation.
mistakes.why: The participation expression is prendre part à. Faire sa partie du travail can be valid for an assigned section; it is not an automatic error.

mistakes.avoid: Dans la deuxième part du rapport, l’auteur conclut.
mistakes.prefer: Dans la deuxième partie du rapport, l’auteur conclut.
mistakes.why: A section of a text is `une partie`.

vocabulary.example: La part de chacun dépend de sa contribution au projet.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; used when something is divided among people.

vocabulary.example: Une partie du rapport doit encore être corrigée.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; used for a section, a proportion, or a match.

vocabulary.example: Je vous transmets ce document de la part du service des permis.
vocabulary.note: Fixed expression; the article contracts after `de`.

vocabulary.example: Une contribution équitable facilite le travail d’équipe.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the ending -tion is a feminine hint.

practice.prompt: Choose the word: « Il a lu la première ___ du dossier, puis il a payé sa ___ des frais. »
practice.hint: Section first, then a share.
practice.answer: Il a lu la première partie du dossier, puis il a payé sa part des frais.

takeaways: Part often presents a share; partie often presents a section, with some overlap.
Section, proportion, or match equals `une partie`.
`Faire sa part`, `prendre part à`, `de la part de` are fixed.
keywords: distinguishing a share from a section

lessons.title: Les échanges et les réactions idiomatiques
lessons.summary: Choose everyday responses for their meaning, tone and context: wellbeing, agreement, reassurance, surprise, gratitude or encouragement. Distinguish casual language from formal reporting without treating informal speech or messages as incorrect French.
objectives: Use the frequent `ça` reactions accurately.
Choose a chunk that matches the formality of the situation.
Choose expressions for the relationship and medium, including informal messages.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Register is the level of formality suited to the audience and situation. Ça is more conversational than cela and is normal in speech and many informal messages. Ça va asks about wellbeing or says that something is acceptable. Ça y est marks an expected point being reached: something may be finished, ready, starting or happening at last. Ça ne fait rien can reassure someone about a minor problem or apology; do not use it to minimise a serious difficulty.

Vas-y and allez-y can mean go ahead; allez-y addresses vous, whether one person politely or several people. Tiens and tenez can accompany handing something over. Le plaisir est partagé or Tout le plaisir est pour moi can reciprocate pleasure after an introduction or a pleasant exchange. Informal expressions can also appear in casual writing; the issue is suitability, not a ban on writing them.

Occupe-toi de tes oignons means mind your own business and can sound rude even between friends. If you want a neutral boundary, Je préfère ne pas en parler is less confrontational. Similarly, choose a neutral description such as l’odeur est désagréable for a formal report rather than the familiar ça ne sent pas la rose.
points: Use `Ça va ?` to ask about someone and `Ça va` to answer.
Use ça y est for an expected point reached, including a beginning or completion.
Use `ça ne fait rien` to dismiss an apology or a small problem.
Use `tenez` with `vous` and `tiens` with `tu` when handing something over.
Recognise occupe-toi de tes oignons as blunt; friendship does not automatically make it polite.
Welcome a visitor with `Faites comme chez vous`, and agree emphatically with `tout à fait`.
Learn three frequent idioms with their register: `poser un lapin` and `avoir le cafard` are informal, while `faire le pont` is neutral.
Keep `ça ne sent pas la rose` for informal speech only; a written report would say `l’odeur est désagréable`.

examples.french: — Ça va ? — Ça va, merci. Tenez, voici votre reçu.
examples.english: “How are you?” “I’m fine, thanks. Here, this is your receipt.”
examples.note: Two everyday chunks in a service exchange.

examples.french: Ça y est, j’ai fini de remplir le dossier en ligne !
examples.english: That’s it, I have finished filling in the file online!
examples.note: « Ça y est » marks completion.

examples.french: Je suis désolé pour le retard. — Cela ne fait rien.
examples.english: I am sorry about the delay. — It does not matter.
examples.note: Slightly more formal variant of « ça ne fait rien ».

examples.french: Puis-je vous poser une question ? — Allez-y, je vous écoute.
examples.english: May I ask you a question? — Go ahead, I am listening.
examples.note: Polite form of « vas-y ».

examples.french: Merci pour cette conversation. — Le plaisir est partagé.
examples.english: Thank you for this conversation. — The pleasure is mutual.
examples.note: Standard way of returning a compliment.

examples.french: Entrez, faites comme chez vous. — Merci, c’est tout à fait aimable.
examples.english: Come in, make yourself at home. — Thank you, that is very kind.
examples.note: A welcoming formula, then « tout à fait » reinforcing an adjective.

examples.french: Il m’a posé un lapin samedi, et depuis j’ai un peu le cafard.
examples.english: He stood me up on Saturday, and I have been feeling a bit down since then.
examples.note: Both idioms are informal; they also fit a casual message, but a formal report may call for neutral wording.

examples.french: Le jeudi est férié, alors beaucoup de collègues font le pont vendredi.
examples.english: Thursday is a public holiday, so many colleagues take the Friday off as well.
examples.note: Faire le pont is neutral and usable in an email to a team.

examples.french: Ça y est, le cours commence !
examples.english: Here we go, the class is starting!
examples.note: The awaited beginning has arrived; the class is not already finished.

mistakes.avoid: Le plaisir est partagée.
mistakes.prefer: Le plaisir est partagé.
mistakes.why: Partagé agrees with masculine le plaisir. The shorter Plaisir partagé ! is also a possible elliptical reply; it is not ungrammatical.

mistakes.avoid: Ça fait rien, je vais attendre le prochain rendez-vous.
mistakes.prefer: Cela ne fait rien, je vais attendre le prochain rendez-vous.
mistakes.why: The first form is normal in casual speech or a casual message. For a formal context, retain ne; cela is a more formal option, not a compulsory replacement for every ça.

mistakes.avoid: Je vous informe que le fournisseur nous a posé un lapin hier.
mistakes.prefer: Je vous informe que le fournisseur ne s’est pas présenté hier.
mistakes.why: For a formal report, ne pas se présenter is more neutral. Poser un lapin is grammatical and may suit a casual exchange with a colleague.

sections.title: Not bad, that's fine, and wow
paragraphs: `Pas mal` means not bad and can be understated praise; it is not necessarily reluctant criticism. Informal `cool` can mean nice, good, or relaxed. `Sympa`, shortened from `sympathique`, means nice or friendly for a person and pleasant or enjoyable for an experience. `Super` and `génial` express stronger approval, like great or brilliant.

`C’est bon` can accept a proposal or confirm that something is sufficient or sorted out: that's fine, that's enough, or we're all set, depending on the exchange. It is not always a judgement about taste. `Oh là là !` expresses a strong reaction such as surprise, admiration, or dismay. `La vache !` is a very familiar exclamation like wow or holy cow, not a literal reference to an animal in this use.
points: Use the exchange and tone to interpret `C’est bon` and `Oh là là !`.
`Cool`, `super`, and `La vache !` belong to relaxed conversation rather than a formal report.

examples.french: Tu as réparé ça tout seul ? Pas mal !
examples.english: You fixed that on your own? Not bad!
examples.note: Understated admiration.

examples.french: On peut venir sans réserver ? Cool !
examples.english: We can come without booking? Cool!
examples.note: Informal approval, not temperature.

examples.french: Ta collègue est sympa ; elle m’a aidé à trouver la salle.
examples.english: Your colleague is nice; she helped me find the room.
examples.note: `Sympa` describes friendly behaviour.

examples.french: Merci pour ton aide, c’est super.
examples.english: Thanks for your help; that’s great.
examples.note: Warm informal appreciation.

examples.french: Vous avez trouvé une solution ? C’est génial !
examples.english: You found a solution? That’s brilliant!
examples.note: Enthusiastic approval.

examples.french: Je peux vous rappeler à quinze heures ? — Oui, c’est bon.
examples.english: Can I call you back at three? — Yes, that’s fine.
examples.note: Accepting the proposed time.

examples.french: Oh là là ! J’ai encore oublié mes clés.
examples.english: Oh dear! I have forgotten my keys again.
examples.note: Dismay, not admiration in this context.

examples.french: La vache ! Tu as parcouru toute cette distance à pied ?
examples.english: Wow! You covered that whole distance on foot?
examples.note: Very familiar surprise among people who know one another.

sections.title: Encouragement, reassurance, and gratitude
paragraphs: `Un choc (m.)` can be a physical impact or an emotional shock; a difficult announcement can therefore be `un choc` without a collision. Standalone `Courage !` encourages someone facing a difficulty: hang in there or keep going. It is not normally used as praise after an easy success.

`Ce n’est rien` reassures someone about a small problem or dismisses an apology: it's nothing, don't worry about it. `Pas de problème` can similarly accept a request or reassure someone. `Être reconnaissant/reconnaissante à quelqu’un de quelque chose` expresses gratitude to a person for something.

`Demander pardon à quelqu’un pour quelque chose` means ask someone to forgive you for something: `à` identifies the person and `pour` the reason. `La patience (f.)` is patience, the ability to wait or tolerate difficulty without becoming angry; `avoir de la patience` and `faire preuve de patience` are natural ways to describe it.
points: Keep the recipient and reason distinct: `pardon à Léa pour mon retard`.
Reassurance such as `Ce n’est rien` suits a minor mishap; it can minimise someone's feelings if used for a serious loss.

examples.french: L’annonce de la fermeture a été un choc pour l’équipe.
examples.english: The announcement of the closure was a shock to the team.
examples.note: An emotional shock.

examples.french: Courage ! Il ne te reste que deux jours de travail.
examples.english: Hang in there! You have only two days of work left.
examples.note: Encouragement while the difficulty continues.

examples.french: Pardon, je vous ai fait attendre. — Ce n’est rien.
examples.english: Sorry, I kept you waiting. — Don’t worry about it.
examples.note: Reassurance after a small inconvenience.

examples.french: Peux-tu m’envoyer le document demain ? — Pas de problème.
examples.english: Can you send me the document tomorrow? — No problem.
examples.note: Readily accepting a request.

examples.french: Je vous suis reconnaissante de votre aide.
examples.english: I am grateful to you for your help.
examples.note: `Vous` identifies the person; `de votre aide` gives the reason.

examples.french: Il a demandé pardon à sa sœur pour ses paroles blessantes.
examples.english: He asked his sister to forgive him for his hurtful words.
examples.note: The person follows `à`; the reason follows `pour`.

examples.french: Merci de votre patience ; je termine la vérification.
examples.english: Thank you for your patience; I am finishing the check.
examples.note: Acknowledging someone's willingness to wait.

mistakes.avoid: Je suis reconnaissant.
mistakes.prefer: Je reconnais cette personne.
mistakes.why: If you intend I recognise this person, use reconnaître. Je suis reconnaissant is grammatical but means I am grateful.

sections.title: Ordinary days and what is happening for now
paragraphs: `Pour le moment` means for now or at present and often leaves open a later change. `Ces jours-ci` means these days, around the current period. `Habituellement` means usually or habitually; `en général` means generally, often introducing a broad tendency rather than an absolute rule.

`Être en voyage` means be away on a trip, not necessarily on holiday. `Rien de spécial` means nothing special. `Ordinaire` describes something ordinary or usual, without automatically judging it as bad. `Se réveiller` means wake up; it is distinct from `se lever`, getting out of bed.

`Prendre une pause` means take a break and is especially common in Canadian French; `faire une pause` is also widespread. `En même temps` literally means at the same time. It can also introduce a balancing consideration in conversation, but its simultaneous-action meaning remains common.
points: A temporary situation (`pour le moment`) is not the same as a recurring habit (`habituellement`).
Waking up does not necessarily mean getting out of bed immediately.

examples.french: Pour le moment, je travaille à la maison.
examples.english: For now, I work from home.
examples.note: The arrangement may change.

examples.french: Ces jours-ci, elle est en voyage pour son travail.
examples.english: These days, she is away on a business trip.
examples.note: A current period and a trip that is not a holiday.

examples.french: Habituellement, je me réveille à sept heures.
examples.english: I usually wake up at seven.
examples.note: A habitual morning routine.

examples.french: Je me réveille tôt, mais je reste parfois au lit quelques minutes.
examples.english: I wake up early, but I sometimes stay in bed for a few minutes.
examples.note: Waking and getting up are separate.

examples.french: Qu’as-tu fait hier ? — Rien de spécial, c’était une journée ordinaire.
examples.english: What did you do yesterday? — Nothing special; it was an ordinary day.
examples.note: An uneventful day, not necessarily an unpleasant one.

examples.french: En général, le bureau ferme à dix-sept heures, sauf le jeudi.
examples.english: The office generally closes at five, except on Thursdays.
examples.note: A broad pattern with an exception.

examples.french: Nous avons beaucoup travaillé ; prenons une pause.
examples.english: We have worked a lot; let’s take a break.
examples.note: Stopping temporarily to rest.

examples.french: Nous sommes arrivés en même temps devant la porte.
examples.english: We arrived at the door at the same time.
examples.note: Two simultaneous arrivals.

mistakes.avoid: Je me lève à sept heures.
mistakes.prefer: Je me réveille à sept heures.
mistakes.why: If you mean only that you wake up, use se réveiller. Se lever is grammatical but says you get up; you might still remain in bed after waking.

sections.title: The same result, a matching item, and an emphatic confirmation
paragraphs: `C’est du pareil au même` means the alternatives come to effectively the same thing, often because the result does not change. It does not automatically mean `ça m’est égal`, I don't mind or I am indifferent. `Correspondant/correspondante` as an adjective means matching or corresponding, as in a numbered item and its matching answer; this is distinct from the noun for a pen pal or correspondent.

`Et même` means and even, adding something noteworthy. Standalone `De même` means likewise or the same to you, and sounds a little more reserved than many casual replies. `C’est comme ça que…` means that's how…, introducing an explanation of a method or how something happened.

`Bien` can confirm an identification: `C’est bien du pain` means it is indeed bread or it really is bread. It does not mean the bread is made well. `Soudain` and `soudainement` mean suddenly, marking an abrupt change or event.
points: Compare equivalent consequences with `du pareil au même`; express personal indifference with `ça m’est égal`.
In an identification, emphatic `bien` confirms the statement rather than describing manner.

examples.french: Partir par cette rue ou par l’autre, c’est du pareil au même : les deux sont fermées.
examples.english: Taking this street or the other comes to the same thing: both are closed.
examples.note: Equivalent outcomes, not necessarily indifference.

examples.french: Lisez chaque question, puis cochez la réponse correspondante.
examples.english: Read each question, then tick the matching answer.
examples.note: Adjectival `correspondante` links the answer to its question.

examples.french: Il y avait des voisins, des collègues et même notre ancienne enseignante.
examples.english: There were neighbours, colleagues, and even our former teacher.
examples.note: An additional person presented as noteworthy.

examples.french: Je vous souhaite une bonne soirée. — De même.
examples.english: I wish you a pleasant evening. — Likewise.
examples.note: A standalone reciprocal reply.

examples.french: C’est comme ça que j’ai rencontré ma meilleure amie.
examples.english: That’s how I met my best friend.
examples.note: A link back to the story just told.

examples.french: Tu croyais que c’était un gâteau ? Non, c’est bien du pain.
examples.english: You thought it was a cake? No, it really is bread.
examples.note: `Bien` confirms the identification; it does not mean well.

examples.french: Soudain, quelqu’un a frappé à la porte.
examples.english: Suddenly, someone knocked at the door.
examples.note: An abrupt event in the story.

examples.french: La conversation s’est arrêtée soudainement.
examples.english: The conversation stopped suddenly.
examples.note: The longer adverb also describes an abrupt change.

sections.title: Gifts, stories, and sharing a happy occasion
paragraphs: `Un cadeau (m.)` is a gift, and `le bonheur (m.)` is happiness, often a fuller or more lasting sense than a single moment of amusement. `Enchanté/enchantée` can mean delighted about an experience or prospect, not just pleased to meet you in an introduction. `Une histoire drôle (f.)` is a funny story or a joke.

`Briser la glace` means break the ice: help people start interacting comfortably. `Lever son verre` means raise one's glass, usually to make a toast. `Dans mes bras` means in my arms; the headword `un bras (m.)` means an arm. Holding or hugging someone in your arms is different from holding a small object in your hands.

`Le monde entier` means the whole world. The noun is `le monde (m.)`, world; it is not always interchangeable with `tout le monde`, everybody. A project can reach the whole world geographically without literally reaching every person.
points: Read `enchanté de` an experience or prospect as delighted, not as a greeting.
Ice-breaking starts a social exchange; a toast marks a wish or occasion.

examples.french: Merci pour ce cadeau ; je suis enchantée de le recevoir.
examples.english: Thank you for this gift; I am delighted to receive it.
examples.note: Delight about a gift, not an introduction formula.

examples.french: Quel bonheur de vous retrouver après toutes ces années !
examples.english: What happiness it brings to see you again after all these years!
examples.note: `Le bonheur` names happiness.

examples.french: Elle a raconté une histoire drôle pour briser la glace.
examples.english: She told a funny story to break the ice.
examples.note: Humour helps people begin talking comfortably.

examples.french: Nous avons levé notre verre à la réussite de notre amie.
examples.english: We raised our glasses to our friend’s success.
examples.note: A toast, with French singular `notre verre` understood individually.

examples.french: Viens dans mes bras, tu m’as tellement manqué !
examples.english: Come into my arms; I have missed you so much!
examples.note: An affectionate invitation to embrace someone close.

examples.french: Ce message a été partagé dans le monde entier.
examples.english: This message was shared around the world.
examples.note: Worldwide reach, not the claim that every individual shared it.

examples.french: Il connaît beaucoup d’histoires drôles, mais il attend le bon moment pour les raconter.
examples.english: He knows many funny stories, but he waits for the right moment to tell them.
examples.note: The plural names jokes or amusing stories, not histories.

mistakes.avoid: Je tiens mon bébé dans mes mains.
mistakes.prefer: Je tiens mon bébé dans mes bras.
mistakes.why: If you mean cradling the baby in your arms, use dans mes bras. Dans mes mains is grammatical but specifies the hands rather than the arms.

vocabulary.example: Ça y est, le formulaire est envoyé et confirmé.
vocabulary.note: Marks completion; informal but very frequent.

vocabulary.example: Vous êtes en retard de cinq minutes ? Ça ne fait rien.
vocabulary.note: `Cela ne fait rien` is the slightly more formal variant.

vocabulary.example: Merci de votre accueil. — Le plaisir est partagé.
vocabulary.note: A full-clause reply; the elliptical Plaisir partagé ! also occurs.

vocabulary.example: Un reçu officiel est remis après chaque paiement.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun, from the past participle of `recevoir`.

vocabulary.example: Installez-vous et faites comme chez vous.
vocabulary.note: Uses the `vous` imperative; the informal version is `fais comme chez toi`.

vocabulary.example: Vous avez tout à fait raison au sujet du délai.
vocabulary.note: Reinforces an adjective, an adverb, or a whole answer.

vocabulary.example: Les participants se sont très bien comportés pendant la visite.
vocabulary.note: Pronominal; `se comporter mal` means to behave badly.

vocabulary.example: Elle m’a posé un lapin sans même envoyer un message.
vocabulary.note: Informal in speech or writing; ne pas se présenter is a neutral alternative.

vocabulary.english: to take the bridging day off
vocabulary.example: Nous faisons le pont entre le jeudi férié et la fin de semaine.
vocabulary.note: Neutral register; describes taking the working day between a holiday and the weekend.

vocabulary.english: to feel down, to have the blues
vocabulary.example: Après trois semaines de pluie, tout le monde a un peu le cafard.
vocabulary.note: Informal for feeling down; avoir le moral bas is a more neutral alternative. The idiom does not diagnose depression.

vocabulary.example: Nous avons rempli le formulaire ensemble à la séance d’accueil.
vocabulary.note: Invariable adverb, often after the verb; it can also open a sentence for emphasis. Un ensemble (m.) is a set or a whole.

vocabulary.english: to smell bad, to be unsavoury
vocabulary.example: Le local n’a pas été aéré depuis une semaine : ça ne sent pas la rose.
vocabulary.note: Informal and almost always negative; unusable in formal written production.

practice.prompt: Complete the exchange: « — ___ ? — ___, merci. ___, voici votre attestation. »
practice.hint: Greeting, reply, and handing something over politely.
practice.answer: — Ça va ? — Ça va, merci. Tenez, voici votre attestation.

takeaways: `Ça va`, `ça y est`, `ça ne fait rien` cover most everyday reactions.
`Tenez` with `vous`, `tiens` with `tu`.
Recognise very familiar idioms, but keep them out of formal writing.
keywords: pas mal, cool, un cadeau, pour le moment, un choc, Courage !
C’est bon, Ce n’est rien, Pas de problème, sympa, être reconnaissant
en voyage, rien de spécial, ordinaire, habituellement, le monde entier
super, génial, demander pardon, prendre une pause, en même temps
du pareil au même, dans mes bras, correspondant, Oh là là !, La vache !
la patience, ces jours-ci, soudain, soudainement, et même, lever son verre
briser la glace, de même, en général, une histoire drôle, C’est comme ça que
C’est bien du pain, se réveiller, le bonheur, enchanté

lessons.title: Les mots abrégés et les petits mots de la conversation
lessons.summary: Clipped words such as un dico and une colo often signal informal register, though established forms such as métro and photo are neutral. Spoken markers — ouais, hein, bah, final quoi — express assent, checks, or reactions. Interpret final ça, requests to repeat, and Et alors ? from their grammatical role, tone, and context.
objectives: Link each clipped form to its full equivalent.
Keep the gender of the complete noun.
Select the form that matches the register of the situation.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Clipping shortens a word. Many familiar examples keep its beginning: un adolescent → un ado, un dictionnaire → un dico, un restaurant → un resto. These nouns keep the gender of the full form: une colonie de vacances → une colo, la faculté → la fac. Other clippings retain a later part, such as un autobus → un bus.

The difference is often one of register. Clipped forms are normal in conversation between peers and in informal messages. In a formal letter or application, fuller forms such as dictionnaire or colonie de vacances are often preferable; this is not a ban on shortened words in all writing. Established forms such as le métro and la photo are neutral in many written contexts too.
points: Match each clipped form with its complete equivalent before using it.
Keep the article and the gender of the original noun.
Use familiar clipped forms in speech and informal messages; check the register of each word.
Prefer an appropriate full form in formal writing when the shortened form is markedly informal.
Note that `métro` and `photo` are now neutral in most writing.

examples.french: Un ado peut dire « un dico » entre amis, mais « un dictionnaire » convient mieux dans un écrit formel.
examples.english: A teenager may say “un dico” among friends, but “un dictionnaire” is better in formal writing.
examples.note: The same object, two registers.

examples.french: Après le bac, elle a travaillé dans une colo pendant l’été.
examples.english: After the baccalaureate exam, she worked at a summer camp during the summer.
examples.note: Two clipped forms in a spoken narrative.

examples.french: Il étudie à la fac de droit et prend le métro chaque matin.
examples.english: He studies at the law faculty and takes the subway every morning.
examples.note: « Fac » stays informal; « métro » has become neutral.

examples.french: Dans sa lettre de motivation, elle a écrit « baccalauréat » et non « bac ».
examples.english: In her cover letter, she wrote “baccalauréat” and not “bac”.
examples.note: The fuller form can be clearer in a formal document; this is a register choice, not a universal spelling rule.

mistakes.avoid: J’utilise une dico bilingue.
mistakes.prefer: J’utilise un dico bilingue.
mistakes.why: Dico keeps the masculine gender of un dictionnaire. Choosing dictionnaire in formal writing is a register preference, not a correction of un dico.

mistakes.avoid: Elle a passé l’été dans un colo près du lac.
mistakes.prefer: Elle a passé l’été dans une colo près du lac.
mistakes.why: The clipped form keeps the feminine gender of `une colonie de vacances`.

sections.title: Ouais, hein, bah, quoi, ça: listen for the function
paragraphs: Ouais is informal assent, like yeah. Hein can check agreement or shared understanding, sometimes insistently depending on tone. Bah often introduces hesitation, resignation, or a reaction, like well. Sentence-final quoi can round off or summarise a thought, roughly you know or I mean; it is not asking what in that use.

Final ça is not automatically an empty filler. In C’est ton ancienne école, ça ?, it points to or resumes the thing being identified, often with extra emphasis. In Je ne comprends pas ça, it is the verb’s object. Do not remove required pronouns by treating every short spoken word as dispensable.

These forms are useful for recognising casual conversation. In a formal exchange, oui and an explicit clarification are often safer than reproducing every tag. Their informality does not make them grammatical errors.
points: Interpret a spoken marker by its conversational function and tone.
Distinguish final quoi as a discourse marker from interrogative quoi.
Check whether ça points to a referent or supplies a required object.

examples.french: Tu viens avec nous ? — Ouais, j’arrive.
examples.english: Are you coming with us? — Yeah, I’m coming.
examples.note: Informal assent.

examples.french: On se retrouve devant la gare, hein ?
examples.english: We’re meeting in front of the station, right?
examples.note: Hein checks a shared arrangement; tone can make it insistent.

examples.french: Bah, on peut attendre le prochain bus.
examples.english: Well, we can wait for the next bus.
examples.note: Bah introduces a relaxed or resigned reaction.

examples.french: On a beaucoup marché; on est fatigués, quoi.
examples.english: We’ve walked a lot; we’re tired, you know.
examples.note: Final quoi rounds off the explanation rather than asking a question.

examples.french: C’est ton ancienne école, ça ?
examples.english: Is that your old school?
examples.note: Ça points to the place or picture being identified.

examples.french: Je ne comprends pas ça. Tu peux m’expliquer ?
examples.english: I don’t understand that. Can you explain it to me?
examples.note: Ça is the object of comprends, not a freely removable tag.

sections.title: Asking again or asking what happened next
paragraphs: When you have not heard, Pardon ? or Comment ? can invite repetition; a fuller Pourriez-vous répéter ? makes the request explicit. Quoi ? is common in spontaneous conversation but can sound abrupt, especially with a stranger or a sharp tone. It is not ungrammatical.

Et alors ? can invite the next part of a story (and then?) or dismiss an objection (so what?). The surrounding exchange and intonation decide. To avoid the dismissive reading, ask Et ensuite, qu’est-ce qui s’est passé ? or another specific follow-up.
points: Choose a repetition request for the relationship and tone, not by a grammar ban on quoi.
Et alors ? may continue a story or dismiss its relevance.

examples.french: Pardon, je n’ai pas entendu. Pourriez-vous répéter le numéro ?
examples.english: Sorry, I didn’t hear. Could you repeat the number?
examples.note: An explicit polite repair request.

examples.french: Comment ? Vous avez dit mardi ou jeudi ?
examples.english: Sorry? Did you say Tuesday or Thursday?
examples.note: Comment asks for clarification, not an explanation of how.

examples.french: J’ai enfin rencontré la responsable. — Et alors, quelle a été sa réponse ?
examples.english: I finally met the person in charge. — And then, what was her answer?
examples.note: A follow-up requesting the next information.

examples.french: Ton téléphone est ancien. — Et alors ? Il fonctionne encore très bien.
examples.english: Your phone is old. — So what? It still works very well.
examples.note: The reply dismisses the relevance of the observation and can sound blunt.

sections.title: School and computer words in their shortened forms
paragraphs: `Un exam (m.)` shortens `un examen (m.)`, an examination; `une interro (f.)` shortens `une interrogation (f.)`, often a classroom quiz or test. `La géo (f.)` is `la géographie (f.)`, geography, and `la récré (f.)` is `la récréation (f.)`, the school break or recess. `Une note (f.)` means a grade or mark in this context, not simply a written note.

`Un instit (m.)` and `une instit (f.)` refer to an elementary-school teacher: `un instituteur (m.)` or `une institutrice (f.)`. `Un prof (m.)` and `une prof (f.)` shorten `un professeur (m.)` and `une professeure (f.)`; the unshortened feminine `une professeur` also occurs. The current French primary-school job title is commonly `un professeur des écoles` or `une professeure des écoles`.

`Un ordi (m.)` is `un ordinateur (m.)`, a computer. `Une info (f.)` is `une information (f.)`, a piece of information. These clipped forms are common in conversation and informal messages; full forms make school reports or administrative communication more explicit.

School terms depend on the education system. In France, le bac normally refers to the baccalauréat at the end of secondary school; in Quebec, un bac commonly names a university bachelor’s degree. Do not infer the qualification level from the shortened word alone.
points: Clipping preserves gender: `un examen → un exam`, but `une interrogation → une interro`.
A school `interro` is a test, not necessarily a police-style interrogation.

examples.french: J’ai un exam de géo lundi ; je révise la géographie ce week-end.
examples.english: I have a geography exam on Monday; I am revising geography this weekend.
examples.note: The same subject appears in clipped and full form.

examples.french: L’instit de ma fille prépare une sortie avec sa classe.
examples.english: My daughter’s elementary-school teacher is preparing a class outing.
examples.note: Informal `instit` identifies a primary-level teacher.

examples.french: Notre prof nous a rendu les copies de l’interro.
examples.english: Our teacher gave us back the quiz papers.
examples.note: Two familiar classroom clippings.

examples.french: J’ai eu une bonne note à cette interrogation.
examples.english: I got a good grade on this test.
examples.note: `Une note` is the assessment result.

examples.french: Les enfants jouent dehors pendant la récré.
examples.english: The children play outside during recess.
examples.note: A school break.

examples.french: Mon ordi ne démarre plus ; je dois emprunter un ordinateur.
examples.english: My computer will not start anymore; I need to borrow a computer.
examples.note: Clipped and full forms name the same device.

examples.french: Tu as une info sur la date de l’examen ?
examples.english: Do you have any information about the exam date?
examples.note: `Une info` is one piece of information, not an English information.

examples.french: Dans mon courrier à l’école, j’ai écrit « professeur » plutôt que « prof ».
examples.english: In my letter to the school, I wrote “professeur” rather than “prof”.
examples.note: Choosing the full form for a more formal document.

mistakes.avoid: Nous avons un interro demain.
mistakes.prefer: Nous avons une interro demain.
mistakes.why: Interro keeps the feminine gender of une interrogation. At school it means a quiz or test.

mistakes.avoid: Tu as un info sur l’examen ?
mistakes.prefer: Tu as une info sur l’examen ?
mistakes.why: Info is feminine, like une information. English uses a piece of information, not an information.

vocabulary.example: Un ado ou une ado peut participer à cet échange scolaire.
vocabulary.note: Clipped form of `un adolescent`; both genders exist.

vocabulary.example: Le bac marque la fin des études secondaires en France.
vocabulary.note: Clipped form of le baccalauréat. The qualification differs between France and Quebec; the full name can be clearer in formal documents.

vocabulary.example: Une colo accueille les enfants pendant les vacances d’été.
vocabulary.note: Clipped form of `une colonie de vacances`; a language stay is `un séjour linguistique`.

vocabulary.example: Un dico bilingue reste utile pour vérifier un sens rapidement.
vocabulary.note: Clipped form of `un dictionnaire`.

practice.prompt: Rewrite formally: « J’ai fait la fac, puis j’ai travaillé dans une colo. »
practice.hint: Restore both complete nouns.
practice.answer: J’ai étudié à la faculté, puis j’ai travaillé dans une colonie de vacances.

takeaways: A clipped noun keeps the gender of the full word.
Choose shortened forms by register; métro and photo are neutral in many written contexts.
Spoken tags have different functions, and final ça is not always a filler.
Tone distinguishes a friendly follow-up from a dismissive Et alors ?.
keywords: marqueurs du discours, demande de répétition, Comment ?, Pardon ?, Quoi ?, Et alors ?
un exam, un examen, la géo, la géographie, une info, une information
un instit, un instituteur, une institutrice, un prof, un professeur
une interro, une interrogation, un ordi, un ordinateur, la récré, la récréation
bac baccalauréat France Québec bachelor degree

modules.title: Le vocabulaire par thème
modules.description: Find practical words by situation: dates, weather, food, home, health, clothing, descriptions, leisure, countries, study, work and community life.

lessons.title: Les jours, les dates, les saisons et les tarifs
lessons.summary: Distinguish a recurring weekday from a specific date using the whole expression, not the article alone. Learn conventional date and season forms, including le 1er mars and au printemps, and use a definite article to express a unit rate.
objectives: Distinguish a habitual day from a specific one.
Write a full date with the right number form.
Use the correct preposition for each season.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Le vendredi, je travaille normally describes a weekly habit; Vendredi, je travaille refers to a particular Friday understood from context. The article alone does not guarantee repetition: le vendredi 5 mars identifies one date. Similarly, le matin can describe a routine, but le matin de mon arrivée is a particular morning. Days and months take lowercase except where a capital is independently required, such as the beginning of a sentence.

In an ordinary sentence, give the date with le and a cardinal number: le 5 mars, le 12 septembre. The first day uses an ordinal: le 1er mars, read le premier mars. Writing premier in full is also correct. Familiar unmodified seasonal forms are en hiver, en été, en automne and au printemps. These are not the only possible constructions: à l’automne is also valid, and modifiers give forms such as cet hiver or le printemps dernier.

A definite article can express a unit price, where English uses per: trois dollars le kilo, deux dollars la pièce, quinze dollars l’heure. The unit, not the noun naming what you buy, determines the article.
points: Le + an unqualified weekday commonly marks a habit; a qualified expression such as le mardi 5 mars can identify a single day.
Write days and months in lowercase.
Use `le` plus a cardinal number in a date, except `le 1er`.
Use `en hiver`, `en été`, `en automne`, but `au printemps`.
Use `le`, `la`, or `l’` before the unit to express a rate.

examples.french: Le vendredi, je suis un atelier de conversation à la bibliothèque.
examples.english: On Fridays, I attend a conversation workshop at the library.
examples.note: The article marks a weekly habit.

examples.french: Mardi, je vais au centre de services pour renouveler mon permis.
examples.english: On Tuesday, I am going to the service centre to renew my permit.
examples.note: No article: one specific day.

examples.french: L’atelier reprendra le mardi 5 mars et se terminera le 1er juin.
examples.english: The workshop will resume on Tuesday, March 5 and will end on June 1.
examples.note: Cardinal numbers in dates, except « 1er ».

examples.french: En hiver, je fais du ski de fond ; au printemps, je marche dans le parc.
examples.english: In winter, I go cross-country skiing; in spring, I walk in the park.
examples.note: « En » for three seasons, « au » for spring.

examples.french: Les pommes coûtent trois dollars le kilo et le stationnement coûte deux dollars l’heure.
examples.english: Apples cost three dollars per kilo and parking costs two dollars per hour.
examples.note: The definite article expresses a rate.

mistakes.avoid: En printemps, la ville organise un grand nettoyage.
mistakes.prefer: Au printemps, la ville organise un grand nettoyage.
mistakes.why: Spring is the one season that takes `au` instead of `en`.

mistakes.avoid: La réunion aura lieu le premier mars, Lundi prochain.
mistakes.prefer: La réunion aura lieu le premier mars, lundi prochain.
mistakes.why: Lundi needs lowercase here. Premier written in full is already correct; le 1er mars is another valid written form.

vocabulary.example: Le vendredi, notre groupe se retrouve à la médiathèque.
vocabulary.note: Le vendredi can express a weekly habit; a qualified date such as le vendredi 5 mars is specific.

vocabulary.example: Le printemps arrive tard dans cette région.
vocabulary.note: The usual unmodified seasonal phrase is au printemps; a modifier can give ce printemps or le printemps dernier.

vocabulary.example: L’hiver apporte souvent de la neige dès novembre.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; used with `en hiver`.

vocabulary.example: Un atelier de conversation a lieu chaque vendredi soir.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; also means a craft workshop.

vocabulary.example: Le stationnement est gratuit après dix-huit heures.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun used in Canada; `le parking` is used in France.

practice.prompt: Say in French: I work on Saturdays, the course starts on 1 September, and it costs twenty dollars an hour.
practice.hint: Habit, date with an ordinal, and a rate.
practice.answer: Le samedi, je travaille ; le cours commence le 1er septembre et il coûte vingt dollars l’heure.

takeaways: Use the whole time expression to distinguish a habit from a particular day.
Dates use cardinals, except `le 1er`.
`En hiver`, `en été`, `en automne`, but `au printemps`.

lessons.title: La météo, les saisons et la nature
lessons.summary: Describe weather with common il fait, il pleut, il y a and le temps est patterns. Distinguish temperature, sunshine and visibility; learn vocabulary for landscapes, the countryside and gardens. Use soir and soirée according to the expression and context, not a rule that every soir must be recurring.
objectives: Ask and answer a question about the weather with the standard formula.
Choose a common weather construction and the words that fit it.
Separate `le soir`, `une soirée`, and `la nuit`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Many weather expressions use an impersonal il: it does not refer to a person or object. Ask Quel temps fait-il ? Learn these common patterns: il fait beau/froid/moins dix; il pleut/neige/gèle; il y a du vent/des nuages/du verglas; le temps est nuageux. The last pattern has an ordinary noun subject, le temps. These are useful patterns, not an exhaustive list: Il fait du vent is also valid, so faire is not limited to adjectives.

Le temps est nuageux and the conversational C’est nuageux describe cloudy weather; Il y a des nuages names the presence of clouds. Choose the description that fits what you mean. Une soirée often presents an evening as a duration or an occasion. Soir names the part of the day: Le soir, je lis describes a habit, but ce soir, hier soir and un soir refer to particular evenings. Compare Bonjour/Bonsoir when greeting someone with Bonne journée/Bonne soirée when wishing them a good day or evening.

Similar pairs are un jour (m.) / une journée (f.) and un matin (m.) / une matinée (f.). The -ée forms often highlight the duration or experience of the period: toute la matinée, une journée agréable. This is a useful tendency, not an absolute opposition between a single event and a habit.
points: Ask with `Quel temps fait-il ?` and answer with one of the four frames.
Use `il fait` plus an adjective or a temperature.
Use an impersonal verb alone: `il pleut`, `il neige`, `il gèle`.
Use `il y a` plus an article and a weather noun: `du vent`, `des nuages`, `du verglas`.
Use `le temps est` plus a descriptive adjective, and treat `c’est nuageux` as its conversational variant.
Le soir can mark a habit; ce soir and hier soir identify particular evenings. Une soirée can describe a duration or an event.

examples.french: — Quel temps fait-il ce matin ? — Il fait froid, mais le temps est ensoleillé.
examples.english: “What is the weather like this morning?” “It is cold, but the weather is sunny.”
examples.note: The standard question, then two different frames in the answer.

examples.french: Il pleut depuis hier soir, alors prends un parapluie.
examples.english: It has been raining since yesterday evening, so take an umbrella.
examples.note: « Pleuvoir » is impersonal and needs nothing after it.

examples.french: Il y a des nuages et du vent ; c’est nuageux sur toute la région.
examples.english: There are clouds and wind; it is cloudy across the whole region.
examples.note: A weather noun with « il y a », then the conversational « c’est nuageux ».

examples.french: Il y avait du verglas toute la matinée, alors les autobus étaient en retard.
examples.english: There was black ice all morning, so the buses were late.
examples.note: « Verglas » is ice on the ground; freezing rain is « la pluie verglaçante ».

examples.french: Les inondations et les glissements de terrain ont coupé deux routes régionales.
examples.english: The floods and landslides cut off two regional roads.
examples.note: Vocabulary for weather events reported in the news.

examples.french: Passez une bonne soirée après la cérémonie d’accueil !
examples.english: Have a good evening after the welcome ceremony!
examples.note: Bonne soirée wishes someone a good evening; Bonsoir is an evening greeting.

mistakes.avoid: Il y a froid et du vent aujourd’hui.
mistakes.prefer: Il y a du vent et il fait froid aujourd’hui.
mistakes.why: Use il fait froid, not il y a froid. Il y a du vent and il fait du vent are both valid ways to say it is windy.

mistakes.avoid: Il fait pleuvoir depuis ce matin.
mistakes.prefer: Il pleut depuis ce matin.
mistakes.why: To report rain, use il pleut. Faire pleuvoir means cause something to rain, literally or figuratively; it is not the ordinary weather report intended here.

mistakes.avoid: Bonne soir et à demain !
mistakes.prefer: Bonne soirée et à demain !
mistakes.why: To wish someone a good evening, use Bonne soirée. To greet someone in the evening, use the single word Bonsoir.

sections.title: Poor visibility and missing-person reports
paragraphs: `Le brouillard (m.)` means fog; `la brume (f.)` means mist. In ordinary descriptions, fog suggests denser conditions and poorer visibility than mist. `Brumeux / brumeuse` means misty or hazy; it describes the conditions rather than naming the substance.

In reports about an outdoor search, `une personne disparue (f.)` means a missing person, whose whereabouts are unknown. It does not by itself mean that the person has died. The phrase remains grammatically feminine even when the missing person is a man.
points: `le brouillard (m.)` — fog; `Il y a du brouillard` — it is foggy.
`la brume (f.)` — mist; `Il y a de la brume` — it is misty.
`brumeux / brumeuse` — misty, hazy: `un matin brumeux`, `une matinée brumeuse`.
`une personne disparue (f.)`, `des personnes disparues (f. pl.)` — missing person, missing people; `disparue` agrees with `personne`.

examples.french: Le brouillard est si dense que le car roule très lentement.
examples.english: The fog is so dense that the coach is moving very slowly.
examples.note: Fog has a direct effect on visibility during travel.

examples.french: Il y a encore de la brume au-dessus du lac, mais on distingue la rive.
examples.english: There is still mist over the lake, but the shore is visible.
examples.note: Mist is presented as lighter than the dense fog in the previous example.

examples.french: La matinée sera brumeuse ; la visite du barrage commencera à onze heures.
examples.english: The morning will be misty; the visit to the dam will begin at eleven.
examples.note: The feminine form brumeuse describes la matinée.

examples.french: La police recherche une personne disparue après une promenade près du camping.
examples.english: The police are looking for a person who went missing after a walk near the campsite.
examples.note: This reports an unknown location, not a confirmed death.

examples.french: Malgré le brouillard, les secours ont retrouvé les deux personnes disparues.
examples.english: Despite the fog, the rescue services found the two missing people.
examples.note: The adjective is feminine plural because it describes les personnes.

mistakes.avoid: Il y a de la brouillard et du brume.
mistakes.prefer: Il y a du brouillard et de la brume.
mistakes.why: Brouillard is masculine; brume is feminine.

mistakes.avoid: Les deux personnes disparus ont été retrouvées.
mistakes.prefer: Les deux personnes disparues ont été retrouvées.
mistakes.why: Disparues agrees with the feminine plural noun personnes, regardless of the people's genders.

sections.title: Seasonal conditions and plans outdoors
paragraphs: `Il fait bon` means the temperature feels pleasantly mild or warm. Unlike `Il fait beau`, it does not primarily describe sunshine or a clear sky. It can feel pleasant outdoors even with some cloud.

`Pluvieux / pluvieuse` means rainy; `orageux / orageuse` means stormy or thundery, often suggesting a thunderstorm is possible. `À cette époque de l’année` means at this time of year, referring to a recurring part of the annual cycle rather than necessarily a historical era.
points: `le ciel (m.)` — sky; `le soleil (m.)` — sun, or sunshine in `Il y a du soleil`.
`pluvieux / pluvieuse` — rainy: `un week-end pluvieux`, `une semaine pluvieuse`.
`orageux / orageuse` — stormy, thundery: `un ciel orageux`, `une journée orageuse`.
`Il fait bon` — the temperature is pleasant or pleasantly warm; it does not mean very hot.
`à cette époque de l’année` — at this time of year; `une époque (f.)` names a period and `une année (f.)` a year.

examples.french: Il fait bon sur la terrasse, même si le ciel est un peu couvert.
examples.english: It is pleasantly warm on the terrace, even though the sky is a little overcast.
examples.note: Pleasant temperature does not require an entirely clear sky.

examples.french: Il y a du soleil, mais il fait trop froid pour déjeuner dehors.
examples.english: It is sunny, but too cold to have lunch outside.
examples.note: Sunshine and comfortable warmth are different observations.

examples.french: À cette époque de l’année, les journées sont souvent pluvieuses.
examples.english: At this time of year, the days are often rainy.
examples.note: The time phrase describes a seasonal pattern.

examples.french: Le ciel devient orageux ; nous allons reporter la sortie en bateau.
examples.english: The sky is becoming stormy; we are going to postpone the boat trip.
examples.note: Orageux suggests storm conditions, not simply light rain.

examples.french: La météo annonce un week-end pluvieux, alors nous visiterons le musée.
examples.english: The forecast says it will be a rainy weekend, so we will visit the museum.
examples.note: Pluvieux describes a period of rainy weather.

examples.french: À cette époque de l’année, le soleil se couche avant la fin de ma journée de travail.
examples.english: At this time of year, the sun sets before the end of my working day.
examples.note: Le soleil names the sun itself, rather than the presence of sunshine.

mistakes.avoid: Il fait bonne sur la terrasse.
mistakes.prefer: Il fait bon sur la terrasse.
mistakes.why: The fixed impersonal expression is il fait bon; bon does not agree with a nearby feminine place noun.

mistakes.avoid: Nous prévoyons une journée pluvieux et orageux.
mistakes.prefer: Nous prévoyons une journée pluvieuse et orageuse.
mistakes.why: Both weather adjectives agree with the feminine noun journée.

sections.title: Mountains, fields, and the countryside
paragraphs: `La campagne (f.)` means the countryside in `vivre à la campagne`. It is not the same as the English word campaign in that phrase. French also has `une campagne (f.)` for an organised campaign, such as a public-awareness campaign; the article and the surrounding words clarify the sense.

`Un paysage (m.)` is a landscape or the scenery you see. `Le feuillage (m.)` means foliage collectively, not a single leaf. `Un barrage (m.)` is a dam when it is a structure holding back water; elsewhere the same noun can describe a barrier or roadblock.
points: `une montagne (f.)` — mountain.
`un paysage (m.)` — landscape; scenery.
`le feuillage (m.)` — foliage, the mass of leaves on plants.
`un barrage (m.)` — dam in a water-management setting.
`la campagne (f.)` — countryside; `une campagne de sensibilisation (f.)` — awareness campaign.
`un champ (m.)`, `les champs (m. pl.)` — field, fields, especially land used for crops or grazing.

examples.french: Notre logement à la campagne donne sur les champs et les montagnes.
examples.english: Our accommodation in the countryside overlooks the fields and the mountains.
examples.note: Three useful terms for describing a rural location.

examples.french: En automne, le feuillage change de couleur et transforme le paysage.
examples.english: In autumn, the foliage changes colour and transforms the landscape.
examples.note: Feuillage is collective; paysage is the wider scene.

examples.french: Le barrage retient l’eau utilisée pour irriguer les champs.
examples.english: The dam holds back the water used to irrigate the fields.
examples.note: Holding back water makes the dam meaning explicit.

examples.french: Depuis la montagne, on voit le barrage et toute la vallée.
examples.english: From the mountain, you can see the dam and the whole valley.
examples.note: The two nouns name distinct features in a landscape.

examples.french: La commune lance une campagne de sensibilisation pour protéger les paysages de la région.
examples.english: The municipality is launching an awareness campaign to protect the region's landscapes.
examples.note: Une campagne names an organised effort here, not a rural place.

examples.french: J’habite à la campagne, mais je travaille en ville trois jours par semaine.
examples.english: I live in the countryside, but I work in town three days a week.
examples.note: À la campagne identifies where someone lives.

mistakes.avoid: Nous vivons au campagne.
mistakes.prefer: Nous vivons à la campagne.
mistakes.why: Campagne is feminine: à la campagne means in the countryside. Une campagne de sensibilisation has a different meaning: an awareness campaign.

mistakes.avoid: Le feuillage du parc sont rouges en octobre.
mistakes.prefer: Le feuillage du parc est rouge en octobre.
mistakes.why: The collective noun feuillage is singular, even though it refers to many leaves.

sections.title: A lawn, its insects, and garden maintenance
paragraphs: `Une pelouse (f.)` is a lawn, an area covered with grass, not the whole garden. In a shared residence, instructions may distinguish walking on the lawn from using a path. `Une libellule (f.)` is a dragonfly; `un papillon (m.)` is a butterfly. Their genders must be learned individually.
`Un tas (m.)` is a heap or pile. `Un tas de feuilles` describes leaves gathered together physically; this is different from the informal quantity expression `un tas de choses`, a lot of things.
points: `une pelouse (f.)` — lawn; `sur la pelouse` — on the lawn.
`une libellule (f.)` — dragonfly, an insect with a long body often seen near water.
`un papillon (m.)` — butterfly.
`un tas (m.)` — heap, pile; `un tas de feuilles` — pile of leaves, from `une feuille (f.)`, a leaf.

examples.french: Après la pluie, la pelouse est trop humide pour y installer les tables.
examples.english: After the rain, the lawn is too wet to set up the tables on it.
examples.note: The lawn is the grassy area used for an outdoor gathering.

examples.french: Une libellule vole au-dessus du bassin, près de la pelouse.
examples.english: A dragonfly is flying over the pond, near the lawn.
examples.note: The long-bodied insect near water is a dragonfly, not a butterfly.

examples.french: Les enfants observent un papillon sur les fleurs sans marcher sur la pelouse.
examples.english: The children are watching a butterfly on the flowers without walking on the lawn.
examples.note: A natural context for distinguishing the planted area from the grass.

examples.french: Le jardinier a laissé un tas de feuilles au bord de la pelouse.
examples.english: The gardener left a pile of leaves at the edge of the lawn.
examples.note: Un tas is a physical pile here, not simply a large number.

mistakes.avoid: Un libellule vole près d’une papillon.
mistakes.prefer: Une libellule vole près d’un papillon.
mistakes.why: Libellule is feminine; papillon is masculine. Insect nouns do not all share one gender.

mistakes.avoid: Il reste un tas des feuilles à déplacer.
mistakes.prefer: Il reste un tas de feuilles à déplacer.
mistakes.why: To describe what an unspecified pile consists of, use un tas de followed by the noun.

vocabulary.example: Le verglas rend les trottoirs dangereux en février.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; freezing rain is `la pluie verglaçante`.

vocabulary.example: Un nuage épais cache le soleil depuis midi.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `il y a des nuages` is the usual plural form.

vocabulary.example: Un parapluie solide est utile pendant tout le mois de novembre.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; regular plural `des parapluies`.

vocabulary.example: Une soirée conviviale a réuni tous les nouveaux voisins.
vocabulary.note: Soirée often treats the evening as a duration or occasion. Soir also occurs in particular-time expressions such as ce soir.

vocabulary.example: Les inondations du printemps ont endommagé plusieurs maisons.
vocabulary.note: Feminine plural noun; the singular `une inondation` also exists.

vocabulary.example: Un glissement de terrain a bloqué la route pendant deux jours.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase; the gender comes from `glissement`.

vocabulary.example: Deux personnes disparues ont été retrouvées en fin de journée.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun phrase; the adjective agrees, giving `des personnes disparues`.

practice.prompt: Ask about the weather, then answer using three different frames: cold, raining, and windy.
practice.hint: One adjective frame, one impersonal verb, one weather noun.
practice.answer: Quel temps fait-il ? Il fait froid, il pleut et il y a du vent.

takeaways: `Quel temps fait-il ?` opens the topic.
Four frames: `il fait` plus adjective, impersonal verb alone, `il y a` plus noun, `le temps est` plus adjective.
Le soir can mark a habit, ce soir a particular evening, and une soirée a duration or occasion.
keywords: weather and parts of the day
le brouillard, la brume, brumeux, une personne disparue
pluvieux, orageux, le ciel, le soleil, il fait bon, à cette époque de l’année
une montagne, le feuillage, un paysage, un barrage, la campagne, les champs
une pelouse, une libellule, un papillon, un tas

lessons.title: La nourriture, les quantités et les portions
lessons.summary: Use partitives for unmeasured portions and de after general quantities: du pain, beaucoup de pain. Keep a definite article when selecting from an identified whole: la moitié du gâteau. Prefixed demi- is invariable and hyphenated: une demi-heure, un demi-litre. A definite article can also express a unit rate: trois dollars le kilo.
objectives: Use partitive articles for unmeasured food.
Distinguish general quantities with de from portions of an identified whole.
Express a unit price with a definite article.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A partitive article presents an unmeasured portion: du lait, de la farine, de l’eau. For unspecified plural items, use des: des légumes. English often leaves these articles untranslated: Je prends du café means I have coffee, not I have the coffee.

General quantities use de: un kilo de pommes, une bouteille d’eau, une tranche de pain, beaucoup de légumes, peu de sel. Keep the definite article when selecting from a known whole: beaucoup des légumes de ce panier (many of the vegetables in this basket), la moitié des repas. De also normally replaces indefinite and partitive articles when negation denies an amount: Je n’ai pas de pain. A definite article expresses a unit price in trois dollars le kilo or deux dollars la pièce.
points: Use `du`, `de la`, `de l’`, `des` for an unspecified amount.
Use de after general weights, containers, and amounts; retain a definite article for an identified whole or set.
Compare Je n’ai pas de lait (no amount) with Ce n’est pas du lait (identifying the substance) and Je n’aime pas le lait (a definite article for the food in general).
Use `la moitié de` plus a determined noun for half of a specific whole.
Use `le`, `la`, or `les` before the unit when giving a rate.
Check the meal names by region: in Canada, `le déjeuner` is breakfast, `le dîner` lunch, and `le souper` dinner; in France, `le petit déjeuner`, `le déjeuner`, and `le dîner`.

examples.french: La banque alimentaire distribue du lait, de la farine et des légumes frais.
examples.english: The food bank distributes milk, flour, and fresh vegetables.
examples.note: Du lait and de la farine are partitives; des légumes introduces unspecified plural items.

examples.french: J’ai acheté un kilo de pommes et beaucoup de légumes au marché.
examples.english: I bought a kilo of apples and a lot of vegetables at the market.
examples.note: These general quantities take de, without a definite article identifying a known set.

examples.french: Le centre communautaire a gardé la moitié des repas pour les bénévoles.
examples.english: The community centre kept half of the meals for the volunteers.
examples.note: « La moitié de » plus a determined noun.

examples.french: Les pommes locales coûtent trois dollars le kilo cette semaine.
examples.english: Local apples cost three dollars per kilo this week.
examples.note: The definite article expresses a rate.

examples.french: Il n’y a plus de café, mais il reste de la soupe et du pain.
examples.english: There is no coffee left, but there is still soup and bread.
examples.note: Negation reduces to « de »; the positive clause keeps the partitive.

examples.french: Au Québec, je prends du café au déjeuner et de la soupe au dîner.
examples.english: In Quebec, I have coffee at breakfast and soup at lunch.
examples.note: Canadian meal names: déjeuner is breakfast and dîner is lunch.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai acheté beaucoup du légumes au marché.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai acheté beaucoup de légumes au marché.
mistakes.why: Use de for this general quantity; singular du cannot determine plural légumes. Des is possible when it is de + les for a known set.

mistakes.avoid: Je voudrais de la pain et du confiture, s’il vous plaît.
mistakes.prefer: Je voudrais du pain et de la confiture, s’il vous plaît.
mistakes.why: Pain is masculine and confiture feminine. Definite articles would also be grammatical if requesting already identified items.

sections.title: A half-unit or half of a particular whole
paragraphs: Before a noun, demi- means half and remains invariable, joined by a hyphen: une demi-heure, un demi-litre, une demi-bouteille. The article follows the noun’s gender; demi- does not acquire a feminine e or a plural s in this position.

La moitié de selects half of a whole that can be identified with a determiner: la moitié du gâteau, la moitié de cette bouteille, la moitié des repas. A demi-litre gives a fixed measurement; half of a particular bottle depends on that bottle’s size.
points: Before a noun, write invariable demi- with a hyphen.
La moitié de names half of an identified whole and keeps its determiner.

examples.french: Laissez reposer la pâte pendant une demi-heure.
examples.english: Leave the dough to rest for half an hour.
examples.note: Une heure (f.) gives une demi-heure, without an e on demi-.

examples.french: Ajoutez un demi-litre de lait.
examples.english: Add half a litre of milk.
examples.note: Un litre (m.) supplies the masculine article; the measured ingredient follows de.

examples.french: Il reste une demi-bouteille de jus dans le réfrigérateur.
examples.english: There is half a bottle of juice left in the refrigerator.
examples.note: Une bouteille (f.) keeps its gender without changing demi-.

examples.french: Gardons la moitié de cette bouteille et partageons la moitié du gâteau.
examples.english: Let’s keep half of this bottle and share half of the cake.
examples.note: Specific wholes: de cette bouteille and de + le gâteau → du gâteau.

mistakes.avoid: Attendez une demie-heure.
mistakes.prefer: Attendez une demi-heure.
mistakes.why: Demi- is invariable before the noun.

mistakes.avoid: Gardez la moitié de le gâteau.
mistakes.prefer: Gardez la moitié du gâteau.
mistakes.why: De contracts with the definite article le to du.

sections.title: Vegetarian meals, plates, and familiar ingredients
paragraphs: `Végétarien / végétarienne` means vegetarian: excluding meat and fish, but not necessarily eggs or dairy products. It is not the same as `végétalien / végétalienne`, which excludes animal-derived foods. State any additional restriction separately when ordering.

`Une assiette (f.)` is a plate; it can also stand for the food served on it. `Le raisin (m.)` normally names grapes collectively as food. English raisins are dried grapes, `les raisins secs (m. pl.)`, not simply fresh `raisin`.
points: `végétarien / végétarienne` — vegetarian: `un repas végétarien`, `une option végétarienne`; a person can say `Je suis végétarien` or `Je suis végétarienne`.
`une assiette (f.)` — plate; `une assiette de légumes (f.)` — a plate of vegetables.
`le beurre (m.)` — butter; it is a dairy product.
`le raisin (m.)` — grapes as a food; `un grain de raisin (m.)` — one grape; `les raisins secs (m. pl.)` — raisins.

examples.french: Je suis végétarienne ; avez-vous une assiette de légumes sans viande ni poisson ?
examples.english: I am vegetarian; do you have a plate of vegetables without meat or fish?
examples.note: The feminine form describes the speaker.

examples.french: Ce repas est végétarien, mais il contient du beurre ; il n’est donc pas végétalien.
examples.english: This meal is vegetarian, but it contains butter, so it is not vegan.
examples.note: Vegetarian does not automatically mean dairy-free.

examples.french: Pour la réunion de midi, prévoyez une assiette par personne et du raisin à partager.
examples.english: For the lunchtime meeting, allow one plate per person and grapes to share.
examples.note: Assiettes are counted; raisin is presented collectively as food.

examples.french: J’ai mis le beurre dans une petite assiette et lavé le raisin pour le petit déjeuner.
examples.english: I put the butter on a small plate and washed the grapes for breakfast.
examples.note: French commonly uses dans une assiette where English says on a plate.

examples.french: Pour le dessert, je préfère le raisin frais aux raisins secs.
examples.english: For dessert, I prefer fresh grapes to raisins.
examples.note: The adjective secs identifies the dried fruit.

mistakes.avoid: Elle cherche une option végétarien.
mistakes.prefer: Elle cherche une option végétarienne.
mistakes.why: The adjective agrees with the feminine noun option; the feminine form has -ienne.

mistakes.avoid: Ces raisins sec sont dans le dessert.
mistakes.prefer: Ces raisins secs sont dans le dessert.
mistakes.why: Sec agrees with plural raisins. Des raisins secs means raisins; du raisin normally means fresh grapes.

sections.title: Taste, sweet and savoury choices, and foam
paragraphs: `Le goût (m.)` means taste or flavour when describing food; `avoir un goût de…` identifies a flavour. In other contexts, it can refer to a person's preferences. `Le sucré (m.)` and `le salé (m.)` group foods into sweet and savoury categories. This use of `le salé` does not claim that every savoury dish tastes excessively salty.

`La mousse (f.)` means foam: a mass of small bubbles, such as milk foam on a drink or soap lather. `Une mousse au chocolat (f.)` is a chocolate mousse, an airy dessert. The foam meaning concerns a physical texture, not every thick or creamy food.
points: `le goût (m.)` — taste, flavour; `avoir un goût de citron` — taste of lemon.
`le sucré (m.)` — sweet foods or sweetness as a category; the adjective `sucré / sucrée` means sweet or sweetened.
