lessons.title: Le corps, la douleur, les odeurs et les sensations
lessons.summary: Avoir mal à normally uses a definite body-part article: à la tête, au dos, aux dents. Avoir mal au cœur is the idiom for nausea. Sentir covers smell and physical perception; se sentir reports a personal state. Faire mal à expresses pain and faire du mal à harm, with physical and emotional meanings overlapping.
objectives: Build `avoir mal à` with the correct contracted article.
Separate `sentir`, `se sentir`, and `faire mal`.
Interpret `avoir mal au cœur` correctly.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: With avoir mal à, the ordinary body-part construction uses a definite article because the subject already identifies the owner: J’ai mal à la tête, Il a mal au dos, Elle a mal aux dents. The contractions apply normally: à + le gives au, à + les gives aux. When the body part is the subject, both Le dos me fait mal and Mon dos me fait mal are possible; a possessive subject is not inherently wrong.

Sentir can mean perceive something or give off a smell. The subject and context distinguish Je sens la peinture (I smell the paint) from La salle sent la peinture (the room smells of paint). In Ce plat sent très bon, bon describes the smell and stays unchanged: Ces fleurs sentent bon. Se sentir reports a personal state: Je me sens fatigué; Je me sens bien.

Avoir mal au cœur usually means feel nauseous in everyday speech; it does not by itself identify a heart condition. If you mean pain in your chest, describe that directly: J’ai une douleur dans la poitrine. A language expression should not be used to infer a medical diagnosis.
points: Use `avoir mal à` plus the definite article of the body part.
Contract to `au` and `aux` where the gender and number require it.
Use `faire mal à` when the body part is the subject.
Use `sentir` for smelling or perceiving, `se sentir` for a personal state.
Read `avoir mal au cœur` as nausea.
Note that fixed body-part idioms also keep the definite article: `avoir les mains dans les poches`.

examples.french: J’ai mal à la tête depuis le début de mon quart de travail.
examples.english: I have had a headache since the start of my shift.
examples.note: Definite article, no possessive.

examples.french: Il a mal au dos et aux épaules après cette journée de déménagement.
examples.english: His back and shoulders hurt after this day of moving.
examples.note: Contractions « au » and « aux ».

examples.french: Comment est-ce que vous vous sentez depuis votre traitement ?
examples.english: How have you been feeling since your treatment?
examples.note: « Se sentir » reports a personal state.

examples.french: Je ne sens rien dans la main gauche depuis l’accident.
examples.english: I have been unable to feel anything in my left hand since the accident.
examples.note: « Sentir » in its perception meaning.

examples.french: Ce plat sent très bon, mais j’ai mal au cœur depuis ce matin.
examples.english: This dish smells very good, but I have been feeling sick since this morning.
examples.note: « Sentir » for a smell, and the idiom « avoir mal au cœur ».

examples.french: Il regardait les autres travailler, les mains dans les poches.
examples.english: He watched the others work, with his hands in his pockets.
examples.note: Fixed idiom with the definite article; it suggests standing idle rather than helping.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai mal à le dos depuis hier.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai mal au dos depuis hier.
mistakes.why: À contracts with le to au.

mistakes.avoid: Je sens fatigué après cette journée.
mistakes.prefer: Je me sens fatigué après cette journée.
mistakes.why: Reporting one’s own state requires the pronominal `se sentir`.

sections.title: Faire mal and faire du mal: pain and harm
paragraphs: Faire mal à quelqu’un means cause someone pain or hurt them. Faire du mal à quelqu’un emphasises harm or injury. This is not a strict physical-versus-emotional division: a remark can faire mal, and something unhealthy can faire du mal to the body.

Both constructions introduce the affected person with à or an indirect pronoun: Cette remarque lui fait mal; Le manque de sommeil lui fait du mal. With a body part, faire mal can also specify where the pain occurs: Ces chaussures me font mal aux pieds.
points: Mal expresses pain; du mal emphasises harm, without an absolute physical/emotional divide.
Use an indirect pronoun for the person affected.

examples.french: Ces chaussures me font mal aux pieds.
examples.english: These shoes hurt my feet.
examples.note: Me identifies the person; aux pieds locates the pain.

examples.french: Sa remarque m’a fait mal, même si elle ne voulait pas me blesser.
examples.english: Her comment hurt me, even though she did not mean to hurt my feelings.
examples.note: Une remarque (f.) is a comment; faire mal can describe emotional pain.

examples.french: Le manque de sommeil lui fait du mal.
examples.english: Lack of sleep is harming him.
examples.note: Faire du mal can concern physical wellbeing, not just emotions.

examples.french: Cette rumeur leur a fait du mal.
examples.english: That rumour harmed them.
examples.note: Une rumeur (f.) is a rumour; leur is an indirect pronoun.

mistakes.avoid: Ces chaussures me fait mal aux pieds.
mistakes.prefer: Ces chaussures me font mal aux pieds.
mistakes.why: The plural subject chaussures requires font.

mistakes.avoid: Cette rumeur les a fait du mal.
mistakes.prefer: Cette rumeur leur a fait du mal.
mistakes.why: Faire du mal à quelqu’un requires indirect leur, not direct les.

sections.title: Identifying the neck, lips, eyebrows, and nails
paragraphs: For an appointment or a personal-care request, name the precise body part. `Le cou (m.)` is the neck; `la gorge (f.)` is the throat. `Les lèvres (f. pl.)` are the lips, and `les sourcils (m. pl.)` are the eyebrows, not the eyelashes.
`Un ongle (m.)` is a fingernail or toenail. Add `de la main` or `du pied` when the location is not clear. English nail can also mean a metal fastener, but that is `un clou (m.)`, not a body part.
points: `le cou (m.)` — neck; distinct from `la gorge (f.)`, throat.
`une lèvre (f.)`, `les lèvres (f. pl.)` — lip, lips.
`un sourcil (m.)`, `les sourcils (m. pl.)` — eyebrow, eyebrows; `les cils (m. pl.)` — eyelashes.
`un ongle (m.)`, `les ongles (m. pl.)` — fingernail or toenail, nails.

examples.french: J’ai mal au cou depuis le trajet en car, surtout quand je tourne la tête.
examples.english: My neck has hurt since the coach journey, especially when I turn my head.
examples.note: The location and the movement identify neck pain rather than a sore throat.

examples.french: Mes lèvres sont sèches depuis que je travaille dehors.
examples.english: My lips have been dry since I started working outdoors.
examples.note: The plural noun lèvres is feminine.

examples.french: La coupure se trouve juste au-dessus du sourcil gauche, pas sur la paupière.
examples.english: The cut is just above the left eyebrow, not on the eyelid.
examples.note: Un sourcil (m.) is an eyebrow; une paupière (f.) is an eyelid.

examples.french: Je me suis cassé un ongle de la main en ouvrant ma valise.
examples.english: I broke a fingernail while opening my suitcase.
examples.note: De la main makes clear that the nail is on a finger.

examples.french: Le médecin examine mes ongles et me demande quand ils ont changé de couleur.
examples.english: The doctor examines my nails and asks when they changed colour.
examples.note: Ils refers back to the masculine plural ongles.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai mal à la cou.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai mal au cou.
mistakes.why: Cou is masculine; à plus le contracts to au.

mistakes.avoid: Mes lèvres sont sec et mes ongles sont cassées.
mistakes.prefer: Mes lèvres sont sèches et mes ongles sont cassés.
mistakes.why: Lèvres is feminine plural, while ongles is masculine plural.

sections.title: An injury, body weight, and a walking stick
paragraphs: `Blessé / blessée` means injured, for example after a fall or accident; it does not mean ill in general. `Une canne (f.)` is a cane or walking stick when someone uses it to walk. These words let you describe mobility needs without assuming a particular diagnosis.
`Le poids (m.)` means weight, for a person or an object. It is a noun; `peser` is the verb to weigh. The final s belongs to the singular spelling of `poids`.
points: `blessé / blessée` — injured: `Il est blessé`, `Elle est blessée`.
`une canne (f.)` — walking stick, cane; `marcher avec une canne` — walk with a cane.
`le poids (m.)` — weight; `le poids du corps` — body weight; `le poids d’un bagage` — the weight of a piece of luggage.

examples.french: Ma collègue est blessée à la jambe et marche avec une canne.
examples.english: My colleague has a leg injury and walks with a cane.
examples.note: The feminine adjective describes the colleague; the noun names her walking aid.

examples.french: Je suis blessé et j’utilise une canne ; pouvez-vous me proposer une chambre près de l’ascenseur ?
examples.english: I am injured and use a cane; can you offer me a room near the lift?
examples.note: A practical accommodation request, using the masculine form for the speaker.

examples.french: Au début du rendez-vous, l’infirmière note mon poids dans le dossier.
examples.english: At the beginning of the appointment, the nurse records my weight in the file.
examples.note: Poids is a measurement, not a description such as heavy or light.

examples.french: Depuis qu’il est blessé, il vérifie le poids de sa valise avant de demander de l’aide pour la porter.
examples.english: Since he was injured, he checks the weight of his suitcase before asking for help carrying it.
examples.note: The same weight noun applies to luggage.

mistakes.avoid: La réceptionniste note mon poid.
mistakes.prefer: La réceptionniste note mon poids.
mistakes.why: Poids keeps its final s even in the singular.

mistakes.avoid: Elle est blessé et utilise un canne.
mistakes.prefer: Elle est blessée et utilise une canne.
mistakes.why: The adjective agrees with elle; canne is a feminine noun.

sections.title: Breathlessness, exhaustion, and stress
paragraphs: `Essoufflé / essoufflée` means out of breath, often after physical effort. `Respirer` means to breathe. `Épuisé / épuisée` means exhausted: it describes severe tiredness, not specifically difficulty breathing. Someone can be exhausted without being out of breath.

`Extrêmement stressé / extrêmement stressée` means extremely stressed. It describes a strong feeling of pressure or anxiety; it does not itself name a medical diagnosis. Use these words to state what you are experiencing and, when relevant, explain the situation.
points: `essoufflé / essoufflée` — out of breath, breathless.
`respirer` — breathe; `avoir du mal à respirer` — have difficulty breathing.
`épuisé / épuisée` — exhausted, very tired; stronger than simply `fatigué / fatiguée`.
`extrêmement stressé / extrêmement stressée` — extremely stressed; extrêmement stays unchanged, while stressé agrees with the person.

examples.french: Je suis essoufflée après avoir monté les escaliers avec les courses.
examples.english: I am out of breath after carrying the shopping up the stairs.
examples.note: The speaker reports breathlessness following physical effort.

examples.french: Pendant la consultation, je lui explique que j’ai du mal à respirer, même au repos.
examples.english: During the consultation, I explain that I have difficulty breathing, even at rest.
examples.note: This states a symptom without suggesting its cause.

examples.french: Après le déménagement, nous sommes épuisés, mais nous ne sommes plus essoufflés.
examples.english: After the move, we are exhausted, but we are no longer out of breath.
examples.note: Tiredness and breathlessness are distinct states.

examples.french: Elle est extrêmement stressée avant son premier entretien et se sent épuisée en fin de journée.
examples.english: She is extremely stressed before her first interview and feels exhausted at the end of the day.
examples.note: Both adjectives agree with elle; the adverb does not change.

examples.french: Je respire normalement maintenant, mais je suis encore épuisé par le voyage.
examples.english: I am breathing normally now, but I am still exhausted from the journey.
examples.note: The breathing verb and the fatigue adjective report different aspects of the person's condition.

mistakes.avoid: Je suis essoufflé signifie toujours je suis épuisé.
mistakes.prefer: Je suis essoufflé décrit le souffle ; je suis épuisé décrit une grande fatigue.
mistakes.why: Being out of breath and being exhausted can occur together, but neither word is a synonym for the other.

mistakes.avoid: Elles sont extrêmements stressé.
mistakes.prefer: Elles sont extrêmement stressées.
mistakes.why: Extrêmement is an invariable adverb; stressées agrees with the feminine plural subject.

vocabulary.example: La tête du patient reste immobile pendant l’examen.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `avoir mal à la tête` means to have a headache.

vocabulary.example: Le dos me fait mal après une longue journée debout.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; contracts to `au dos` after `avoir mal à`.

vocabulary.example: Je me sens beaucoup mieux depuis le début du traitement.
vocabulary.note: Pronominal; followed by an adjective or an adverb.

vocabulary.example: Un quart de travail de nuit demande une bonne organisation du sommeil.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase used in Canada; `un poste` is used in France.

vocabulary.example: Un traitement de six semaines a été prescrit par la clinique.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; the ending -ment is a masculine hint.

vocabulary.example: Une épaule douloureuse limite les mouvements du bras.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `avoir mal à l’épaule` for the pain construction.

vocabulary.example: Après son opération, il marche avec une canne pendant six semaines.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the same word appears in `une canne à pêche`, a fishing rod.

vocabulary.french: avoir les mains dans les poches
vocabulary.english: to stand idle, to do nothing to help
vocabulary.example: Personne n’avait les mains dans les poches pendant le déménagement.
vocabulary.note: Fixed idiom keeping the definite article, like other body-part expressions.

practice.prompt: Say in French: my teeth hurt, I feel tired, and this room smells of paint.
practice.hint: Three different structures, one of them with a contraction.
practice.answer: J’ai mal aux dents, je me sens fatigué et cette salle sent la peinture.

takeaways: `Avoir mal à` plus a definite article, contracted as needed.
`Sentir` perceives or gives off a smell; `se sentir` reports a state.
`Avoir mal au cœur` equals nausea.
keywords: the body, pain, smell, and feeling
douleur, faire mal à, faire du mal à
le cou, les lèvres, les sourcils, les ongles
blessé, blessée, le poids, une canne

lessons.title: S’habiller : « mettre », « essayer » et « aller à »
lessons.summary: `Mettre` is the ordinary verb for putting clothes on: `Je mets une veste`. `Essayer` is trying a garment on before buying it, often after seeing it `en vitrine`. `Aller à` expresses suitability, and the roles are the reverse of English: the item is the subject and the person is an indirect object (`Cette veste lui va bien`). `Aller avec` matches two items, and `convenir à` is the more formal way of saying that something suits a person or a situation.
objectives: Use `mettre` and `essayer` in a shopping or dressing situation.
Put the item, not the person, in subject position with `aller à`.
Choose between `aller à`, `aller avec`, and `convenir à`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Three verbs cover the everyday clothing situation. `Mettre` means to put on and takes a direct object: `Je mets un manteau`, `Elle a mis une tenue sobre pour l’entrevue`. `Porter` is the state that follows: `Elle porte un manteau`. `Essayer` is trying a garment on: `Puis-je essayer cette veste ?`, typically after noticing it `en vitrine`, in the shop window.

`Aller à` expresses suitability and reverses the English word order: the clothing, the colour, or the hairstyle is the subject, and the person is an indirect object introduced by `à` or replaced by `me`, `te`, `lui`, `nous`, `vous`, `leur`. English says She looks good in that jacket; French says `Cette veste lui va bien`. Two neighbours must be kept apart: `aller avec` links two items rather than an item and a person (`Cette cravate va bien avec la chemise bleue`), and `convenir à` is the more formal equivalent of `aller à`, usable for people and also for situations (`Cette tenue convient à un entretien`, `Cet horaire ne me convient pas`). The adverbs `bien`, `très bien`, and `mal` grade the judgement.
points: Use `mettre` plus a direct object for putting a garment on.
Use `porter` for the state of wearing it.
Use `essayer` for trying on, and `en vitrine` for what is displayed in the window.
Make the item the subject of `aller à` and the person an indirect object.
Use `aller avec` between two items and `convenir à` in a formal register.

With clothing, aller can mean fit in size or look good on someone. Context and bien clarify the judgement: Cette veste me va, mais sa couleur ne me plaît pas (This jacket fits me, but I do not like its colour).

examples.french: Je mettrai une veste sobre pour l’entrevue de demain.
examples.english: I will wear an understated jacket for tomorrow’s interview.
examples.note: « Mettre » takes a direct object.

examples.french: J’ai vu ce manteau en vitrine ; puis-je l’essayer ?
examples.english: I saw this coat in the window; may I try it on?
examples.note: « En vitrine » for the display, « essayer » for trying on.

examples.french: Cette veste sobre va bien à la candidate.
examples.english: This understated jacket suits the candidate.
examples.note: The item is the subject; the person follows « à ».

examples.french: Le rose pâle lui va très bien, mais le vert foncé lui va mal.
examples.english: Pale pink suits her very well, but dark green does not suit her.
examples.note: A colour as subject plus lui va mal means it is unflattering on that person. Elle va mal instead means she is unwell or doing badly; changing the subject changes the meaning.

examples.french: Cette cravate va bien avec la chemise bleue.
examples.english: This tie goes well with the blue shirt.
examples.note: « Aller avec » links two items.

examples.french: Cette tenue convient à un entretien, mais cet horaire ne me convient pas.
examples.english: This outfit is suitable for an interview, but this schedule does not suit me.
examples.note: « Convenir à » works for a situation as well as a person.

mistakes.avoid: Elle va bien cette veste pour l’entrevue.
mistakes.prefer: Cette veste lui va bien pour l’entrevue.
mistakes.why: The item that suits is the subject and the person is an indirect object.

mistakes.avoid: Je mets à mon manteau avant de sortir, puis je pars.
mistakes.prefer: Je mets mon manteau avant de sortir, puis je pars.
mistakes.why: Mettre takes the garment directly, without à. Porter mon manteau is also grammatical, but describes wearing or carrying it rather than the act of putting it on.

sections.title: Clothes you slip on and jewellery you wear
paragraphs: `Un habit (m.)` is a garment or an item of dress, but everyday French often uses the plural `des habits (m. pl.)` for clothes. For a whole coordinated outfit, `une tenue (f.)` is usually clearer. The singular `un habit` can also refer to a formal dress coat in an appropriate context; it is not the English noun habit, which is `une habitude (f.)`.

`Enfiler` means slip on or pull on clothing, highlighting the putting-on action rather than the state of wearing it. `Un caleçon (m.)` usually means boxer shorts in a men's-underwear context. `Un bijou (m.)`, plural `des bijoux (m. pl.)`, is a jewel or piece of jewellery; English jewellery is normally uncountable, but French can count individual pieces.
points: `Enfiler` describes putting clothing on; `porter` describes wearing it.
Use `des habits` for clothes and `une tenue` when the coordinated outfit matters.

examples.french: Il a préparé des habits propres pour demain.
examples.english: He has prepared clean clothes for tomorrow.
examples.note: The everyday plural refers to clothes collectively.

examples.french: Pour la cérémonie, elle a choisi une tenue sobre.
examples.english: For the ceremony, she chose an understated outfit.
examples.note: `Une tenue` identifies a complete outfit.

examples.french: Attends une minute, j’enfile ma veste et j’arrive.
examples.english: Wait a minute; I am slipping on my jacket and then I will be there.
examples.note: `Enfiler` focuses on the action.

examples.french: Il enfile un caleçon propre avant de mettre son pantalon.
examples.english: He puts on clean boxer shorts before putting on his trousers.
examples.note: French uses a singular noun for this garment.

examples.french: Ce bijou appartenait à ma grand-mère.
examples.english: This piece of jewellery belonged to my grandmother.
examples.note: A single countable piece.

examples.french: Elle porte deux bijoux discrets avec cette tenue.
examples.english: She is wearing two understated pieces of jewellery with this outfit.
examples.note: `Porter` describes the resulting state; `bijoux` counts the pieces.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai un habit de lire le soir.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai l’habitude de lire le soir.
mistakes.why: To mean I have a habit of reading in the evening, use avoir l’habitude de + infinitive. Un habit (m.) is clothing; une habitude (f.) is a customary behaviour.

mistakes.avoid: Elle porte deux bijous.
mistakes.prefer: Elle porte deux bijoux.
mistakes.why: Bijou has the irregular plural bijoux. Translate deux bijoux as two pieces of jewellery, not two jewelleries: French counts the pieces directly.

vocabulary.example: Elle met un manteau léger dès que la température monte.
vocabulary.note: Direct object; participle `mis`, present `je mets`, `nous mettons`.

vocabulary.example: Puis-je essayer ce manteau en taille moyenne ?
vocabulary.note: `-yer` verb: `j’essaie` or `j’essaye`, both accepted.

vocabulary.english: to suit, to be suitable for
vocabulary.example: Cet horaire ne convient pas aux parents de jeunes enfants.
vocabulary.note: Formal equivalent of `aller à`; also used for situations.

vocabulary.example: Une vitrine bien éclairée attire les passants le soir.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `en vitrine` means on display.

vocabulary.example: Une veste sobre convient à un entretien d’embauche.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `un veston` is used in Canada for a suit jacket.

vocabulary.example: Une tenue soignée fait bonne impression dès l’accueil.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `être en tenue de travail` means to be in work clothes.

vocabulary.example: Elle porte une veste bleue et elle porte aussi un dossier volumineux.
vocabulary.note: Durative: the state of wearing, unlike the punctual `mettre`; it also means to carry.

practice.prompt: Say that you saw a coat in the window, ask to try it on, and say it suits you.
practice.hint: Three different verbs, and the item is the subject of the last one.
practice.answer: J’ai vu ce manteau en vitrine. Puis-je l’essayer ? Il me va très bien.

takeaways: `Mettre` puts on, `porter` wears, `essayer` tries on.
With `aller à`, the item is the subject and the person is indirect.
`Aller avec` matches two items; `convenir à` is the formal equivalent.
keywords: un habit, des habits, enfiler, un caleçon, un bijou, des bijoux

lessons.title: Décrire l’apparence, le caractère et les impressions
lessons.summary: Choose adjectives for weight, shape, condition, personality and impressions. Distinguish literal from figurative meanings, talent from fame, and a cool temperature from an approving reaction.
objectives: Choose a descriptive adjective whose meaning fits the noun.
Distinguish physical description, personal judgement and figurative criticism.
Use masculine and feminine adjective forms in realistic descriptions.

sections.title: Weight, shape, appearance, and condition
paragraphs: `Lourd/lourde` means heavy. `Pointu/pointue` describes a pointed end or shape, rather than every kind of sharpness: a pointed pencil is `un crayon pointu`, whereas a sharp cutting blade is normally `une lame tranchante`. `Mince` means thin for an object and slim for a person; it does not necessarily suggest unhealthy thinness.

`Laid/laide` and the more informal `moche` mean ugly. Both can sound hurtful when applied to a person. `Pourri/pourrie` literally means rotten, but its figurative meaning changes with the noun: terrible or lousy for an experience, corrupt for a person or system. Those are separate contextual uses, not descriptions of physical decay.
points: Distinguish weight (`lourd`) from thickness or build (`mince`).
Keep literal rotten food separate from the familiar criticism `un temps pourri` and the strong accusation `un politicien pourri`.

examples.french: Cette valise est lourde ; peux-tu m’aider à la porter ?
examples.english: This suitcase is heavy; can you help me carry it?
examples.note: `Lourde` describes weight.

examples.french: Attention, ces ciseaux ont des pointes très pointues.
examples.english: Careful, these scissors have very pointed tips.
examples.note: `Pointues` describes the shape and agrees with `des pointes (f. pl.)`.

examples.french: Ce livre est mince, mais il contient beaucoup d’idées.
examples.english: This book is thin, but it contains many ideas.
examples.note: For an object, `mince` can refer to thickness.

examples.french: Il est grand et mince, comme son frère.
examples.english: He is tall and slim, like his brother.
examples.note: For a person's build, `mince` commonly means slim.

examples.french: Je trouve ce bâtiment laid ; mon frère dit qu’il est vraiment moche.
examples.english: I find this building ugly; my brother says it is really ugly.
examples.note: `Moche` gives the second judgement a more informal tone.

examples.french: Cette pomme est pourrie ; il faut la jeter.
examples.english: This apple is rotten; we need to throw it away.
examples.note: Literal deterioration.

examples.french: Nous avons eu un temps pourri pendant tout le séjour.
examples.english: We had lousy weather throughout the stay.
examples.note: Informal criticism of the weather, not literal rotting.

examples.french: Le personnage dénonce un système pourri par la corruption.
examples.english: The character denounces a system rotten with corruption.
examples.note: A strong figurative judgement about corruption.

mistakes.avoid: Cette pomme est pourri.
mistakes.prefer: Cette pomme est pourrie.
mistakes.why: `Une pomme (f.)` requires feminine `pourrie`. Here the meaning is rotten, not corrupt; the noun selects the sense.

sections.title: Strange, wonderful, pleasant, or simply cool
paragraphs: `Incroyable` means incredible or unbelievable and can express admiration or disbelief. `Étrange` means strange or unusual; it is not `étranger/étrangère`, meaning foreign. `Agréable` means pleasant or enjoyable. `Merveilleux/merveilleuse` is stronger praise: wonderful. `Immense` describes very great size or extent, not necessarily something good.

`Frais/fraîche` can describe cool temperature: cool air, a cool room, or a cool evening. With food, the same adjective often means fresh. For the approving reaction “That's cool!”, a broadly useful expression is `C’est sympa !` or the more enthusiastic `C’est génial !`. Do not use the temperature sense of `frais` as your general translation of approval; slang uses vary with the speaker and context.
points: Use the surrounding noun to distinguish a fresh product from a cool temperature.
`Étrange` evaluates how unusual something seems; `étranger` identifies a foreign origin or connection.

examples.french: Le résultat est incroyable : elle a terminé en une heure.
examples.english: The result is incredible: she finished in an hour.
examples.note: `Incroyable` expresses surprise and admiration here.

examples.french: Ce message est étrange : personne ne l’a signé.
examples.english: This message is strange: nobody signed it.
examples.note: Something unusual, not something foreign.

examples.french: C’était une conversation agréable, et votre accueil était merveilleux.
examples.english: It was a pleasant conversation, and your welcome was wonderful.
examples.note: `Merveilleux` conveys stronger appreciation than `agréable`.

examples.french: La salle est immense, mais nous n’attendons que vingt personnes.
examples.english: The room is huge, but we are expecting only twenty people.
examples.note: `Immense` describes size without implying suitability.

examples.french: L’air est frais ce matin ; je vais prendre une veste.
examples.english: The air is cool this morning; I am going to take a jacket.
examples.note: Temperature, not freshness of food.

examples.french: La chambre reste fraîche, même quand il fait chaud dehors.
examples.english: The bedroom stays cool, even when it is hot outside.
examples.note: `Fraîche` is the feminine form in this temperature sense.

mistakes.avoid: Cette chambre reste frais en été.
mistakes.prefer: Cette chambre reste fraîche en été.
mistakes.why: `Une chambre (f.)` requires the feminine adjective `fraîche` (also spelled `fraiche`). Here it means cool in temperature.

sections.title: Personality, ability, and reputation
paragraphs: `Timide` means shy; `extraverti/extravertie` means extroverted or outgoing. These describe social disposition, not kindness or competence. `Cruel/cruelle` means cruel, causing or disregarding suffering. It is much stronger than simply strict.

`Exigeant/exigeante` describes someone who expects a lot, or work that makes substantial demands. `Talentueux/talentueuse` means talented, whereas `célèbre` means famous. A person can have talent without being well known, or fame without the particular skill being discussed.
points: Distinguish a demanding task from a demanding person through the noun.
Fame (`célèbre`) and ability (`talentueux`) are different claims.

examples.french: Lina est timide au début, mais elle parle volontiers avec ses amis.
examples.english: Lina is shy at first, but she readily talks with her friends.
examples.note: Shyness does not mean an inability to communicate.

examples.french: Son collègue est extraverti et aime rencontrer de nouvelles personnes.
examples.english: Her colleague is outgoing and likes meeting new people.
examples.note: `Extraverti` describes social disposition.

examples.french: Se moquer de sa peur serait cruel.
examples.english: Making fun of her fear would be cruel.
examples.note: A judgement about causing hurt, not merely being demanding.

examples.french: La formatrice est exigeante, mais elle explique clairement ses attentes.
examples.english: The trainer is demanding, but she clearly explains her expectations.
examples.note: A person who sets high standards.

examples.french: Ce travail est exigeant et demande beaucoup de concentration.
examples.english: This work is demanding and requires a lot of concentration.
examples.note: A task that requires effort.

examples.french: Cette jeune artiste est talentueuse, mais elle n’est pas encore célèbre.
examples.english: This young artist is talented, but she is not famous yet.
examples.note: Ability contrasted with public recognition.

mistakes.avoid: Cette artiste est talentueux.
mistakes.prefer: Cette artiste est talentueuse.
mistakes.why: `Cette artiste` identifies a woman, so the adjective takes the feminine `talentueuse`. This describes ability; `célèbre` would describe fame instead.

sections.title: Net and pareil: describe the right kind of similarity or clarity
paragraphs: `Net/nette` can mean neat or clean-looking in an appearance, clear in an answer, or sharp and in focus in an image. It is not a universal substitute for tidy: an organised room is most naturally `une chambre bien rangée`, whereas `une apparence nette et soignée` concerns a clean, well-groomed appearance.

`Pareil/pareille` means the same or alike. Two things described as `pareils` may be separate objects with identical characteristics. With an explicit comparison, use `pareil à`. This does not imply that the speaker is indifferent between them.
points: Choose clear, sharp, or neat as the English translation of `net` according to what it describes.
Compare identical-looking objects with `pareil`; use `bien rangé` for orderly storage.

examples.french: Il a une apparence nette et soignée pour son entretien.
examples.english: He has a neat, well-groomed appearance for his interview.
examples.note: The appearance sense behind English neat.

examples.french: Sa réponse est nette : il refuse.
examples.english: His answer is clear: he refuses.
examples.note: An unambiguous answer, not a tidy answer.

examples.french: La photo est nette, mais le bureau qu’on y voit est mal rangé.
examples.english: The photo is sharp, but the desk in it is untidy.
examples.note: Image clarity and tidiness are independent.

examples.french: Ma veste est pareille à la tienne ; nous avons choisi le même modèle.
examples.english: My jacket is just like yours; we chose the same model.
examples.note: `Pareille à` compares two separate jackets.

mistakes.avoid: La photo est net.
mistakes.prefer: La photo est nette.
mistakes.why: `Une photo (f.)` needs the feminine `nette`, with a double t. In this context the adjective means sharp or in focus, not tidy.

vocabulary.example: Cette artiste est talentueuse, mais elle n’est pas encore célèbre.
vocabulary.note: Ability is different from fame.

vocabulary.example: Ce crayon a une pointe très pointue.
vocabulary.note: Pointed shape is not the same property as a sharp cutting edge.

practice.prompt: Describe a female artist as talented but not yet famous.
practice.hint: Express ability and reputation separately, with feminine agreement.
practice.answer: Cette artiste est talentueuse, mais elle n’est pas encore célèbre.

takeaways: Interpret an adjective together with the noun it describes.
Keep a literal physical property separate from a figurative judgement.
Choose tactful descriptions of people; grammatical accuracy does not make a remark polite.
keywords: description appearance character personality impressions adjectives vocabulary
lourd lourde pourri pourrie pointu pointue laid laide moche mince
incroyable étrange agréable merveilleux merveilleuse immense
net nette pareil pareille frais fraîche fraiche cool

lessons.title: Les sports, les activités et les instruments
lessons.summary: Learn `jouer à` for games such as `jouer au tennis`, `jouer de` for instruments such as `jouer de la guitare`, and `faire` plus a partitive article for activities: `faire de la natation`, `faire du ski`. The partitive presents an activity without counting individual outings; it does not require a habit. Contrast `faire du vélo` with a counted ride, `faire un tour à vélo`, and `faire de la randonnée` with `faire une randonnée`.
objectives: Learn the preposition with jouer and the partitive article with faire.
Separate an uncounted activity from a counted outing or session.
Use tense and context to distinguish a habit from a particular event.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Learn the construction with the activity. Games use `jouer à`: `jouer au soccer`, `jouer au hockey`, `jouer aux échecs`. Instruments use `jouer de`: `jouer de la guitare`, `jouer du violon`. With jouer, prepositions contract with definite articles where required: `à + le → au`, `de + le → du`. With faire, the activity instead takes a partitive article: `faire de la natation`, `faire du vélo`, `faire de la randonnée`. Do not describe this as adding a second `de` before a partitive.

The article contrasts uncounted activity with counted units, not necessarily habit with a single event. `Je fais du vélo` may mean that I cycle regularly or that I am cycling now. `J’ai fait du vélo ce matin` describes past cycling with the same partitive. A countable noun identifies an outing or a unit: `faire un tour à vélo`, `faire une randonnée`, `faire une séance de yoga`, `faire quelques longueurs`, `faire une partie de tennis`. These can recur too: `Je fais une randonnée chaque dimanche`. Tense and context establish when and how often the activity happens.

In French, `le footing (m.)` means jogging, not the usual English meaning of footing. `Le jogging (m.)` can name the same activity: `faire du footing`, `faire du jogging`. To count an outing, say `faire un footing de vingt minutes` or `faire un jogging de vingt minutes`. Context matters because `un jogging (m.)` can also mean a tracksuit: `porter un jogging` concerns clothing, not running.
points: Learn jouer à with the activities that take it, such as le tennis, le hockey and les échecs; not every sport uses jouer.
Use `jouer de` for a musical instrument.
Use `faire` plus a partitive article to name an activity, whether habitual or particular.
Use a countable noun to count outings or units: `un tour à vélo`, `une randonnée`, `une partie de tennis`.
Use tense and time expressions, not the partitive alone, to identify a habit or a particular event.
Read `la batterie` from its context: the drum kit, a car battery, or a set of equipment.

examples.french: Il joue au tennis au centre communautaire et fait une partie avec sa voisine le samedi.
examples.english: He plays tennis at the community centre and plays a game with his neighbour on Saturdays.
examples.note: « Jouer au tennis » for the sport, « une partie » for one match.

examples.french: Je joue de la guitare pendant le festival francophone.
examples.english: I play the guitar during the Francophone festival.
examples.note: « Jouer de » for an instrument.

examples.french: Je fais du vélo toute l’année, mais hier j’ai simplement fait un tour à vélo.
examples.english: I cycle all year round, but yesterday I just went for a bike ride.
examples.note: General practice, then one occasion.

examples.french: Elle fait de la randonnée depuis dix ans et elle a fait une randonnée facile dimanche.
examples.english: She has been hiking for ten years and she did an easy hike on Sunday.
examples.note: The countable noun marks a single outing.

examples.french: Pendant le cours de natation, nous avons fait quelques longueurs.
examples.english: During the swimming lesson, we swam a few lengths.
examples.note: Quelques longueurs counts lengths of the pool rather than naming the activity as an uncounted whole.

examples.french: J’ai fait du yoga ce matin, mais je ne fais pas de yoga régulièrement.
examples.english: I did yoga this morning, but I do not do yoga regularly.
examples.note: A completed time marker bounds the event, even with the partitive.

examples.french: L’orchestre répète la partition, et le chef d’orchestre reprend le refrain plus lentement.
examples.english: The orchestra is rehearsing the score, and the conductor goes over the chorus more slowly.
examples.note: Core music vocabulary for describing a rehearsal or a concert.

examples.french: En ce moment, je fais du vélo ; d’habitude, je fais une randonnée chaque dimanche.
examples.english: Right now I am cycling; usually, I go for a hike every Sunday.
examples.note: A partitive can describe current activity, and a countable outing can belong to a habit.

examples.french: Je fais du footing dans le parc le dimanche, et hier j’ai fait un jogging de vingt minutes.
examples.english: I go jogging in the park on Sundays, and yesterday I went for a twenty-minute jog.
examples.note: Le footing (m.) and le jogging (m.) both name jogging. Du names the activity; un counts an outing. The time expressions distinguish the routine from yesterday’s run.

examples.french: J’ai acheté un jogging confortable pour faire du sport.
examples.english: I bought a comfortable tracksuit for exercising.
examples.note: Here un jogging (m.) is clothing, not a run; the verb acheter makes the intended meaning clear.

mistakes.avoid: Elle joue de la piano depuis trois ans.
mistakes.prefer: Elle joue du piano depuis trois ans.
mistakes.why: Piano is masculine: de + le contracts to du in jouer du piano.

mistakes.avoid: Nous jouons à la natation le mardi.
mistakes.prefer: Nous faisons de la natation le mardi.
mistakes.why: The activity is expressed with `faire` plus the partitive `de la`: `faire de la natation`, not `jouer à la natation`.

mistakes.avoid: Hier après-midi, j’ai fait de la randonnée de trois heures.
mistakes.prefer: Hier après-midi, j’ai fait une randonnée de trois heures.
mistakes.why: Use `une randonnée de trois heures` to describe the duration of one hike. The partitive is also possible with `pendant`: `J’ai fait de la randonnée pendant trois heures`.

mistakes.avoid: Il joue à la batterie dans un groupe du quartier.
mistakes.prefer: Il joue de la batterie dans un groupe du quartier.
mistakes.why: An instrument takes `jouer de`; `jouer à` is reserved for games and sports.

sections.title: Exercise, coaching, skiing, and time in the sun
paragraphs: `Un entraîneur (m.)` or `une entraîneuse (f.)` is a coach who trains a person or team. `Un entraînement (m.)` is training or a training session, not the person leading it. `Faire de l’exercice` means to exercise for physical activity; it need not involve a competitive sport.

`Skier` means to ski and is an alternative way to name the activity already expressed by `faire du ski`. `Bronzer` means to tan or get a tan through exposure to the sun. It describes the skin becoming darker, whether or not the person was deliberately sunbathing.
points: `un entraîneur (m.)`, `une entraîneuse (f.)` — sports coach.
`un entraînement (m.)` — training, training session; `l’entraînement (m.)` can also refer to training generally.
`faire de l’exercice` — exercise, be physically active; `un exercice (m.)` can separately name one specific exercise.
`skier` — ski: `Je skie`, `Nous skions`.
`bronzer` — tan, get a tan: `Je bronze`, `Elle a bronzé`.

examples.french: Notre entraîneuse a déplacé l’entraînement à dix-huit heures pour les personnes qui travaillent.
examples.english: Our coach moved the training session to six p.m. for people who work.
examples.note: The coach is the person; the training session is the scheduled activity.

examples.french: Je fais de l’exercice pendant ma pause de midi, même quand je n’ai pas d’entraînement.
examples.english: I exercise during my lunch break, even when I do not have a training session.
examples.note: General physical activity does not require a club session.

examples.french: L’entraîneur nous propose trois exercices avant l’entraînement.
examples.english: The coach suggests three exercises before the training session.
examples.note: Individual exercises can be counted, unlike exercise as a general activity.

examples.french: Nous skions le matin, puis nous rentrons au logement pour déjeuner.
examples.english: We ski in the morning, then return to our accommodation for lunch.
examples.note: Skions is the nous form of skier.

examples.french: Je sais skier, mais je préfère réserver un cours pour reprendre après plusieurs années.
examples.english: I can ski, but I prefer to book a lesson to get back into it after several years.
examples.note: Skier is the infinitive naming the skill.

examples.french: Elle a bronzé en skiant, même si elle n’est jamais allée à la plage.
examples.english: She got a tan while skiing, even though she never went to the beach.
examples.note: Tanning concerns the skin's response to sun exposure, not a particular place or activity.

mistakes.avoid: Mon entraînement m’a envoyé l’horaire.
mistakes.prefer: Mon entraîneur m’a envoyé l’horaire.
mistakes.why: The coach can send the schedule; the training session is not a person.

mistakes.avoid: Je ski et nous skions le dimanche.
mistakes.prefer: Je skie et nous skions le dimanche.
mistakes.why: The verb is skier; its je form ends in -e.

sections.title: Choirs, symphonic music, and musical chords
paragraphs: `Une chorale (f.)` is a choir, a group of singers; `une chorale d’enfants (f.)` is a children's choir. `Un orchestre symphonique (m.)` is a symphony orchestra, typically combining string, woodwind, brass, and percussion sections. `Symphonique` means symphonic or relating to this kind of orchestral music, not simply musical.

`La musique classique (f.)` is classical music in the broad everyday sense. It includes more than symphonies: solo piano and chamber music can be classical too. In a musical setting, `un accord (m.)` is a chord, several notes heard together; it is not grammatical agreement or a social agreement.
points: `une chorale (f.)` — choir; `une chorale d’enfants (f.)` — children's choir.
`un orchestre symphonique (m.)` — symphony orchestra.
`symphonique` — symphonic; the singular adjective has the same form with a masculine or feminine noun.
`un accord (m.)`, `les accords (m. pl.)` — musical chord, chords.
`la musique classique (f.)` — classical music, a broad musical category rather than only music from the historical Classical period.

examples.french: La chorale d’enfants répète le mercredi après l’école.
examples.english: The children's choir rehearses on Wednesdays after school.
examples.note: The group consists of singers, not instrumentalists.

examples.french: Pour le concert de fin d’année, la chorale chantera avec un orchestre symphonique.
examples.english: For the end-of-year concert, the choir will sing with a symphony orchestra.
examples.note: Two different ensembles perform together.

examples.french: J’écoute de la musique classique en travaillant, surtout des œuvres pour piano.
examples.english: I listen to classical music while working, especially piano works.
examples.note: Classical music does not have to be orchestral.

examples.french: Ce soir, la salle propose un programme symphonique ; demain, elle accueillera un pianiste seul.
examples.english: Tonight, the venue is offering a symphonic programme; tomorrow, it will host a solo pianist.
examples.note: Symphonique identifies the orchestral character of the programme.

examples.french: Je travaille les accords à la guitare avant d’accompagner la chorale.
examples.english: I practise the guitar chords before accompanying the choir.
examples.note: Accords are combinations of musical notes in this setting.

examples.french: Ces trois accords suffisent pour accompagner la chanson des enfants.
examples.english: These three chords are enough to accompany the children's song.
examples.note: The number counts musical chords, not agreements between people.

mistakes.avoid: La chorale d’enfants est un groupe d’instruments.
mistakes.prefer: La chorale d’enfants est un groupe de jeunes chanteurs.
mistakes.why: A choir is made up of singers; an orchestra is an instrumental ensemble.

mistakes.avoid: Je travaille les accord de cette chanson.
mistakes.prefer: Je travaille les accords de cette chanson.
mistakes.why: Use plural accords after les. In this musical context un accord means a chord, not an agreement between people.

sections.title: Video games, films, and cultural outings
paragraphs: `Les jeux vidéo (m. pl.)` are video games. `Des activités culturelles (f. pl.)` are cultural activities, such as exhibitions, concerts, films, or theatre outings; the phrase is common in community, university, and holiday programmes.
`Un film (m.)` is a film or movie. `Une pièce de théâtre (f.)` is a play written for or performed on stage. It is not a room inside a theatre: in this phrase, `pièce` names the dramatic work.
points: `un jeu vidéo (m.)`, `les jeux vidéo (m. pl.)` — video game, video games; `jouer aux jeux vidéo` — play video games.
`une activité culturelle (f.)`, `des activités culturelles (f. pl.)` — cultural activity, cultural activities.
`un film (m.)` — film, movie; `voir un film au cinéma` — see a film at the cinema.
`une pièce de théâtre (f.)` — play; `voir une pièce de théâtre` — see a play.

examples.french: Après les cours, mes colocataires jouent aux jeux vidéo dans le salon.
examples.english: After classes, my flatmates play video games in the living room.
examples.note: The plural games phrase uses aux.

examples.french: L’université propose des activités culturelles à prix réduit, dont des films et des pièces de théâtre.
examples.english: The university offers discounted cultural activities, including films and plays.
examples.note: The general category includes distinct types of entertainment.

examples.french: Nous avons vu le film au cinéma ; la pièce de théâtre raconte la même histoire autrement.
examples.english: We saw the film at the cinema; the play tells the same story differently.
examples.note: The screen work and the stage work are different versions of the story.

examples.french: Pendant son voyage de travail, elle a réservé une place pour une pièce de théâtre.
examples.english: During her business trip, she booked a ticket for a play.
examples.note: A realistic cultural outing alongside work travel.

examples.french: Le centre organise une soirée de jeux vidéo vendredi et projette un film dimanche.
examples.english: The centre is organising a video-game evening on Friday and screening a film on Sunday.
examples.note: The two events involve different activities despite both using screens.

mistakes.avoid: Je joue à les jeux vidéo après les cours.
mistakes.prefer: Je joue aux jeux vidéo après les cours.
mistakes.why: À + les contracts to aux in jouer aux jeux vidéo.

mistakes.avoid: Nous avons vu un pièce de théâtre.
mistakes.prefer: Nous avons vu une pièce de théâtre.
mistakes.why: Pièce is feminine. The full phrase une pièce de théâtre means a play, not a room in a theatre.

vocabulary.example: Le tennis demande de la précision et une bonne endurance.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `jouer au tennis`, but `faire une partie de tennis` for one match.

vocabulary.example: La guitare acoustique accompagne doucement la chanteuse.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `jouer de la guitare`.

vocabulary.example: Une randonnée de deux heures suffit pour découvrir le parc.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `faire une randonnée` counts a hike, while `faire de la randonnée` names the activity without counting outings.

vocabulary.example: Un tour à vélo le long du canal prend environ une heure.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase naming a counted ride; `faire du vélo` names the activity and can also refer to one occasion.

vocabulary.example: Le footing me permet de me détendre après le travail.
vocabulary.note: French usage: faire du footing names jogging; faire un footing counts a run.

vocabulary.example: Un jogging de vingt minutes suffit pour commencer la journée en mouvement.
vocabulary.note: The meaning depends on context: faire un jogging is going for a jog; porter un jogging is wearing a tracksuit.

vocabulary.example: Les jeux de société occupent les enfants pendant l’atelier.
vocabulary.note: Masculine plural of `un jeu`, which takes -x.

vocabulary.example: Un débutant est accueilli dans le groupe du mardi soir.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; feminine `une débutante`.

vocabulary.example: Un orchestre communautaire donne un concert gratuit en juin.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun despite its final -e.

vocabulary.example: Un chef d’orchestre invité dirigera le concert de fin d’année.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase; the gender comes from `chef`.

vocabulary.example: Une partition annotée circule entre les musiciens.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; not to be confused with `une partie`.

vocabulary.example: Un refrain simple aide la classe à retenir la chanson.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `un couplet` is a verse.

vocabulary.example: La batterie du groupe est installée au fond de la salle, et la batterie de la voiture est déchargée.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun with several meanings decided by context: drums, a car battery, or a set of equipment.

practice.prompt: Say that you swim regularly, then that you swam a few lengths this morning.
practice.hint: Use the partitive to name swimming and régulièrement to express the habit; count pool lengths with quelques longueurs.
practice.answer: Je fais de la natation régulièrement, et ce matin j’ai fait quelques longueurs.

takeaways: Learn `jouer à` with games, `jouer de` with instruments, and `faire` plus a partitive article with activities.
The partitive names uncounted activity; a countable noun identifies outings or units.
Tense and context establish habit or a particular event; either article pattern can occur with a habit.
keywords: un entraîneur, une entraîneuse, un entraînement, faire de l’exercice, skier, bronzer
une chorale, une chorale d’enfants, symphonique, un orchestre symphonique, les accords, la musique classique
les jeux vidéo, des activités culturelles, un film, une pièce de théâtre

lessons.title: Les pays et les nationalités
lessons.summary: Connect country names to their articles and masculine/feminine nationality adjectives. An alphabetical reference gives the country forms and English meanings, including names normally used without an article. Distinguish nationality adjectives, capitalised person nouns, and language names; recognise a county as un comté.
objectives: Store a country, its adjective, and its person noun as one set.
Form the feminine adjective, including the doubled-consonant group.
Apply the capitalisation rule consistently.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Learn related forms together: l’Allemagne (f.), allemand / allemande, un Allemand / une Allemande; le Canada (m.), canadien / canadienne, un Canadien / une Canadienne. Comparing the family helps you notice the endings and retain the article and gender rather than guessing them from English.

Several patterns recur. Add -e: allemand → allemande, français → française, roumain → roumaine. Double n in -ien and -éen: canadien → canadienne, coréen → coréenne. Keep an existing final -e: belge, russe, suisse. Learn other changes explicitly: grec → grecque and turc → turque. Capitalisation depends on function: lowercase for the adjective and for the language, capital for the noun naming a person.

In the reference below, adjective forms are written masculine first, then feminine; a repeated form means that gender does not change its spelling. To name a person, normally capitalise the same form and add an article: portugais / portugaise → un Portugais / une Portugaise. Suisse also has the established feminine person noun une Suissesse; the adjective remains suisse. A nationality does not tell you which languages someone speaks.

Most country names take an article, shown here with the gender. Chypre, Malte, Monaco, and Saint-Marin normally appear without one; do not add an artificial le or la to those names. A preposition may change or remove an article: la France → en France, le Portugal → au Portugal, les Pays-Bas → aux Pays-Bas. The country reference records the name itself, not a ready-made destination phrase.
points: Record the country with its article, then both adjective forms, then the person noun.
Add `-e` for most feminine adjectives.
Double the final consonant in the `-ien` and `-éen` groups.
Leave adjectives already ending in `-e` unchanged.
Keep capitals on country names and person nouns; use lowercase for nationality adjectives and language names.

examples.french: Elle est canadienne et travaille dans un organisme d’aide à l’intégration.
examples.english: She is Canadian and works for a settlement support organisation.
examples.note: Lowercase adjective after « être ».

examples.french: C’est un Britannique installé au Québec depuis dix ans.
examples.english: He is a British man who has lived in Quebec for ten years.
examples.note: Capitalised noun naming a person.

examples.french: L’Allemagne compte seize Länder et partage une frontière avec la France.
examples.english: Germany has sixteen states and shares a border with France.
examples.note: Feminine country with its article.

examples.french: Une étudiante roumaine et un collègue russe ont présenté le projet.
examples.english: A Romanian student and a Russian colleague presented the project.
examples.note: « Roumaine » adds -e; « russe » is identical in both genders.

examples.french: Le Royaume-Uni réunit quatre nations et reste un partenaire commercial important.
examples.english: The United Kingdom brings together four nations and remains an important trading partner.
examples.note: Masculine country name with a compound form.

mistakes.avoid: Elle est Canadienne et elle parle Anglais.
mistakes.prefer: Elle est canadienne et elle parle anglais.
mistakes.why: Here canadienne describes the subject and is an adjective; anglais names the language. Both take lowercase.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai rencontré une italien pendant la formation.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai rencontré une Italienne pendant la formation.
mistakes.why: The noun naming a person is capitalised and agrees in gender.

sections.title: Country reference: Albanie to Croatie
paragraphs: Read each entry as French country name — English country name — masculine / feminine adjective. Keep the two adjective forms together instead of guessing the feminine from the English name. In particular, autrichien refers to Austria, not Australia; Austrian is not australien.
points: l’Albanie (f.) — Albania — albanais / albanaise
l’Allemagne (f.) — Germany — allemand / allemande
l’Andorre (f.) — Andorra — andorran / andorrane
l’Arménie (f.) — Armenia — arménien / arménienne
l’Autriche (f.) — Austria — autrichien / autrichienne
l’Azerbaïdjan (m.) — Azerbaijan — azerbaïdjanais / azerbaïdjanaise
la Belgique (f.) — Belgium — belge / belge
la Biélorussie (f.) — Belarus — biélorusse / biélorusse
la Bosnie-Herzégovine (f.) — Bosnia and Herzegovina — bosnien / bosnienne
la Bulgarie (f.) — Bulgaria — bulgare / bulgare
Chypre (f.; normally no article) — Cyprus — chypriote / chypriote
la Croatie (f.) — Croatia — croate / croate

examples.french: Une collègue albanaise m’a expliqué comment remplir le formulaire.
examples.english: An Albanian colleague explained to me how to fill in the form.
examples.note: Albanaise describes feminine une collègue (f.); it is not a person noun here.

examples.french: Une entreprise autrichienne propose un stage à un étudiant arménien.
examples.english: An Austrian company is offering an internship to an Armenian student.
examples.note: Autrichienne ends in -ienne; arménien remains masculine with un étudiant (m.).

examples.french: Une association belge accueille une famille bosnienne.
examples.english: A Belgian association is welcoming a Bosnian family.
examples.note: Belge is unchanged in the feminine; bosnien becomes bosnienne.

examples.french: Elle vient de Chypre et présente un projet chypriote.
examples.english: She comes from Cyprus and is presenting a Cypriot project.
examples.note: Chypre normally has no article; chypriote is the adjective.

examples.french: Un visiteur croate et une bénévole bulgare ont participé à la rencontre.
examples.english: A Croatian visitor and a Bulgarian volunteer took part in the meeting.
examples.note: Croate and bulgare keep the same singular spelling in both genders.

mistakes.avoid: Une entreprise autrichien recrute.
mistakes.prefer: Une entreprise autrichienne recrute.
mistakes.why: The adjective agrees with feminine une entreprise (f.): autrichienne.

sections.title: Country reference: Danemark to Italie
paragraphs: The -ais group usually adds -e for the feminine: danois → danoise, finlandais → finlandaise. Do not extend this spelling to every name: espagnol → espagnole, but grec → grecque. The country name itself keeps its initial capital.
points: le Danemark (m.) — Denmark — danois / danoise
l’Espagne (f.) — Spain — espagnol / espagnole
l’Estonie (f.) — Estonia — estonien / estonienne
la Finlande (f.) — Finland — finlandais / finlandaise
la France (f.) — France — français / française
la Géorgie (f.) — Georgia — géorgien / géorgienne
la Grèce (f.) — Greece — grec / grecque
la Hongrie (f.) — Hungary — hongrois / hongroise
l’Irlande (f.) — Ireland — irlandais / irlandaise
l’Islande (f.) — Iceland — islandais / islandaise
l’Italie (f.) — Italy — italien / italienne

examples.french: Une étudiante danoise partage son logement avec une chercheuse finlandaise.
examples.english: A Danish student shares her accommodation with a Finnish researcher.
examples.note: Both feminine adjectives add -e; the nationalities do not determine which languages they speak.

examples.french: Un collègue espagnol nous a recommandé une association française.
examples.english: A Spanish colleague recommended a French association to us.
examples.note: Espagnol agrees with un collègue (m.); française agrees with une association (f.).

examples.french: Elle vient de Grèce et travaille dans une entreprise grecque.
examples.english: She comes from Greece and works for a Greek company.
examples.note: The feminine adjective is grecque: retain c and add que.

examples.french: L’Irlande et l’Islande figurent dans le programme du voyage.
examples.english: Ireland and Iceland are included in the travel itinerary.
examples.note: These are different countries: irlandais / irlandaise versus islandais / islandaise.

examples.french: J’ai rencontré une Italienne qui organise des ateliers de conversation.
examples.english: I met an Italian woman who organises conversation workshops.
examples.note: Une Italienne is a person noun, so it takes a capital; une formatrice italienne would use a lowercase adjective.

mistakes.avoid: Elle travaille pour une entreprise grec.
mistakes.prefer: Elle travaille pour une entreprise grecque.
mistakes.why: Use the feminine form grecque with une entreprise (f.).

sections.title: Country reference: Kazakhstan to Monténégro
paragraphs: Keep the written distinction between letton → lettone and lituanien → lituanienne. Names such as Liechtenstein and Luxembourg have much longer adjectives; learning the whole family is more reliable than attaching a guessed ending. Monaco and Malte normally stand without a country article.

For Kazakhstan, distinguish kazakhstanais / kazakhstanaise, which explicitly refers to the state or its citizenship, from kazakh / kazakhe, which also names the Kazakh people and their language. The latter is used more broadly in some contexts, but citizenship and ethnicity are not interchangeable.
points: le Kazakhstan (m.) — Kazakhstan — kazakhstanais / kazakhstanaise (Kazakhstani); kazakh / kazakhe (Kazakh)
le Kosovo (m.) — Kosovo — kosovar / kosovare
la Lettonie (f.) — Latvia — letton / lettone
le Liechtenstein (m.) — Liechtenstein — liechtensteinois / liechtensteinoise
la Lituanie (f.) — Lithuania — lituanien / lituanienne
le Luxembourg (m.) — Luxembourg — luxembourgeois / luxembourgeoise
la Macédoine du Nord (f.) — North Macedonia — macédonien / macédonienne
Malte (f.; normally no article) — Malta — maltais / maltaise
la Moldavie (f.) — Moldova — moldave / moldave
Monaco (normally no article) — Monaco — monégasque / monégasque
le Monténégro (m.) — Montenegro — monténégrin / monténégrine

examples.french: Une étudiante lettone échange des conseils avec une collègue lituanienne.
examples.english: A Latvian student is exchanging advice with a Lithuanian colleague.
examples.note: Lettone has double t but only one n. Lituanienne has double n.

examples.french: Une entreprise luxembourgeoise recrute une ingénieure kazakhstanaise.
examples.english: A Luxembourg company is recruiting a Kazakhstani engineer.
examples.note: Luxembourgeoise and kazakhstanaise are feminine adjective forms. Kazakhstanaise identifies nationality without asserting ethnicity.

examples.french: Nous irons à Malte pour rencontrer une partenaire maltaise.
examples.english: We will go to Malta to meet a Maltese partner.
examples.note: À Malte has no article; maltaise is the feminine adjective.

examples.french: Une association monégasque a invité un chercheur moldave.
examples.english: A Monegasque association has invited a Moldovan researcher.
examples.note: Monégasque refers to Monaco; both adjectives keep their singular spelling across genders.

examples.french: Une famille monténégrine et un étudiant kosovar se sont inscrits au cours.
examples.english: A Montenegrin family and a Kosovar student have enrolled in the class.
examples.note: Monténégrine describes feminine une famille (f.); kosovar describes masculine un étudiant (m.).

mistakes.avoid: Une étudiante letton participe à l’atelier.
mistakes.prefer: Une étudiante lettone participe à l’atelier.
mistakes.why: The feminine adjective is lettone; preserve tt and add e.

sections.title: Country reference: Norvège to Russie
paragraphs: Les Pays-Bas is a plural country name, while the nationality adjective néerlandais agrees with the person or thing described, not with that country's grammatical number. Britannique refers to the United Kingdom; do not replace it automatically with anglais, which specifically means English.
points: la Norvège (f.) — Norway — norvégien / norvégienne
les Pays-Bas (m. pl.) — the Netherlands — néerlandais / néerlandaise
la Pologne (f.) — Poland — polonais / polonaise
le Portugal (m.) — Portugal — portugais / portugaise
la République tchèque (f.) — the Czech Republic — tchèque / tchèque
la Roumanie (f.) — Romania — roumain / roumaine
le Royaume-Uni (m.) — the United Kingdom — britannique / britannique
la Russie (f.) — Russia — russe / russe

examples.french: Une chercheuse norvégienne et un étudiant polonais présenteront leurs résultats.
examples.english: A Norwegian researcher and a Polish student will present their findings.
examples.note: Norvégienne doubles n; polonais stays masculine with un étudiant (m.).

examples.french: Elle vient des Pays-Bas et dirige une entreprise néerlandaise.
examples.english: She comes from the Netherlands and runs a Dutch company.
examples.note: De + les becomes des; néerlandaise is feminine singular because entreprise is feminine singular.

examples.french: Une Portugaise m’a conseillé de contacter une association locale.
examples.english: A Portuguese woman advised me to contact a local association.
examples.note: The person noun une Portugaise takes a capital. Une collègue portugaise would use a lowercase adjective.

examples.french: Une délégation tchèque et une équipe roumaine ont participé au projet.
examples.english: A Czech delegation and a Romanian team took part in the project.
examples.note: Tchèque is unchanged; roumain becomes roumaine.

examples.french: Cette université britannique propose un échange avec une université russe.
examples.english: This British university offers an exchange with a Russian university.
examples.note: Britannique and russe have the same masculine and feminine singular spelling.

mistakes.avoid: Elle vient du Pays-Bas.
mistakes.prefer: Elle vient des Pays-Bas.
mistakes.why: The country name is plural: les Pays-Bas; de + les contracts to des.

sections.title: Country reference: Saint-Marin to Vatican
paragraphs: The compound saint-marinais retains its hyphen: une association saint-marinaise. Distinguish suédois / suédoise (Swedish) from suisse (Swiss). Similarly, link slovène to Slovenia and slovaque to Slovakia rather than treating them as interchangeable.
points: Saint-Marin (m.; normally no article) — San Marino — saint-marinais / saint-marinaise
la Serbie (f.) — Serbia — serbe / serbe
la Slovaquie (f.) — Slovakia — slovaque / slovaque
la Slovénie (f.) — Slovenia — slovène / slovène
la Suède (f.) — Sweden — suédois / suédoise
la Suisse (f.) — Switzerland — suisse / suisse
la Turquie (f.) — Türkiye / Turkey — turc / turque
l’Ukraine (f.) — Ukraine — ukrainien / ukrainienne
le Vatican (m.) — Vatican City — vaticanais / vaticanaise

examples.french: Une délégation saint-marinaise participera à la rencontre.
examples.english: A delegation from San Marino will take part in the meeting.
examples.note: Saint-marinaise is a lowercase, hyphenated adjective agreeing with une délégation (f.).

examples.french: Une étudiante slovaque et une formatrice slovène échangent leurs coordonnées.
examples.english: A Slovak student and a Slovenian trainer are exchanging contact details.
examples.note: Slovaque refers to la Slovaquie (f.); slovène refers to la Slovénie (f.).

examples.french: Une association suédoise travaille avec une équipe suisse.
examples.english: A Swedish association works with a Swiss team.
examples.note: Suédois becomes suédoise; suisse does not change.

examples.french: Une collègue turque aide une famille ukrainienne à préparer le dossier.
examples.english: A Turkish colleague is helping a Ukrainian family prepare the application.
examples.note: Turc becomes turque, whereas ukrainien becomes ukrainienne.

examples.french: Un citoyen vaticanais a pris part à la conférence.
examples.english: A Vatican citizen took part in the conference.
examples.note: Vaticanais is a nationality adjective; the feminine form is vaticanaise.

mistakes.avoid: Une collègue turc a répondu.
mistakes.prefer: Une collègue turque a répondu.
mistakes.why: Use the feminine form turque with une collègue (f.).

sections.title: A country is not a county
paragraphs: Un pays (m.) is a country; un comté (m.) is a county, an administrative or historical area in certain places. Do not confuse comté with un compte (m.), an account, or un comte (m.), a count in the nobility. The English names country and county are close, but the French words and meanings are distinct.
points: un pays (m.) — a country
un comté (m.) — a county
une ville (f.) — a town or city
une région (f.) — a region

examples.french: Le service est ouvert aux habitants du comté.
examples.english: The service is available to residents of the county.
examples.note: Du comté is de + le comté; it names a local area, not a whole country.

examples.french: Elle a changé de ville, mais elle habite toujours dans le même pays.
examples.english: She has moved to a different city, but she still lives in the same country.
examples.note: Une ville and un pays describe different geographical scales.

examples.french: Je cherche un logement dans cette région, près de mon travail.
examples.english: I am looking for accommodation in this region, near my workplace.
examples.note: Une région (f.) is a region; its precise administrative role depends on the place.

mistakes.avoid: Les habitants du compte peuvent utiliser ce service.
mistakes.prefer: Les habitants du comté peuvent utiliser ce service.
mistakes.why: To mean county, use un comté. Un compte is an account, not an inhabited area.

vocabulary.example: L’Allemagne accueille chaque année de nombreux travailleurs qualifiés.
vocabulary.note: Feminine country; adjective `allemand`, `allemande`.

vocabulary.example: Le Royaume-Uni réunit quatre nations.
vocabulary.note: Masculine country; the adjective is `britannique` for both genders.

vocabulary.example: La Roumanie possède de nombreuses régions montagneuses.
vocabulary.note: Feminine country; adjective `roumain`, `roumaine`.

vocabulary.example: Une entreprise canadienne a financé une partie du projet.
vocabulary.note: The feminine doubles the final consonant before -e.

vocabulary.example: Un organisme communautaire accompagne les familles nouvellement arrivées.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; the ending -isme is a masculine hint.

practice.prompt: Give the three forms for `le Portugal` and use the person noun in a sentence.
practice.hint: Masculine adjective, feminine adjective, capitalised noun.
practice.answer: portugais, portugaise, un Portugais / une Portugaise : Une Portugaise a présenté son parcours professionnel.

takeaways: One country equals four linked forms.
`-ien` doubles its consonant in the feminine; `-e` adjectives do not change.
Capitals for countries and person nouns; lowercase for nationality adjectives and languages.
